title: Laboratory Capacity, Diagnostic Performance, and Operational Barriers in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Cross-Sectional Study from Al-Dhalea and Radfan Districts
description:
This project contains all data, materials, and analysis scripts for the research study: "Laboratory Capacity, Diagnostic Performance, and Operational Barriers in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Cross-Sectional Study from Al-Dhalea and Radfan Districts."

Study Overview

A comprehensive cross-sectional assessment of diagnostic laboratory services in two conflict-affected districts of Yemen (Al-Dhalea and Radfan), conducted from July to December 2025. The study evaluated 20 laboratories, interviewed 60 laboratory personnel, and analyzed 700 patient samples to assess operational capacity, diagnostic accuracy (malaria RDTs and CBC), and identify barriers to reliable service delivery.

Key Findings

· Malaria RDTs demonstrated high accuracy (sensitivity: 95.4%, specificity: 94.5%)
· Significant operational barriers: reagent stockouts (40% of labs), intermittent electricity (30%), staff training gaps (45% untrained)
· Mean turnaround time: 2.1 days, with only 26.7% of results reported within 24 hours
· Overall error rate: 5.0%, primarily from RDT-microscopy discordance

title: Serum placental growth factor (PlGF) for the prediction of early-onset pre-eclampsia in the first trimester of pregnancy: a systematic review
description: Pre-eclampsia remains a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality worldwide, with 99% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries. The standard first-trimester screening model, combining maternal characteristics with mean arterial pressure (MC + MAP), detects fewer than half of cases destined to develop early-onset pre-eclampsia at a 10% false-positive rate. This systematic review evaluated the incremental diagnostic accuracy of adding serum placental growth factor (PlGF) to the MC + MAP model for the prediction of early-onset pre-eclampsia in the first trimester of pregnancy.

title: RELIABILITY, APPLICABILITY AND EXPANSION OF ACCESS TO DIAGNOSIS THROUGH TELECONSULTATION IN STOMATOLOGY: a scoping review
description: Teledentistry comprises several modalities of remote dental care, notably teleconsultation—defined as the exchange of clinical information among healthcare professionals—and telediagnosis, which involves issuing diagnostic reports. However, the impact of teleconsultation on the early diagnosis of oral lesions remains uncertain. This study aims to synthesize the available evidence and provide a comprehensive overview of the reliability, applicability, and potential to expand access to the diagnosis of oral lesions, including malignant and potentially malignant disorders, through teleconsultation in oral medicine. A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, LILACS, and gray literature up to January 2025, with no language restrictions. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using specific tools: Newcastle-Ottawa (cohort studies), JBI (cross-sectional studies), QUADAS-2 (diagnostic accuracy studies), and GRADE (certainty of evidence). A narrative synthesis was performed. A total of 25 observational studies (cross-sectional, cohort, and diagnostic accuracy) were included, involving 8,746 patients assessed via teleconsultation, although not all studies reported the exact number of participants. Among the evaluated cases, 612 were confirmed as malignant. Diagnostic agreement between general practitioners and specialists ranged from 60% to 100%, being higher in studies with standardized protocols, prior training, or those conducted by specialists. Remote diagnostic accuracy reached up to 97% compared to the gold standard. Overall satisfaction with the service was high (96.5%), and 75% of patients reported the procedure as comfortable. Some studies demonstrated that teleconsultation contributes to expanding access to diagnosis in oral medicine, as reflected in an increase in referrals. Despite promising findings, the high methodological heterogeneity (>85%) among studies precluded a robust meta-analysis and limited the generalizability of results.

title: Application of Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) in Resource-Limited Areas: A Scoping Review
description: Trauma ranks among the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. According to World Health Organization (WHO) data, 4.4 million people die annually from injuries resulting from accidents or violence. This burden is particularly pronounced among individuals aged 15 to 44, with low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) bearing the primary impact—accounting for over 90% of these global trauma-related deaths. In these resource-constrained regions, relatively weak infrastructure, scarce medical resources, and inadequate emergency response systems compound frequent trauma incidents. Costs associated with readmissions, surgical interventions, and mortality rates rise significantly, placing immense pressure on medical resources and overwhelming healthcare systems. Patients often fail to receive timely diagnosis and treatment due to lack of imaging examinations and sufficient medical resources, posing severe challenges to trauma management. Currently, routine trauma imaging examinations commonly include computed tomography (CT) and ultrasound imaging. Although CT offers high sensitivity and specificity in trauma detection and diagnosis, concerns persist regarding its high cost and radiation exposure. Furthermore, the inability to move critically ill patients limits CT application in resource-constrained settings [1]. Ultrasound examinations can be performed at the bedside, but conventional ultrasound imaging is time-consuming. Compared to CT and conventional ultrasound, Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) is the current primary diagnostic tool for trauma patients. First proposed by Rozychi et al. and widely recognized at an international conference in 1996, FAST is a bedside ultrasound method for rapidly assessing visceral hemorrhage in trauma patients. Its application has since expanded to include acute abdominal conditions such as abdominal aortic aneurysms and gallbladder stones. The FAST examination typically covers the subxiphoid region, right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, and pelvis. It examines the hepatic-renal and splenic-renal spaces, the rectovesical pouch (uterovesical pouch), and the pericardial cavity for free fluid, determining the presence of hemorrhage in the abdominal cavity, pelvic cavity, and pericardial cavity. As a simple, low-cost, non-invasive imaging modality, FAST is particularly well-suited for resource-limited settings, especially those lacking advanced imaging equipment. It has become an indispensable alternative for managing trauma patients, effectively enhancing the timeliness and efficacy of trauma care. However, despite FAST's significant potential in resource-limited settings, current research predominantly focuses on trauma populations outside these regions and is often limited to single-center studies with small sample sizes. Therefore, this study systematically reviews the literature on FAST application in trauma care within resource-limited settings. The aim is to provide evidence-based guidance for trauma care practices and personnel training in such regions, while analyzing implementation barriers and strategies for adaptive improvements.

title: Eye Tracking during Visual Paired-Comparison Tasks for Detecting Cognitive Decline
description:
To provide a more comprehensive understanding of the capability of this assessment tool, the present systematic review and meta-analyses aim to evaluate the effectiveness and usefulness of paired visual comparisons based on eye tracking movement as a tool for assessing memory deficits in individuals with age-related cognitive changes.

2 Methods
2.1 Study protocol
This systematic review followed the “Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis” (PRISMA) guidelines (see the PRISMA checklist).18 A predefined protocol was developed and is available upon request from the corresponding author. The inclusion criterion for this systematic review was the participation of impaired memory participants and/or healthy participants, with a focus on evaluating recognition memory using VPC with ETM. Key outcomes are novelty preference scores, percent looking time at novel images, total looking time, and total fixations. Both observational and experimental studies will be considered.
2.2 Eligibility criteria
Studies including participants classified as healthy and with impaired memory, where their memory was assessed based on the VPC task, which has been published or accepted for publication in peer-reviewed journals and written in any language, were considered. No restrictions were applied in terms of study design, setting, country, or time frame. Descriptive or review articles, conference proceedings, and articles for which the full text was unavailable were excluded. Only studies that included assessments of novelty preference scores based on the VPC task were included.
2.3 Search strategy
Six electronic databases, namely, PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, SportDiscuss, ProQuest, and the OpenGrey, were searched from inception to November 2023, without applying any time limits or filters. The research strategy employed appropriate Boolean operators (AND, OR, and NOT) to combine the relevant keywords. Additionally, field tags, wild-card options (such as truncated words), and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms were used where applicable. Additionally, to minimize the risk of missing relevant publications, the reference lists of the included manuscripts and related citations from other journals identified via Google Scholar were reviewed. Furthermore, a search of personal files was also performed. The full research strategy and keywords used are presented in Table S1.
2.4 Selection process
The process used for selecting articles is outlined in Figure 1. EndNote software (version 20) was used to remove duplicate articles recorded in the initial search results. Titles and abstracts of all unique hits were screened by the first two authors (MAB and KT) for eligibility, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. The full texts of the selected studies were subsequently screened for eligibility, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. The reasons for excluding an article during the abstract and full-text screening were recorded.
2.5 Data extraction
Using a pilot-tested extraction form, the two first authors (MAB and KT) independently collected the data and resolved disagreements by consensus. The extracted data included participant characteristics (number of participants, age, educational level), study characteristics (country, methodology), and key outcomes, and the results are presented in Table 1.
2.6 Quality assessment
Two examiners independently assessed the methodological quality of the studies using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2) tool.19 The tool evaluates the methodological quality of diagnostic accuracy studies in four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. It assesses bias within each domain and examines the applicability of findings in the first three domains. Independent evaluators assigned assessments of "low", "high", or "unclear" risk of bias to each guiding question within the domains.
2.7 Statistical analysis
The random-effects model was constructed using the restricted maximum likelihood estimation with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) method20 to determine the effect size of the VPC and its pooled sensitivity and specificity. Three studies were considered the minimum number of studies needed to be included in the meta-analysis. The standardized mean difference (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to investigate whether differential effects existed between the nap and control groups/interventions for declarative memory across all studies. The SMD (Hedges’ g) was used to measure effect size and was considered small at g < 0.5, moderate at 0.5 < g < 0.8, and large at g > 0.8.21 Forest plots were generated to illustrate point estimates of Hedges’ g and 95% CIs. The between-study variance tau-square (Tau2) test was used for heterogeneity, and the I2 statistic was used to assess the heterogeneity among studies; I2 statistics were considered low at I2 < 50%, moderate at 50%< I2 < 75%, and high at I2 > 75%.22 The 95% prediction interval for the true outcomes was calculated.23 As indicated by Rothstein et al.,24 funnel plots of potential asymmetries were constructed, and Begg and Mazumdar’s rank correlation test,25 Egger’s linear regression test,26 and Duval and Tweedie’s trim and fill method27 were used to identify publication bias. Outliers were assessed using the “dmeta” package (version 0.0.9000);28 after all outliers were retrieved, a second random effects meta-analysis was performed. The stability of each study’s pooled SMD was assessed via leave-one-out sensitivity analyses involving the removal of individual studies from the analysis and computing the excluded study’s impact on the overall effect estimate. The statistical significance level was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses. This meta-analysis was conducted using the R programming language (version 4.2.3)29, 30 with the “metafor” package (version 3.8.1).31

title: MRD/PET-CT Concordance and Prognostic Value in Multiple Myeloma: Systematic Study-Level Analysis
description:
Objectives
- Quantify agreement between MRD and PET-CT at the same timepoint using κ statistics.
Evaluate the prognostic significance of dual negativity vs other categories (MRD−/PET+, MRD+/PET−, MRD+/PET+). 
- Explore heterogeneity by risk of bias, detection method, and study design.

Eligibility Criteria
- Population: Adults with multiple myeloma after therapy assessment.
- Interventions/exposures: MRD (flow or NGS, any sensitivity) and PET-CT performed within ±30 days.
- Outcomes: Concordance (2×2 tables) and time-to-event (PFS/OS) per dual-negativity status.
- Study types: Prospective or retrospective studies with ≥10 paired patients.
- Time frame: January 1, 2015 – June 30, 2025. The original systematic search covered publications up to April 30, 2025; two additional eligible studies published in May–July 2025 were identified through manual surveillance of recent issues and conference proceedings before database lock.
- Exclusions: Reviews, abstracts without extractable data, and studies with non-overlapping timepoints.

Information Sources and Search Strategy
PubMed and Cochrane CENTRAL: (Multiple Myeloma"[MeSH Terms] OR "multiple myeloma"[All Fields]) AND ("Neoplasm, Residual"[MeSH Terms] OR "residual disease"[All Fields] OR MRD[All Fields]) AND ("Positron-Emission Tomography"[MeSH Terms] OR "PET"[All Fields] OR "PET-CT"[All Fields] OR "FDG-PET"[All Fields]). Manual addition of cited or related studies. Full strings included in Supplement Material.

Data Extraction and Items
Extract: study ID, n, MRD method, imaging modality/criteria, 2x2 concordance data, HRs or KM curves, follow-up, ASCT status, risk of bias. Two reviewers independently cross-checked entries.

Risk of Bias Assessment
Concordance outcomes: QUADAS-2
Prognostic outcomes: QUIPS
Each domain judged Low / High / Unclear; disagreements resolved by consensus.

Statistical Analysis Plan
Agreement metrics: observed proportion, Cohen’s κ (and AC1 sensitivity).
Random-effects pooling (REML + Hartung-Knapp), report τ², I², 95 % PI.
Directional discordance model (MRD-/PET+ vs MRD+/PET-).
Prognosis: log-HR pooling for dual-negativity; include reconstructed HRs if needed.

Sensitivity analyses:
Exclude high-risk or misaligned studies.
Alternative continuity corrections.
Subgroup/meta-regression by MRD method or imaging criteria.
Publication bias: Egger’s test, contour funnel plots.

All code executed in R (4.4+) with meta/metafor; scripts deposited in Github.

Deviations from PROSPERO Policy
Because initial data extraction had begun before we learned of PROSPERO’s requirement for prospective registration, this project is retrospectively registered on OSF instead.

Data Availability
Screening logs, extraction sheets, and analytic code are uploaded as read-only CSV/R files; patient-level data are not included.

title: Validation of an Agentic-Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model System for Dermatology Decision Support
description:
Dermatology presents significant diagnostic complexity, with unevenly distributed specialist access. Decision support tools that surface traceable evidence at the point of care represent a high-value intervention if they can demonstrably improve physician accuracy.

Existing RAG evaluations rely on automated benchmarks and do not assess clinical evidence trustworthiness, answer grounding, or impact on physician decision-making. This study addresses these gaps through a physician reader study.

Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a transformative technology in medical question answering, demonstrating the ability to process complex clinical narratives and generate clinically relevant responses, with leading systems approaching or exceeding physician-level performance on standardized assessments such as the USMLE. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems employing iterative gap-aware retrieval loops represent a further extension, with preliminary evidence suggesting improved evidence coverage on complex queries.

In the dermatology domain, in silico studies have shown that LLMs can match or outperform dermatologists in diagnostic accuracy across a range of skin conditions. However, no study has evaluated a RAG system via a physician reader study in dermatology, and no prior work has assessed evidence grounding of RAG outputs using physician judgement. This study addresses both gaps. For the specific system evaluated here automated MCQ accuracy on the a dermatology-relevant subset of the MedQA dataset constructed for this study was assessed during development and serves as the pre-clinical evidence base. No prior clinical validation has been conducted for this system configuration.

title: Automated Scoring of Drawings from a Tablet-Based Complex Figure Copy task
description:
Objective 
Complex Figure Copy Tasks are one of the most commonly employed neuropsychological tests. However, manual scoring of this test is time-consuming, requires training, and can then still be inconsistent between different examiners. We aimed to develop and evaluate a novel, automated method for scoring a tablet-based Figure Copy Task. 

Method 
A cohort of 261 healthy adults and 203 stroke survivors completed the computerised Oxford Cognitive Screen – Plus Figure Copy Task. Responses were independently scored by two trained human raters and by a novel automated scoring program.  

Results 
Overall, the Automated Scoring Program was able to reliably extract and identify the separate figure elements (sensitivity and specificity of 92.10% and 90.20% respectively) and assigned total scores which agreed well with manual scores (ICC = .83). Receiver Operating Curve analysis demonstrated that, compared to overall impairment categorisations based on manual scores, the Automated Scoring Program had an overall sensitivity and specificity of 80% and 93.40% respectively (AUC = 86.70%). Automated total scores also reliably distinguished between different clinical impairment groups with acute stroke survivors scoring significantly worse than longer term survivors, which in turn scored worse than neurologically healthy adults.  

Conclusions 
These results demonstrate that the novel automated scoring algorithm was able to reliably extract and accurately score Figure Copy Task data, even in cases where drawings were highly distorted due to comorbid fine-motor deficits. This represents a significant advancement as this novel technology can be employed to produce immediate, unbiased, and reproducible scores for Figure Copy Task responses in clinical and research environments.

title: Exploration of Differentially Expressed circulating microRNAs as Diagnostic Biomarkers for Primary Aldosteronism
description:
Primary Aldosteronism (PA) is the most common cause of secondary hypertension and is associated with significant cardiovascular morbidity when left undiagnosed. Despite its clinical importance, the condition remains underdiagnosed due to the lack of reliable, minimally invasive biomarkers that can effectively distinguish PA from primary (essential) hypertension (PH). The current diagnostic pathway relies on screening with aldosterone-to-renin ratio, confirmatory tests, and adrenal vein sampling, which are invasive, costly, and not widely available.

This project aims to explore circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) as potential diagnostic biomarkers for PA. miRNAs are small, non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression and are increasingly recognized for their stability in blood and disease-specific expression patterns. Leveraging machine learning and bioinformatics approaches, we will analyze miRNA expression profiles obtained from plasma/serum samples of patients with confirmed PA compared to those with PH. Differential expression analysis will identify candidate miRNAs that show significant and reproducible differences between the two groups.

We will then employ supervised machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) to evaluate the discriminatory power of these candidate miRNAs. Feature selection methods will be used to derive a parsimonious diagnostic signature with optimal sensitivity and specificity. Cross-validation and independent validation subsets will be applied to minimize overfitting and assess generalizability.

The expected outcome of this research is the identification of a panel of circulating miRNAs that can serve as non-invasive biomarkers for distinguishing PA from PH. Such a biomarker panel could improve early diagnosis, reduce dependence on invasive procedures, and ultimately guide more targeted and effective management of patients with hypertension. Beyond diagnostic utility, this study may also provide insights into the molecular pathways underlying aldosterone excess and its cardiovascular consequences.

title: Data collection and analysis from the Informatics Department of the Unified Health System in Brazil, using open source programming languages: a scoping review
description:
1 INTRODUCTION
The consolidation of the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) brought with it the need to develop instruments capable of recording, organizing, and providing information to support health management (Lima et al., 2009). Since its creation, SUS has required information systems capable of consolidating data in a structured and standardized manner, supporting both epidemiological surveillance and health planning. In this process, the Department of Informatics of SUS (DATASUS) assumed a strategic role by gathering, processing, and providing nationwide data, becoming one of the main sources of information for managers, researchers, and health professionals (Brazil, 2020a).
The availability of reliable and accessible data is a central requirement for public policy formulation, indicator evaluation, and the development of research in public health (Costa et al., 2025). However, the use of these databases still faces challenges related to the decentralization of sources, heterogeneity of records, data quality, and periodic system updates, which may limit their applicability in more complex analyses (Brazil, 2020a).
To overcome these limitations, the National Health Information and Informatics Policy (PNIIS) and the Digital Health Strategy for Brazil 2020–2028 (ESD28) have established guidelines focused on information governance, interoperability, and strengthening the technological infrastructure of SUS (Brazil, 2020b).
Established in 2004, the PNIIS defined principles for the use of Information and Communication Technologies within SUS, emphasizing the integration of national information systems, improvement of data quality, and strengthening of health management (Brazil, 2004). These guidelines were later updated to incorporate goals related to interoperability and information governance (Brazil, 2021).
Among the structuring initiatives for the modernization of SUS, the National Health Data Network (RNDS) stands out as a central platform integrating information from different systems and levels of care, promoting interoperability and providing essential data to support decision-making. Other initiatives include SUS Digital, through the “Meu SUS Digital” tool, and the PQDAS Program, which standardizes and improves the quality of supplementary health data in alignment with SUS data (Brazil; Ministry of Health; Secretariat of Digital Health Information, 2024).
The adoption of digital technologies not only modernizes infrastructure but also transforms the interaction between citizens, professionals, and managers, increasing efficiency and integration of care. This approach represents the evolution of the concept of eHealth, expanding the use of digital resources beyond service informatization. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data, telemedicine, wearable devices, and mobile applications have been used to improve management, access, and quality of care (World Health Organization, 2021).
According to the Ministry of Health (Brazil, 2020a), DATASUS integrates systems covering various areas of health care, such as the Hospital Information System (SIH), Ambulatory Information System (SIA), Mortality Information System (SIM), Live Birth Information System (SINASC), and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN), among others.
Despite the breadth of these databases, challenges persist regarding data quality, updating, standardization, and interoperability, which may limit reliable analyses and evidence-based decision-making. Ensuring efficient integration among systems is essential so that managers and professionals have access to consistent and up-to-date information.
Data collection and management in Brazil are directly linked to PNIIS and ESD28. While PNIIS establishes standards for organization, integration, and governance of health information, ESD28 defines priorities for digital technology use, including interoperability, professional training, and innovation. The articulation between these initiatives allows DataSUS data to be used strategically at different management levels (Brazil, 2020b; Costa et al., 2025).
Access to public health data in Brazil has advanced significantly, even before the Access to Information Law (LAI) came into effect in 2012. Tools such as TabNet and TabWin, developed by DATASUS, enable the creation of tables, graphs, and indicators to support epidemiological analyses (Saldanha et al., 2019; Silva, 2009). TabNet allows quick tabulations from public data, while TabWin enables microdata import and spatial representations.
Despite their usefulness, these tools have operational limitations, require specific training, and demand repetition of procedures for each new period analyzed. In this context, programming code emerges as an alternative to automate, speed up, and standardize data collection and processing.
The increased availability of SUS microdata, combined with the expansion of digital health tools, has driven the adoption of open-source programming languages for data manipulation and analysis (Costa et al., 2025). These languages enhance scientific reproducibility, integration with public databases, and automation of complex analyses such as risk modeling and time series (Wilson et al., 2014).
Despite these advances, there is a knowledge gap regarding systematic mapping of the use of open-source programming specifically applied to DATASUS. While isolated studies exist, comprehensive discussions of methods and tools remain scarce. The scoping review by Restrepo et al. (2023) on open health datasets in Latin America highlights this gap.
Although DataSUS has consolidated itself as a national repository, challenges such as heterogeneity, lack of standardization, variable data quality, and integration difficulties between systems still limit reproducibility.
At the same time, there is growing use of open-source programming in health data science. However, a systematic mapping is needed to identify how these tools are applied to DataSUS, which methods are used, and which gaps remain.
The absence of this overview hinders the consolidation of best practices and the development of more accessible technological solutions. Therefore, conducting a scoping review to systematize existing knowledge is necessary to support open science, improve public health analyses, and strengthen evidence-based decision-making within SUS.

2 OBJECTIVE
To map the evidence in the scientific literature on the use of open-source programming for the collection and analysis of data from Brazilian Health Information Systems.

3 METHOD
3.1 Study Design
This study consists of a scoping review, characterized as applied research with a technological development approach. The review will be conducted in accordance with the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses – Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), aiming to ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and greater detail in the conduct and reporting of the study.
3.2 Data Sources
The databases selected for this review are: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, LILACS, BVS (Virtual Health Library), Google Scholar, and the Brazilian Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations (BDTD). 
The choice of these databases is justified by their relevance to the topic, coverage of high-quality journals, and multidisciplinary scope. While databases such as PubMed, Embase, and LILACS are specialized in health and biomedical sciences, Scopus and Web of Science provide a multidisciplinary perspective, and IEEE Xplore contributes the necessary technical focus for topics related to programming and data analysis. Searches will also be conducted in Google Scholar and BDTD to capture gray literature not indexed in journal databases.
3.3 Identifying the Research Question 
The first step consists of formulating a well-focused research question, with the objective of mapping what has already been published on the use of open-source programming languages and tools in the context of DATASUS, as well as identifying potential gaps in the existing literature. 
Research question: What evidence is available in the literature on the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and analysis of DATASUS data? 
Based on this guiding question, it will be possible to identify the most commonly used open-source programming languages for the collection and analysis of DATASUS data, recognize the libraries, frameworks, or tools frequently employed in these processes, and understand the main methods and techniques used for data collection, extraction, and analysis. Moreover, through this scoping review, it will be possible to map the key challenges reported in the literature regarding the use of open-source programming for working with DATASUS data, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of the topic.
3.4 Identifying the Most Significant Terms in the Question
To identify the most relevant terms present in the research question, a concept mapping was carried out a structured methodology aimed at identifying and organizing the key elements of a research question. The objective of concept mapping is to translate the identified concepts into search terms (keywords and controlled descriptors), which will be used in databases. This approach is essential to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive, precise, and aligned with the research objectives, being especially useful in systematic reviews, scoping reviews, and other types of literature reviews.
From this research question, the main elements identified were: terms related to open-source programming languages, data collection, extraction, analysis, and DataSUS. To structure the search strategy, the PCC (Population, Concept, and Context) framework was used, which best represents the components of the research. This structuring allows for a more targeted and efficient search, ensuring that the results obtained are aligned with the research objectives and cover the essential aspects of the investigated topic, as presented in Table 1 describing the PCC strategy.


The process of mapping and refining terms, using the main term and the translation of terms between DeCS (Health Sciences Descriptors) and MeSH (Medical Subject Headings), is a robust methodological approach to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive and precise, facilitating the retrieval of articles in bibliographic databases. 
3.5 Search Strategy
The search terms will be defined based on subject descriptors from the databases using the Health Sciences Descriptors (DeCS) and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). 
The search strategies were adapted for each database, using controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR). The construction of the search strategy was carried out in two steps: first, the terms related to each concept were combined using the Boolean operator OR (e.g., “Programming Languages” OR “Python Programming” OR “R Programming”) to ensure search comprehensiveness. Next, the groups of terms were combined with each other using the Boolean operator AND (e.g., [Group 1] AND [Group 2] AND [Group 3] AND [Group 4]), ensuring the precision and relevance of the results. The entire process was conducted using the PubMed Advanced Search tool (available at: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/advanced/). 
No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date, in order to ensure broad and inclusive coverage of the literature. 
These strategies were adapted to improve the sensitivity and specificity of the searches while maintaining the same framework initially established in the strategy developed for PubMed. The combination of terms, based on controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR), resulted in the following search strategies for each database, as presented in the appendices of this work through Table 2: Search Strategy in Databases.


3.6 Selection Process
Publications identified through the descriptors will be exported to the Rayyan application for duplicate removal and selection of articles/documents based on eligibility criteria, followed by full-text review and data extraction.
Studies addressing the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and/or analysis of DataSUS data will be included. Documents describing data extraction methods from other information sources or systems will be excluded from the sample.
3.7 Data Management and Analysis
Both the selection process through title and abstract screening and full-text review, and the data extraction will be carried out by two researchers. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus.
Due to the heterogeneity of the documents to be analyzed, quality assessment will be performed only for scientific articles indexed in databases, using the AGREE II instrument.
Data will be stored using the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) software.

3.8 Ethical Considerations and Conflicts of Interest
In accordance with Brazilian Resolutions No. 466 of December 12, 2012, and No. 510 of April 7, 2016, this study is exempt from review by a Research Ethics Committee (REC). There are no conflicts of interest in this protocol. 
4 EXPECTED RESULTS
The scoping review will comprehensively map the scientific production related to the use of open-source programming languages applied to DataSUS, identifying the state of the art in the collection, processing, and analysis of data from Brazil’s national health information systems. It is expected to characterize the types of published studies, application contexts, the most explored SUS information systems, and the predominant methodological approaches, providing a consolidated overview of current practices in the field. The use of open-source code enables researchers and developers to access and contribute to the improvement of tools. Well-developed code supports efficient data integration and analysis, accelerating the development of new solutions tailored to community needs.
In addition, the review will enable the identification of the main tools, languages, and libraries used to handle SUS microdata, including Python, R, and other open-source resources. This characterization will allow an assessment of the accessibility, documentation, and reproducibility of existing solutions, contributing to an understanding of how these technologies have been applied in research and health management.
The mapping process is also expected to reveal gaps in the literature, such as the lack of methodological standardization, limitations in interoperability between systems, scarcity of automated tools, and insufficient studies addressing integration across different DataSUS databases. Identifying these gaps will provide guidance for the development of new technological solutions and for shaping future research agendas.
The review will further systematize the methodologies employed in the analyzed studies, describing strategies for data collection, preprocessing, statistical analysis, modeling, and data visualization. This systematization will help compare manual and automated approaches, highlighting best practices, limitations, and opportunities for improvement in the use of public health data.
From the perspective of management and public policy, the expected results include demonstrating the potential of open-source tools to enhance transparency, efficiency, and reproducibility in epidemiological and administrative analyses. The review should show how automation in data collection and processing can support managers, researchers, and SUS professionals in evidence-based decision-making.
Finally, the study is expected to produce a consolidated, up-to-date, and replicable body of knowledge capable of supporting the development of new technologies, guiding training processes, and strengthening open science in the context of Brazilian public health.
In the future, it is expected that these tools will become more accessible, customizable, and user-friendly, increasing transparency in analyses. This will enable more robust studies aligned with the needs of health professionals and researchers. Additionally, new methodologies may be developed to handle large-scale data, optimizing the use of DataSUS for epidemiological analyses, outbreak prediction, and public policy evaluation using big data technologies.

title: Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing Technologies in Respiratory Critical Care: A Living Scoping Review Protocol
description: This living scoping review aims to comprehensively map and describe the use of metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) for diagnosing respiratory infections in critically ill patients. It will examine the sequencing workflows employed, their diagnostic accuracy, and how mNGS findings are integrated into clinical decision-making within intensive care units (ICUs). Following JBI and Cochrane methodologies, the review will systematically identify and synthesise studies that apply mNGS to lower respiratory tract samples from ICU patients, describing technologies used, diagnostic performance, and clinical impact. Updated regularly, the review will provide an evolving overview of mNGS applications in respiratory critical care, highlighting current practices, challenges, and evidence gaps to inform future research and guide the implementation of mNGS in clinical diagnostics.

title: Grammatical Correction and Morphological Productivity Tasks as Potential Identifiers of Developmental Language Disorder in Spanish-Catalan Bilingual Children: A Pilot Study
description: A critical problem for Catalan-Spanish bilinguals is the lack of assessment tools to conduct valid and accurate oral language evaluations. The purpose of this study was to provide initial pilot data for a new assessment tool in Catalan. We examined the possibility that two novel tasks, a grammatical correction (GramCorr) and morphological productivity (MP; nonword and word subtasks), could differentiate between Catalan-speaking children with and without developmental language disorder (DLD) with good diagnostic accuracy. Twenty-seven school-aged children with DLD (Mage = 9;1 years) and twenty-seven age/sex-matched typically developing (TD) children (Mage = 9;0 years) participated in the study. Group differences and diagnostic accuracy analyses (sensitivity and specificity and likelihood ratios) were conducted. Results showed that the global percentage of correct answers of children with DLD was significantly poorer than that of the TD controls in the two tasks. The preliminary diagnostic accuracy results suggested that the overall test (GramCorr+MP) can be used as an accurate tool to discriminate between children with DLD and children with TD. In addition, the MPnonword subtask on its own seems to provide sufficient information to diagnose DLD. When GramCorr and MPword task are used together, they can serve as tool to rule out a language disorder. Finally, the nature of both tasks, their usefulness for practitioners and future steps in the design of valid tools for the identification of Catalan speaking children with DLD were discussed.

title: Predicting Three-Month Pain and Disability in Frozen Shoulder: Protocol for the Development and Internal Validation of a Clinical Prognostic Model
description:
Frozen shoulder (FS) is a pathological condition affecting the glenohumeral joint and its surrounding soft tissues, leading to severe pain, restricted range of motion (ROM), disability, and a diminished quality of life (1). In particular, patients frequently report severe, drug-resistant pain—both during the day and at night—which is typically exacerbated at end-range or by abrupt movements (2). This is accompanied by multiplanar active and passive ROM limitations, particularly in external rotation with the arm by the side (3). Additionally, compensatory scapular dyskinesia and muscle atrophy of the whole shoulder girdle may be observed, especially in the later stages of the condition (1).
Although FS has historically been recognized as a localized, joint-specific pathology, growing evidence indicates that it is a musculoskeletal epiphenomenon driven by metabolic, inflammatory, and systemic dysregulation, alongside a clear influence from the patient's psychological profile (4). Consequently, the therapeutic paradigm is evolving toward a comprehensive, multi-system approach that integrates sleep hygiene, nutritional strategies, and psychological support (4–6).
The prognosis of FS is often challenging. Although some authors have characterized FS as a self-limiting pathology , current evidence recognises that symptoms can persist for years after onset (7). Specifically, moderate-to-severe ROM limitation, moderate pain, and functional issues have been reported from two to seven years following symptom onset. Furthermore, at a two-year follow-up, one-third of patients with FS remained dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with their rehabilitation pathway (7).
Prognostic research in FS is extensive and focuses on a wide range of outcome measures. For instance, diabetes mellitus, bilateral presentation, and a longer duration of symptoms are strong prognostic factors for poorer outcomes, potentially identifying patients who require early surgical intervention (8); conversely, age below 60 has been linked to a favorable response to non-surgical treatment (9). Notably, more severe baseline pain and functional limitations have been reported as negative predictors for both functional recovery and mobility improvement (10). Furthermore, diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, and autonomic symptoms negatively impact the quality of life of patients suffering from FS (11).
In parallel, psychological factors such as kinesiophobia, catastrophizing, anxiety, depression, and low health-related quality-of-life scores have emerged as significant predictors of persistent pain and disability (12). Finally, higher levels of kinesiophobia and comorbidities are associated with poorer disability and quality-of-life recovery (13), while higher baseline anxiety is negatively associated with functional outcomes at a three-month follow-up (14).
In clinical practice, accurately estimating a patient's prognosis is essential for guiding clinical decision-making. Prognostic prediction models can support this process by integrating multiple patient characteristics to generate individualized risk or recovery predictions. Indeed, prognostic prediction models are algorithms that combine multiple variables to estimate the likelihood of a specific outcome of interest for an individual patient, typically developed using a specific dataset (15). These models can be integrated into clinical decision support systems or presented as (online) calculators that require clinicians to manually input the values for each predictor to obtain the final prognostic estimate (15). Specifically, by utilizing these tools, clinicians can input a priori selected patient information, which the model processes to generate an individualized probability of achieving or not achieving a clinical outcome.
To the best of the authors’ knowledge, within the international literature on shoulder disorders, there is currently only one prognostic model, which assesses which patients will not have repeat shoulder instability after first-time traumatic anterior dislocation (16). However, although prognostic research is increasingly identifying various variables that impact outcomes in patients with FS, no prognostic model has yet been developed for this pathology. Therefore, this study will aim to develop and internally validate a prognostic model for patients suffering from FS.
Having a methodologically robust prognostic model available could allow clinicians to accurately estimate a patient’s prognosis, thereby informing clinical decision-making. Moreover, this tool could improve tailored treatment strategies by identifying different risk gradients for individuals who may require either minimal or more intensive interventions to achieve a positive outcome. Prognostic information is also essential for managing expectations and communicating with patients about their likely clinical trajectory.

METHODS

Study Design and Setting

This study is a retrospective prognostic model development study using data from three prospective cohorts. This study will be reported according to the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis with artificial intelligence (TRIPOD+AI) guidelines (17), which provide harmonised guidance for reporting prediction model studies.

Ethical approval

The dataset used to prepare the present prognostic model will be aggregated from three separate datasets derived from previously published prospective cohort studies (13,14,18). Ethics Committee of University of Molise (Italy) approved all studies (24/2024 on October 02, 2024; 06/2025 on June 19, 2025; 16/2025 on 05 November 2025). All study-related procedures will be performed in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Setting and participants

Adult individuals meeting the eligibility criteria were recruited during their initial specialist consultation for FS across three private physiotherapy practices in Roma, Lecce and Genova (Italy). The recruitment period was from November 2024 to February 2026. All participants were recruited seeking their first physiotherapy consultation for FS and had the same diagnosis supported by the same diagnostic criteria (Figure 1). Moreover, in all centers, during the recruitment process, one expert physiotherapist with more than eight years of clinical practice focused on shoulder disorders screened the participants for inclusion in the study.
All eligible participants were provided with detailed information regarding the research aims and procedures. A comprehensive information letter with dedicated information was provided to any individual who expressed interest. All individuals who met the inclusion criteria and agreed to participate in the study provided written, voluntary informed consent, while individuals who declined to participate were directed to standard rehabilitation.
During the 12-week prospective follow-up period, participants received standardised rehabilitation. Specifically, all patients underwent identical clinical management throughout the study. Therefore, this clinical management was not considered an exposure of interest, but rather an usual physiotherapy care provided to all participants.
All participants attended an educational session featuring standardized content across centers. This session addressed the natural history of FS, predisposing and prognostic factors, management options, home exercise recommendations, and expected recovery timelines. After the initial consultation, participants were referred to a qualified clinician for pharmacological management. Physical therapy rehabilitation commenced within few days of the initial consultation and consisted of joint mobilization, exercise therapy, and stretching, complemented by detailed instructions for a daily 30-minutes home exercise program.
Supervised sessions lasted approximately 45 minutes and were scheduled twice weekly during the first 2 weeks, once weekly for the subsequent 6 weeks, and once every 2 weeks during the final month. In all clinical settings, care was delivered by physiotherapists with over 12 years of experience in shoulder pathologies.
Two hundred and eight-three participants met all inclusion criteria; in particular, 80 participants were recruited for the cohort 1 (13), 120 participants from the cohort 2 (14), and 83 participants from the cohort 3 (18).

Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Participants eligible for this study were adults with a diagnosis of unilateral FS. FS is defined as a restriction of external rotation of the affected shoulder exceeding 50% compared to the contralateral side, along with limitations of less than 25% in at least two additional planes of movement (19). Symptoms were required to be stable or progressively worsening over the previous month, in line with the criteria established by Kelly et al. (2013) (19). Eligible participants were also required to be proficient in Italian and have no contraindications to corticosteroid therapy.
Exclusion criteria encompassed a history of shoulder trauma or fracture within the past year, previous rotator cuff repair or other shoulder surgical procedures within the same timeframe, and recent shoulder dislocations. Individuals with serious, specific shoulder pathologies (such as tumors or infections), as well as those with severe neurological or psychiatric disorders that could potentially interfere with study participation, were also excluded. Additionally, a negative radiographic evaluation for significant glenohumeral osteoarthritis was mandatory; specifically, a grade of 2 or higher on the Kellgren–Lawrence scale (20) was classified as an exclusion criterion to ensure the sample was accurately representative of individuals with FS rather than joint degeneration. Finally, pain elicited or worsened by neck movement and positive Wainner cluster (21) results was applied as further exclusion criteria.

Variables included in the model

Outcomes of interest for the model: Pain and disability were assessed as dependent variables, as they are the major concerns for people suffering from FS.
These dimensions were assessed using the two Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI) subscores (22). The SPADI is a self-report questionnaire used to assess the severity of shoulder pain and its impact on daily activities, assessing the degree of pain and difficulty experienced by the individual when performing various shoulder-related tasks, such as reaching, lifting, and sleeping (23). The questionnaire consists of 13 items divided into a pain subscale (5 items) and a disability subscale (8 items). For each item, the patient must assign a score ranging from 0 to 10 points, where a higher score indicates a greater level of pain or disability (22). The total score of each subscore of the SPADI is calculated by adding the single-question score and then normalising to 100. This study used the Italian version of SPADI since it showed robust psychometric properties in subjects with FS (24).

Independent predictors included in the model: 

Baseline score for pain and disability (continuous variable). Baseline scores for pain and disability have been identified as prognostic factors across multiple studies (10,13,18) and will be incorporated into our predictive models. Specifically, the baseline pain score will be included in the pain model, whereas the baseline disability score will be included in the disability model.

Age (continuous variable). Age as a predictor of conservative treatment failure has yielded somewhat conflicting results in the literature. Levine et al. (2007) (25) found that younger patients were more likely to fail non-operative management, and Rill et al. (2011) (26) identified age as a strong predictor of progression to surgery. This latter finding was recently supported by Kingston et al. (2018) (27), who demonstrated that younger age was significantly associated with surgical intervention. Ages of 60 or over were a better prognostic factor for non-operative treatment for FS (9). Conversely, in a systematic review, Mertens et al. (2021) (10) concluded that there is Level 2 evidence regarding factors influencing treatment outcomes in patients with FS, indicating that younger age is actually associated with better overall functionality.

Daily pain intensity (continuous variable). Two studies investigated the association between daily pain and outcomes in FS patients. Results revealed that higher initial pain was associated with a worse final disability (10), and those patients with the most severe symptoms at onset carry the worst prognosis (28).

Comorbidities (Yes/no for diabetes and thyroid; dichotomous variable). Various studies found that patients with diabetes had worse results in range of motion and pain recovery than patients without diabetes after conservative treatment (29). Moreover, few studies found an influence of diabetes for lower final functionality after conservative treatment (26,29). Lastly, diabetes is a significant risk factor for undergoing shoulder arthroscopy for the diagnosis of FS (30). Patients with diabetes mellitus would benefit from early surgery (8), as diabetes was a poor prognostic factor for non-operative treatment for FS (9). Presence of diabetes and thyroid disorder at baseline emerged to be a negative prognostic factor for shoulder pain, disability and quality of life in patients with FS (11,13).

Symptoms onset (Two classes: < or >5months). Evidence suggests that duration of symptoms is predictive for change in SPADI after 8 weeks (31), with shorter duration predicting larger improvements in SPADI. In addition, shorter duration of symptoms predicted better final function (26) and successful treatment after a home-based exercise program (7). Lastly, patients who suffer from chronic symptoms would benefit from early surgery (8).
Sex (dichotomous variable). Female sex (specifically women>45 years old) was found as a significant risk factor for undergoing shoulder arthroscopy for the diagnosis of FS (30). 


Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics will be used to summarise participant characteristics, candidate predictors, and outcome measures. Continuous variables will be reported as means and standard deviations or medians and interquartile ranges, as appropriate according to their distribution, while categorical variables will be summarised using frequencies and percentages. The extent and patterns of missing data will be explored for all candidate predictors and outcomes. Assuming that data are missing at random, missing values in candidate predictors will be handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) (32). The imputation model will include all candidate predictors and both outcome variables to maximise the plausibility of the MAR assumption. Parameter estimates obtained from analyses across the imputed datasets will be combined using Rubin's rules (33). Participants with missing outcome data will not contribute to the development of the corresponding prognostic model.
Separate multivariable linear regression models will be developed for the two prespecified continuous outcomes: SPADI Pain and SPADI Disability. Continuous predictors will be modelled using restricted cubic splines with three knots (34).
Model performance will be evaluated in terms of discrimination (i.e., area under the curve), calibration (i.e., calibration plot, calibration intercept, and calibration slope), and clinical utility (i.e., decision curve analysis) (35). 
Internal validation will be performed using 500 bootstrap resamples. A uniform shrinkage factor will be derived from the bootstrap calibration slope and applied to all regression coefficients to reduce overfitting. Following coefficient shrinkage, the model intercept will be re-estimated to ensure appropriate calibration of the final model (36). The final optimism-adjusted regression coefficients and model performance measures will be reported. 

Sample size calculation

As this is a retrospective study, the sample size was fixed by the number of eligible participants available in the study database and could not be determined a priori. Therefore, rather than estimating the required sample size, we assessed the maximum complexity of the prognostic models that could be reliably developed with the available data.
The allowable model complexity was estimated using the pmsampsize package in R (https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/pmsampsize/versions/1.1.3/topics/pmsampsize), following the methodology proposed by Riley and colleagues for the development of multivariable prediction models with continuous outcomes (37). This approach determines the maximum number of predictor parameters that can be estimated while minimising the risk of model overfitting and ensuring adequate model performance.
For the SPADI Pain outcome, assuming an anticipated model performance of R2 = 0.20, a mean follow-up score of 20.31, a standard deviation of 16.69, and the available sample size of 283 participants, the analysis indicated that a model containing up to 9 predictor parameters (regression coefficients) could be reliably estimated.
Similarly, for the SPADI Disability outcome, assuming an anticipated model performance of R2 = 0.20, a mean follow-up score of 18.85, a standard deviation of 19.87, and the same available sample size, up to 9 predictor parameters (regression coefficients) could be estimated.

OPEN SCIENCE POLICIES AND CORE OPEN SCIENCE PRACTICES IN MAJOR MEDICAL JOURNALS: DEVELOPMENT OF AN AUTOMATIZED TOOL BASED ON A LLM
description:
Open science policies and core open science practices in major medical journals: development of an automatized tool based on a LLM

GUILLAUME FREYERMUTH / CONSTANT VINATIER / GAUTHIER LE-BARTZ-LYAN / SARAH BUET / PERRINE LUNEL / NICOLAS ROBILLARD / GWENAEL DUMONT / FLORIAN NAUDET / MATHIEU ACHER

BACKGROUND

Monitoring the use and application of Open Science practices is key to fostering Open Science and to understanding barriers and facilitators of open science practices. Monitoring also aids in measuring the impact of open science policies and can serve as a possible intervention to improve transparency and reproducibility. For instance, the Hong Kong principles support the assessment of researchers on the use of Open Science practices. Open Science Monitoring is a key priority for organizations such as the UNESCO [and the G7. The scientific community is also beginning to agree on key indicators to measure. For instance, in biomedicine, a core set of 19 open science practices has been developed to monitor various open science practices such as preregistration, open data, open access, open code, conflict of interest statements etc. 

In recent years, biomedical journals have implemented some policies that promote open science practices. Most notably, the influential International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) made prospective registration a requirement to publish clinical trial results in 2005. In 2018, it required a specific data-sharing statement to be included in each newly submitted paper (and prespecified in study registration). The impact of these policies have been studied previously showing an major influence on trial registration practices, and mixed results regarding actual data sharing. 

Automatized options are being developed to track change within the biomedical literature. It is therefore useful to assess the impact of the various open science policies adopted by biomedical journals using those tools. 

OBJECTIVES
 
This aim of this study, targeting major medical journals, is three-fold:
1. to describe open science policies in these journals, 
2. to develop and validate automatic tools that can be used to monitor key transparency practices 
3. to describe retrospectively changes on open science and transparency practices for articles published in those journals.

METHODS

Selection criteria

We will include in our study a sample of 10 major medical journals. 

Population: We will include research studies published in 2020 or 2021 in journals of interest:
- Annals of internal medicine 
- BioMed Central Medicine 
- The British Medical Journal
- Canadian Medical Association Journal 
- Journal of the American Medical Association 
- JAMA Network Open 
- Lancet
- Nature Medicine 
- Public Library Of Science 

Study design: All types of research articles will be included with a proportional number of 1/RCTs, 2/ meta-analyses and 3/ other research articles. 

Data sources: 
All articles and supplementary materials will be extracted from Pubmed and from the journal website. If an article isn’t open access, academic access will be used to get it. 

Automatized tool

Here we want to develop a tool using machine learning and to explore the feasibility of a tool based on a large language model (LLM) such as Mixtral or llama to extract the presence and absence of open science practices inside. Ideally this tool should be automatized, open source (or failing that, open weights). and used locally to enforce reproducibility. It should be able to identify journal articles (either in XML or pdf format) and all supplementary material (in pdf format) and to extract core Open Science practices. The task of extracting content out of a scholar article with an LLM involves optional innovations to ensure accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, such as embedding of raw data into vector stores, refining the method of prompting the LLM, and employing techniques like retrieval augmented generation (RAG) or fine-tuning.

Creation of the validation database: 

Data collection occurred from February 25th to March 18th 2024, following a standardized approach. For each journal, a stratification about study type was realized to select 10 RCT, 10 meta research and 10 other research articles per journal. To perform article selection, 1/ the algorithm of research from PubMed was used as described in table 1. Then, in each journal/category, we randomly selected 10 articles. As it, the database is composed of 30 articles from each journal with an equal representation of the different type of study designs for a total of 300 articles. In case the required number of articles of a given type wasn’t available in a given journal, the total number of articles was completed by articles with the same study design published in other journals (that were each time from a different journal). This was done by a first group of master 1 students (SB, PL, NR).

Search strategy and article selection process
 
All articles were classified by the publication date, the latest will get the number 1 and the oldest the max. After assigning these numbers, for each journal and type of study, each was given a random number and eligibility of articles will be assessed – for each journal and type of study- using this random number and included if those are in line with our selection criteria (data and code available on the Open Science Framework). As soon as the target number of included articles was reached, the same selection process was applied for the next journal and type of study.

Description of tools’ performance

Development will use the validation database of 300 papers selected from articles published in the journals of interest during the year 2020-2021 (30 per journal).

Statistical analysis: 

Tool’s performance will be determined by the computation of metrics: sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPC and the F1 score and the plotting of the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC). 
As highlighted in the literature (2), any error may also come from human. For each disagreement, a manual verification of the result by an expert (CV or FN) will be done to determine if the LLM is truly false or not.

title: Effectiveness of Multidisciplinary (MDT) Team Activation Models and Algorithms in Collaborative Care for Pediatric Cancer Patients in Hospital
description:
Multidisciplinary Teams (MDTs) have been widely recognized as a critical approach to improving the quality, safety, and overall outcomes of healthcare services, particularly in oncology (Prades et al., 2015; Soukup et al., 2018). However, the implementation of MDTs across hospital settings shows significant variation, particularly regarding team activation mechanisms (Lamb et al., 213; Taylor et al., 2019). Most existing literature focuses on MDTs as collaborative structures or discussion forums, while MDT activation mechanisms as systematic, protocol-driven decisions are rarely studied (Fleissig et al., 2006). In routine practice, MDT activation is often ad hoc, relying heavily on individual clinician experience without the support of standardized algorithms or decision rules. This situation has the potential to lead to inefficiencies, delayed decision-making, fragmented care pathways, and inconsistent adherence to clinical guidelines (Pillay et al., 2016).
Pediatric cancer care, in particular, requires highly coordinated efforts across multiple disciplines (e.g., oncology, surgery, nursing, pharmacy, and psychosocial support) to optimize diagnostic accuracy, reduce treatment delays, and enhance clinical outcomes (Pritchard-Jones et al., 2020). While MDTs or tumor boards are widely recommended in pediatric oncology guidelines, their activation in routine practice remains inconsistent. Many hospitals still rely on ad hoc consultations or rigid, fixed-schedule meetings, which may not align with the dynamic and urgent needs of pediatric patients (Hahlweg et al., 2 and Hong et al., 2014). Trigger-based activation models and clinical algorithms offer a systematic approach to mobilize MDT expertise precisely when clinical, pathway, or digital thresholds are met (Kawamoto et al., 2005; Sutton et al., 2020).
This review will generate evidence to inform the design of a context-adaptive MDT activation model for pediatric cancer care, with explicit relevance to both high-resource and resource-constrained hospital settings.

title: Completeness of Reporting in AI Diagnostic Studies for Skin Cancer: A Protocol for a Systematic Review of Adherence to CLAIM, TRIPOD-AI, and STARD 2015 Standards
description: This systematic review evaluates the completeness of reporting in AI diagnostic and classification studies for skin cancer against three established reporting checklists: CLAIM (42 items), TRIPOD-AI (27 items), and STARD 2015 (30 items). The primary outcome is checklist-specific adherence rates. Secondary outcomes include item-level and domain-level adherence, temporal trends in reporting completeness (pre-CLAIM 2010–2019, post-CLAIM/pre-TRIPOD-AI 2020–2024, post-TRIPOD-AI 2025–2026), and correlation between reporting completeness and methodological quality. The review will search PubMed (MEDLINE), Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov from 1 January 2010 to 30 June 2026. Two reviewers will independently screen, extract data, and assess risk of bias using QUADAS-2. Adherence data will be synthesised descriptively with median and IQR per checklist, stratified by publication period, journal type, impact factor, geographic region, imaging modality, validation design, and public dataset use.

title: Accuracy of inflammatory biomarkers in assessing outcomes in Chagas disease: a scoping review
description: This scoping review aims to map and synthesize the existing literature on inflammatory biomarkers in Chagas disease (CD), focusing on identifying gaps in current knowledge and providing guidelines for future research. (2) Which aspects of this area have not yet been sufficiently explored or understood? Studies that meet the inclusion criteria will be incorporated into the review, and any discrepancies between reviewers will be resolved by a third reviewer. Cross-sectional (diagnostic accuracy) and cohort studies will be considered, including individuals with CD in the indeterminate, digestive, cardiac, or mixed forms, of both sexes, regardless of age, and from any healthcare setting.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence in detecting vertical root fractures: A systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Vertical root fracture (VRF) is a challenging endodontic complication that frequently results in tooth extraction due to diagnostic difficulty and delayed detection. Conventional periapical radiographs and clinical examination demonstrate limited sensitivity because of anatomical superimposition and subtle fracture lines. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) improves visualization but is associated with artifacts, radiation exposure, and interpretation variability.
Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning and machine learning-based image analysis models, has recently been applied to dental imaging for automated fracture detection. Although numerous experimental and clinical studies report promising outcomes, the actual diagnostic accuracy remains uncertain due to methodological variability, dataset bias, and differences in imaging modalities. Therefore, a systematic synthesis of available evidence is required

title: Protocol for a systematic review and prognostic accuracy meta-analysis of tests and prediction models in first-trimester threatened miscarriage
description:
This project is a systematic review and prognostic accuracy meta-analysis evaluating biochemical, ultrasound, clinical, and multivariable prediction models for women presenting with first-trimester threatened miscarriage and an ultrasound-confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy. Threatened miscarriage is one of the most common obstetric emergencies worldwide, yet counselling is often based on experience rather than rigorously quantified risk. Over four decades, many individual tests and composite models have been proposed, but their true prognostic performance, risk of bias, and incremental value over routine assessment remain uncertain.
The primary objective is to identify and compare the accuracy of candidate prognostic markers and models for predicting subsequent miscarriage versus ongoing pregnancy or live birth in this high-risk group. We will include prospective or nested cohort studies and high-quality evidence syntheses that report first-trimester biochemical markers (for example, progesterone, hCG, CA-125), ultrasound parameters (such as fetal heart rate, crown–rump length, gestational sac morphology), clinical factors, or multivariable and machine-learning models. The review follows PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-DTA guidance, and uses CHARMS for model framing, QUADAS-2 for study-level risk of bias, and PROBAST for prediction model appraisal. Where at least four comparable studies report a given threshold, we will use random-effects bivariate or HSROC models to estimate pooled sensitivity, specificity, and summary ROC curves; otherwise, accuracy will be synthesised narratively.
Expected outputs include: (1) a fully documented protocol and data extraction tools; (2) a curated dataset of study-level accuracy estimates and model characteristics; (3) reproducible analysis code for all meta-analyses and figures; and (4) a set of evidence-based recommendations for future large, multicentre, TRIPOD-compliant cohorts and model validation studies. By making these materials openly available on OSF, we aim to increase transparency, facilitate replication and extension of our work, and provide a robust evidentiary foundation for future clinical guidelines and decision-support tools for the millions of women worldwide who experience threatened miscarriage each year.
