Title
Deep Learning Methods for Breast Cancer Analysis Using MRI: A Systematic Review

Review Question
What deep learning methods have been applied to breast cancer detection, classification, and segmentation using MRI, and what are their reported performance characteristics and limitations?

Eligibility Criteria
The inclusion criteria were:
(1) studies applying deep learning (DL) models for breast cancer diagnosis or classification,
(2) the use of MRI-based imaging as the primary modality,
(3) evaluation using standard metrics (e.g., accuracy, AUC, sensitivity).
(4) availability of experimental design or dataset details.
(5) Written in English.
The exclusion criteria included:
(1) studies relying solely on machine learning (ML) without explicit comparison to or integration with DL models.
(2) imaging modalities other than MRI,
(3) papers lacking full methodological or evaluation details.
(4) studies focusing on other cancer types.
(5) Conference papers.

Information Sources
PubMed, Google Scholar, Web of Science

Search Strategy
The search was conducted using explicit Boolean strings for each database syntax: (“breast cancer” OR “breast tumour”) AND (“MRI” OR “magnetic resonance imaging”) AND (“deep learning” OR “convolutional neural network” OR “CNN” OR “YOLO”) AND (“classification” OR “segmentation” OR “detection”).

Study Selection
Titles/abstracts screened → full-text review → inclusion.
Following PRISMA 2020 framework to ensure reproducibility, transparency, and methodological rigor in the identification, screening, and study selection.

Data Extraction
MRI modality, metrics.

Risk of Bias / Quality Assessment
Qualitative methodological assessment (dataset size, validation strategy).
The reliability of the included studies evaluated based on different standards: Data integrity: where verified ground truth was met by utilizing trusted publicly available datasets (e.g., Duke, QIN-Breast, TCGA-BRCA). Imbalance Handling: where a key risk of bias in BC detection is the prevalence of imbalanced data, here specific techniques like balanced patch sampling were used to mitigate this effect. Clinical Transparency: due to the black box nature of DL models which could be considered as a limitation, studies combined XAI or heatmaps visualization to provide higher clinical utility.
Most studies showed solid methodological design, especially those utilized large datasets or multi-modal inputs of MRIs, however some sources of bias couldn’t be exempted including lack of external confidential validation and limited dataset sizes.

Data Synthesis
The review synthesized findings from 8 studies focusing on advanced DL architectures for breast MRI. Among the reviewed studies, hybrid and multi-modal models consistently outperformed single-modal, and YOLO-based detectors demonstrated higher real-time localization abilities. While diagnostic accuracy shown to remain above 90%, the evidence base remains geographically and institutionally narrow due to many reasons.
In terms of addressed challenges for the transition of these models into clinical routines, most studies relied on limited set of publicly available datasets (e.g. Duke, QIN Breast), suggesting that while the architecture is good, the evidence base still needed and validation is still required for clinical standards. Moreover, the high computational costs remain as a barrier to adopting real-world deployment, which raises the need for something like a lightweight model that can be integrated into existing radiology workstations. Furthermore, the transparency issue in AI-Assisted decision-making tools needs a collaborative effort to utilize high quality, annotated, and diverse MRI data to ensure generalizability and validated frameworks.
In conclusion, DL is showing great promise for transforming breast MRI analysis from early detection and segmentation to personalized treatment planning. The combination of data diversity, explainable models, and clinical settings will shape the next era of computer-aided BC diagnosis, ultimately reduce human tedious workload and improve patient outcomes, while considering the limitations and challenges addressed previously.

Timeline
Review conducted between [September 2025 – January 2026].

title: Prognostic value of procalcitonin for bacteremia in pediatric oncologic febrile neutropenia in a Peruvian population
description: This project evaluates the prognostic value of serum procalcitonin measured at hospital admission for the detection of bacteremia in pediatric oncology patients presenting with febrile neutropenia. Using a diagnostic test design nested within a retrospective cohort, the study analyzes the first episode of febrile neutropenia in hospitalized children with cancer between 2021 and 2025 at a specialized referral center in Peru. Clinical characteristics, admission procalcitonin levels, and blood culture results obtained within the first 48 hours are assessed. Diagnostic accuracy measures, including ROC curve analysis, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and likelihood ratios, are used to determine the optimal procalcitonin cutoff. This project aims to generate local evidence to improve risk stratification and support timely clinical decision-making in pediatric febrile neutropenia.

title: ⁠Effect of the use of Artificial Intelligence tools on the diagnostic accuracy of medical students during clinical rotations: A scoping review.
description:
Introduction: Medical education is at an inflection point due to the rapid technological evolution, marked by the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Tools such as Machine Learning and Large Language Models (LLMs) are being integrated into the medical and educational fields, offering promising applications such as virtual patient simulation, the creation of personalized learning platforms, and support for clinical decision-making. However, despite the great interest and potential of AI, its integration into the medical curriculum is still early and fragmented. There is a need for rigorous scientific literature that specifically evaluates the impact of using these tools on the clinical judgment and diagnostic accuracy of medical students during their clinical rotations. Therefore, conducting a scoping review is justified to synthesize the available evidence, identify knowledge gaps, and propose strategies for optimal AI integration into medical training.


Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the guidelines of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The search will be performed in key electronic databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Bireme, complemented by a review of gray literature (government reports, theses). Search terms will be developed using controlled vocabulary (MeSH, DeCS) and related keywords, focusing on the intersection of "Artificial Intelligence", "Diagnostic Accuracy", and "Medical Students in Clinical Rotations". Scientific articles, reviews, and technical documents in Spanish, English, and Portuguese, published between January 2015 and November 2025, will be included. The study selection process will be managed with Rayyan software and will involve title and abstract screening, followed by full-text review by two independent reviewers, with a third for conflict resolution. Data extraction will focus on bibliographic information, study objectives, methodological design, population, the type of AI used, and the documented effects on diagnostic accuracy.


Expected Results: This scoping review is expected to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence, allowing for: Identification of the specific types of AI tools that have been used for educational purposes in medical students during clinical rotations. Analysis of the positive and negative effects of AI use on students' diagnostic accuracy, differentiating the clinical areas of greatest application, as well as examination of the ethical and pedagogical implications associated with incorporating AI into clinical training settings and proposal of a framework for integrating artificial intelligence into medical education that optimizes its use as a learning resource while minimizing its potential adverse effects. The results of this research will serve as a fundamental guide for trainees, educators, healthcare professionals, and educational policy makers, facilitating informed decision-making regarding the implementation of AI in the training of future physicians.

title: Accuracy of Intraoperative Surgical Margin Assessment Techniques in Veterinary Oncology
description:
Accurate determination of surgical margin status is fundamental for detecting residual microscopic residual cancer in patients, predicting clinical outcomes, and optimizing treatment planning. Postoperative histopathology following surgical tumor resection is considered the gold standard for margin evaluation; however, this process typically takes one or two weeks to obtain results and only a limited sample of the surgical margins are assessed. Consequently, this delay results in a missed opportunity to evaluate surgical margins in real time and to utilize that information for immediate intraoperative decision-making, which could improve patient outcomes. Several techniques are available for intraoperative surgical margin assessment, each with different levels of accuracy, including frozen tissue section biopsy, imprint cytology margin, near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) which has the potential to guide surgical-decision making in real-time.

This review aims to compare the diagnostic accuracy of intraoperative surgical margin evaluation techniques as individual studies focus on the reporting of accuracy of one technique in comparison to histopathology. Only studies on canine cutaneous or subcutaneous tumors will be included in the review. 
The primary outcome of the review is comparison of diagnostic accuracy for detection of positive surgical margins in cutaneous and subcutaneous tumors across techniques.

title: DEEP LEARNING FOR AUTOMATED DETECTION AND CLASSIFICATION OF TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT DISORDERS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
Title: Deep Learning for Automated Detection and Classification of Temporomandibular Joint Disorders: A Scoping Review

Temporomandibular Joint Disorders (TMDs) are a significant clinical challenge associated with pain, functional impairment, and reduced quality of life. Traditional diagnostic approaches—such as manual interpretation of MRI, CBCT, CT, or panoramic images—can be time-consuming, subjective, and affected by inter-observer variability. With recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) techniques, automated detection and classification of TMDs has emerged as a promising solution to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency.

This scoping review systematically maps current evidence on deep learning applications for diagnosing TMDs, including anterior disc displacement (ADD), osteoarthritis, condylar degeneration, and degenerative joint disease. Using PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a comprehensive search across PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and Wiley identified 15 eligible studies published between 2015 and 2025.

Across these studies, models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), U-Net, ResNet, VGG16, MobileNetV2, YOLO, and ensemble architectures demonstrated high diagnostic performance—achieving accuracy levels up to 99%, sensitivity up to 98%, and significant improvements in segmentation precision. Findings indicate that deep learning can reduce diagnostic time by up to 50%, standardize interpretation, and serve as an effective decision-support tool for clinicians.

Despite promising results, challenges remain related to dataset diversity, external validation, reproducibility, and clinical integration. Future research should focus on multi-center datasets, multimodal learning, standardized benchmarking, explainability methods such as Grad-CAM, and ethical frameworks for AI deployment in healthcare.

This review highlights the potential of deep learning to transform TMD diagnostics, contributing to faster, more accurate, and more consistent radiologic evaluation, ultimately improving clinical outcomes for patients.

title: Clinical Utility and Necessity of Preoperative CT Imaging in Functional and Aesthetic Nasal Surgery: A Systematic Review
description:
Overview and rationale 
Rhinoplasty, septoplasty and septorhinoplasty are among the most frequently performed operations worldwide. With a wide variety of indications like external deformities and internal dysfunctions, preoperative evaluations are necessary to inform sound, patient oriented surgical decisions. As such a wide variety of preoperative assessment methods are used, most common of which are physical examination, rhinoscopy, nasal endoscopy and CT imaging. These operations are costly, and most insurance companies require patients to have CT-documentation for clinical justification to proceed with payment. While CT scans provide ample insight into anatomical structures of the sinonasal region to help make informed decisions, they could also harm patients if used frequently due to their utilization of ionizing radiation. And since they are costly procedures, frequent use would also force significant financial burden on healthcare systems. Consequently, some recent studies have advocated for its limited use in complicated cases to ensure patient safety and cost-effectiveness. This PRISMA-2020-conformant systematic review was designed to respond to these controversies and assess CT scans overall utility and necessity in comparison to other preoperative assessment methods. 
Objective 
The main objective of this study was to compare various preoperative assessment methods in patients undergoing rhinoplasty, septoplasty or septorhinoplasty, with a specific focus on the utilization of CT imaging. 
Methods 
Eligibility: studies with patients undergoing rhinoplasty, septoplasty and septorhinoplasty (any age/indication) that utilized preoperative assessment with direct comparisons (CT vs other modalities). Included studies where Randomized trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, case series or cross-sectional studies reporting comparative outcomes. case reports, animal/in vitro studies, reviews, editorials, conference abstracts without full data, or studies lacking direct comparison between CT and alternative methods where excluded. 
Search and databases: an initial search was performed on April 14th,2025 in PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane library using MeSH terms and keywords. An updated search was performed on November 8th,2025 with same queries to cover the time gap. Language and publication date were not restricted. Also, reference list of relevant articles and systematic reviews were hand-searched to limit potential article-misses. 
Study selection and data extraction: two independent reviewers screened and data extracted articles with a third reviewer to resolve any disagreements. extracted domains included author(s), country, year of publication, sample size, study design, objective, patient characteristics, preoperative assessment methods (including computed tomography (CT) and alternative assessment methods as comparators), surgery type, surgery indication, relevant outcomes (diagnostic or clinical) and limitations. 
Risk of bias: MMAT 2018 was implemented to do study appraisal and risk of bias assessment. Studies where qualitatively categorized (low, medium, high) and no numerical scoring was applied, per MMAT guidance. 
Synthesis and certainty: although meta-analysis was considered initially, narrative synthesis was done due to significant heterogeneity. Certainty was graded using GRADE. 
Transparency: complete search strategies, PRISMA flow, extractions, risk-of-bias justifications and summary will be provided on OSF project page. AI assistance (ChatGPT) was only used for translation of non-English articles for screening and data extraction, with translations manually checked by reviewers. AI was not used to generate scientific content, analysis or conclusion. 
Current status and preliminary evidence map: From 2,334 records, 29 studies were included. The evidence base comprised two parallel-group randomized controlled trials (RCTs); 23 cohort or cross-sectional clinical studies; one technical study; and three laboratory or cadaveric studies. Population included both adult and pediatric; with three studies addressing adult nasal fracture; one pediatric series addressing congenital nasal dermoids; one small prospective case series focusing on adults undergoing secondary rhinoseptoplasty, comparing 3D volume-rendered CT with standard clinical examination; and three cadaveric investigations simulating functional rhinoplasty interventions. most common included preoperative modalities were nasal endoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy, or plain radiography; outcome domains included diagnostic agreement/accuracy, detection of specific anatomic or pathologic findings, changes in surgical planning, and patient-reported outcomes (NOSE, ROE, VAS, SNOT-22).
Expected outcomes and contributions: 
Deliverables: PRISMA-2020 flow diagrams; study characteristics, surgery types, comparator modalities (CT vs alternative preoperative assessment methods), outcomes measured tables; risk of bias summary; GRADE-style summary of findings; SWiM compliant narrative synthesis
Knowledge gains: the study will lead to a clean and complete map of human studies involving comparison of preoperative assessment methods in nasal surgeries, with emphasis on preoperative CT imaging and how it measures up in comparison to other preoperative modalities. This will highlight CT imaging areas of necessity and areas of redundancy, providing a clear map guiding physicians on how and where to use it in their assessments to ensure patients safety. 
Impact: this will help committees to come up with necessary guidelines and protocols for CT usage, inform future study designs to derive deeper paradigms, guide relative regulatory bodies such as ethics committees and insurance companies on appropriate comparators and their use, and help guide physicians for possibly more appropriate choices of preoperative modalities to ensure patient safety
Limitations and Risk Management: possible anticipated limitations in studies are small sample size, unclear randomization and blinding methods, heterogenous study designs, inconsistent outcome definitions, limited objective statistical analysis. To address these, appropriate risk of bias tools, transparent use of GRADE for certainty evaluation and SWiM for narrative synthesis are utilized. 
Ethics, Roles, Dissemination: due to utilization of previously published human studies in this study, ethics approval was non-applicable. The study received no external funding. Team roles covered otolaryngologist, sinus and nasal surgery fellow, and biostatistician/methodologists. 
Corresponding author is Dr. Mehdi Bakhshaee (BakhshaeeM@mums.ac.ir; https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9590-4798)

title: Mapping the interplay between anxiety symptoms during the COVID-19 lockdown in Belgium: A undirected and Bayesian network perspective
description: Template: We are preregistering this exploratory data analysis of preexisting data, as suggested by Weston, Ritchie, Rohrer, and Przybylski (2019). https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919848684 More details regarding the template can be found here: https://osf.io/v4z3x/ Context and Research Questions: Pandemic yields severe and long-lasting consequences on mental health (for a systematic review, see Brooks et al., 2020), and the COVID-19 pandemic is no exception to this statement. Early data indicate that the COVID-19 pandemic has a significant impact on mental health (e.g., Asmunsdon & Taylor, 2020; Wang et al., 2020; for a systematic review, see Xiong et al., 2020), with anxiety symptoms being one of the most commonly reported problems (e.g., Quiu et al., 2020; Mertens et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). In Belgium, the number of people reporting anxiety symptoms increased substantially during the lockdown of March 2020 compared to similar data collected two years before (Sciensano, 2020). And similar findings have been reported across different countries (e.g., González-Sanguino et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020). And that should not come as a surprise. The profound health, economic, and social consequences of COVID-19 lockdown are likely to be anxiogenic for many, regardless of whether or not they have had direct exposure to the virus (Heeren, 2020; Park, Velez, Kannan, Chorpita, 2020). However, in most of the studies that have been published so far regarding the impact of the lockdown on anxiety symptoms, researchers have relied on a unitary approach to anxiety by collapsing the different features of anxiety into one sum-score and thus ignoring any possibility that these distinct features could interact in different ways. Recently, a network approach to psychopathology has appeared, conceptualizing mental disorders as network systems of interacting symptoms. In this way, instead of investigating mental disorders as reflecting a single, unitary construct, a network approach allows an investigation into the structure of, and associations between, the symptoms themselves. Though only recently pioneered by Borsboom and his colleagues (e.g., Borsboom et al., 2011, Borsboom & Cramer, 2013), this approach has quickly become a hot topic in contemporary clinical psychology. Many studies have accordingly used this framework to investigate the interrelations between systems of symptoms and speculate as to the clinical implications (for systematic reviews, see Contreras et al., 2019; Robinaugh et al., 2019). Although a few studies have already applied a network analytic framework to examine the interdependence between different factors assumedly involved in the psychological responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, and especially regarding the fear of infection or the anxious response to the structural impact of the pandemic (e.g., Papini et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2020), none of these studies focused on the network structure of the connections between the distinct features of anxiety during the lockdown. In this project, we thus seek to map the network structure of the hallmark features of anxiety during the lockdown. To do so, we will implement the network computational tools via a reanalysis of an existing dataset (Lits et al., 2020; see below) that includes the GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006)—one of the most commonly used self-reported screening tools in epidemiological and clinical research of anxiety disorders (e.g., Schalet et al., 2014)—in a large and representative sample of participants living in the French-speaking part of Belgium who took part to an online survey conducted during the first weeks following the (first) Belgian national lockdown (March 2020). Especially, we have three primary goals. First, we endeavor to clarify the pairwise connections among the distinct anxiety symptoms during the lockdown. To do so, we will compute a graphical Gaussian model (GGM). In this undirected network, edges signify conditional independence relationships between nodes (here, symptoms of anxiety), controlling for the effects of all other nodes. Of critical interest is the computation of centrality metrics that disclose the most potentially influential nodes maintaining the GGM network structure. We will then test whether these nodes cohere as a unitary network system of interacting elements or whether they instead constitute distinct communities (or subnetworks) of nodes (i.e., symptoms) serving different functions. Finally, we will use Bayesian computational methods to compute a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to estimate the probabilistic dependencies among the distinct anxiety features. A DAG is a directed network whereby each edge has an arrow tip on one end, signifying the direction of probabilistic dependence (McNally, 2016; McNally, Heeren, & Robinaugh, 2017). To generate directed edges, DAGs encode the conditional independence relationships and characterize the variables' joint probability distribution. DAGs can thus be decomposed as a product of the conditional distribution of each node given its parent nodes in the graph, thus rendering DAG analysis capable of indicating whether the existence of node A ("downstream") probabilistically implies the existence of node B ("upstream") more than vice versa (e.g., Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2020). Although DAGs have occasionally been used in clinical psychology, they have increasingly become popular in other fields, especially in epidemiology and environmental sciences, wherein numerous illustrations are available. Therefore, we computed DAGs to generate a computationally driven model of the probabilistic dependencies among the distinct symptoms of anxiety reported during the lockdown. These complementary computational approaches can provide a novel perspective and clues to generating new hypotheses about the functional relations among the anxiety symptoms reported during the COVID-19 lockdown. Data description: The data we plan to use come from an online survey carried out between March 30 and April 10 by the Observatoire de Recherche sur les Médias et le Journalisme (ORM – UCLouvain; i.e., Lits et al., 2020). This survey aimed to gauge the extent of the COVID-19 infodemic in French-speaking Belgium during the COVID-19 lockdown. The survey also included data related to anxiety symptoms (as assessed using the well-validated and broadly used Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale, hereafter GAD-7) because the authors also wanted to evaluate the association between infodemic related behaviors and anxiety feelings during the Belgian lockdown. To do so, they rely on a sum-score of the seven items of the GAD-7. The final report of this survey (i.e., Lits et al., 2020) involves 1,817 French-speaking Belgians. The present re-analysis will focus on the item's responses of GAD-7's (and not the tally-score of the GAD-7) of these participants. Is the data publicly available: Yes, a summarized version can be found here: https://osf.io/z3r4e/ Date of access: 5 October, 2020 Data source: Collected by Grégoire Lits, Louie-Amélie Cougnon, Alexandre Heeren, Bernard Hanseeuw, & Nathan Gurnet, all from UCLouvain, Belgium. Note that the statistical analyst of this pre-registered data re-analysis (i.e., Alexandre Heeren) was involved in the initial data collection. Sampling and data collection procedures: The data collection procedure is well documented in the following research report (available online): Lits, G., Cougnon, L.-A, Heeren, A., Hanseeuw, B., & Gurnet, N. (2020, May 11). Analyse de « l’infodémie » de Covid-19 en Belgique francophone. https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/wsuj3. The sample was built upon a quota sampling method based on age, gender, and education level, and weighted by gender and educational level (following the results of the STATBEL 2019 governmental survey on workforce) to be representative of the characteristics of the population living in the French-speaking part of Belgium over the age of 16. Prior work based on the dataset: The statistical analyst of this preregistration (i.e., Alexandre Heeren) was not the statistical analyst of the two previous research reports based on the initial dataset. So far, the data have been analyzed and reported by Nathan Gurnet and Grégoire Lits for Lits et al., 2020) and by Bernard Hanseeuw and Nathan Gurnet for Hanseeuw et al., 2020). Prior knowledge of current dataset: The variable we are interested in from this dataset has already been processed in two previous publications aiming at depicting the COVID-19 infodemic-related behaviors in French-speaking Belgium (e.g., Hanseeuw, Cougnon, Heeren, Gurnet, & Lits, 2020; Lits, G., Cougnon, L.-A, Heeren, A., Hanseeuw, B., & Gurnet, N., 2020). However, these publications did not focus on the GAD-7, and only relied on a sum-score of the GAD-7 (i.e., there was no distinction between the seven features of anxiety). Finally, this dataset has never been analyzed via a graph theoretical framework. Here, for the first time, we will re-analyze the data related to anxiety in an exploratory fashion using a network approach (aka graph-theoretical framework). Moment of preregistration: Registration before any analyst on this team handling or analyzing the GAD-7 data using a network approach. Measured variables (that will be included in analyses): Given our research questions (see above), we plan to include the seven items of the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7). Transformations: Following guidelines in using network analysis in clinical psychology (e.g., Epskamp & Fried, 2018), we will apply, for each variable, the nonparanormal transformation via the R package huge (Jiang et al., 2019). Data Inclusion: We will include all participants of the research report of Lits et al. (2020). Outliers: N/A Sample size: For our analyses, the sample size will be 1,817 (as in Lits et al., 2020). Missing data: The final sample of Lits et al. (2020) does not include participants with missing values. Statistical plan: The measured variables (i.e., the 7 variables of the GAD-7; see above) will be included as nodes in the network models and processed as follows: 1. Data Preparation. First, we will test whether our correlation matrix is positive definite (reflecting that nodes are not linear combinations of other nodes). Second, we will search for potential pairs of redundant nodes, that is, nodes that are highly inter-correlated and that correlate to the same degree with other variables. To do so, we will implement the Hittner method for comparing dependent correlations (Hittner, May, & Silver, 2003) via the goldbricker function of the R package networktools (Jones, 2018). If pairs of redundant nodes are identified, they will be combined via the reduce_net function of networktools—i.e., reducing the redundant variables via a principal component analysis of the two variables and creating a new variable. 2. Graphical Gaussian Model. We will use a graphical Gaussian model (GGM) to estimate the undirected network. In this network, edges signify conditional independence relationships between nodes, controlling for the effects of all other nodes (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). We will present GGMs that will be regularized via the graphical LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) algorithm, which serves two primary functions (Friedman, Hastie, & Tibshirani, 2011). First, it computes regularized partial correlations between pairs of nodes, thereby eliminating spurious associations (edges) attributable to the influence of other nodes in the network. Second, it shrinks trivially small associations to zero, thereby removing potentially “false positive” edges from the graph and producing a sparse graph comprising only the strongest edges. We will use the R package qgraph (Epskamp et al., 2012) that automatically implements the graphical LASSO regularization in combination with Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC) model selection (Foygel & Drton, 2011). In this procedure, 100 models with varying degrees of sparsity are estimated; a final model is selected according to the lowest EBIC value, given a specific hyperparameter gamma (γ), which controls the trade-off between including false-positive edges and removing true edges. The hyperparameter γ is usually set between zero and 0.5 (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). The closer one chooses a value of γ near 0.5, the more the EBIC will favor a simpler model containing fewer edges, whereas the closer one chooses a value of γ near zero, the more the EBIC will favor a model with more edges. We will opt to set γ to 0.5 to be confident that our edges are genuine, assuming that the true model is, indeed, sparse (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). To estimate the stability of edges, we will bootstrap the confidence regions of the edge weights via the R package bootnet (Epskamp, Borsboom, & Fried, 2018). We will set the bootstraps to 1,000. To quantify the importance of each node in the resulting graphical LASSO network, we will compute the expected influence centrality index (Robinaugh, Millner, & McNally, 2016). The expected influence of a node is the sum of the edge weights incident on a given node, including positive and negative values. Higher expected influence values indicate greater centrality and thus greater importance in the network. We will evaluate the stability of the centrality metrics by implementing a subset bootstrap procedure (Costenbader & Valente, 2003). To do so, we will repeatedly correlate the centrality metrics of the original dataset with the metrics calculated from a subsample of participants missing via person-dropping bootstraps (we will set the bootstraps to 1,000) as implemented in the R package bootnet (Epskamp et al., 2018). We will also calculate the centrality stability correlation coefficient (CS-coefficient) to quantify the effects of this person-dropping procedure. The CS-coefficient represents the maximum proportion of participants that can be dropped while maintaining a 95% probability that the correlation between centrality metrics from the full data set and the subset data are at least .70. Based on a simulation study (Epskamp et al., 2018), a minimum CS-coefficient of .25 (and preferably ≥ .50) is recommended for interpreting centrality indices. Using a bootstrapped difference test, we will then capitalize on this subset bootstrap procedure to test whether nodes statistically differ between them in terms of expected influence values. Because recent commentators have argued that differential variability—that is, the phenomenon that variables have drastically different variances—may distort conclusions about node centrality (e.g., Fried, 2016; Terluin, de Boer, & de Vet, 2016), we will also compute the correlations between the standard deviation and the expected influence centrality value of each variable. This approach will allow us to test whether there is an association between nodes' importance in the network and its variability. Finally, we will test whether the nodes denoting the hallmark features of anxiety feelings during COVID-19 cohere as one or multiple subnetworks (“communities”). Following prior network research (e.g., Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2018; Robinaugh, LeBlanc, Vuletich, & McNally, 2014), we will implement the spin-glass algorithm (Reichardt & Bornholdt, 2006), a modularity-based community detection procedure suitable for uncovering the structure of relatively small networks with negative edge values (e.g., Traag & Bruggeman, 2009). We will use the spinglass.community function (γ = 1, start temperature = 1, stop temperature = .01, cooling factor = .99, spins = 7) of the R package igraph (Csardi & Nepusz, 2006). Nodes within a community are more strongly interconnected than they are with nodes in another community. In case of community structure, we will identify important nodes that may serve as bridges between the resultant communities by computing the bridge expected influence index via the bridge function of the R package networktools (Jones, 2018). Bridge expected influence is the sum of the edge weights connecting a given node to all nodes in the other community or communities (Jones, Ma, & McNally, 2019). As for the centrality metrics, in the case of a community structure, we will evaluate the stability of the bridge centrality estimates via person-dropping bootstraps (we will set the bootstraps to 1,000) as implemented in the R package bootnet and compute the related CS-coefficient (Epskamp et al., 2018). Using a bootstrapped difference test, we will also capitalize on this subset bootstrap procedure to test whether nodes statistically differ between them in terms of bridge expected influence values. 3. Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Finally, we will compute a DAG to estimate a directed, potentially “causal” structure of the system (Pearl et al., 2016). We will use a Bayesian hill-climbing algorithm implemented via the R package bnlearn (Scutari, 2010). As implemented by bnlearn, the bootstrap function computes the structural aspects of the network model by adding edges, removing them, and reversing their direction to ultimately optimize the goodness-of-fit target score, i.e., the Bayesian Information Criterion. This involves an iterative process of randomly restarting this process with different possible edges linking different node pairs, perturbing the system, and using 50 different random restarts to avoid local maxima. Following our previous works (Bernstein, Heeren, & McNally, 2017; Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2020; McNally, Heeren, & Robinaugh, 2017), we will perform 100 perturbations (i.e., attempts to insert, delete, or reverse an edge) for each restart. As this iterative procedure unfolds, the function returns the best fitting network based on this random restart/perturbation procedure. To ensure the stability of the resultant DAG, we will then bootstrap 10,000 samples (with replacement), compute a network for each sample, and average across the resulting networks to produce a final network structure (e.g., Blanchard, Roskam, Mikolajczak, & Heeren, 2020; Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2020; McNally, Heeren, & Robinaugh, 2017), involving a two-step procedure. First, we will determine how frequently a given edge appeared in the 10,000 bootstrapped networks. We will then use the optimal cut-point method of Scutari and Nagarajan (2013) for retaining edges, which yields networks having both high sensitivity and high specificity. Second, we will ascertain the direction of each surviving edge in the 10,000 bootstrapped networks. If a given edge points from node X to node Y in at least 51% of the bootstrapped networks, then this direction will be represented in the final network. In summary, we will first determine the network structure (i.e., whether an edge is present or not), and then determine the direction of each surviving edge. References Asmundson, G., & Taylor, S. title: Circulating Tumor DNA-Based Molecular Residual Disease After Curative-Intent Therapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: An Umbrella Review of Diagnostic Accuracy, Recurrence Prediction, and Adjuvant-Treatment Guidance
description:
This project is an umbrella review evaluating the role of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based molecular residual disease (MRD) assessment after curative-intent therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The review synthesizes evidence from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, reconstructed individual-patient-data analyses, pooled analyses, and diagnostic test accuracy studies to assess the prognostic value, diagnostic performance, and potential clinical utility of ctDNA-MRD for recurrence prediction, survival outcomes, and adjuvant-treatment guidance.

The review includes evidence from multiple databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, Europe PMC, Embase, and Semantic Scholar. Outcomes of interest include recurrence-free survival (RFS), disease-free survival (DFS), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, area under the curve (AUC), and molecular lead time. The study also evaluates methodological quality using an AMSTAR-2-informed framework and quantifies overlap among included evidence syntheses using corrected covered area (CCA) analysis.

The findings suggest that ctDNA-MRD positivity is consistently associated with poorer recurrence-related and survival outcomes, particularly in post-treatment and longitudinal surveillance settings. The study highlights the potential of ctDNA-MRD as a prognostic and trial-enrichment biomarker while emphasizing current limitations related to assay heterogeneity, review overlap, and lack of randomized MRD-guided intervention evidence.

This OSF project contains materials related to the umbrella review, including the manuscript, supplementary materials, methodological documentation, and associated research outputs.

title: Performance of Large Language Models in Automated Medical Literature Screening: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
This project aims to systematically evaluate the performance, reliability, and heterogeneity of large language models (LLMs) in the automated screening of medical literature. As the volume of scientific publications continues to grow exponentially, the screening phase of systematic reviews has become increasingly time-consuming and labor-intensive. Recent advances in artificial intelligence—particularly large language models such as GPT-series, LLaMA, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek, and Qwen—have shown the potential to automate key steps of evidence synthesis. However, the accuracy, consistency, and generalizability of these models across different screening tasks and clinical domains remain unclear.

This study will conduct a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis to summarize existing evidence on the use of LLMs for title/abstract screening, citation filtering, and study selection in medical and health-related systematic reviews. We will assess multiple performance indicators, including sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1-score, workload reduction, and time efficiency. We also aim to explore sources of heterogeneity, such as model type, prompt design, clinical field, screening task complexity, dataset characteristics, and evaluation methodology.

The review will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Searches will be conducted across PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and preprint servers. Eligible studies will include evaluations of LLM-assisted or fully automated literature screening workflows, using either real-world systematic review datasets or curated benchmark sets. Risk of bias will be assessed using adapted tools for AI performance studies. Where feasible, meta-analysis will be performed to synthesize quantitative performance metrics.

title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Acne Severity Assessment: A Systematic Benchmarking Study of Diagnostic Accuracy and Fitzpatrick Skin Type Bias Using Open-Access Dermatological Datasets
description: This cross-sectional benchmarking study evaluates the agreement between contemporary multimodal large language models (LLMs) — including GPT-4o/GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, SkinGPT-4, and LLaVA-Med — and a consensus reference standard established by board-certified dermatologists, for the task of acne severity grading using the Global Acne Grading System (GAGS) and the Investigator's Global Assessment (IGA). The study uses exclusively publicly available, openly licensed dermatological image datasets (ACNE04, SCIN, DermNet NZ, PAD-UFES-20). The primary analysis quantifies overall diagnostic agreement using quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa; pre-specified secondary analyses examine performance disparities across Fitzpatrick skin types I–VI using established algorithmic fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, false negative rate parity). Additional analyses include prompt sensitivity, run-to-run reliability, inter-model agreement, and clinical impact of misclassifications on guideline-based treatment recommendations. The study is reported in full compliance with the CLEAR Derm, TRIPOD-AI, CLAIM 2024, STARD 2015, and PROBAST-AI guidelines.

title: MENSTRUAL HEALTH POLICIES AND THEIR IMPACTS ON SCHOOL LIFE AND QUALITY OF LIFE OF ADOLESCENTS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
Objective: The objective of this scoping review is to map the available evidence regarding the repercussions of public menstrual health policies on adolescents’ school life and quality of life.

Type of review: This study is characterized as a scoping review conducted according to the methodological recommendations of the Joanna Briggs Institute (PETERS et al., 2020) and guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines (TRICCO et al., 2018). The review protocol will be previously registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF), a platform dedicated to the registration and sharing of scientific protocols and preprints.

Description of the research question: The research question was developed based on the PCC strategy, an acronym for Population, Concept, and Context, as recommended by the Joanna Briggs Institute (2021). In this review, the following elements were defined: P (Population) – adolescents; C (Concept) – menstrual health policies; and C (Context) – school and community settings or national and international policies related to health and education. Based on this structure, the following guiding question was established: “How do public menstrual health policies impact adolescents’ school life and quality of life?”

Descriptors: The search strategy will be developed using descriptors indexed in DeCS and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), including: Adolescent; Menstruation; Menstrual Hygiene Products; Educational Status; Quality of Life; Health Policy, and their corresponding terms in Portuguese. Keywords related to the topic will also be used, such as: Menstrual Health; Period Poverty; Menstrual Health Policies; Menstrual Hygiene Management Policies; School Attendance; Academic Performance; School Performance; saúde menstrual; pobreza menstrual; frequência escolar; desempenho escolar; and políticas de saúde menstrual. The Boolean operators “AND” and “OR” will be employed to combine terms, aiming to increase the sensitivity and specificity of the search strategy.

Search strategy: The search strategy will be developed through access to the CAPES Journal Portal, including the following databases and information sources: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, LILACS, CINAHL, Embase, Web of Science, CAPES Theses and Dissertations Catalog, Google Scholar, ENAP portal, Ministry of Education portal, and Ministry of Health portal. The Rayyan online platform will be used for the organization and selection of studies. The process of screening titles, abstracts, full-text reading, and data extraction will be independently carried out by two reviewers. Any disagreements will be discussed among the researchers until consensus is reached.

Search string: In the MEDLINE database, the following search strategy will be applied:
((((((Adolescent OR Adolescents OR Teenager OR Youth)) AND ((Menstruation OR "Menstrual Health" OR "Period Poverty" OR "Menstrual Hygiene Products" OR "Menstrual Hygiene Management"))) AND (("Menstrual Health Policies" OR "Menstrual Hygiene Management Policies" OR "Public Policy" OR "Health Policy"))) AND (("Educational Status" OR "School Attendance" OR "Academic Performance" OR "School Performance" OR Education OR School))) AND (("Quality of Life"))).

Inclusion and exclusion criteria: The inclusion criteria will comprise studies available in the selected databases addressing public policies, programs, strategies, or interventions related to menstrual health and their repercussions on school attendance, academic performance, and adolescents’ quality of life. Studies involving actions such as distribution of menstrual products, menstrual health education, combating period poverty, improvement of sanitation and menstrual hygiene conditions in school and community environments, as well as governmental or institutional policies aimed at promoting menstrual dignity, will be considered. Research conducted with adolescents, regardless of sex, language, country of origin, or year of publication, will be included. Duplicate studies, publications not available in full text, review studies, editorials, letters to the editor, conference abstracts, opinions, research protocols, and investigations that do not directly address the relationship between menstrual health policies and outcomes related to school attendance/academic performance or adolescents’ quality of life will be excluded.

title: Evaluation of a conversational AI system for simulated clinical scenarios in medical education: a mixed-methods multi-centre study
description:
Effective consultation skills remain fundamental to high-quality healthcare delivery, influencing diagnostic accuracy, patient satisfaction, and clinical outcomes. This protocol describes a mixed-methods evaluation of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for simulated clinical scenarios in undergraduate medical education. The study will recruit the entire third-year cohort of medical students (n=271) at the University of Bristol to compare AI virtual patients with traditional actor-based simulations across four standardised primary care scenarios. Quantitative assessment will employ validated measures including an abridged version of the Immersive Technology Evaluation Measure (ITEM) (see appendix A), the User Experience Questionnaire-Short (UEQ-S), and an adapted educational AI technology feedback questionnaire based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), whilst qualitative data will be collected through focus groups analysed using Braun and Clarke's thematic framework. The primary outcome measures perceived realism, technical usability factors, and educational value of AI consultations compared to actor simulations. Secondary outcomes include AI’s comparative performance across (four) different clinical scenarios, feedback quality assessment, and recommendations for curricular integration. Statistical analysis will employ non-parametric methods with effect size calculations and confidence intervals, whilst qualitative analysis will be conducted independently by two researchers with subsequent consensus meetings. This comprehensive evaluation will provide evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI virtual patients for communication skills training, informing future integration into medical curricula whilst addressing stakeholder concerns about the role of technology in clinical education.

title: Diagnostic Assessment for Professional Performance Improvement
description:
Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) positions Diagnostic Assessment for Professional Performance Improvement as a foundational scholarly contribution that reframes professional performance assessment from a summative, judgment-oriented practice into a diagnostic, developmental, and ethically grounded system. The book responds to a global organizational challenge in which performance evaluations often fail to identify underlying causes of performance gaps, leading to ineffective interventions and diminished professional trust.
From the perspective articulated by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), diagnostic assessment serves as an analytical mechanism to understand not only what level of performance is achieved, but why performance emerges in a particular form. This distinction is critical in complex professional environments where performance is influenced by competence, motivation, psychosocial context, organizational design, and systemic constraints.
The central objective advanced by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) is to establish a scientifically grounded framework for diagnosing professional performance that integrates psychometric rigor, organizational psychology, and human-centered management principles. Rather than treating performance deficits as individual failure, the book conceptualizes them as multidimensional signals requiring structured interpretation.
Methodologically, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) adopts an interdisciplinary approach, synthesizing diagnostic logic from educational assessment, clinical psychology, and strategic human resource management. This approach enables performance assessment to function as a learning-oriented process embedded within continuous professional development systems.
A key contribution articulated by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) is the differentiation between evaluative assessment and diagnostic assessment. While evaluative assessment categorizes outcomes, diagnostic assessment identifies causal patterns, developmental needs, and contextual misalignments that hinder professional effectiveness.
The book further examines the role of digital tools and analytics, as discussed by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), emphasizing their potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy while warning against reductive performance metrics detached from human meaning.
Implications outlined by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) extend to leadership decision-making, talent development, performance coaching, and organizational learning systems. Diagnostic assessment is positioned as a strategic capability that aligns performance improvement with ethical responsibility.
Overall, Diagnostic Assessment for Professional Performance Improvement, as developed by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), offers a comprehensive, evidence-based, and humanistic framework for advancing professional performance in contemporary organizations.

title: Deep Learning for Whole-Slide Histologic Subtyping of Lung Cancer: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis
description:
This project is a systematic review and restricted exploratory diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis evaluating deep learning models for whole-slide histologic subtyping of lung cancer using H&E-stained digital pathology images. The review focuses on clinically relevant classification tasks, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, small-cell carcinoma, and benign or histologic mimic categories. Seven electronic databases (Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Online Library, Europe PMC, and Semantic Scholar) were searched through April 25, 2026.

The study synthesizes evidence regarding the diagnostic performance, methodological quality, and clinical applicability of artificial intelligence systems in computational pathology. Quantitative synthesis was restricted to clinically interpretable whole-slide, slide-, or case-level datasets with extractable 2 × 2 diagnostic accuracy data for adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma. Secondary analyses summarize reported AUCs, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratios, risk of bias, and evidence gaps across different diagnostic tasks.

This review highlights both the promise and current limitations of deep learning for lung cancer histologic classification and emphasizes the need for external validation, standardized reporting, clinically relevant operating thresholds, and pathologist-supervised implementation before routine clinical adoption.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Diagnosis and Segmentation in Laryngoscopy: A Systematic Review
description:
Objective: To systematically evaluate the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI) in laryngoscopic imaging and to compare the diagnostic accuracy and clinical applicability across various imaging modalities and AI architectures.
Methods: Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was performed across PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases for studies published between 2018 and 2025. Original research articles that applied AI to laryngoscopic images or videos for diagnosis, detection, or segmentation were included. Two reviewers independently conducted the literature screening and data extraction.
Results: A total of 42 studies were included. Deep learning models demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to that of clinical experts in the identification of laryngeal lesions. Models utilizing NBI imaging demonstrated superior performance in the detection of early-stage laryngeal cancer compared with standard WLI models. However, the QUADAS-2 assessment revealed that 80% of the studies exhibited a high risk of bias in the "Patient Selection" domain, primarily attributed to the retrospective pre-selection of high-quality images with limited sample sizes.
Conclusion: AI holds significant potential in laryngeal lesion detection and can effectively augment clinicians workflows. However，despite the high-performance metrics reported, significant challenges persist . Future research should prioritize the development of high-quality datasets and facilitate the clinical translation of AI systems.

title: BipoSense Statistical Process Control Method
description: Early detection of emerging affective episodes is crucial in managing bipolar disorder (BD). Passive sensing - passive data collection via smartphone or wearable - offers a promising solution by potentially capturing altered activity, communication, and sleep patterns, indicative of manic and depressive episodes. Recently, statistical process control (SPC) has been introduced to psychopathology as a novel approach to identify out-of-control processes. However, its application to mobile sensing data and to bipolar disorder remains unexplored. To investigate SPC’s potential in detecting emerging affective episodes, we utilized the BipoSense study, which monitored patients with BD. The BipoSense data covers 12 months of continuously collected passive sensing data via smartphone app, daily e-diary data and bi-weekly expert interviews, i.e. 26 in a row, to assess the psychopathological status. Compliance was excellent. A total of 29 depressive and 20 (hypo)manic emerging episodes in 28 patients were included in the analyses. SPC charts and multilevel analyses revealed heterogenous results. Passive sensing, despite its potential as a low-burden, continuous measurement tool, did not demonstrate robust detection of affective episodes or prodromal states. Self-rated current bipolar mood, assessed via e-diary, outperformed passive sensing parameters in predicting current episodes, whereas predicting prodromal phases was also limited. Notably, SPC with personalized control limits did not surpass established clinical cut-off scores. Even after systematic optimization of SPC settings, the combination of detected emerging episodes in relation to false alarms was insufficient for clinical use. Future studies warrant mobile sensing parameters closer aligned to psychopathology, therewith increasing validity, sensitivity, and specificity.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection of Colorectal Cancers Using Capsule Endoscopy Data: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to weigh heavily on public health worldwide, with the latest GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates pointing to 1.9 million new diagnoses and more than 900,000 fatalities in the last year, cementing CRC’s position as the third-most diagnosed cancer and the second-deadliest across the globe (6). Projections suggest that by 2040, the annual case load will swell to beyond 3.2 million, marking a 63% steep climb driven chiefly by aging populations, dietary choices, rising obesity rates, and related metabolic syndromes (6). Observers note that the increase is not confined to any single continent, surfacing in high Human Development Index (HDI) nations and spreading rapidly through many areas of Asia, with particular acceleration evident in North America, Australasia, and several Latin American nations (6). While screening technologies and therapeutic advances have improved, the stubbornly high death toll underscores the imminent requirement for more effective early-detection initiatives on a worldwide scale (6).

Capsule Endoscopy (CE) has transformed the assessment of the gastrointestinal tract by providing a comfortable, silent, and awake-viewed tour through the GI tract via a tiny wireless camera that patients simply swallow in a gel-encased pill. The pioneer of this approach, the PillCam (originally named M2A), first targeted the often-cryptic small bowel and achieved FDA clearance in the United States in August 2001 (4,12,13). Following this advance, the colon capsule innovation arose, offering a gentler second look at the colon for patients hesitant to endure the rigors of colonoscopy preparation or those whose index colonoscopy was incomplete. The PillCam Colon 2, developed by Given Imaging and later acquired by Medtronic, received de novo FDA clearance in November 2012 and was marketed in 2014 to address the clinical need for accurate polyp detection in carefully selected patients (1,4,12). Multiple studies and meta-analyses confirm that, with appropriate indications, colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) detects the majority of clinically relevant colonic polyps, showing 88–95% agreement for polyps ≥6 mm compared with standard colonoscopy (2,3,12).

Manual review of CCE data involves tens of thousands of images per procedure, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has emerged as a transformative tool to automate lesion detection, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and reduce interpretation time (1,4,14–17). Studies report AI polyp detection sensitivities of up to 98.1% in CCE datasets, with significant reductions in reading time by as much as 70% compared with expert human reviewers (1,4,14,15). Recent research also emphasizes the importance of developing explainable AI models to improve clinical acceptance and integrate trusted decision support into clinical workflows (5).

Despite the promising advances, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding AI algorithms, study methodologies, evaluated capsule platforms, target lesions (e.g., polyp size, dysplasia vs. carcinoma), and performance metrics (1–4,7,8,14,15,17). A comprehensive scoping review is therefore crucial to systematically map existing global evidence, classify AI and machine learning approaches applied to capsule endoscopy data for early CRC detection, synthesize diagnostic performance metrics, and identify current knowledge gaps and limitations. This will support future research planning, clinical translation, and deployment of AI-augmented capsule endoscopy as a scalable CRC screening tool. The purpose of the study is to identify and categorize artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches including deep learning, convolutional neural networks, and other AI algorithms applied to colon capsule endoscopy for the early detection of colorectal cancer and precursor lesions and to summarize and report diagnostic performance metrics (such as sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy) and highlight key gaps, limitations, and challenges in the current evidence base to inform future research and clinical adoption.

title: NyameriNet
description: The development of "Nyameri," a hypothetical next-generation mobile application for diabetic retinopathy (DR) image analysis, represents a synthesis of cutting-edge academic research and commercial product features into a cohesive, plausible technology. The core of the Nyameri system is its custom-designed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), named NyameriNet. This architecture is engineered to deliver high diagnostic accuracy while operating efficiently on mobile devices without constant reliance on cloud connectivity. While specific architectural details like the exact number of layers are not provided in the source materials, the design philosophy aligns with state-of-the-art models known for their balance of performance and efficiency. For instance, NyameriNet's estimated size of approximately 40 MB is comparable to DRNet13, which was reported to be 35 MB. This suggests an architecture that may incorporate techniques such as depthwise separable convolutions or other forms of model optimization to maintain a small footprint. The primary function of NyameriNet is a five-class classification task: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative DR. This multi-stage grading is a standard benchmark in the field, reflecting the clinical need for precise disease staging. The simulated performance of NyameriNet is projected to exceed current clinical standards, positioning it as a highly advanced tool. The model is expected to achieve an accuracy rate between 96% and 98%, a figure supported by numerous studies on complex CNN architectures. For example, a DenseNet-121 model using CLAHE and ESRGAN preprocessing on the APTOS 2019 dataset achieved 98.36% accuracy , while a hybrid Inception v3 model reached 98.7% accuracy on the same dataset. Similarly, a modified VGGNet-based transfer learning model trained on the Kaggle EyePACS dataset achieved 96.6% accuracy after extensive data augmentation. Sensitivity and specificity are critical metrics for any screening tool, and NyameriNet's projected values aim to surpass established benchmarks. An estimated sensitivity of 97-98% significantly outperforms the minimum requirements set by bodies like the British Diabetic Association (BDA) of 80%. This level of performance is consistent with top-tier models; for instance, a study on the Messidor-2 dataset achieved a sensitivity of 97.63% , and another model reached 99.21% on the Kaggle test dataset. Specificity is projected to be in the range of 95-97%, also exceeding the BDA's 95% minimum requirement. Models like DeB5-XNet have demonstrated 97.1% specificity on the DDR dataset , and a WFDLN model achieved 98.0% specificity on the Messidor dataset. These figures underscore the potential of modern deep learning to provide highly reliable screening results. The model's precision and F1-score are also projected to be very high, at 0.96-0.98, indicating a low rate of false positives and a strong balance between precision and recall.

title: Giving Voice to the COVID Generation: Assessing Language Development and Risk for Impairments
description:
Children born during the COVID-19 pandemic (BDC) are now in preschool and have experienced unprecedented social and educational restrictions as well as reduced linguistic input during critical developmental years. The long-term consequences of these constraints on language acquisition remain critically understudied, creating an urgent need for research. This project undertakes the timely research endeavor of providing a systematic characterization of language development in BDC preschoolers, and developing an evidence-based, open-access multivariable risk calculator to estimate individual risk for language impairments.
Portugal, one of the EU countries that implemented the strictest COVID-19 measures, offers a unique setting to assess the impact of pandemic- related constraints on child development. Our previous research has highlighted significant developmental delays in BDC infants, toddlers, and preschoolers, reinforcing the importance of this project. By leveraging advanced statistical modeling and interdisciplinary expertise, this project will identify key predictors of language impairments and translate findings into a practical tool that enhances early identification and intervention.

Over 18 months, this project will follow a structured four-phase approach:

Phase 1 | Systematic Literature Review: A systematic literature review will synthesize quantitative findings to establish a comprehensive overview of the pandemic's impact on early language development. These findings will directly inform the design of the parental questionnaires used in the subsequent phase, ensuring that the study focuses on the most critical environmental and social factors.

Phase 2 | Longitudinal Study: This phase will include a large-scale longitudinal study with two cohorts of typically developing BDC children (4- year-olds with one year of pandemic exposure and 5-year-olds with two years of exposure, n=400). Data will be collected at two-time points, with a one-year interval between each collection. Caregivers will complete questionnaires based on the relevant findings from the systematic literature review conducted in Phase 1. Children will undergo individual standardized language assessments to evaluate their language skills. Data analysis will employ Structural Equation Modeling to uncover the direct and indirect effects of pandemic-related restrictions on language development, accounting for critical environmental and social factors.

Phase 3 | Development of a Multivariable Risk Model: Building on the findings from Phase 2, a predictive model will be developed to identify key risk factors, such as sociodemographic, environmental, and developmental variables contributing to language delays. Logistic regression will be employed to construct the model, estimating the likelihood of language impairments based on these factors. The model will output a probability score categorized into low, moderate, and high risk. Cross-validation will be performed to ensure model robustness using measures of sensitivity and specificity. Post-validation adjustments will refine the model based on data analysis.

Phase 4 | Creation of the Risk4LI Calculator: The model developed in Phase 3 will be used to create the Risk4LI calculator, implemented as a free interactive web-based form. This will ensure accessibility for professionals in education, healthcare, and related fields. The tool will allow personalized, real-time assessment of child-specific risk factors, facilitating referrals for more comprehensive assessments and early interventions before language difficulties escalate. By providing a free, user-friendly platform, this project bridges the gap between scientific research and practice, offering a solution with applicability beyond the scope of this study.

This research is both timely and critical. Language development is foundational for academic success and social integration, yet pandemic-born cohorts remain at risk for long-term difficulties. The project's interdisciplinary approach, integrating linguistics, psychology, education, speech therapy, clinical sciences, and informatics expertise, ensures a robust analysis of developmental trajectories while delivering tangible solutions for language assessments. The resulting research will have a lasting impact on scientific research and contribute to the development of educational and clinical policies.

Beyond its immediate impact, this project sets the stage for future advancements in early language screening. Risk4LI's framework can be adapted for other populations and enhanced using machine learning techniques to refine predictive accuracy. These potential applications position Risk4LI as a transformative tool in childhood research, education, and clinical practice, helping to identify and support children at risk of language delays, ultimately ensuring better outcomes for BDC children and future generations.

title: Coverage of the rapid molecular test for the diagnosis of Tuberculosis in different global contexts: scoping review protocol
description: Introduction: Tuberculosis (TB) is a disease that stands out for its prevalence in areas characterized by high social vulnerability and densely populated regions. Among the main challenges faced by management and healthcare are delays in the diagnosis of the disease. Although sputum smear microscopy is a low-cost and simple diagnostic technique, it has significant limitations, such as low sensitivity and specificity. In light of these limitations, the increase in new TB cases in recent years, and with the goal of achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) related to social and health responses for combating the disease, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the global implementation of Rapid Molecular Testing for TB (RMT-TB) starting in December 2010. Therefore, the objective of this study is to analyze the coverage of RMT-TB in different global contexts. Methods and Analysis: This is a scoping review protocol, where eligible studies will be screened using the PCC strategy, through publications indexed in the MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, LILACS databases, and the Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations (BDTD). Keywords from the literature and descriptors indexed to the Health Sciences Descriptors and Medical Subject Headings platforms will be used, connected through the boolean operators “OR” and “AND.” A specific form will be developed for extracting variables of interest from the studies included in the review, and the data will subsequently undergo descriptive analysis and narrative synthesis by the authors.
