Detailed Description of Research Project

Title: Agentic AI in Medical Image Analysis: A Preliminary PRISMA-Guided Evidence Map of Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Multi-Agent Systems, and Model Context Protocol Integration in Radiology and Pathology

Authors: Pedram M. Aghaei, Behnam Kiani Kalejahi, Kamila Khalimova, Mohammad Javad Rajabi Institution: Department of Computer Science and Biomedical Engineering, School of Engineering, Central Asian University, Tashkent 111221, Uzbekistan Corresponding author: p.aghaei@cau.uz Registration date: June 2026

1. Background and Motivation

Medical imaging generates more than one billion radiological examinations annually worldwide. Global radiologist supply is severely constrained — the World Health Organisation estimates that two-thirds of the global population lacks access to diagnostic imaging services, and in high-income countries radiologist workload has increased by approximately 40% over the past decade. These pressures are making AI-assisted workflow support increasingly important. At the same time, the complexity of clinical imaging decisions is growing: integration with genomic data, treatment planning systems, multi-disciplinary team inputs, and longitudinal patient histories demands a fundamentally different class of AI tool than the narrow classifiers developed over the past decade.

Deep learning transformed specific, well-defined imaging tasks — lesion detection, organ segmentation, cancer screening — with landmark studies achieving expert-level performance on narrow benchmarks. However, these systems operate in isolation. They process single inputs and return single outputs, cannot retrieve guidelines, cannot integrate clinical history or prior reports, provide no natural-language interface, and offer no mechanism for workflow integration beyond a single prediction score. Their clinical adoption has accordingly been limited relative to their technical performance.

A second, structurally distinct transformation is now underway. Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and vision-language models (VLMs) enable simultaneous reasoning over imaging data and clinical text. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), originally proposed for knowledge-intensive natural language processing, has been adapted to ground clinical AI outputs in retrieved guidelines, protocols, and domain-specific documents, with early evidence of substantially reduced hallucination rates. Agentic architectures — systems capable of planning multi-step tasks, invoking external tools, querying clinical databases, and coordinating specialised processing modules — represent an emerging layer that may enable dynamic, context-sensitive imaging workflow support. The recent standardisation of agent-infrastructure connectivity through protocols such as Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) further opens pathways to integration with DICOM/PACS servers, electronic health records, reporting templates, and clinical knowledge bases.

Together, these five architectural layers — passive LLMs/VLMs, RAG, agentic RAG, autonomous agents, multi-agent systems, and MCP-style integration — are creating an entirely new class of clinical AI. The published evidence on this transition is growing exponentially, concentrated almost entirely in 2025–2026. However, the evidence base is highly heterogeneous across architecture, task, modality, evaluation method, clinical domain, and deployment context, making narrative reviews unreliable and meta-analysis impossible without a preliminary systematic mapping exercise.

2. Knowledge Gap

Despite the rapid growth of published work, no PRISMA-guided systematic evidence map exists that comprehensively characterises the full architectural spectrum from passive LLMs through RAG, autonomous agents, multi-agent systems, and MCP-style integration infrastructure specifically within medical imaging. Several reviews address adjacent topics — RAG in radiology, foundation models in pathology, LLMs in healthcare broadly — but none maps the complete architectural landscape, proposes a unifying taxonomy, conducts comparative quality appraisal across tiers, or provides a structured governance and clinical readiness framework. This evidence map is designed to address that gap.

3. Purpose and Research Question

The primary purpose of this study is to produce a preliminary PRISMA-guided systematic evidence map of agentic AI architectures in medical image analysis — characterising the available evidence, proposing a unifying taxonomy, identifying research priorities, and establishing the methodological foundation for a completed systematic scoping review.

Primary research question: What LLM, VLM, RAG, autonomous-agent, multi-agent, and MCP-style architectures have been applied to radiology and pathology imaging workflows, and what evidence — at any maturity stage — exists for their design, performance, safety, governance, and deployment readiness?

Five specific objectives:

Provisionally characterise the medical imaging tasks, clinical domains, and imaging modalities addressed by agentic and foundation-model AI systems across radiology and pathology.
Propose and validate a novel six-tier architecture taxonomy (T0: Passive LLM/VLM → T1: RAG → T2: Agentic RAG → T3: Autonomous Agent → T4: Multi-Agent System → T5: MCP-style Integration) that organises the current evidence landscape and is designed to remain applicable as foundation model capabilities evolve.
Map data sources, clinical tools, and infrastructure connections (DICOM/PACS, EHR, clinical guidelines, WSI platforms, report templates) used by each architecture tier.
Assess, in a representative subsample, the evaluation methods, performance metrics, validation design, hallucination assessment approaches, and clinical readiness levels of identified systems.
Propose a governance and safety framework and a five-priority research agenda to guide both the completion of this review and the broader research field.
4. Study Design and Methods

This study is a preliminary PRISMA-guided systematic scoping review, following PRISMA 2020 for review reporting, PRISMA-ScR for scoping review extensions, and PRISMA-S for systematic search strategy documentation. A scoping design was selected because the evidence base is too heterogeneous in architecture, task, modality, evaluation method, and clinical context for meta-analysis to be appropriate or valid at this stage.

This work is explicitly a preliminary evidence map, not a completed systematic scoping review. Three major databases (Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library) have not yet been searched due to institutional authentication constraints, and human dual-review of the full 223-record eligible pool is underway. The present registration documents the protocol in its current state. The completed systematic review — incorporating all database searches, full human dual-review, complete data extraction, and comprehensive quality appraisal — is the planned final output.

Information sources and search strategy: Formal Boolean searches were executed in Scopus (330 records, official RIS export, 8 June 2026) and PubMed/MEDLINE (10 records, official NBIB export, 8 June 2026; note: this primary query is acknowledged as a likely undercount and will be supplemented with six broader queries covering report generation, digital pathology, multimodal AI, clinical decision support, agentic AI, and vision-language models). A peer-maintained grey-literature supplementary source was accessed (GitHub: Awesome-AI-Agents-for-Healthcare; 169 unique records after deduplication). Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library were not searchable due to institutional access restrictions; all documented search strings for these databases are included in this registration and will be executed to complete the review. After cross-source deduplication, 500 unique candidate records were identified.

Selection process: Automated four-tier title/abstract classification was applied to all 500 records: P0 (core agentic/RAG/MCP + imaging domain confirmed — 126 records), P1 (LLM/VLM/FM + imaging confirmed — 97 records), P2 (uncertain — 172 records, retained for secondary consultation), P3 (excluded — 105 records). A total of 223 P0+P1 records were identified for full-text retrieval. Human dual-review of all 223 records with inter-rater reliability calculation (target Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.80) and conflict-resolution protocol is currently underway.

Representative subsample: To anchor the preliminary evidence map before full-text review is complete, a purposive representative subsample of 40 studies was selected across all six architecture tiers, prioritising peer-reviewed studies, maximising domain diversity (radiology: n = 22; pathology: n = 14; infrastructure/governance: n = 4), and including the five highest-cited or most recently published records per tier. Of these, 32 met final eligibility on full-text review and are reported in the evidence map tables.

Data extraction: For all 32 included subsample studies, data extraction covered: bibliographic identifiers; clinical domain and imaging modality; architecture tier assignment (T0–T5); specific model(s) and version; retrieval mechanism; tool specification; dataset; evaluation metrics with confidence intervals; validation design; human-in-the-loop status; hallucination assessment; governance features; and clinical readiness level (L0–L4). Full extraction will be applied to all final included studies in the completed review.

Quality appraisal: Applied to the 32-study subsample using: QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies (n = 8); CLAIM for medical imaging AI papers (n = 18); DECIDE-AI for clinical decision support evaluation papers (n = 6); and a custom five-domain checklist for agentic/RAG/MCP papers not covered by existing instruments (n = 12), assessing retrieval source authority, tool-call reliability, output faithfulness and hallucination risk, auditability and explainability, and human oversight provision.

Evidence strength labelling: All cited studies carry evidence level labels applied consistently throughout: Peer-reviewed clinical (indexed clinical journal); Peer-reviewed benchmark (indexed CS/AI venue); Preprint (arXiv/bioRxiv/medRxiv, not yet peer-reviewed); Grey literature (technical specification, GitHub repository, or institutional documentation). This stratification ensures preprint results and grey literature are not inadvertently presented as peer-reviewed clinical evidence.

Synthesis approach: Narrative synthesis across six themes: architecture taxonomy, clinical domain and modality, evaluation methodology, clinical readiness, governance and safety, and deployment context. Quantitative meta-analysis is not attempted owing to fundamental heterogeneity.

5. Expected Outcomes

Primary deliverable — Preliminary evidence map (current): A preliminary PRISMA-guided evidence map providing the following original contributions: (1) a novel six-tier architecture taxonomy for agentic AI in medical imaging; (2) a comparative preliminary evidence synthesis across radiology (12 representative studies) and pathology (10 representative studies), stratified by evidence strength tier; (3) a clinical readiness distribution table mapping all architecture tiers to deployment levels L0–L4; (4) a governance and safety framework covering hallucination risk, auditability, human oversight, EU AI Act compliance, and FDA SaMD pathways; (5) a five-priority provisional research agenda: prospective RAG clinical validation, standardised agentic benchmarks, clinical governance infrastructure, agentic protocol-modification safety, and regulatory science engagement.

Secondary deliverable — Completed systematic scoping review (planned): Upon completion of the WoS, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library searches; expanded PubMed queries; human dual-review of all 223+ eligible records with kappa reporting; complete data extraction; comprehensive quality appraisal of all included studies; final PRISMA flow diagram with complete counts; and OSF registration identifier confirmed — the full systematic scoping review will supersede this preliminary evidence map. This completed review is expected to cover approximately 600–700 unique records after all database coverage is included, with an estimated 80–120 final included studies across all six architecture tiers.

Specific anticipated findings (provisional, subject to confirmation in completed review):

Within the representative subsample reviewed, RAG architectures (T1) appeared to be the most clinically mature tier, with seven peer-reviewed studies tentatively suggesting accuracy improvements of 6–22% over baseline LLMs in radiology QA tasks and consistent hallucination reduction — however, no prospective multi-centre clinical trial has been conducted for any RAG system. Pathology WSI foundation models (T0) appeared to be the most technically mature category, with several Nature-published models reporting AUROC > 0.90 on pan-cancer benchmarks with external validation, though prospective deployment data are absent. Multi-agent systems (T4) showed promising benchmark performance but uniformly lacked prospective validation and safety documentation. MCP-style integration architectures (T5) were at the conceptual and early prototype stage. All architecture tiers remained at clinical readiness Level 1–2 (retrospective, single-site validation); no agentic system in the representative subsample had completed prospective multi-centre clinical evaluation.

All findings are explicitly provisional and will be confirmed, extended, or revised in the completed systematic review.

6. Significance and Anticipated Impact

This evidence map is expected to make four specific contributions to the field. First, the six-tier architecture taxonomy provides a common language for researchers, clinicians, and regulators to describe and compare agentic AI systems in clinical imaging — a contribution designed to remain applicable as specific foundation models and commercial products evolve. Second, the governance and clinical readiness framework provides a practical tool for radiology departments, AI developers, and regulatory bodies to assess where specific systems stand in the deployment readiness spectrum and what steps are needed to advance. Third, the research priority agenda provides an evidence-based direction for funding bodies and research groups to invest effort most effectively. Fourth, the PRISMA-S documented search strings — including strings for WoS, IEEE, ACM, and four expanded PubMed queries — provide a replicable, extensible foundation that any research group worldwide can use to update or extend this evidence base.

The study builds directly on a progressive research trajectory from the authors' group in deep-learning medical imaging (bone tumour classification, brain tumour GAN segmentation, skin lesion synthesis, liver CAD systematic review, bone age estimation), and extends a companion PRISMA review of LLMs and generative foundation models in cloud-enabled IoMT medical imaging. Together, these works map the transition from narrow discriminative models through generative AI to the fully agentic, workflow-integrated systems characterised in the present evidence map.

7. Limitations Acknowledged at Registration

The following limitations are acknowledged in advance and documented transparently as required by good systematic review practice:

Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library have not yet been searched — the primary coverage limitation of this preliminary map.
The primary PubMed query (n = 10) likely underestimates PubMed coverage; expanded queries are planned.
Human dual-review of the 223-record full-text pool is underway; results presented in the preliminary map are from an automated screening plus a 32-study purposive subsample.
Quality appraisal is indicative, applied to the 32-study subsample only.
OSF registration identifier is pending confirmation.
The evidence base is concentrated in English-language, North American and European, arXiv-published computer science literature — publication bias risk is high.
The field is growing so rapidly that additional relevant records will have been published between the search date (8 June 2026) and any future publication of this review.
8. Funding and Conflicts of Interest

This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sector. All authors declare no competing interests. No commercial AI products or platforms are endorsed by this evidence map.

title: Diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive cardiac troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction: A protocol of randomized double-blind diagnostic trial
description:
Abstract
Background: The sensitivity and specificity of the routine detection of acute myocardial infarction(AMI) in early diagnosis are not high, which can not meet the clinical needs. Copeptin combined with hypersensitive cardiac troponin T(hs-cTnT) is a new detection scheme, and its value in the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction is still unclear. Accordingly, the aim of this study is to evaluate the diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction.
Methods: This is a prospective, randomized, double-blind diagnostic trial to investigate the diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction. Approved by the clinical research ethics of our hospital. Patients were randomly divided into one of two test protocols: (A) copeptin combined with hs-cTnT group and (B) cardiac troponin I (cTnI) group. Patients, doctors, nurses, inspectors, and data-gathering assistants were blinded to group allocation. We will focus on the sensitivity comparison of the two detection methods at different time periods and the sensitivity and specificity comparison of the two detection methods. Data were analyzed using the statistical software package SPSS version 25.0 (Chicago, IL). 
Discussion: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive cardiac troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction. The results of this study will establish clinical evidence for the detection of high sensitivity cardiac troponin T in the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction.

title: The Effectiveness of Deep Learning-Based Convolutional Neural Networks for Automated Detection of the Inferior Alveolar Nerve Canal on Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) Scans: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Reliability, and Clinical Applicability
description:
Background:
Accurate identification of the Inferior Alveolar Nerve Canal (IANC) is crucial in dental sur-gical procedures to prevent complications such as nerve damage. Manual detection of the IANC on Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) scans is time-consuming and prone to operator variability. Deep learning-based Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) offer a promising alternative for automating this process, but their generalizability and clinical ap-plicability remain underexplored.
Objective:
To evaluate the effectiveness, reliability, and clinical applicability of CNNs in the automated detection of the IANC on CBCT scans, identify limitations in current approaches, and pro-pose directions for future research.
Methods:
A systematic review was conducted using databases including PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore. Inclusion criteria focused on studies employing CNNs for IANC detection, reporting key metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB2 tool, and data on CNN architecture, dataset size, and performance were extracted.
Results:
Nine studies were included, employing architectures such as U-Net, ResNet, and DenseNet. CNN models demonstrated high accuracy (85%-97%), sensitivity (84%-95%), and specifici-ty (85%-96%), outperforming manual detection in consistency and reliability. However, lim-itations included small sample sizes, lack of dataset diversity, and overfitting risks, impact-ing generalizability across populations.
Conclusion:
CNNs exhibit significant potential for automating IANC detection on CBCT scans, improv-ing diagnostic precision and reducing variability. Addressing challenges such as dataset di-versity, standardization of evaluation metrics, and external validation is critical for clinical adoption.

description: This repository contains the replication materials for a peer-reviewed study evaluating the reliability of Claude Code (Claude Opus 4.6, agentic deployment) for grading handwritten university exam papers. title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Systematic Review
description:
Breast cancer remains one of the most prevalent cancers affecting women globally. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for improving treatment outcomes and survival rates. In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have emerged as powerful tools in the field of medical diagnostics, particularly in oncology. These technologies have shown promise in enhancing diagnostic accuracy, reducing human error, and streamlining workflows in radiology, pathology, and genomic analysis.
This systematic review aims to comprehensively evaluate existing literature on the application of AI and ML techniques in breast cancer diagnosis. The review will focus on assessing the diagnostic performance (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) of these models across various diagnostic modalities such as mammography, ultrasound, MRI, histopathological images, and genetic biomarkers.
The purpose of this review is to Synthesize evidence on how AI and ML are being utilized in breast cancer diagnosis, Identify which algorithms and datasets are most commonly used, Compare the performance of AI/ML models with conventional diagnostic methods, Highlight gaps in current research and provide recommendations for future studies, The expected outcomes include a detailed summary of current AI/ML technologies in breast cancer diagnostics, an evaluation of their diagnostic accuracy, and an identification of challenges and future opportunities for clinical implementation. This review will contribute to the body of knowledge that can inform clinicians, researchers, and healthcare policymakers about the readiness and reliability of AI-assisted diagnostic tools in breast cancer care.

title: Monitoring of Open Science practices in major medical journals - a case study
description:
BACKGROUND

Monitoring (evaluating and quantifying) the use and application of open science practices is key to fostering open science and to understanding barriers and facilitators of open science practices. Monitoring also aids in measuring the impact of open science policies and can serve as a possible intervention to improve transparency and reproducibility. For instance, the Hong Kong principles (1) propose tracking open science practices as a key metric for researcher assessment. Open science monitoring is a key priority for organizations such as the UNESCO (2) and the G7 (3). The scientific community has begun to develop both principles covering which open science practices should be tracked (4) and how to monitor them. For instance, in biomedicine, a core set of 19 open science practices has been developed (5) covering areas such as preregistration, open data, open access and open code. 

Many biomedical journals have also begun to implement policies that promote open science practices. Most notably, the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) made prospective registration a requirement to publish clinical trial results in 2005 (6). In 2018, it required a specific data-sharing statement to be included in each newly submitted paper (and prespecified in study registration) (7). The impact of these policies has been studied previously, showing a major impact on trial registration practices (8) and mixed results regarding actual data sharing (9)(10). Beyond the common policies set out by the ICMJE, there is variation across biomedical journals regarding other open science policies. In 2007, the Annals of Internal Medicine encouraged, without mandating, data-sharing practices (11). The BMJ encouraged data-sharing in 25 March 2009 (12), made it mandatory in 01 September 2013 for trials of drugs and devices (13) and in 01 July 2015 for all clinical trials (14). Starting in May 2024, all trials published in The BMJ will be required to share their underlying data (15). PLOS journals enforced clinical trial data-sharing in 03 March 2014 (16). This diversity in journals’ open science policies can be monitored by using the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) factor (17), a metric proposed by the Center for Open Science (18) to assess journals’ open science policies. 

Various automated tools have been developed to track changes in behavior across the biomedical literature (e.g.(19)). These tools can be used to assess and monitor open science practices (20), and aid in developing an observatory of open science practices across scientific journals. If those tools are indeed able produce accurate and reproducible results, such an observatory could allow 1/ to determine the real percentage of open science practices, 2/ to assess whether changes in journal’s policies were followed by changes in published articles, and 3/ to point what needs to be improved by researchers and editors. 
 
OBJECTIVES
 
This aim of this study is three-fold:
 to set up a proof-of-concept observatory of major medical journals using automatic tools that can be used to monitor key transparency practices; 
 to describe open science policies in major medical journals;
 to describe retrospectively changes on open science and transparency practices for articles published in the major medical journals with a longitudinal description of registration and data sharing practices following major changes in their policies
METHODS

This protocol will be pre-registered on the open science Framework (link). 
Selection of journals 

Our study will assess a sample of major medical journals (Table 1). We will not rely on impact factor to select target journals as this metric has several limitations (21). Instead, we will focus on a purposeful sample of ten internationally recognized generalist medical journals (specialists medical journals will be excluded) with a majority of current (or former) members of the International Committee of Medical Journals Editors (ICMJE). Furthermore, two major open access journals in the field of medicine, JAMA Network Open and BMC Medicine (the flagship medical journal of the BMC series) will also be included.

In order to monitor key transparency practices in the target journals, we will include all research articles published in the 2020-2023 period.

We will retrospectively describe changes in data-sharing practices for clinical trials. Search strategies
All eligible articles from the target journals will be identified via searches on PubMed detailed in the following subsection for the articles used for the analysis of key transparency practices. These search strings have been validated according to the PRESS guideline (24) with a specific reviewing by an information specialist (it is the same search string as our study that aims to develop the LLM tool, available on the OSF at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3V6JW ). 
Research articles
We will use the following search string: ((2020:2023[Date - Publication]) AND "hasabstract" NOT ("comment"[Publication Type]) NOT ("letter"[Publication Type]) NOT ("editorial"[Publication Type]) NOT ("published erratum"[Publication Type]) NOT ("news"[Publication Type]) NOT ("introductory journal article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("biography"[Publication Type]) NOT ("portrait"[Publication Type]) NOT ("congress"[Publication Type]) NOT ("interview"[Publication Type]) NOT ("retraction of publication"[Publication Type]) NOT ("personal narrative"[Publication Type]) NOT ("retracted publication"[Publication Type]) NOT ("patient education handout"[Publication Type]) NOT ("lecture"[Publication Type]) NOT ("autobiography"[Publication Type]) NOT ("clinical conference"[Publication Type]) NOT ("classical article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("address"[Publication Type]) NOT ("legal case"[Publication Type]) NOT ("expression of concern"[Publication Type]) NOT ("festschrift"[Publication Type]) NOT ("overall"[Publication Type]) NOT ("bibliography"[Publication Type]) NOT ("corrected and republished article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("interactive tutorial"[Publication Type]) NOT ("duplicate publication"[Publication Type]) NOT ("directory"[Publication Type]) NOT ("newspaper article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("periodical index"[Publication Type]) NOT ("dictionary"[Publication Type]) NOT ("meta analysis"[Publication Type]) NOT ("randomized controlled trial"[Publication Type])) AND ("Annals of Internal Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMC Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMJ"[Journal] OR "CMAJ"[Journal] OR "JAMA"[Journal] OR "JAMA Netw Open"[Journal] OR "Lancet"[Journal] OR "Nat Med"[Journal] OR "N Engl J Med"[Journal] OR "PLOS Med"[Journal]). 
Randomised controlled trials
We will use the following search string: (2020:2023[Date - Publication] AND "hasabstract" AND randomizedcontrolledtrial[Filter] AND ("Annals of Internal Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMC Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMJ"[Journal] OR "CMAJ"[Journal] OR "JAMA"[Journal] OR "JAMA Netw Open"[Journal] OR "Lancet"[Journal] OR "Nat Med"[Journal] OR "N Engl J Med"[Journal] OR "PLOS Med"[Journal])). 

After further development we will also try to use a IA Tool that we are developing (refer to box 1 and to research protocol: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3V6JW ) to identify all RCTs in case it outperforms our search strategy.
Similar search strings adapted to the different journals and timeframe will be used for analyses of registration and data sharing practices following policy changes.
Systematic review and meta-analyses
We will use the following search string: (2020:2023[Date - Publication] AND "hasabstract" AND meta-analysis[Filter] AND ("Annals of Internal Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMC Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMJ"[Journal] OR "CMAJ"[Journal] OR "JAMA"[Journal] OR "JAMA Netw Open"[Journal] OR "Lancet"[Journal] OR "Nat Med"[Journal] OR "N Engl J Med"[Journal] OR "PLOS Med"[Journal])). 

After further development we will also try to use our IA Tool to identify all systematic review and meta-analyses in case it outperforms our search strategy.
Collection of relevant articles
We will use R [version 4.2.2 RRID:SCR_001905], and the packages rvest and RSelenium to create web scraping scripts that extract eligible articles (PDF) and any supplementary materials from the website of each of the ten journals included in our sample. Two main strategies will be adapted to each journal:
- A strategy for open access articles, as detailed with an example using articles from The BMJ (Appendix 1); 
- A strategy for articles under a paywall, that will require institutional access and the use of another method using RSelenium packages, as detailed with an example using articles from JAMA (Appendix 2). 
In addition, for each eligible article, the XML file will be extracted either from PubMed, PubMed Central, Unpaywall or Alexandria3k if available, or through the API of the respective journal if accessible.
In case no solution is found to retrieve the pdf, XML and/ or the supplementary materials, we will contact the different journals to ask for an access to all the needed documents. 
Manual extraction of data in research articles
In order to determine the diagnostic performance of each tool to detect each open science practice, we will use a manual extraction of open science practices as a gold standard. Therefore 3 distinct manual extractions will be performed for 1/ key transparency practices, 2/ registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes and 3/ data sharing practices for clinical trials following policy changes (see below for more details including sample size computations). Because of time constraint (availability of researchers in charge of data extraction) data extractions have started on 29/04/2024 prior the registration of the protocol and are being performed by two independent reviewers (MS, FJA), but no interventions began before it. The first 100 extracted articles will be triple checked by CV and disagreements identified in the following articles will be resolved by consensus with a third reviewer (FN or CV). About 150 articles were extracted by one researcher as of registration and extractions are still on going without any analysis being carried out when the protocol is registered. 
Identification of automatized tools
We will identify existing automatic tools that can monitor any of the previously established 19 core open science practices (5). Those tools will be searched by reviewing the ScreenIT pipeline (20) curated by the Automated Screening Working Groups and by contacting several public (e.g., Rtransparent and ODDPub) and private groups (e.g., SciScore and DataSeer) performing open science monitoring. Box 1 lists some tools/initiatives identified in preliminary searches. 

RTransparent: R package that automatically identifies and extracts indicators of transparency (data availability, code availability, statements of conflicts of interest, statements of funding, statements of protocol registration) from TXT and PMC XML versions of published research articles in biomedicine (https://github.com/serghiou/rtransparent). For data and code, rTransparent uses ODDPub effectively with only small adjustments. We will expand the code for registration to cover OSF and PROSPERO and if needed all other)*.
ODDPub: R package that facilitates detecting open data and open code (https://github.com/quest-bih/oddpub)**.
ctRegistries: Checking for registration statement for clinical trials (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/17407745221087456, https://github.com/maia-sh/trn-pop).*
DataSeer: Artificial Intelligence based tool that facilitates checking data sharing policies (https://dataseer.ai/).*
SciScore: Machine learning based tool to evaluate items in the MDAR checklist and use of key biological resources (https://sciscore.com/). 
ContriBOT: A R tool, that detects and extracts Author contribution statements and acknowledgements from scientific papers. (https://github.com/quest-bih/ContriBOT) **.
IA Tool: We are currently developing and IA tool (see our protocol for both development and validation https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3V6JW ) based on a large language model (LLM) such as Mixtral to extract the presence and absence of open science practices inside medical journal articles. Ideally this tool will be automatized, open source (or failing that, open weights). It should be able to identify journal articles and supplementary material that is in .pdf format and to extract core open science practices. The task of extracting content out of a scholar article with an LLM involves optional innovations to ensure accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, such as embedding of raw data into vector stores, refining the method of prompting the LLM, and employing techniques like retrieval augmented generation (RAG) or fine-tuning*.

We do not expect that all open science practices will be covered by existing tools but tools are already available for many of these practices such as data sharing and pre-registratio

Outcomes 
Key transparency practices
For each open science practice (Table 3) in which an automated tool will be identified, we will use the tool on the sample of papers from 2020 to 2023 (included, Table 2). In case certain tools only apply to open access articles, we will restrict our analysis using those specific tools to those articles and document the number of open access articles used and the number of articles that were not used. We will therefore record the open access status of all research articles included in the study. In order to assess the diagnostic accuracy of the tools, we will randomly sample 10 articles from each articles type (RCT, meta-analysis or other research article) per journal for manual assessment (i.e. a total of 300 research articles) from 2022-2023. This sample size ensures a precision of ± 6% to estimate percentages in the worst-case scenario for precision estimations (i.e. if the percentage is 50%). These 300 articles will be manually extracted and will serve as the gold standard. This manual extraction will also be used to estimate how many papers retrieved using our search strategy are actually false positives (i.e. how many are not research articles). 
Registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes
In order to explore whether the tools are able to detect a change following the 2005 ICMJE policy that mandated registration, we will monitor registration practices for all available randomized control trials published 2 years before and 5 years after the policy (i.e. 01/07/2005) in all selected journals (when applicable), which means from 01/07/2003 to 01/07/2010 (Table 2). 
In order to assess the diagnostic accuracy of the tools, we will randomly select 15 articles per journal for manual assessment from 2003 to 2010. This sample size (150) ensures a precision of ± 8% to estimate percentages in the worst-case scenario for precision estimations (i.e. if the percentage is 50%). These 150 articles will be manually extracted and will serve as the gold standard. This manual extraction will also be used to estimate how many papers retrieved using our search strategy are actually false positives (i.e. how many are not randomised controlled trials). 
Data sharing practices for clinical trials following policy changes
In order to explore whether the tools are able to detect changes following implementation of the various data sharing policies, we will monitor data sharing practices for all available randomized control trials (RCT): 
- Published 2 years before and after the policy (i.e. 01/04/2007 (11)) that encouraged data sharing in Annals of Internal Medicine which means from 01/04/2005 to 01/04/2009;
- Published 2 years before and after the policies that encouraged (i.e. 25/03/2009 (12)), mandated for drug and devices (i.e. 01/01/2013 (13)) and then mandated for all trials (i.e. 01/07/2015 (14)), in The BMJ which means from 25/03/2007 to 01/07/2017;
- Published 2 years before and after the policy (i.e. 01/04/2014 (16)) that mandated data sharing in PLOS Medicine which means from 01/04/2012 to 01/04/2016;
- Published 2 years before and up to date after the ICMJE policy that encouraged data sharing (i.e. 01/07/2018 (7)), in all remaining journals which means from 01/07/2016 to 01/07/2020;
Longitudinal descriptions will be performed separately for each journal.
In order to assess the diagnostic performance of the tools, we will assess 50 articles randomly sampled articles from all 4 groups defined above (Annals, BMJ, PLOS, and ICMJE) over the selected period, i.e. a total of 200 articles. This sample size ensures a precision of ± 7% to estimate percentages in the worst-case scenario for precision estimations (i.e. if the percentage is 50%). These 200 articles will be manually extracted and will serve as the gold standard. This manual extraction will also be used to estimate how many papers retrieved using our search strategy are actually false positives (i.e. how many are not randomised controlled trials). 
Analysis
General approach
For each open science indicator and for each specific validation sample, we will use a 2x2 table (e.g. table 4) with the manual extraction as gold standard and the extraction by automatic tool as intervention. Due to the lack of consensus on a gold standard for automatic extraction, manual extraction is considered the most reliable method for obtaining information and will be regarded as the gold standard.

We will estimate the diagnostic accuracy of each tool by deriving sensitivity, specificity per indicator and F-score (25), by using the value identified by manual inspection as the gold standard. Systematic differences between journals will be explored by performing a subgroup analysis by journal. Estimated parameters will be presented with their 95% confidence intervals. Performance of different tools tracking the same open practices may vary because tools have been optimized on different training data and may also rely on different operational definitions of what is being tracked. If certain articles are unavailable, we maintain the predetermined power level by replacing them with alternative articles chosen at random from the same journal, or, if needed, from another randomly selected journal with a similar publication type.

Table 4: Describe of the performance of each automatic tool. 
 
Key transparency practices
A descriptive analysis of each of the parameters described above will be carried out by journal. Categorical variables will be described over the time period using number and percentages (with their 95% confidence intervals). For registration and data sharing, subgroup analyses will be specifically performed for clinical trials and for meta-analyses separately.
Registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes
A descriptive analysis of clinical trial registration will be carried for all journals around 01/07/2005. Categorical variables will be described over the time period using number and percentages for each year. This analysis will be descriptive with no specific strategy regarding statistical inference.

Data sharing practices for clinical trials following policy changes
A descriptive analysis of clinical trial data sharing will be carried for all journals around 01/07/2018. Categorical variables will be described over the time period using number and percentages for each year. This analysis will be descriptive with no specific strategy regarding statistical inference.

Exploratory analysis 
A secondary analysis will assess whether performance differs between pdf vs. XML files, for papers for which both are available in order to help to interpret data
PERSPECTIVES
Implications 
In this study, we will explore various automated tools to monitor open science practices at major generalist biomedical journals. This work will inform the development of a broader open science observatory of biomedical journals. The leading biomedical journals in this study will hence provide important information about these journals that are considered as trusted sources by the medical community. Last, by tracking the open science practices, we will be able to describe changes occurring around implementation of various policy changes on selected open science practices (clinical trial data sharing and registration). Finally, if the accuracy of the automatic tools is good, we will be able to expand the observatory to other journals to more holistically measure the landscape, depending validation. 
Limitations
Because it will be based on a selected sample of major journals, this study will lack external validity regarding core open science practices in other journals (including specialty journals) (10). But given the complexity of the task, it is important that, before further development of the observatory, we start with a small sample of journals. These journals were chosen as we are sure they publish all the different types of research articles that are targeted by the open science practices we are interested in monitoring. In addition, because some automated indicators only detect mention of a registration, or mention of data sharing, it is likely that we won’t be able to detect failure to comply with study registration and/or data sharing plans (26). Finally, because journals can change their reporting practices over time and software tools can improve, it is possible that the diagnostic properties assessed in our study will differ in the future evaluations. Regarding this specific point, the potential identification of challenges in line with reporting in our study may be useful to inform future journal policies in order to reach a better harmonization and to ease monitoring of core Open Science practices.

title: Simulationen zur Förderung der diagnostischen Kompetenzen in der heil- und sonderpä-dagogischen Hochschulbildung: Strukturiertes Klickspiel oder Einsatz GPTAvatar - ein Vergleich mit Noviz:innen und Expert:innen
description:
Diagnostische Kompetenzen sind eine zentrale Qualifikation für heil- und sonderpädagogische Fachkräfte, um Kinder mit besonderem Förderbedarf frühzeitig zu erkennen und darauf aufbau-end passgenaue, datengestützte Fördermassnahmen zu planen und umzusetzen. Entsprechend bildet die Diagnostik einen Schwerpunkt in der heil- und sonderpädagogischen Aus- und Weiter-bildung. Dabei sind für die hochschulische Ausbildung unterschiedliche Kompetenzniveaus von Noviz:innen bis Expert:innen zu berücksichtigen.
Zur Förderung der diagnostischen Kompetenz werden in der Lehre derzeit Fachbücher und meist papierbasierte Fallvignetten eingesetzt. Zur Vertiefung eignen sich interaktive Simulatio-nen (Heitzmann et al., 2019), die anhand von Fallbeispielen den diagnostischen Prozess mit mehreren Entscheidungsmöglichkeiten spielerisch darstellen. Klickbasierte Simulationsspiele sind stark strukturiert. Freier sind hingegen KI-gestützte Avatare, die adaptiv auf die Person reagieren und Audio-, Bild- und Videodaten verarbeiten können. Dadurch unterstützen sie das Lernen, geben gezielte Hilfestellungen und fungieren als virtuelle Mentoren (Fink et al., 2024).
Fragestellung
In einem 2x2-Experiment wird ein strukturiertes Klickspiel mit dem GPTAvatar (Robinson, 2023) im Expert:innen-Noviz:innen-Vergleich untersucht. In beiden Spielen holen die Teilnehmenden Informationen über jeweils ein Kind mit Leseschwierigkeiten ein, treffen möglichst datengestütz-te und fundierte Förderentscheidungen und begründen diese. Der Avatar sichert das gesamte Gespräch in Logdaten und ist für das Spiel mit einem Fallbeispiel konfiguriert sowie mit Verhal-tensregeln versehen worden. Untersucht wird das diagnostische Vorwissen (DaKI; Jungjohann & Gebhardt, 2023), und der Einfluss der Selbsteinschätzung des Cognitive Load (Krieglstein et al.,2023) auf die Qualität diagnostischer Entscheidungen (Heitzmann et al., 2019). Die Fragestellung ist, ob sich die Noviz:innen von den Expert:innen in der Bearbeitung der beiden Simulatio-nen unterscheiden, gemessen an der kognitiven Belastung und der diagnostischen Qualität, und inwiefern sie unterschiedliche Begründungen für die Förderentscheidungen geben. 
Design und Methode
In die Studie werden N = 25 Noviz:innen und N = 25 Expert:innen der Heil- und Sonderpädago-gik aus Deutschland und der Schweiz einbezogen. Alle Teilnehmenden bearbeiten zwei diagnos2tische Fälle - einen im Klickspiel und einen mit dem GPTAvatar. Die Reihenfolge der Bearbeitung erfolgt randomisiert im Sinne eines 2 x 2-within-Designs mit Messwiederholung. 
Die Förderentscheidungen werden als Index auf Basis der diagnostischen Qualität nach Kriterien von Heitzmann et al. (2019) kodiert, auf einer Skala von (1) unpassend bis (3) ausreichend-datengestützt und passend zum Erwartungshorizont. Die abhängige Variable diagnostische Qualität der Förderentscheidung wird mit dem diagnostischen Vorwissen (Selbsteinschätzung DaKI) als Covariate und dem Einfluss der Reihenfolge der Bearbeitung in Beziehung gesetzt und im ANOVA-Modell analysiert.
Die Ergebnisse werden aufzeigen, inwiefern der Einsatz KI-gestützter Avatare im Vergleich zu strukturierten Klickspielen eine Förderung diagnostischer Kompetenzen ermöglicht. Weiter könnten die Ergebnisse genutzt werden, verschiedene Lernspiele für Noviz:innen und Ex-pert:innen zu entwickeln, um unterschiedliche diagnostischen Kompetenzniveaus zu adressieren.

title: Multiplex Testing for HIV, Viral Hepatitis, and STIs: A Scoping Review
description:
The global commitment to ending the HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI epidemics by 2030 has placed a strong emphasis on integrated testing services to improve early diagnosis and linkage to care. Expanding access to multiplex testing, which allows for the simultaneous detection of multiple infections, is a key strategy in achieving universal health coverage and improving public health outcomes. These tests are particularly important in addressing co-infections among priority populations, such as pregnant women, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals, and people at high risk for STIs and viral hepatitis. By enabling early diagnosis and timely treatment, multiplex testing plays an important role in reducing transmission rates and enhancing disease management at both individual and population levels.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are considered gold standards in evidence-based medicine, typically drawing from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to guide clinical interventions. However, in public health research, where interventions often extend beyond controlled settings, scoping reviews have become a valuable approach to synthesizing evidence from a variety of study designs, including observational, qualitative, and grey literature sources. Scoping reviews allow for a broader examination of available evidence, capturing implementation challenges, policy gaps, and emerging innovations in disease prevention and control.
This scoping review integrates data from indexed scientific literature and grey literature sources (e.g., technical reports, conference abstracts, and dissertations) to provide a comprehensive understanding of the feasibility, usability, and diagnostic accuracy of multiplex testing for HIV, viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV), and STIs. The review examines studies published between 2019 and 2024, focusing on different types of multiplex tests, including molecular diagnostics, serology-based rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), and self-testing platforms. Key outcomes include diagnostic performance, patient acceptance, and barriers to implementation across various healthcare settings.
By summarizing barriers, limitations, and successes of multiplex testing, this review aims to generate actionable evidence to inform public health policies, advocacy efforts, and the integration of multiplex diagnostics into routine healthcare services. Findings will provide insights into how multiplex testing can be optimized for different populations and settings, helping to advance evidence-based strategies for disease prevention, early detection, and linkage to care.

title: Future Pulse: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health
description:
Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2021. Future Pulse: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health. Book of Primary Care & Community Health Publishing, Thousand Oaks Special Issue, 2021. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/87ahk



"Future Pulse: AI-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health" by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, published in 2021 by the Book of Primary Care & Community Health Publishing in Thousand Oaks, delves into the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern diagnostics. The book emerges from the need to explore how AI technologies can revolutionize healthcare, particularly in diagnostics, offering a more efficient, accurate, and personalized approach to medical care.
Definition and Basic Concepts
The book begins by introducing the fundamental concepts of AI and its application in healthcare. It outlines how AI has evolved over the years to become an integral part of modern medical diagnostics. AI is defined as a branch of computer science that develops algorithms and systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, and problem-solving. In healthcare, AI is utilized to analyze complex medical data, aiding in diagnostics and treatment planning.
Underlying Phenomena
The motivation behind this book is the rapid advancement and integration of AI technologies in the healthcare sector. The author highlights the increasing volume of healthcare data, the demand for personalized medicine, and the need for more efficient diagnostic tools as key phenomena driving the exploration of AI in diagnostics. The book underscores the potential of AI to address these contemporary challenges and improve patient outcomes.
Problem Statement
The primary problem addressed by the book is the integration of AI into healthcare diagnostics. It examines the challenges and opportunities of incorporating AI technologies in medical diagnostics, aiming to understand how these technologies can be effectively utilized to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency while addressing ethical and privacy concerns.
Research Objectives
The book aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the role of AI in healthcare diagnostics, exploring its applications, benefits, and challenges. It seeks to outline strategies for successful implementation, emphasizing the importance of ethical guidelines and regulatory frameworks to ensure the responsible use of AI in diagnostics.
Indicators
Key indicators of successful AI integration in healthcare diagnostics, as identified in the book, include improved diagnostic accuracy, faster diagnostic processes, enhanced data analysis capabilities, and more personalized treatment plans. The book also considers the development of robust ethical and legal frameworks as critical indicators.
Operational Variables
Operational variables in the book include AI technologies such as machine learning algorithms, neural networks, and natural language processing tools. The book also explores variables related to healthcare outcomes, data management practices, and regulatory compliance.
Determining Factors
The determining factors for the successful implementation of AI in healthcare diagnostics include technological advancements, data availability and quality, regulatory environments, and healthcare professionals' readiness to adopt AI-driven tools. The author emphasizes the role of interdisciplinary collaboration in overcoming technical and ethical challenges.
Implementation and Strategy
The book outlines various strategies for integrating AI into healthcare diagnostics, such as investing in AI research and development, fostering collaboration between technology developers and healthcare professionals, and establishing comprehensive training programs for healthcare workers. It also highlights the need for continuous monitoring and evaluation to adapt to evolving technologies and healthcare needs.
Challenges and Supportive Factors
The book identifies several challenges, including data privacy concerns, algorithmic biases, and the potential for job displacement within the healthcare sector. Supportive factors include technological innovations, supportive regulatory policies, and public acceptance of AI in healthcare. The author calls for a balanced approach to address these challenges while leveraging supportive factors to maximize the benefits of AI.
Determining Factors of the Book
The relevance and impact of the book are determined by its timely exploration of emerging technologies, its comprehensive analysis, and its practical recommendations for healthcare professionals and policymakers. The book’s ability to address ethical considerations and propose actionable strategies also contributes significantly to its importance.
Research Findings
The book presents several case studies demonstrating successful AI applications in diagnostics. These include enhanced imaging analysis, personalized medicine through genetic profiling, and efficient epidemiological data analysis. These findings illustrate the tangible benefits of AI integration, providing evidence of its potential to transform healthcare delivery.
Conclusion and Recommendations
In conclusion, the book emphasizes the vital role of AI in modernizing healthcare diagnostics. It advocates for their ethical and responsible adoption, emphasizing the need for regulatory frameworks and continuous evaluation. The author recommends fostering interdisciplinary collaborations, investing in technological innovations, and developing comprehensive regulatory frameworks to ensure the successful integration of AI in diagnostics.
"Future Pulse: AI-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health" offers a detailed exploration of how AI can enhance traditional diagnostic practices and pave the way for new approaches in healthcare. It underscores the importance of innovation, ethical responsibility, and strategic implementation to harness the full potential of these transformative technologies.

title: Translation of oral health research priorities into research topics in an equity-based priority setting exercise
description: Background: In the context of research priority setting, participants express their research priorities and ideas in various forms, ranging from narratives to explicit topics or questions. However, the transition from these expressions to well-structured research topics or questions is not always straightforward. Challenges intensify when research priorities pertain to interventions or diagnostic accuracy, requiring the conversion of narratives into the PICO (Participant, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) format. Scope and findings: This project aimed to understand the challenges of engaging a diverse, multilingual population in setting oral health research priorities. While not a comprehensive priority-setting effort, we modified James Lind Alliance's (JLA) methods and used thematic analysis to establish a list of priority research topics and questions. This was accomplished by conducting interviews with 40 community participants and 14 dentists from various ethnic backgrounds in Malaysia. The interview language depended on participant preferences, including English, Malay, and Mandarin, with translations handled collaboratively by bilingual research assistants. The process involved thematic analysis, discussion with a research committee, and necessary modifications. Our interpretations revealed distinct categories of participant statements: explicit, complicated, implicit, and incomplete. In this study, we identified a three-step approach to translate research ideas that are presented either as explicit statements or as complicated narratives.

title: Protocol: In multi-reader multi-case study designs, do AI-diagnostic tools improve accuracy outcomes for radiologists in cancer risk stratification?
description:
The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques in healthcare has become a topic of significant discussion. Methods using such algorithms have demonstrated remarkable improvements in terms of accuracy and sensitivity in medical image recognition tasks1. In clinical practice, evidence has shown that AI technology can be used as a clinical decision tool to diagnose numerous diseases when using radiological techniques such as X-ray, CT, MRI, or ultrasound1. ML algorithms thus are seen as being able to efficiently provide diagnostically accurate data to patients on a shorter timescale. 

Challenges and complications
Although AI has been lauded as a revolutionary technique and can be suggested to perform better than humans in healthcare on several issues regarding their accuracy and utility in clinical practice, some of the main issues that have arisen are: 
• Algorithms are normally inputted with a specific output in mind while a doctor may be able to make a more flexible decision. For example, an AI tool that has been developed to consider lymph node metastasis in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma may be able to outperform radiologists2. However, this model will not be able to then make decisions that only a doctor can on the best course of action for the patient. 
• Overdiagnosis3: The algorithms from AI detect and diagnose conditions whether they cause harm for a patient or not. For example, if we consider a CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) to detect pulmonary emboli (PE) in the lungs, this is usually an incidental finding and even when detected, PE only needs to be treated on a symptomatic basis. AI tools for CTPA may detect this at a much higher rate. Are smaller lesions therefore being detected with the extra sensitivity that are less harmful? The question then arises on how we should approach this data: who should be treated and who should not? 



AI application in medical imaging analysis
The future of AI seems to be as a diagnostic support tool integrated within a radiologist’s workflow, allowing an increase in efficiency and a reduction in errors1. Studies that thus compare AI models with radiologist or clinician-mediated diagnosis may not highlight the effects AI may have in a clinical setting and quantify the gain in accuracy from AI in reading images. 

More radiological test studies have thus shifted to implementing a multi-reader multi-case (MRMC) design4. This design is popular as once a radiologist has viewed twenty cases there is less information to be gained by asking them to view a further twenty than asking a different radiologist to view the same twenty5. The study design asks multiple radiologists to view the same cases and means that results can correlate within readers meaning that bootstrapping and modelling can account for these parameters to enhance statistical power. These studies’ primary outcome arises as a receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve that describes a plot of sensitivity vs. 1-specificity for diagnostic tests6. The AUC can then be used as a measure to combine both sensitivity and specificity to compare diagnostic tools. 

In recent years, several systematic reviews regarding artificial intelligence and radiology have been published7,8. These have focussed on diagnostic performance and how AI models compare to a radiologist. Due to the heterogeneity of data across the field of AI tools these have often been narrative syntheses. By solely considering the MRMC study design this allows examination of a more homogenous dataset. The study design outlined above also will help interpretation of how AI-diagnostic tools may help optimise cancer management in healthcare. Studies using this as a primary outcome are often required by regulatory bodies for licensing new radiological devices9. Furthermore, by solely analysing MRMC studies this also will allow consideration of detailed methodological components across studies to consider data presentation and analysis within the field of AI and radiology. 

This systematic review thus aims to assess MRMC studies using ROC AUC outcome measures to consider whether AI-assisted clinician diagnosis may be beneficial. The review will also examine design, analysis, and reporting of MRMC studies regarding AI to consider how these may influence the data that is ultimately presented.

title: Improving cut-off determination of Neuropsychological tests: a Bayesian approach
description:
Traditional validation approaches in neuropsychology typically rely on normative data from healthy individuals to establish cut-off scores. While this method provides estimates of specificity, it does not inform sensitivity, and the resulting cut-off is generic rather than pathology-specific. This limitation becomes critical when assessing clinical populations, as neuropsychological tools are often validated on very small patient samples. Such constraints make it difficult to apply standard Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analyses, which require sufficiently large and balanced datasets to produce reliable estimates.

To address this issue, we propose a Bayesian adaptation of the ROC framework. The rationale behind this approach is that Bayesian methods naturally incorporate uncertainty arising from sample size, allowing for more robust inference even when patient data are scarce. Unlike simple simulation techniques, Bayesian modeling provides posterior distributions for key parameters, enabling credible intervals for cut-off scores, sensitivity, and specificity.

In our conceptual example, we consider a dataset with 200 healthy controls and only 10 patients. Using Bayesian regression, we estimate model parameters and generate simulated datasets from posterior distributions. For each simulated dataset, we compute ROC curves and derive credible intervals for diagnostic metrics. This approach leverages prior assumptions about the relationship between patients and controls and models data distributions using Student’s t-distribution, which accounts for heavier tails and greater variability in small samples. Consequently, the Bayesian framework offers a principled solution for neuropsychological validation in contexts where traditional ROC analysis is impractical.

title: Artificial intelligence in optical coherence tomography and magnetic resonance imaging for optic neuropathies: Scoping Review
description: Introduction: Optic neuropathies are diseases that affect the optic nerve and cause visual loss of varying degrees. Among the most common are glaucoma and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, both major causes of irreversible blindness worldwide. Early diagnosis depends on imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which allow precise evaluation of structural and functional changes in the optic nerve. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool in neuro-ophthalmology, capable of processing large volumes of images with high diagnostic accuracy. However, the rapid expansion of scientific evidence calls for a review that synthesizes current advances, applications, and limitations of this technology. Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted of studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of AI models applied to the analysis of OCT and MRI in optic neuropathies. The search will include databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, and BIREME, using MeSH and DeCS descriptors related to artificial intelligence, deep learning, and optic neuropathies. Grey literature will be included, and the snowball technique will be applied. Expected results: It is expected to generate an updated overview of the evidence on AI in the diagnosis of optic neuropathies, identifying the most used models, their benefits, limitations, and perspectives for clinical integration in neuro-ophthalmology.

title: Comparison of different methods for the meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies – a simulation study
description: Meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies is, due to its co-primary endpoint of sensitivity and specificity, methodologically more challenging than its univariate counterpart in intervention studies. In medical practice, methods for the meta-analysis of DTA studies often do not distinguish between diagnostic thresholds in the primary studies and only use information from a single threshold per study. In contrast, more recent approaches incorporate all available information by considering all diagnostic thresholds and can express summary estimates depending on the threshold. We will systematically compare eleven methods for the meta-analysis of DTA studies, five of which consider a single diagnostic threshold per study, while the other six consider all available thresholds. Using simulation scenarios that resemble realistic meta-analysis datasets, we will investigate the methods’ bias, empirical coverage and convergence behavior for diagnostic tests on both the continuous and ordinal scale. Our aim is to detect situations in which certain methods are superior or inferior to others and thus aiding practitioners in an adequate choice of method when performing meta-analysis in a specific setting.

title: The Oxford Digital Multiple Errands Test (OxMET): Validation of a Simplified Computer Tablet Based Multiple Errands Test
description:
Impairments in executive functioning are common following Acquired Brain Injury, though there is a lack of screening tools which present both a time efficient and ecologically valid approach to assessing the consequences of executive impairments. We present the Oxford Digital Multiple Errands Test (OxMET), a novel and simplified computer-tablet version of a Multiple Errands Test.
We recruited 124 neurologically healthy controls and 105 stroke survivors to complete the OxMET task. Normative data and internal consistency were established from the healthy control data. Convergent and divergent validation was assessed in a mixed subset of 158 participants who completed the OxMET and the OCS-Plus. Test-retest reliability was examined across a mixed subset of 39 participants. Finally, we investigated the known-group discriminability of the OxMET.
The OxMET demonstrated very high internal consistency, and stable group level test-retest performance as well as good convergent and divergent validity. The OxMET demonstrated high sensitivity and good specificity in overall differentiation of stroke survivors from controls. Stroke survivors made significantly more errors than healthy controls, as well as being less accurate and slower to complete the task. 
This paper presents the Oxford Digital Multiple Errands Test as a brief, easy to administer tool, designed to quickly screen for potential consequences of executive impairments in a virtual environment shopping task on a computer tablet. Initial normative data and validation within a chronic stroke cohort is presented.

title: STAndards for ReporTing Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (START-EDI)
description: START-EDI reporting guidelines will provide a list of minimum items that should be reported by healthcare researchers, ensuring that diversity is incorporated in essential areas such as research design, data collection, public involvement, dissemination and impact. title: Use and appropriateness of Reporting Guidelines in physical therapy research: a protocol for a meta-research study
description:
INTRODUCTION: Problems about reporting of a scientific study can affect dissemination of research in different manners. It is known that study methods are frequently not described in adequate detail and that results are presented ambiguously or selectively. To overcome these problems, reporting guidelines (e.g. CONSORT, PRISMA, STARD and STROBE statements) have been developed to increase the transparency of research. While recent evidence suggested that these guidelines are frequently used inappropriately in studies published in the major medical journals, the extent and appropriateness of use in physical therapy research has not been systematically evaluated. The aim of this meta-research study will be to evaluate the frequency of using reporting guidelines and their appropriate use in physical therapy published research.
METHODS: A cross-sectional analysis is planned on a random sample of 200 studies published in the last ten years (2010-2019) in the five generic rehabilitation journals with the highest 5-year impact factor. Randomization will be stratified for publication date to include an equal number of studies from 2010 to 2014 (n=100), and from 2015 to 2019 (n=100). Randomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, diagnostic accuracy studies and observational studies will be included. Crude prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals of using and appropriateness of using will be estimated. A bivariate analysis will assess the relationship between the use of reporting guidelines and the year of publication.
DISSEMINATION PLANS: Several studies have shown the positive influence of reporting guidelines on the completeness of research reporting but no one investigated the use and the appropriateness of reporting guidelines in physical therapy research. Therefore, this study will add relevant knowledge that may contribute to improve further the reporting of rehabilitation research. The results of this research will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and will be presented at relevant (inter)national scientific events.

title: Differential diagnosis checklists reduce diagnostic error differentially: a randomized experiment
description:
Introduction Wrong and missed diagnoses contribute substantially to medical error. Can a prompt to generate alternative diagnoses (prompt) or a differential diagnosis checklist (DDXC) increase diagnostic accuracy? How do these interventions affect the diagnostic process and self-monitoring?
Methods Advanced medical students (N = 90) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions to complete six computer-based patient cases: Group 1 (prompt) was instructed to write down all diagnoses they considered while acquiring diagnostic test results, and to finally rank them. Groups 2 and 3 received the same instruction plus a list of 17 differential diagnoses for the chief complaint of the patient. For half of the cases, the DDXC contained the correct diagnosis (DDXC+) and for the other half, it did not (DDXC-; counterbalanced). Group 4 (control) was only instructed to indicate their final diagnosis. Mixed-effects models were used to analyze results.
Results Students using a DDXC that contained the correct diagnosis had better diagnostic accuracy, mean (standard deviation), 0.75 (0.44), compared to controls without a checklist, 0.49 (0.50), P < 0.001, but those using a DDXC that did not contain the correct diagnosis did slightly worse, 0.43 (0.50), P = 0.602. The number and relevance of diagnostic tests acquired were not affected by condition, nor was self-monitoring. However, participants spent more time on a case in the DDXC-, 4:20 minutes (2:36), P ≤ 0.001, and DDXC+ condition, 3:52 minutes (2:09), than in the control condition, 2:59 minutes (1:44), P ≤ 0.001.
Discussion Being provided a list of possible diagnoses improves diagnostic accuracy compared with a prompt to create a differential diagnosis list, if the provided list contains the correct diagnosis. However, being provided a diagnosis list without the correct diagnosis did not improve and might have slightly reduced diagnostic accuracy. Interventions neither affected information gathering nor self-monitoring.

title: Adaptation, external validation and refinement of two children’s homes Swiss-French topic search filters on RERO DOC
description:
Abstract
Objectives:
To adapt, validate and refine topic search filters meant to retrieve Swiss social work bachelor theses focusing on children’s homes written in French and indexed in RERO DOC
Study design:
Search filter external validation, refinement and internal validation
Methods:
Full-text assessment of all 385 bachelor theses published by HETS Valais students and indexed in RERO DOC, extraction of titles and assessment of whether they focus or not on children’s homes. Adaptation of the two previously built filters for RERO DOC, measurement of their performances on this new dataset. Development of three new 
Results:
Performances of the original topic search filters dropped significantly when applied to this external validation set. The highly sensitive children’s homes search filter performance went from 79.45%/95.12% sensitivity/specificity to 66.32%/78.89% and the highly specific search filter performance went from 69.86%/98.37% sensitivity/specificity to 54.74%/83.39% when tested on the RERO DOC dataset. Reasons included: a lower prevalence of specific keywords within children’s homes titles (now out of date or highly canton-specific) and limited functionality of searches making use of character accentuations.
A highly sensitive (“exhaustive”), a highly specific (“focused”) and a balanced (“best trade-off”) RERO DOC specific search filters were developed iteratively using a search simulator. The “exhaustive” search filter achieved 87.37% sensitivity and 71.88% specificity. The “focused” search filter achieved 62.11% sensitivity and 93.40% specificity. And the “best trade-off” filter achieved 74.74% sensitivity and 84.38% specificity.
Novel keywords included in these filters include: reference, fugue, mineur, rupture, plainte and St-Raphael/Saint-Raphael.
Limitations:
The RERO DOC search filters were used without using data from abstracts or the full extent of advanced search features available and could be improved further. The new search filters should be used with caution on different databases, if used to search works from non-Swiss settings (for instance works from France), if used to search for works published prior to 1980/1990 or if used to search for works published in the following decades.
