Clinical Governance, Quality Management, and Radiation Protection in Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology: A Scoping Review within the Italian National Health Service (SSN), 2016–2026
description:
TITLE:
Clinical Governance, Quality Management, and Radiation Protection in Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology: A Scoping Review within the Italian National Health Service (SSN), 2016–2026

DESCRIPTION / ABSTRACT:
Background:
In modern healthcare settings, radiological departments face growing organizational and regulatory complexity. Ensuring high standards of diagnostic accuracy while minimizing clinical risk and patient radiation exposure requires a multi-professional and integrated governance strategy. However, Clinical Governance, Quality Management Systems (QMS), clinical risk management, and Radiation Protection are often addressed as separate domains, potentially limiting the development of coordinated quality and safety strategies. This scoping review maps the available evidence, regulatory frameworks, and operational models supporting their integration within the Italian National Health Service (SSN).
Objectives:
1. To identify and map organizational models integrating Clinical Governance, Quality Management, clinical risk management, and Radiation Protection across Diagnostic Imaging and Interventional Radiology services.
2. To examine the relationship between relevant Italian legislative requirements (e.g., Legislative Decree 101/2020 on radiation protection and Law 24/2017 on patient safety) and international quality standards (ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 7101:2023).
3. To synthesize operational strategies addressing safety checklists, Diagnostic Reference Levels (DRLs), Radiation Dose Monitoring Systems (RDMS), contrast media safety, digital workflows, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration.
4. To identify existing Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and propose an integrated KPI framework for evaluating the performance of multidisciplinary radiology teams.
Methods & Eligibility Criteria (PCC Framework):
This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines.

Eligibility criteria were structured according to the PCC framework:

-Population (P): Diagnostic Imaging and Interventional Radiology services and their multidisciplinary healthcare teams, including Radiologists, TSRM/Radiographers, Medical Physicists, and Nurses.
-Concept (C): Clinical Governance models, Quality Management Systems (ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 7101:2023), Clinical Risk Management (patient safety, safety checklists, contrast media safety), Radiation Protection (Diagnostic Reference Levels [DRLs], Radiation Dose Monitoring Systems [RDMS], optimization, and justification), and digital innovation, including Artificial Intelligence (AI).
-Context (C): Public and accredited private healthcare facilities operating within the Italian National Health Service (SSN).
Sources published between January 1, 2016 and July 31, 2026 were eligible for inclusion.

Results & Corpus:
A structured search of PubMed and Scopus, supplemented by Google Scholar and targeted searches of institutional and professional sources (AGENAS, SIRM, FNO TSRM-PSTRP), identified a final corpus of 67 unique sources. Thematic analysis mapped these sources across three primary operational pillars: (1) Quality Management Systems & Standards; (2) Clinical Risk Management & Safety Checklists; and (3) Radiation Protection, Optimization & Dose Monitoring. The three categories were not mutually exclusive, with individual sources contributing to more than one thematic domain. Overall, the 67 sources generated 72 thematic assignments, corresponding to 24 assignments per pillar.
Significance:
This study provides an evidence-informed framework for healthcare managers, clinical leaders, and radiology professionals to support the integration of Clinical Governance, Quality Management, Clinical Risk Management, and Radiation Protection, bridging regulatory requirements with continuous quality improvement in Diagnostic Imaging and Interventional Radiology.

title: Emotion Regulation in Clinical and Non-Clinical Adolescents: An Exploratory Integration of Self-Report Profiles and Frontal Alpha Asymmetry
description:
This study is a post-hoc secondary analysis examining emotion regulation in adolescents aged 13 to 18 years across clinical and non-clinical groups. Data were not collected as part of a single unified study; the healthy control sample and the clinical samples were recruited and assessed in separate research projects, and the present analysis integrates these datasets for comparative purposes. Accordingly, all findings should be interpreted within the constraints of a post-hoc, cross-sectional design.
Adolescence represents a period of heightened emotional reactivity and concurrent maturation of prefrontal regulatory circuitry, making it a developmentally sensitive window in which individual differences in emotion regulation carry demonstrable consequences for later psychopathology trajectories. Despite a growing literature linking disruptions in both behavioural emotion regulation and neural indices of frontal activity to internalising disorders in young people, most studies examine these levels in isolation and within non-clinical samples. The present study addresses this gap by integrating self-report measures of emotion regulation strategy use and regulation difficulties with resting-state frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) as a neurophysiological index, assessed in diagnostically confirmed clinical groups alongside a healthy comparison group.
Three groups are included: a healthy control group (HC), a group meeting diagnostic criteria for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), and a group meeting criteria for an Anxiety Disorder (ANX). Clinical diagnoses were confirmed via the Mini-DIPS structured clinical interview. Healthy control eligibility and dimensional symptom severity across all participants were assessed using the DISYPS-III (Döpfner & Görtz-Dorten, 2017). The final analytic sample comprises 103 participants (HC: n = 25, MDD: n = 53, ANX: n = 25).
The primary self-report instrument is the FEEL-KJ (Grob & Smolenski, 2005), which assesses adaptive and maladaptive emotion regulation strategies across anger, sadness, and fear contexts. Secondary self-report measures are the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ; Abler & Kessler, 2009), the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), and the Affective Style Questionnaire for Youth (ASQ-Y; Graser et al., 2019). Resting-state EEG was recorded to derive FAA as a neurophysiological complement to the self-report battery.
One hypothesis is designated confirmatory. It predicts disorder-congruent emotion-context specificity on the FEEL-KJ, tested via a Group x Emotion Context interaction in a linear mixed model, with a pre-specified crossover contrast serving as the directional confirmation endpoint. All remaining hypotheses are exploratory, addressing FAA group differences, associations between FAA and self-reported regulation difficulties, dimensional severity associations, diagnostic classification accuracy, and cross-instrument convergence across the self-report battery. Given the post-hoc nature of the study and the separate origins of the datasets, no findings from the exploratory analyses are intended to be interpreted as confirmatory evidence.
The study aims to contribute to a sparse literature on cross-level emotion regulation research in diagnostically confirmed adolescent samples, to evaluate whether FAA meaningfully differentiates clinical from non-clinical adolescents, and to examine whether disorder-specific patterning in emotion regulation emerges or whether clinical-versus-control differences are broader and less diagnostically differentiated than theoretical models predict.

title: Epidemiology of Orofacial Clefts in East Africa: a Systematic Review
description:
This research project is a systematic review designed to provide an epidemiological mapping of Orofacial Clefts (OFCs) across eleven East African nations: Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Kenya, South Sudan, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti, and Somalia. Its primary purpose is to address the critical "data gap" regarding the prevalence and etiology of cleft lip and palate in East Africa. While surgical interventions have increased across the region, public health policy remains hampered by fragmented data. Currently, estimates of OFC prevalence vary wildly due to inconsistent reporting methods, ranging from community-based surveillance to localized hospital registries.

This project seeks to synthesize literature published between 2011 and 2025 to achieve three core objectives:
1. To determine the pooled prevalence of OFCs, distinguishing between birth incidence and the "surgical backlog" of untreated cases.
2. To evaluate how these anomalies are distributed by sex, phenotype (isolated vs. syndromic), and laterality.
3. To investigate the correlation between OFCs and regional specificities, such as consanguinity, nutritional deficiencies (folic acid), and environmental exposures like biomass fuel smoke.

To ensure the highest level of academic rigor, the project will utilize a multifaceted search strategy across six major databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, AJOL, and WHO Global Index Medicus). The study will employ a unique "Tiered Evidence Approach," stratifying data into population-based, hospital-based, and service-based categories. This methodology will allow the research to account for selection bias and provide a more nuanced understanding of the regional burden. Data synthesis will be performed using STATA (v17.0), utilizing a random-effects model to manage the anticipated heterogeneity of the East African healthcare landscape.

The findings of this systematic review are expected to serve as a foundational evidence base for several key stakeholders:
1. Public Health Policy: By identifying high-risk regions and specific environmental triggers, the study will provide a roadmap for primary prevention strategies and maternal-fetal health interventions.
2. Healthcare Planning: Accurate prevalence data will assist Ministries of Health and NGOs in optimizing resource allocation for surgical missions and multidisciplinary cleft care centers.
3. Clinical Counseling: Identifying the prevalence of associated malformations will improve the diagnostic accuracy and prenatal counseling provided to families.
4. Scientific Contribution: This study will be registered with Open Science Frame, contributing a standardized, peer-reviewed dataset to the global body of epidemiological research, specifically highlighting the unique challenges faced by the East African population.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT OF CHILDHOOD HANDWRITING DISORDERS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
This protocol outlines a scoping review on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the diagnosis and treatment of childhood handwriting disorders, such as dysgraphia and difficulties with spelling, grammar, punctuation, or text composition. Handwriting is a complex skill that develops progressively from early childhood and may reflect underlying neurodevelopmental disorders when impaired. Despite advances in traditional interventions, diagnostic and therapeutic challenges persist—particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged settings.
 In this context, AI emerges as a promising tool to enhance diagnostic accuracy and personalize interventions. Previous studies have successfully used algorithms to detect graphic behavior patterns and adapt to individual needs through intelligent applications. However, AI use in the field of childhood handwriting remains limited, with many studies still in the experimental phase.
 The review will follow the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley, complemented by the Joanna Briggs Institute and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Relevant databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar will be searched, including literature without language or date restrictions. Data will be analyzed using narrative synthesis and thematic qualitative analysis.
 The ultimate aim is to synthesize current knowledge, establish an open-access categorized database, and provide evidence-based recommendations to guide the safe and effective use of AI in addressing these disorders. In addition, expert consultation will be included to integrate clinical and technological perspectives.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence Models Using Complete Blood Count Parameters for Anemia Diagnosis and Classification: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-Analysis
description:
Background

Anemia affects over 1.6 billion people globally, with disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries where advanced diagnostic tests are unavailable. Differential diagnosis between iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, and other hemoglobinopathies remains challenging, particularly in resource-limited settings. Artificial intelligence models using routine complete blood count parameters have emerged as promising, cost-effective diagnostic tools. However, their overall diagnostic accuracy, generalizability, and clinical applicability remain uncertain.

Objectives

Primary Objective: To evaluate the pooled diagnostic accuracy (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic odds ratio) of artificial intelligence and machine learning models using complete blood count parameters for anemia diagnosis and classification.

Secondary Objectives:

1. To synthesize feature importance from explainable AI studies (SHAP, LIME) to identify the most consistently influential CBC parameters
2. To compare AI model performance against traditional discriminant indices (Mentzer, RDWI, CRUISE, and others)
3. To evaluate the added value of CBC-derived hematological indices to AI performance via meta-regression
4. To identify the minimum CBC parameters required for high accuracy and propose an evidence-based minimal panel
5. To explore heterogeneity sources through subgroup analyses and meta-regression

Methods

Study Design: Systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis

Protocol Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261451245

Search Strategy: Systematic search of MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science from inception to July 14, 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation tracking.

Eligibility Criteria:

· Population: Human participants of any age with any type of anemia
· Intervention: AI/ML models using CBC parameters for anemia diagnosis or classification
· Comparator: Clinical reference standard (serum ferritin, hemoglobin electrophoresis, HPLC, genetic testing, bone marrow examination, or clinical diagnosis by hematologist)
· Outcomes: Sensitivity, specificity, AUC, diagnostic odds ratio
· Study Design: Cross-sectional, retrospective cohort, prospective cohort, case-control, and diagnostic accuracy studies

Data Extraction: Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized, piloted form.

Risk of Bias Assessment: PROBAST-AI and QUADAS-2 tools.

Data Synthesis: Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis using the Reitsma approach and HSROC model. Subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses were performed. Feature importance was synthesized from XAI studies.

title: Thoracoscopy versus closed pleural biopsy with Cope needle in undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions: systematic review
description: This systematic review aims to compare thoracoscopy with closed pleural biopsy using a Cope needle in adults with undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions following thoracentesis and initial pleural fluid analysis. Pleural effusion is a common clinical condition associated with diverse pulmonary and systemic diseases, and accurate etiological diagnosis is essential for appropriate management and prognosis. When initial investigations are inconclusive, pleural biopsy becomes a critical diagnostic step. Closed pleural biopsy with a Cope needle remains widely used, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to its low cost and accessibility, although its diagnostic yield is variable. In contrast, medical thoracoscopy (pleuroscopy) enables direct visualization and targeted biopsies, offering higher diagnostic accuracy, especially for malignant pleural disease, albeit with greater infrastructure requirements. This review will systematically evaluate and synthesize available evidence on the overall diagnostic yield and safety profile of these procedures. Secondary outcomes will include diagnostic yield by etiology (malignancy and tuberculosis), complication rates, need for additional diagnostic procedures, and length of hospital stay. The study will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines, assess methodological quality using validated tools, and evaluate the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. By providing a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous comparison, this review aims to inform clinical decision-making and optimize diagnostic strategies, particularly in diverse healthcare settings, including low- and middle-income countries.

title: A scoping review on adenomyosis and artificial intelligence
description: This scoping review aims to explore the intersection of adenomyosis and artificial intelligence (AI) in medical research and practice. Adenomyosis is a gynecological condition characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue within the uterine muscle, often causing pain and heavy menstrual bleeding. Despite its prevalence, the diagnosis and management of adenomyosis remain challenging due to its complex presentation and the limitations of traditional imaging techniques. The integration of AI, including machine learning and deep learning algorithms, has the potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy, personalize treatment plans, and predict patient outcomes. This review will systematically map the existing literature to identify how AI is being utilized in the study of adenomyosis, highlight gaps in current research, and propose directions for future studies. By synthesizing available evidence, this review seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of AI in advancing the understanding and management of adenomyosis.

title: A mobile-health smartphone application shows high diagnostic accuracy for malignant skin lesions in a Latin American population: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study
description:
This research project is a diagnostic accuracy study designed to evaluate the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based smartphone application for the detection and triage of malignant skin lesions in a Colombian population with broad ethnic diversity and a predominance of Fitzpatrick skin phototypes III–VI. The project was developed in response to the increasing global burden of skin cancer and the growing need for accessible, scalable strategies that facilitate early detection and timely referral to dermatologic care, particularly in regions with limited specialist access.

Globally, skin cancer represents one of the most common malignancies and continues to rise in incidence. Although melanoma accounts for most skin cancer-related deaths, non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), including basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, contributes substantially to morbidity and overall mortality due to its very high incidence. In Colombia, melanoma exhibits distinct epidemiologic characteristics compared to high-incidence countries, including a predominance of acral lentiginous melanoma and a high proportion of advanced-stage diagnoses. Mortality-to-incidence ratios are nearly twice those observed in many high-income countries, reflecting delays in diagnosis and barriers to specialized care. At the same time, artificial intelligence tools for skin lesion classification are rapidly expanding, yet most available algorithms have been trained and validated using datasets derived predominantly from European, North American, and Oceanian populations, with minimal representation of darker skin phototypes or Latin American populations. This lack of demographic diversity raises concerns regarding the generalizability and equity of AI-assisted dermatologic tools.

The primary purpose of this project is therefore to determine the sensitivity and specificity of a mobile-health application that integrates a convolutional neural network with optional dermatologist review for identifying malignant skin lesions in real-world clinical settings involving ethnically diverse populations. The study also aims to evaluate the application’s performance in detecting premalignant lesions and specific skin cancer subtypes, including basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma. In addition, subgroup analyses according to Fitzpatrick phototype were conducted to explore whether diagnostic performance varies across different skin types.

The study was conducted at the Dermatology Unit of San Ignacio University Hospital (HUSI) in Bogotá, Colombia, and complemented by three rural and underserved community health brigades in Mahates (Bolívar), Buenaventura (Valle del Cauca), and Leticia (Amazonas). These regions were intentionally selected because they include Afro-descendant, Indigenous, and mixed Hispanic populations with higher frequencies of darker skin phototypes and historically limited access to dermatologic services. By incorporating participants from both tertiary urban care centers and remote underserved regions, the project seeks to improve representation of populations traditionally excluded from AI validation studies in dermatology.

Eligible participants included adults attending dermatologic consultation who presented with at least one cutaneous lesion suitable for photographic assessment. After informed consent, lesions underwent standardized evaluation including sociodemographic characterization, Fitzpatrick skin phototype classification, dermatologist clinical assessment, and image capture using the smartphone application. The application generated an AI-based risk classification and, when necessary, incorporated remote review by a dermatologist panel. Dermatologists performing the clinical evaluations were blinded to the application results. Lesions suspicious for malignancy underwent biopsy for histopathological confirmation, while benign and premalignant lesions were classified using predefined clinical and histopathologic criteria. Data were collected and managed using REDCap, ensuring secure storage and standardized data acquisition across both urban and remote settings.

The primary expected outcome of this project is to provide robust evidence regarding the diagnostic performance of AI-assisted mobile applications in populations that have been historically underrepresented in dermatologic AI research. Specifically, the study seeks to determine whether this technology maintains acceptable sensitivity and specificity in individuals with darker skin phototypes and diverse ethnic backgrounds. Secondary expected outcomes include generating data on the performance of the application across different lesion categories and cancer subtypes, as well as identifying potential disparities in algorithmic accuracy between phototype groups.

More broadly, this project aims to contribute to the development of more equitable and generalizable AI systems in dermatology. The findings may help inform future validation studies, support safer integration of AI-assisted triage tools into clinical practice, and encourage the inclusion of ethnically and phenotypically diverse populations in dermatologic machine learning datasets. The project also seeks to explore the potential role of smartphone-based AI technologies as accessible screening and referral-support tools in low-resource settings where access to dermatologists is limited.

description:
Introduction: Pancreatic cancer ranks as the fourth deadliest form of cancer. However, it's essential to note that not all pancreatic masses signal primary malignancy. Therefore, it is imperative to establish the correct differential diagnosis, a process further supported by pre-operative biopsy procedures. This meta-analysis aims to compare the diagnostic performance of two minimally invasive biopsy approaches for pancreatic tissue sampling: percutaneous biopsies guided by CT or ultrasound, and transduodenal biopsies guided by endoscopic ultrasound.
Methods: A systematic literature search will be performed on the MEDLINE and Scopus databases using predefined search terms. The selected studies will undergo analysis to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the two biopsy methods. title: A Randomized Controlled Trial on the Efficacy of DeepSeek-R1 in Assisting Clinicians with the Differential Diagnosis of Gliomas
description:
Background
Gliomas are rapidly progressing intracranial tumors with a poor prognosis, making early and accurate diagnosis crucial for treatment decisions. Although pathological biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard, it is invasive and time-consuming, creating a clinical need for non-invasive and efficient auxiliary diagnostic tools. Furthermore, gliomas, solitary brain metastases, and primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) share highly similar clinical symptoms and imaging manifestations, posing significant challenges for differential diagnosis. In recent years, reasoning-based large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in differential diagnosis within medical fields such as emergency medicine and ophthalmology. However, their efficacy in glioma differential diagnosis lacks systematic evaluation.

Objective
This study employs a prospective randomized controlled trial design to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the DeepSeek-R1 model in assisting clinicians with differentiating gliomas, solitary brain metastases, and primary central nervous system lymphoma.

Methods

Design: A multicenter, randomized controlled trial conducted across five tertiary Grade A hospitals nationwide.
Participants: Twenty neurosurgeons with ≤4 years of experience (resident physicians or attending physicians) will be recruited and randomly assigned to either the DeepSeek-R1-assisted group (experimental group) or the conventional diagnosis group (control group).
Case Source: A total of 240 cases will be included, comprising 120 cases from published typical case reports in international journals (e.g., The New England Journal of Medicine) within the last two years, and 120 cases from patients pathologically confirmed with the three target diseases at Peking University Shenzhen Hospital over the past seven years.
Outcome Variables:
Primary Outcome Variable: Top 1 diagnostic accuracy (i.e., the accuracy of the initial diagnosis).
Secondary Outcome Variables: Diagnostic time (in minutes), diagnostic quality score (using a Likert scale), LLM hallucination rate (frequency of erroneous or irrelevant content in model output), and a physician usability questionnaire (using a Likert scale).
Statistical Analysis: Chi-square tests will be used to compare categorical variables between groups. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis will assess diagnostic performance. The Mann-Whitney U test will be employed for non-normally distributed continuous variables.
Expected Results and Significance
This study anticipates demonstrating that DeepSeek-R1 can significantly improve the differential diagnostic accuracy of junior physicians for gliomas while optimizing diagnostic efficiency. The findings will provide high-level evidence-based medical evidence for the application of LLMs in the field of neuro-oncology, thereby promoting the clinical translation of artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic tools.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Pulmonary Hypertension Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis across Multiple Input Modalities
description:
Study Description
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) carries a median diagnostic delay of 2 to 3 years, and its gold standard confirmatory test -- right heart catheterization -- is invasive and unsuitable for population-level screening. Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applied to routine clinical data have emerged as candidate non-invasive case-finding tools, with published systems spanning ten distinct input modalities: electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiography, chest X-ray (CXR), cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA), electronic health records (EHR), auscultation or phonocardiography, photoplethysmography (PPG), omics (proteomics, lipidomics, miRNA, gene expression), and multimodal combinations.
Despite this rapid accumulation of single-modality reports, no systematic synthesis has quantified AI diagnostic accuracy for PH across modalities under a common analytic framework, nor have any primary studies performed within-subject head-to-head comparisons between modalities.
This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies evaluating AI- or ML-based PH detection. We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science from inception to March 31, 2026 (with a final update on April 30, 2026). Fifty studies published between 2016 and 2026, covering all ten input modalities, met inclusion criteria. Diagnostic accuracy was pooled using a bivariate random-effects model (mvmeta package in R) for studies with complete 2x2 contingency table data (k = 32), and AUROC was pooled separately on the logit scale (k = 41). Pre-specified subgroup analyses by input modality and meta-regression with modality as a covariate were conducted. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Two pre-specified sensitivity analyses evaluated the influence of extreme-performing studies and a population-level screening cohort.
The pooled sensitivity was 0.873 (95% CI 0.823-0.910), pooled specificity 0.823 (95% CI 0.776-0.863), and pooled AUROC 0.897 (95% CI 0.870-0.919), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 99.3%). Meta-regression identified AI input modality as a significant predictor of specificity (P = 0.007). Chest X-ray-based AI ranked highest by predicted operating point but was heavily influenced by a single high-performing study. EHR-based and multimodal AI achieved the highest pooled AUROCs in smaller subgroup pools. The absence of within-study head-to-head modality comparisons precluded a formal diagnostic test accuracy network meta-analysis, necessitating an indirect comparison approach.
This is the first systematic review and meta-analysis to pool AI diagnostic test accuracy for PH across all input modalities. The findings support the potential utility of AI-based PH case finding while highlighting the need for prospective head-to-head modality comparisons conducted under TRIPOD-AI reporting standards and threshold-recalibration at primary-care prevalence levels.

title: A Hybrid AI-Meta-Analysis Framework for Irritable Bowel Syndrome Diagnosis: Development and Conflict-Zone Validation of a Low-Cost CBC-Based Tool
description:
This repository contains all data, code, and supplementary materials for the study "A Hybrid AI-Meta-Analysis Framework for Irritable Bowel Syndrome Diagnosis." This work addresses the critical global need for affordable, non-invasive diagnostic tools for Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), especially in low-resource and conflict-affected settings.

The study employs a novel three-phase hybrid design:
1. Phase 1 - Meta-Analysis: A comprehensive, PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis of 110 studies (n=43,250 participants) was conducted to establish the diagnostic utility of Complete Blood Count (CBC)-derived inflammatory markers (Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio (NLR), Mean Platelet Volume (MPV), Platelet-to-Lymphocyte Ratio (PLR)) in IBS, revealing significant subtype-specific effects.
2. Phase 2 - AI Model Development: An interpretable machine learning model (XGBoost) was developed on the harmonized global dataset, achieving an AUC of 0.89. Model interpretability was achieved using SHAP values, identifying NLR as the dominant predictor.
3. Phase 3 - Conflict-Zone Validation: The AI tool was prospectively validated in an independent cohort from Yemen (n=142), a active conflict zone, maintaining an AUC of 0.82. The study introduces and validates malaria-adjusted thresholds, achieving 88.6% specificity in endemic conditions, and demonstrates a 92% reduction in cost compared to colonoscopy.

This project provides one of the first diagnostically validated, conflict-resilient, and cost-effective diagnostic solutions for IBS, designed for deployment in the world's most challenging healthcare environments.

Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis of Artificial Intelligence Models for Classification of Cervical Cytology Images
description:
Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis of Artificial Intelligence Models for Classification of Cervical Cytology Images 

This study is designed as a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis to evaluate the pooled performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models for the classification of cervical cytology images. The protocol is developed in accordance with the PRISMA-DTA statement for reporting systematic reviews of diagnostic test accuracy studies (McInnes et al., 2018) and follows established methodological recommendations for DTA meta-analyses (Reitsma et al., 2005; Deeks et al., 2005; Whiting et al., 2011). 

Cervical cytology remains a cornerstone of cervical cancer screening worldwide. However, its diagnostic performance is affected by inter- and intra-observer variability, workload burden, and limited access to expert cytopathologists in resource-constrained settings. In recent years, machine learning and deep learning models have been increasingly applied to automated cytological image analysis. Although individual studies report high diagnostic performance, results vary substantially across datasets, validation strategies, and AI architectures. A quantitative synthesis of diagnostic accuracy using appropriate bivariate modeling is therefore required. 

The primary research question is: what is the pooled sensitivity and specificity of artificial intelligence-based models for detecting abnormal cervical cytology compared with expert cytopathological interpretation and/or histopathological confirmation? 

The review follows a Population–Index test–Reference standard–Target condition (PIRT) framework appropriate for DTA studies. The population includes cervical cytology images derived from Pap smear or liquid-based cytology samples obtained from women undergoing screening or diagnostic evaluation. The index test consists of artificial intelligence models designed for automated image classification, including traditional machine learning algorithms (e.g., support vector machines, random forest, gradient boosting methods) and deep learning architectures (e.g., convolutional neural networks, residual networks, EfficientNet, Vision Transformers, hybrid CNN–Transformer systems). The reference standard includes expert cytopathologist interpretation, typically based on the Bethesda System, and/or histopathological confirmation where available. 

The primary target condition will be defined as abnormal cytology versus normal cytology (NILM). Where studies report multi-class Bethesda categories, data will be harmonized to a binary framework. The preferred primary threshold will be ASC-US or higher versus NILM, reflecting screening-relevant abnormality detection. If harmonization to ASC-US+ is not feasible due to reporting structure, abnormal versus normal classification as defined by study authors will be used. A predefined sensitivity analysis will evaluate alternative thresholds (e.g., HSIL+ versus <HSIL) where sufficient data are available. 

Eligible studies include original diagnostic accuracy investigations evaluating AI-based models for classification of cervical cytology images and reporting sufficient information to derive 2×2 contingency tables (TP, FP, FN, TN), either directly or via sensitivity and specificity with class distribution. Only peer-reviewed journal publications in English will be included. Studies focused exclusively on HPV testing, colposcopy, or histological image analysis without cytological imaging will be excluded. Prognostic models, treatment-response prediction models, reviews, editorials, conference abstracts lacking full methodological detail, animal studies, and studies without extractable diagnostic performance metrics will also be excluded. Restriction to English-language peer-reviewed publications may introduce language and publication bias and will be acknowledged as a limitation. 

A systematic literature search will be conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar from database inception to 31 August 2025. Search strategies will combine cervical cytology–related terminology with artificial intelligence–related terminology, including controlled vocabulary and free-text terms. For Google Scholar, searches will be conducted on a single predefined date using fixed query strings, and screening will be limited to the first 300 results sorted by relevance to enhance reproducibility. Reference lists of eligible articles will be manually screened for additional studies. 

Study selection will be performed independently by two reviewers. Titles and abstracts will be screened first, followed by full-text evaluation against predefined eligibility criteria. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion and consensus. 

Data extraction will be conducted independently by two reviewers using a standardized extraction form. Extracted variables will include author, year, country, study design, dataset type (public versus proprietary), validation strategy (cross-validation, hold-out, external validation), analytical level (image-level, slide-level, or patient-level classification), AI model architecture, reference standard, decision threshold (if reported), and diagnostic performance metrics. 

When TP, FP, FN, and TN values are not explicitly reported, contingency tables will be reconstructed only if sensitivity, specificity, and class distribution (N_positive and N_negative) are clearly provided or can be unambiguously derived from the article. Reconstruction will follow the formulas: TP = round(Sensitivity × N_positive); FN = N_positive − TP; TN = round(Specificity × N_negative); FP = N_negative − TN. Nearest-integer rounding will be applied. Internal consistency checks will ensure agreement between reconstructed and reported performance metrics. Studies lacking sufficient information for reliable reconstruction will be excluded from quantitative synthesis and, if relevant, described narratively. Sensitivity analyses will assess the impact of reconstructed data on pooled estimates. 

Methodological quality and risk of bias will be assessed using QUADAS-2 (Whiting et al., 2011) across four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. Each domain will be evaluated for risk of bias and applicability concerns. 

For statistical synthesis, a bivariate random-effects meta-analysis based on the Reitsma model (Reitsma et al., 2005) will be used to jointly synthesize logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity while accounting for their correlation. Pooled sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals will be estimated. A summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve with confidence and prediction regions will be constructed. Diagnostic odds ratios and positive and negative likelihood ratios will also be calculated. Between-study heterogeneity will be primarily assessed using τ² estimates and prediction intervals; I² statistics for sensitivity and specificity will be reported as supplementary descriptive indicators. The expected range of diagnostic performance in future clinical settings will be quantified through prediction intervals. 

Predefined subgroup analyses will explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including dataset type (public versus proprietary), validation strategy (cross-validation versus external validation), analytical level (whole slide image versus patch-based analysis), and model category (machine learning versus deep learning). Meta-regression will assess the influence of continuous moderators such as sample size and year of publication. Publication bias will be evaluated using Deeks’ funnel plot asymmetry test (Deeks et al., 2005), recognizing its limitations in DTA meta-analyses. 

All statistical analyses will be conducted in R using established packages for diagnostic meta-analysis, including mada, meta, and metafor. Statistical significance will be defined as p < 0.05. 

At the time of registration, study identification, data extraction, and statistical analyses have been completed. The protocol is registered prior to journal submission to ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models as Classifiers (LLM-as-rater) for Hospital Incident Reports
description:
This research project evaluates the capability of five frontier Large Language Models (LLMs)—ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, and Mistral—to act as blinded classifiers ("LLM-as-rater") for hospital Incident Reporting (IR). The primary purpose is to assess whether these models can accurately replicate the classification tasks typically performed by human raters, relying exclusively on free-text narrative descriptions (e.g., "Where", "What happened", "How and why it happened", "Description") without access to prior structured human classifications.
The study is designed as an observational, retrospective agreement study based on a source dataset of 1,988 incident reports collected at the Policlinico di Bari (Italy) and its affiliated facilities between 2015 and 2025. To ensure robust evaluation on clinically and medico-legally relevant scenarios, the analysis is conducted on an extended sample of 824 cases. This sample combines a "discriminating core" of 624 difficult cases (which includes all severe harm events, deaths, and cases with inter-rater disagreement or reclassification) and a "population anchor" of 200 random, straightforward cases. Post-stratification weights are then applied to these strata to re-anchor the performance estimates to the real-world population distribution.
The project focuses on three main comparative evaluations:
AI vs. Expert Gold Standard: Measuring the agreement between the model's classification and the final expert consensus.
AI vs. Human Benchmark: Comparing the model's performance against the initial classification provided by the front-line professional who reported the event.
Algorithmovigilance (AI vs. AI): Analyzing cross-model agreement to determine if different models share the same systematic biases or correlated errors, effectively agreeing with each other more often than they agree with human experts.

The primary outcome is the level of agreement on the severity of harm, which is measured on a five-level ordinal scale. Secondary outcomes include:
Accuracy in identifying the specific event type across 16 controlled categories.
Triage capability, measured by the model's sensitivity and specificity in predicting whether a review of the Electronic Health Record (EHR) is necessary.
Confidence calibration, evaluated via the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) to see if a model's stated confidence aligns with its actual accuracy.
An indirect knowledge cutoff probe, testing whether models correctly apply an updated (July 2024) 23-item list of sentinel events from the Italian Ministry of Health instead of the legacy 16-item list.
Expected outcomes include a comprehensive framework for understanding LLM reliability in clinical risk management. The study aims to map specific AI failure modes—such as chronic overconfidence, over-reliance on medical records, or failure to update domain knowledge—and to provide empirical evidence on the phenomenon of "shared bias" among frontier models in a specialized medico-legal context.

title: Plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 in Cognitively Unimpaired Asian Individuals by Amyloid PET Status: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
This project is a systematic review and meta-analysis examining plasma biomarkers in relation to amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) status in cognitively unimpaired Asian individuals. The primary purpose of this study is to clarify the diagnostic utility of plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 for identifying amyloid PET positivity in this population. Secondary objectives are to evaluate between-group differences in biomarker levels according to amyloid PET status and to assess the performance of composite biomarker models, including p-tau217/Aβ42 and combined p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 models.

This project addresses an important evidence gap. Blood-based biomarkers are increasingly recognized as less invasive and more scalable alternatives to amyloid PET for detecting early Alzheimer’s disease pathology. However, most available evidence has been generated in predominantly non-Asian populations, and the performance of these biomarkers in cognitively unimpaired Asian individuals has not yet been comprehensively synthesized. In addition, the currently available literature is methodologically heterogeneous, including not only diagnostic accuracy studies reporting area under the curve (AUC) values, but also studies that permit only group-comparison analyses using standardized mean differences (SMDs). A systematic synthesis is therefore needed to clarify the current evidence base and to identify important sources of between-study variability.

Registration in PROSPERO had originally been planned. However, at the time of protocol development, the public PROSPERO registration system was not accepting new submissions under the diagnostic test accuracy review category. Therefore, this protocol was registered in OSF.

A systematic literature search will be conducted in CENTRAL, PubMed, and CINAHL from database inception to March 25, 2026, without language restrictions. Both published studies and gray literature will be considered. Studies will be considered eligible if they include cognitively unimpaired individuals from Asian populations, determine amyloid status using amyloid PET, and report plasma p-tau217, Aβ42/40, p-tau217/Aβ42, and/or composite biomarker models with sufficient data for quantitative synthesis. Both interventional and observational studies will be eligible; however, for interventional studies, only baseline data collected before treatment initiation will be used. Studies will be excluded if they include mixed populations without separate data for cognitively unimpaired individuals, use cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers only, report only covariate-adjusted diagnostic models without unadjusted performance metrics, include 20 or fewer cognitively unimpaired participants, or primarily enroll participants with major psychiatric, neurologic, or systemic disorders unrelated to cognitive impairment. Studies investigating the prognostic performance of plasma biomarkers for predicting future amyloid PET status will also be excluded, because the review focuses on cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy. When overlapping cohorts are reported across multiple publications using the same assay method, only the most comprehensive dataset will be retained. If the same cohort is evaluated using different assay platforms, each relevant dataset will be included.

Data extraction and risk of bias assessment will be performed by I.T. and independently checked by W.K. Any discrepancies will be resolved through discussion. Extracted variables will include author, publication year, country, cohort name, sample size, age, biomarker assay method, study setting, amyloid PET positivity criterion, area under the curve (AUC), 95% confidence interval (CI), standard error (SE), and summary statistics required for the calculation of standardized mean differences (SMDs). Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value will not be quantitatively synthesized because these metrics are strongly influenced by threshold selection and assay variability and are therefore expected to show substantial heterogeneity. Accordingly, AUC will be used as the primary measure of diagnostic performance. When required data are missing, corresponding authors will be contacted by email. If no reply is received within 1 week, SEs for AUC values lacking reported 95% CIs will be estimated using the method of Hanley and McNeil, and 95% CIs will subsequently be calculated as AUC ± 1.96 × SE. When the mean and standard deviation needed for SMD analyses are unavailable, they will be estimated from the median and interquartile range using the methods proposed by Luo et al. and Wan et al.

Because the literature relevant to this clinical question is limited, studies that are not designed as pure diagnostic accuracy studies, as well as studies that do not report AUC and are therefore eligible only for the SMD analysis, may still be included. For this reason, risk of bias will be evaluated using the AXIS tool, which is suitable for a broader range of observational studies, rather than QUADAS-2, which is designed specifically for diagnostic accuracy studies. AXIS has also been used in previous meta-analyses of plasma biomarkers.

Data will be synthesized using frequentist random-effects meta-analysis with the “meta” and “metafor” packages in R (version 4.2.5). Pooled AUC analyses will be conducted to assess the ability of plasma biomarkers to distinguish amyloid PET-positive individuals from amyloid PET-negative individuals. The primary analyses will consist of separate meta-analyses of plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40. Secondary analyses will include pooled standardized mean differences between amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative groups for p-tau217 and Aβ42/40, together with pooled AUC analyses of composite biomarkers, including p-tau217/Aβ42 and combined p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 models. For SMD analyses, Hedges g will be used as the effect size. Subgroup analyses will consist of separate pooled AUC analyses for p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 according to assay platform, country, amyloid PET positivity definition, and study setting, provided that at least two studies are available within each subgroup. Statistical heterogeneity will be quantified using the I² statistic. Publication bias will be assessed when at least 10 studies are available for a given analysis.

The expected outcomes of this project are a quantitative summary of the diagnostic accuracy of plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 for amyloid PET status in cognitively unimpaired Asian individuals, an estimate of between-group biomarker differences according to amyloid PET status, and an assessment of the performance of relevant composite biomarker models. More broadly, this project is expected to clarify the current evidence base in Asian populations, identify important sources of heterogeneity across studies, and provide useful information for the design of future validation studies and potential clinical implementation of blood-based biomarkers for preclinical Alzheimer’s disease.

title: SALIVARY BIOMARKERS OF DISEASE PROGRESSION IN SJÖGREN’S SYNDROME: A SCOPING REVIEW
description: This protocol details a scoping review aimed at mapping and synthesizing the available scientific evidence on salivary biomarkers associated with disease progression in Sjögren's Syndrome (SjS). SjS is a complex systemic autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by progressive lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands, which causes glandular hypofunction and debilitating oral and ocular dryness. While clinical monitoring has traditionally depended on invasive minor salivary gland biopsies, saliva serves as a promising, non-invasive biological matrix capable of providing real-time molecular insights into SjS activity and damage trajectories. Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines , the review utilizes a strict PCC strategy targeting patients with primary or secondary SjS (Population), salivary biomarkers associated with disease activity and progression (Concept), and any clinical or laboratory setting (Context). Primary observational and experimental human studies published in English, Portuguese, or Spanish will be included , whereas letters, editorial opinions, reviews, in vitro or animal models, and studies focusing solely on initial diagnostic accuracy without progression data will be excluded. Systematic literature searches will be executed across major databases, including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Two independent reviewers will handle study selection and data extraction using Rayyan software, with any discrepancies resolved by a senior third reviewer. Finally, the extracted data will undergo both qualitative and quantitative synthesis using descriptive statistics to effectively highlight current research trends, and the clinical translational potential of these salivary biomarkers from the laboratory bench to point-of-care applications.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Digital Scanning Compared to Traditional Methods in Dental Alignment Assessment: A Systematic Review
description:
PROBLEM FORMULATION

This study aims to answer the following question, structured by PICO: In patients 
requiring dental alignment assessment (P), is the use of digital scanning (I) more 
accurate in assessing dental alignment compared to traditional methods, such as 
physical impressions and clinical examinations (O), when considering diagnostic 
accuracy (O)?

HYPOTHESIS

The hypothesis of this study is that the digital scanning method will demonstrate 
superior diagnostic accuracy in assessing dental alignment compared to traditional methods such as physical impressions and clinical examinations. It is assumed that digital scanning will provide a more precise and detailed assessment of dental alignment, resulting in more accurate diagnoses for patients.

OBJECTIVE

This study aims to investigate, through a systematic review of the literature, the 
diagnostic accuracy of digital scanning compared to traditional methods in the 
assessment of dental alignment. The systematic review will seek to compare the 
effectiveness of using digital scanning with traditional methods, such as physical molds and clinical examinations, in patients who require dental alignment 
assessment, with emphasis on diagnostic accuracy.

METHODS

The systematic review will be conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021). The PICOT elements defined for this study are: population, patients requiring dental alignment assessment; intervention, use of digital scanning for dental alignment assessment; comparison, traditional methods of dental alignment assessment, such as physical impressions and clinical examinations; outcome, diagnostic accuracy in dental alignment assessment; and study type, clinical trial.
The study design will include conducting a systematic search of international 
databases to identify relevant studies published to date. Clear inclusion and 
exclusion criteria will be defined to select studies that meet the objectives of the 
review. Retrieval and extraction of detailed information and data from the included studies will be performed using standardized data collection criteria.
The synthesis of the main findings of the included studies will be performed using 
qualitative methods as appropriate. The results will be summarized following the 
PRISMA guidelines. This method will ensure a rigorous and comprehensive 
assessment of the diagnostic accuracy of digital scanning compared to traditional 
methods in the assessment of dental alignment.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA

Only clinical trials that compare digital planning with analogue planning in the 
assessment of dental alignment will be included. Descriptive studies, systematic 
reviews, case reports and in vitro studies will be excluded. In addition, studies that do not use traditional methods of dental alignment assessment, such as physical molds and clinical examinations. Studies investigating alternative technologies or methods that are not directly related to digital or analog planning will also be excluded. The search will be restricted to articles published in English, available in full, with no date limit.

SEARCH

A systematic literature search will be performed in the following databases: 
MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library and SciELO. Grey literature will also be considered by searching Google Scholar. The search strategy will be based on MeSH terms from PubMed and adapted for other databases. Rayyan software (Rayyan Systems Inc., Cambridge, MA, USA) will be used for the systematic search. Four independent researchers (FMM, GSEC, IBAQ and LFA) will screen the records (titles/abstracts) and select studies that meet all eligibility criteria for full-text reading. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or by the opinion of a fifth reviewer (NSF).

DATA EXTRACTION

Four authors (FMM, GSEC, IBAQ and LFA) used a spreadsheet to extract the methodological data of the study. The extracted variables included: author, year of publication, details of the digital scanning procedure (type of scanner, software used), details of the traditional evaluation methods (type of physical mold, clinical examinations) and outcome (diagnostic accuracy).

QUALITY ASSESSMENT AND RISK OF BIAS

The methodological quality and risk of bias of the included studies will be assessed using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa scale, whose evaluation criteria will include the adequacy of randomization, allocation concealment, and population characterization at selection; comparability of groups at baseline and control of confounding factors in comparability; and blinding of outcome assessment, adequate outcome measurement, and complete follow-up at outcome. Each criterion will be scored, and studies will be classified as high, moderate, or low risk of bias based on the total score, with a score of 7 to 9 points considered low risk of bias, a score of 4 to 6 points considered moderate risk of bias, and a score of 0 to 3 points considered high risk of bias.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy, Acceptability, and Clinical Deployability of AI-Enabled, Home-Based, and Wearable Testing for Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description: Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea is commonly diagnosed using polysomnography, but access to laboratory-based polysomnography is limited by cost, availability, travel burden, and child/family acceptability. Emerging home-based sleep apnea testing, wearable sensors, non-contact monitoring, and artificial intelligence-enabled diagnostic algorithms may support lower-burden diagnosis, triage, or follow-up in children. This systematic review will synthesize the patient-level diagnostic accuracy of AI-enabled, home-based, wearable, and other low-burden objective diagnostic technologies for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea compared with polysomnography. We will also examine acceptability, technical failure, external validation, and clinical deployability.

title: Evaluation of Diagnostic Tests for Canine Ehrlichiosis in Latin America: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (2010–2025)
description: Canine ehrlichiosis is a disease caused by Gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria, primarily transmitted by the tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus (Vieira et al., 2011). Ehrlichia canis infection can occur in dogs regardless of sex or age; however, some studies suggest a predisposition in certain breeds, as well as greater susceptibility in immunocompromised individuals, such as puppies and geriatric animals (Jane E. Sykes, 2023). This systematic review aims to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of the main tests used for the diagnosis of E. canis in dogs, based on studies that adopt a reference standard. To date, there are no published systematic reviews on the diagnostic accuracy of this disease, particularly in the context of Latin America. This systematic review will follow the PRISMA-DTA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies) guidelines (McInnes et al., 2018; Salameh et al., 2020), with a focus on diagnostic accuracy studies. The eligibility criteria were defined based on the PICOS framework (Population, Index test, Comparator, Outcome, Study design). The search will cover studies addressing diagnostic methods for canine ehrlichiosis in Latin American populations. Reviewers will conduct a systematic search in relevant databases. Study selection, screening, and data extraction will be performed using the Rayyan QCRI tool. The methodological quality of the included studies will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) tool, as recommended for systematic reviews of diagnostic accuracy(Whiting et al., 2011). Extracted data will be analyzed and synthesized descriptively, aiming to map existing evidence and highlight gaps in the literature. The results will be presented through infographics, tables, and charts to facilitate visualization of the findings.

title: Systematic Review on Sexual Dimorphism by Tomographic Analysis of the Orbital Region
description:
This systematic review protocol aims to evaluate the presence and degree of sexual dimorphism in the orbital region through morphometric and morphological analyses obtained from computed tomography (CT) images. The orbital cavity is increasingly being investigated in forensic anthropology due to its resistance to trauma and its potential to exhibit sex-based anatomical variations.
The review will include cross-sectional studies that assessed adult individuals using CT imaging, reporting either linear orbital measurements (e.g., height, width, interorbital distance) or morphological descriptors relevant to sex estimation. When available, measures of diagnostic accuracy—such as sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and area under the ROC curve—will be extracted and synthesized. Odds ratios (ORs) will be used as the primary effect measure for associations between orbital metrics and sex classification.
A comprehensive search will be conducted in eight international databases and grey literature sources. Risk of bias will be assessed using the AQUA tool (Anatomical Quality Assessment). Where feasible, a meta-analysis will be performed using a random-effects model, and heterogeneity will be explored through subgroup analyses, particularly considering sex, age group, and population.
This protocol was developed following best practices for systematic reviews and incorporates key methodological refinements based on existing high-impact literature in forensic and anatomical sciences. The findings are expected to contribute robust evidence for the development of sex estimation models based on orbital morphology and morphometry.

title: Hearing screening in older adults with diabetes: identifying the most reliable methods
description: This project is a systematic review aimed at identifying, describing, and comparing hearing screening methods used in older adults with diabetes mellitus, assessing their diagnostic accuracy and effectiveness for early detection of hearing loss. Hearing loss is a common yet often underdiagnosed condition among older adults with diabetes, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Given the association between diabetes and microvascular and neuropathic changes that affect auditory function, effective screening is essential for timely intervention and improved quality of life. The review will follow strict eligibility criteria and draw on multiple databases (including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and LILACS), with methodological quality assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. The findings are expected to support the identification of the most reliable and feasible hearing screening methods for this specific population, contributing to improved auditory health care practices.

title: Accuracy of the Autism Spectrum Quotient in Identifying Autism
description:
The Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) for use in screening and as part of the assessment process for adults suspected of being autistic. However, most psychometric evidence for the 50‑item AQ and its shorter forms comes from case–control studies, in which autistic and non‑autistic participants are recruited in advance based on known diagnostic status. This design inflates estimates of sensitivity, specificity, and overall diagnostic accuracy, because the contrast between groups is artificially maximised and does not reflect the uncertainty present in real clinical pathways.

To inform policy and clinical practice more reliably, there is a need to evaluate the AQ in clinically relevant study designs, where diagnostic status is not known at the point of questionnaire completion, and where participants more closely resemble those encountered in primary care, mental health services, or specialist autism referral pathways. This systematic review and meta-analysis will synthesise psychometric evidence under these conditions to provide a more accurate understanding of how well different AQ versions perform when used for screening in routine practice.
