title: Data collection and analysis from the Informatics Department of the Unified Health System in Brazil, using open source programming languages: a scoping review
description:
1 INTRODUCTION
The consolidation of the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) brought with it the need to develop instruments capable of recording, organizing, and providing information to support health management (Lima et al., 2009). Since its creation, SUS has required information systems capable of consolidating data in a structured and standardized manner, supporting both epidemiological surveillance and health planning. In this process, the Department of Informatics of SUS (DATASUS) assumed a strategic role by gathering, processing, and providing nationwide data, becoming one of the main sources of information for managers, researchers, and health professionals (Brazil, 2020a).
The availability of reliable and accessible data is a central requirement for public policy formulation, indicator evaluation, and the development of research in public health (Costa et al., 2025). However, the use of these databases still faces challenges related to the decentralization of sources, heterogeneity of records, data quality, and periodic system updates, which may limit their applicability in more complex analyses (Brazil, 2020a).
To overcome these limitations, the National Health Information and Informatics Policy (PNIIS) and the Digital Health Strategy for Brazil 2020–2028 (ESD28) have established guidelines focused on information governance, interoperability, and strengthening the technological infrastructure of SUS (Brazil, 2020b).
Established in 2004, the PNIIS defined principles for the use of Information and Communication Technologies within SUS, emphasizing the integration of national information systems, improvement of data quality, and strengthening of health management (Brazil, 2004). These guidelines were later updated to incorporate goals related to interoperability and information governance (Brazil, 2021).
Among the structuring initiatives for the modernization of SUS, the National Health Data Network (RNDS) stands out as a central platform integrating information from different systems and levels of care, promoting interoperability and providing essential data to support decision-making. Other initiatives include SUS Digital, through the “Meu SUS Digital” tool, and the PQDAS Program, which standardizes and improves the quality of supplementary health data in alignment with SUS data (Brazil; Ministry of Health; Secretariat of Digital Health Information, 2024).
The adoption of digital technologies not only modernizes infrastructure but also transforms the interaction between citizens, professionals, and managers, increasing efficiency and integration of care. This approach represents the evolution of the concept of eHealth, expanding the use of digital resources beyond service informatization. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data, telemedicine, wearable devices, and mobile applications have been used to improve management, access, and quality of care (World Health Organization, 2021).
According to the Ministry of Health (Brazil, 2020a), DATASUS integrates systems covering various areas of health care, such as the Hospital Information System (SIH), Ambulatory Information System (SIA), Mortality Information System (SIM), Live Birth Information System (SINASC), and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN), among others.
Despite the breadth of these databases, challenges persist regarding data quality, updating, standardization, and interoperability, which may limit reliable analyses and evidence-based decision-making. Ensuring efficient integration among systems is essential so that managers and professionals have access to consistent and up-to-date information.
Data collection and management in Brazil are directly linked to PNIIS and ESD28. While PNIIS establishes standards for organization, integration, and governance of health information, ESD28 defines priorities for digital technology use, including interoperability, professional training, and innovation. The articulation between these initiatives allows DataSUS data to be used strategically at different management levels (Brazil, 2020b; Costa et al., 2025).
Access to public health data in Brazil has advanced significantly, even before the Access to Information Law (LAI) came into effect in 2012. Tools such as TabNet and TabWin, developed by DATASUS, enable the creation of tables, graphs, and indicators to support epidemiological analyses (Saldanha et al., 2019; Silva, 2009). TabNet allows quick tabulations from public data, while TabWin enables microdata import and spatial representations.
Despite their usefulness, these tools have operational limitations, require specific training, and demand repetition of procedures for each new period analyzed. In this context, programming code emerges as an alternative to automate, speed up, and standardize data collection and processing.
The increased availability of SUS microdata, combined with the expansion of digital health tools, has driven the adoption of open-source programming languages for data manipulation and analysis (Costa et al., 2025). These languages enhance scientific reproducibility, integration with public databases, and automation of complex analyses such as risk modeling and time series (Wilson et al., 2014).
Despite these advances, there is a knowledge gap regarding systematic mapping of the use of open-source programming specifically applied to DATASUS. While isolated studies exist, comprehensive discussions of methods and tools remain scarce. The scoping review by Restrepo et al. (2023) on open health datasets in Latin America highlights this gap.
Although DataSUS has consolidated itself as a national repository, challenges such as heterogeneity, lack of standardization, variable data quality, and integration difficulties between systems still limit reproducibility.
At the same time, there is growing use of open-source programming in health data science. However, a systematic mapping is needed to identify how these tools are applied to DataSUS, which methods are used, and which gaps remain.
The absence of this overview hinders the consolidation of best practices and the development of more accessible technological solutions. Therefore, conducting a scoping review to systematize existing knowledge is necessary to support open science, improve public health analyses, and strengthen evidence-based decision-making within SUS.

2 OBJECTIVE
To map the evidence in the scientific literature on the use of open-source programming for the collection and analysis of data from Brazilian Health Information Systems.

3 METHOD
3.1 Study Design
This study consists of a scoping review, characterized as applied research with a technological development approach. The review will be conducted in accordance with the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses – Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), aiming to ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and greater detail in the conduct and reporting of the study.
3.2 Data Sources
The databases selected for this review are: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, LILACS, BVS (Virtual Health Library), Google Scholar, and the Brazilian Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations (BDTD). 
The choice of these databases is justified by their relevance to the topic, coverage of high-quality journals, and multidisciplinary scope. While databases such as PubMed, Embase, and LILACS are specialized in health and biomedical sciences, Scopus and Web of Science provide a multidisciplinary perspective, and IEEE Xplore contributes the necessary technical focus for topics related to programming and data analysis. Searches will also be conducted in Google Scholar and BDTD to capture gray literature not indexed in journal databases.
3.3 Identifying the Research Question 
The first step consists of formulating a well-focused research question, with the objective of mapping what has already been published on the use of open-source programming languages and tools in the context of DATASUS, as well as identifying potential gaps in the existing literature. 
Research question: What evidence is available in the literature on the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and analysis of DATASUS data? 
Based on this guiding question, it will be possible to identify the most commonly used open-source programming languages for the collection and analysis of DATASUS data, recognize the libraries, frameworks, or tools frequently employed in these processes, and understand the main methods and techniques used for data collection, extraction, and analysis. Moreover, through this scoping review, it will be possible to map the key challenges reported in the literature regarding the use of open-source programming for working with DATASUS data, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of the topic.
3.4 Identifying the Most Significant Terms in the Question
To identify the most relevant terms present in the research question, a concept mapping was carried out a structured methodology aimed at identifying and organizing the key elements of a research question. The objective of concept mapping is to translate the identified concepts into search terms (keywords and controlled descriptors), which will be used in databases. This approach is essential to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive, precise, and aligned with the research objectives, being especially useful in systematic reviews, scoping reviews, and other types of literature reviews.
From this research question, the main elements identified were: terms related to open-source programming languages, data collection, extraction, analysis, and DataSUS. To structure the search strategy, the PCC (Population, Concept, and Context) framework was used, which best represents the components of the research. This structuring allows for a more targeted and efficient search, ensuring that the results obtained are aligned with the research objectives and cover the essential aspects of the investigated topic, as presented in Table 1 describing the PCC strategy.


The process of mapping and refining terms, using the main term and the translation of terms between DeCS (Health Sciences Descriptors) and MeSH (Medical Subject Headings), is a robust methodological approach to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive and precise, facilitating the retrieval of articles in bibliographic databases. 
3.5 Search Strategy
The search terms will be defined based on subject descriptors from the databases using the Health Sciences Descriptors (DeCS) and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). 
The search strategies were adapted for each database, using controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR). The construction of the search strategy was carried out in two steps: first, the terms related to each concept were combined using the Boolean operator OR (e.g., “Programming Languages” OR “Python Programming” OR “R Programming”) to ensure search comprehensiveness. Next, the groups of terms were combined with each other using the Boolean operator AND (e.g., [Group 1] AND [Group 2] AND [Group 3] AND [Group 4]), ensuring the precision and relevance of the results. The entire process was conducted using the PubMed Advanced Search tool (available at: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/advanced/). 
No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date, in order to ensure broad and inclusive coverage of the literature. 
These strategies were adapted to improve the sensitivity and specificity of the searches while maintaining the same framework initially established in the strategy developed for PubMed. The combination of terms, based on controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR), resulted in the following search strategies for each database, as presented in the appendices of this work through Table 2: Search Strategy in Databases.


3.6 Selection Process
Publications identified through the descriptors will be exported to the Rayyan application for duplicate removal and selection of articles/documents based on eligibility criteria, followed by full-text review and data extraction.
Studies addressing the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and/or analysis of DataSUS data will be included. Documents describing data extraction methods from other information sources or systems will be excluded from the sample.
3.7 Data Management and Analysis
Both the selection process through title and abstract screening and full-text review, and the data extraction will be carried out by two researchers. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus.
Due to the heterogeneity of the documents to be analyzed, quality assessment will be performed only for scientific articles indexed in databases, using the AGREE II instrument.
Data will be stored using the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) software.

3.8 Ethical Considerations and Conflicts of Interest
In accordance with Brazilian Resolutions No. 466 of December 12, 2012, and No. 510 of April 7, 2016, this study is exempt from review by a Research Ethics Committee (REC). There are no conflicts of interest in this protocol. 
4 EXPECTED RESULTS
The scoping review will comprehensively map the scientific production related to the use of open-source programming languages applied to DataSUS, identifying the state of the art in the collection, processing, and analysis of data from Brazil’s national health information systems. It is expected to characterize the types of published studies, application contexts, the most explored SUS information systems, and the predominant methodological approaches, providing a consolidated overview of current practices in the field. The use of open-source code enables researchers and developers to access and contribute to the improvement of tools. Well-developed code supports efficient data integration and analysis, accelerating the development of new solutions tailored to community needs.
In addition, the review will enable the identification of the main tools, languages, and libraries used to handle SUS microdata, including Python, R, and other open-source resources. This characterization will allow an assessment of the accessibility, documentation, and reproducibility of existing solutions, contributing to an understanding of how these technologies have been applied in research and health management.
The mapping process is also expected to reveal gaps in the literature, such as the lack of methodological standardization, limitations in interoperability between systems, scarcity of automated tools, and insufficient studies addressing integration across different DataSUS databases. Identifying these gaps will provide guidance for the development of new technological solutions and for shaping future research agendas.
The review will further systematize the methodologies employed in the analyzed studies, describing strategies for data collection, preprocessing, statistical analysis, modeling, and data visualization. This systematization will help compare manual and automated approaches, highlighting best practices, limitations, and opportunities for improvement in the use of public health data.
From the perspective of management and public policy, the expected results include demonstrating the potential of open-source tools to enhance transparency, efficiency, and reproducibility in epidemiological and administrative analyses. The review should show how automation in data collection and processing can support managers, researchers, and SUS professionals in evidence-based decision-making.
Finally, the study is expected to produce a consolidated, up-to-date, and replicable body of knowledge capable of supporting the development of new technologies, guiding training processes, and strengthening open science in the context of Brazilian public health.
In the future, it is expected that these tools will become more accessible, customizable, and user-friendly, increasing transparency in analyses. This will enable more robust studies aligned with the needs of health professionals and researchers. Additionally, new methodologies may be developed to handle large-scale data, optimizing the use of DataSUS for epidemiological analyses, outbreak prediction, and public policy evaluation using big data technologies.

description:
# Offline-First Mobile OCR and FHIR Interoperability for Bedside Vital Sign Digitisation in Geriatric Care under Power and Network Constraints: A Ghanaian District Hospital Study

**Author:** Titus Afeo Azure Aduku, BSN, RN 
**Affiliation:** Department of Nursing, Tatale District Hospital, Ghana Health Service, P. O. Box YD 9, Tatale, Northern Region, Ghana 
**Corresponding Email:** titusafeoazureaduku@gmail.com 

---

## Abstract

### Background
Manual transcription of bedside vital signs in resource-limited district hospitals across Sub-Saharan Africa is slow, error-prone, and burdensome for health personnel. Although digital health platforms offer potential solutions, existing cloud-based artificial intelligence (AI) and optical character recognition (OCR) systems consistently fail in remote border facilities due to frequent power blackouts, cross-border network dropouts, high API costs, and strict data privacy regulations (e.g., Ghana's Data Protection Act, 2012 [Act 843] and Cybersecurity Act, 2020 [Act 1038]). Furthermore, human expert usability testing of mobile health (mHealth) applications remains unscalable due to severe clinical workforce shortages.

### Objective
To design, benchmark, and validate an offline-first mobile clinical OCR pipeline that digitizes paper-based vital sign charts on low-cost commodity hardware into standardized Health Level Seven Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (HL7 FHIR R4) `Observation` payloads mapped to Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes (LOINC), and to evaluate its interface usability using a local, automated Large Language Model (LLM)-as-a-Judge framework.

### Methods
We benchmarked an edge-computing OCR pipeline (combining local OpenCV image filtering and Google ML Kit text recognition) on physical bedside tablet hardware (Samsung SM-X210: Qualcomm Snapdragon 695 5G, 4 GB RAM) and a throttled single-core ARM Cortex-A53 virtual device emulator representing entry-level smartphones ($\le \$130\text{ USD}$). Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated across a validated dataset of $N = 250$ distorted clinical vital sign charts derived from the open-access VitalDB repository. Extracted parameters (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature) were converted into HL7 FHIR R4 JSON payloads, bound to standard LOINC codes, and validated using the HAPI FHIR Engine. User interface usability was evaluated locally using an offline quantized model (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) scored against Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics and validated against gold-standard expert human benchmarks. Resilience to power outages was tested across 50 off-grid "Ward-to-OPD" deferred batch-synchronization scenarios using 256-bit AES-encrypted local SQLite queues.

### Results
The on-device OCR pipeline achieved a mean processing latency of $120.30\text{ ms}$ ($\text{SD} = \pm 24.16\text{ ms}$) on physical tablet hardware and $243.80\text{ ms}$ ($\text{SD} = \pm 54.39\text{ ms}$) under single-core emulation. Automated OCR charting significantly outperformed manual keyboard entry speed ($t_{249} = 103.50, p < 0.001$; Wilcoxon $W = 31380, p < 0.001$). The pipeline yielded an overall Character Error Rate (CER) of $0.8\%$ ($0.008$), with minimal Mean Absolute Errors:

* **Systolic BP MAE:** $0.428\text{ mmHg}$
* **Diastolic BP MAE:** $0.288\text{ mmHg}$
* **Heart Rate MAE:** $0.192\text{ bpm}$
* **Respiratory Rate MAE:** $0.116\text{ breaths/min}$
* **Temperature MAE:** $0.015^\circ\text{C}$

All generated JSON payloads ($250/250, 100.0\%, p = 1.000$) achieved full HL7 FHIR R4 schema compliance and correct LOINC terminology bindings. The local Llama-3-8B judge model demonstrated strong agreement with human expert ratings ($r = 0.840, p < 0.001$), achieving $87.20\%$ classification accuracy ($\text{F1} = 0.729$, Cohen’s $\kappa = 0.645$, Krippendorff’s $\alpha = 0.646$, $\chi^2_1 = 104.60, p < 0.001$). Over off-grid blackout periods averaging $12.15\text{ hours}$ (accumulating up to 115 queued records per device), the physical deferred sync protocol achieved a $100.0\%$ record preservation rate ($0\%$ data loss) with a mean batch upload latency of $3.738\text{ seconds}$.

### Conclusions
On-device OCR combined with local rule-based FHIR parsing enables rapid, highly accurate, and fully offline bedside vital sign digitization on commodity mobile hardware, eliminating transcription errors while maintaining interoperability with central electronic medical record systems. Executing all computations on-device bypasses electrical grid and network failures, eliminates recurring mobile data fees, and guarantees statutory data sovereignty under national cybersecurity and privacy laws. Furthermore, localized LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation provides a zero-cost, privacy-preserving, and human-aligned software quality auditing mechanism for continuous mHealth optimization in resource-constrained healthcare environments.

---

**Keywords:** Optical Character Recognition; Edge AI; HL7 FHIR R4; LOINC; Vital Signs; Offline-First mHealth; LLM-as-a-Judge; Usability Heuristics; Data Sovereignty; Sub-Saharan Africa.

The Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Identifying Cephalometric Landmarks: A Scoping Review
description:
Background: Manual identification of cephalometric landmarks is time-consuming and susceptible to human error. Artificial intelligence (AI) can automate this task, potentially improving efficiency, consistency, and diagnostic accuracy.
Aim: To evaluate the accuracy and reliability of AI algorithms for automated cephalometric landmark identification.
Methods: This scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, EMBASE, and Medline were searched up till April 2024, yielding 68 eligible studies. Extracted data included datasets used, number of landmarks assessed and expert examiners involved, AI algorithms, and accuracy metrics.
Results: The included studies collectively analysed approximately 450,000 lateral cephalograms, often using the IEEE ISBI Grand Challenge 2015 dataset, with most algorithms using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Several AI models demonstrated accuracy comparable to human experts (within 2 mm), whereas others had variable performance. However, heterogeneity in study design, dataset quality, and reporting limited the generalisability of the findings.

title: AI stridor analysis
description:
Objective: This review examines artificial intelligence (AI) applications in analyzing respiratory sounds, specifically stridor, to address limitations in traditional, operator-dependent diagnostic methods. 

Data Sources: A structured search across PubMed, Scopus, and Ovid was conducted, focusing on studies from 2010 to 2024 relevant to AI and stridor detection. 

Review Methods: The review synthesizes findings from studies employing machine learning (ML) models like Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Support Vector Machines (SVM) to enhance stridor diagnosis by analyzing respiratory sound patterns. 

Results: The reviewed studies demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy, with models such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) and Personalized Federated Learning with Self-Distillation (PFL-SD) achieving accuracies up to 100% and 96.1%, respectively. AI techniques showed potential to classify stridor types, identify anatomical locations of obstructions, and guide clinical decision-making, particularly in pediatric cases requiring prompt intervention. 

Conclusion: AI-driven respiratory sound analysis offers promising advancements in stridor diagnosis through improved accuracy and early detection, though limitations in data standardization and underexplored pediatric applications present challenges and opportunities. Future research on larger, standardized datasets could expand the potential of AI tools in this critical clinical setting.

title: Automated Data Extraction from PDFs Using a Multi-Stage, Large Language Model-Enabled Process: A Proof-of-Concept Study
description:
Objective
The objective of this study is to compare automated data extraction using a multi-stage, LLM-enabled process with a conventional, human-led data-extraction approach. Specifically, we aim to evaluate the accuracy metrics and error types associated with each process.
Research Questions
1. What is the comparative accuracy of an automated, multi-stage, LLM-enabled evidence extraction process versus a conventional, human-only data extraction approach?
2. How do types and distribution of errors compare between the two approaches?
Methods 
Study design: We will use a validation study design within a diagnostic test accuracy framework to evaluate the performance of a multi-stage, automated, LLM-enabled evidence extraction process against a reference standard.
Sample size: Our study sample will consist of randomized and nonrandomized studies drawn from three rapid reviews. Because this is an exploratory study, we will not conduct a formal sample size calculation.
Selection of source studies: To avoid any risk of data contamination, we will use three rapid reviews, which have been completed but not yet published. The topics of the rapid reviews focus on 1) the efficacy and harms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines[8], 2) the efficacy and harms of coronavirus disease (COVID)-19 vaccines[9], and 3) values and preferences of patients receiving pharmacologic and psychologic treatments for chronic insomnia.[10] Together, these rapid reviews encompass a broad range of study designs (e.g., randomized trials, nonrandomized studies of interventions, qualitative studies) and outcomes (e.g., categorical, continuous, patient-reported measures). 
Conventional human-led data extraction [Refence Standard]: Data for the rapid reviews were extracted by a single investigator and checked for correctness and completeness by a second, senior reviewer. Data elements include 1) Study characteristics (e.g., registration number, first author); 2) Characteristics of study participants (e.g., mean age, inclusion/exclusion criteria); 3) Numerical data related to participant flow (e.g., number of randomized individuals overall and per study group); 4) Outcome data (e.g., the proportion of individuals experiencing an event, or rankings of values and preferences).
Automated data extraction: 
For automated data extraction, we will use a 6-step multi-stage, LLM-enabled evidence extraction process. It begins by using an external parsing service, Landing AI (https://landing.ai/), to parse Portable Document Format (PDF) files of study publications (Step 1), then employs an LLM—specifically Google Gemini 3 Pro, though the architecture supports other models—to extract data and information from a study report (i.e., the main study reporting article or ‘index’ article) and any associated study supplements, appendices, and related companion articles (i.e., publications or study registrations reporting information related to the index article) (Step 2). The system links these supplementary data to the main index article (Step 3) and, to improve recall, conducts multiple runs of the extraction step (Step 4). Step 5 uses a voting algorithm to identify the most frequent value extracted for each data point across the multiple data extraction runs, and exports these values into the final dataset for comparison with the reference standard (Step 6).
Data management: A data manager will oversee the data collection process. The data manager will receive completed tasks, verify data completeness, perform data cleaning as needed, and organize outputs into standardized formats to enable comparison between data extraction approaches. We will store data electronically in Excel datasheets. All investigators will have access to the data. The final LLM prompts, model configuration settings, and human- and model generated data extractions will be saved and shared as part of dissemination. Likewise, we will make the final data available upon request. 
Adjudication panel: The data manager will compile a single standardized sheet containing the outputs of both data extraction approaches, with group identifiers removed, and submit it to the adjudication panel. The credibility of any validation study depends on the quality of its reference standard. Because human data extraction is error-prone, an adjudicated ground truth is required. The adjudication panel will resolve disagreements between automated and human data extraction to determine the most accurate information for each data point. This adjudicated reference standard will then serve as the ground truth for calculating performance metrics.
To avoid bias for or against the automation tool, the adjudication process will be blinded. The panel will include senior members of the team who were not involved in conducting the rapid reviews. Adjudication panelist tasks will first assess whether data are concordant between the two approaches. We define concordance as ‘the proportion of data items that are factually congruent between the two methods, regardless of differences in style or presentation’.[11] Data elements that are concordant will be assumed to reflect accurately extracted data compared with the ground truth. Next, panelists will adjudicate discordant data elements between the two approaches by consulting the original source documents to establish the ‘ground truth’. Both data extractions will then be recompared against the ground truth to determine whether an error is present. Lastly, the panelists will judge the severity of errors in terms of their potential impact on review results and conclusions. A second adjudicator will review any discordances flagged by the first adjudicator and will either accept the first adjudicator’s determinations or engage in dialogue to come to a consensus determination. Every final decision about the presence and severity of an error, together with the supporting rationale, will be documented to ensure a transparent and auditable trail. 
Performance Metrics: Outcomes of interest include:
• Accuracy metrics (accuracy, recall, precision, F1-score). In the context of data extraction, accuracy refers to the proportion of data items that are either correctly extracted or correctly identified as unavailable. To calculate these performance metrics, we will use the ground truth as the reference standard.
• Concordance. We will use percent agreement rather than kappa statistics, as chance agreement is minimal when extractors rely directly on source material.
• Error Analysis. We will determine the types of errors (e.g., missed data, unsupported data) and the potential severity of errors. 

Ethical and Privacy Considerations. 
The study is solely aimed at advancing knowledge and understanding in the field of AI-based data extraction, without involving any human subjects or sensitive data. Therefore, ethical considerations and associated procedures are not applicable for this research. We will use an LLM that does not train on uploaded PDFs or user interactions unless explicitly permitted, ensuring that the intellectual property rights of copyrighted study reports are fully respected.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Post-Treatment Circulating Tumor DNA for Minimal Residual Disease Detection in Early-Stage Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy
description:
This project contains the prespecified protocol for a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis evaluating the performance of post-treatment circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for minimal residual disease (MRD) detection in early-stage breast cancer (stage I–III).

The review follows PRISMA-DTA guidelines and applies a bivariate random-effects model to jointly estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity. Risk of bias is assessed using QUADAS-2.

The objective is to quantify diagnostic performance parameters including sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio, and area under the summary ROC curve (AUC), and to evaluate clinical utility through pre-test to post-test probability transitions.

This registration was completed prior to final data synthesis and manuscript submission.

title: Abstract
description:
Introduction: Oral cancer, the sixteenth most common cancer worldwide, presents a significant health burden, particularly in regions like South Asia and Europe, due to risk factors such as tobacco use, betel quid, and alcohol consumption. VELscope, a diagnostic device, aids in early detection by identifying abnormal fluorescence in oral tissues. This scoping review will evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of VELscope in detecting oral premalignant and malignant lesions, identify research gaps, and provide insights into its utility in clinical practice.The objective of this scoping review is to comprehensively assess the available evidence regarding the clinical and cost-effectiveness of VELscope for detecting oral premalignant lesions, and oral cancer. 
Method & Analysis: Adhering to JBI Scoping Review Methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we will systematically map evidence from peer-reviewed studies in English published until January 2025. Key outcomes include diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity) and cost-effectiveness. Databases such as MEDLINE (PubMed), Scopus, Embase, and Cochrane will be searched, with screening and data extraction conducted independently by two reviewers by using appropriate software (e.g. Rayyan and Microsoft Excel). Findings will be synthesized using tables, figures, and a PRISMA flow diagram to highlight gaps and inform future research and clinical practice.
Ethics and Dissemination: This scoping review does not involve primary data collection; therefore, ethics approval is not required. The findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, presentations at national and international conferences, and workshops aimed at healthcare professionals and policymakers.

title: The experiences of artificial intelligence utilization in healthcare services and healthcare professionals workloads: a scoping review
description: In recent years, the landscape of healthcare services has undergone transformative changes with the incorporation of Artificial Intelligence. (AI). AI encompasses a range of technologies including, but not limited to, machine learning, natural language processing, and deep learning, which have been progressively employed to optimize healthcare services and manage workloads effectively. The penetration of AI in healthcare is premised on its potential to automate routine tasks, offer decision support systems, and enhance diagnostic accuracy, thereby ostensibly reducing the workloads of healthcare professionals and enhancing efficiency. Therefore, evaluating the impacts of AI utilization in healthcare services on the workloads of healthcare professionals becomes imperative to delineate the nuanced implications it harbors for the healthcare workforce.

title: Development and internal validation of a search filter meant to identify Swiss graduate theses focusing on children’s homes written in French
description:
Abstract
Background and rationale:
Swiss social work students from higher education universities (HETS Lausanne, HETS Fribourg, HETS Valais and HETS Genève) have published over 4000 theses from 2008-2018, many of which report primary qualitative research (mainly interview studies). The current number of social work theses (thousands), variation in indexing, terminology and keywords used by students (foyer, maison, home, lieu de vie, institution, etc.) (or used in different universities) and database limitations (no abstracts available online for almost all theses) has made it difficult for to find Swiss works focusing on this topic. Children’s home research not identified by end-users and stakeholders are unlikely to be read, could be unnecessarily undertaken again and may therefore contribute to research waste. Neglecting children’s home research found in graduate theses also means that children in care and care workers would have given their time to contribute to research that may end up having little to no impact. A well-developed topic search filter meant to help identify children’s home research could prove to be a useful tool to limit research waste in this context.
Objective:
To develop and validate search filters meant to retrieve Swiss social work graduate theses focusing on children’s homes (topic search filter) written in French and indexed in Swissbib.
Study design:
Search filter development study and internal validation of the filters on one (1) dataset of relevant records and one (1) dataset of irrelevant records
Methods:
First, consecutive theses published by HETS Lausanne social work students from 1960-2015 were manually sought and assessed until 10 children’s home theses were found for each decade. Based on a brief assessment of their contents, 73 theses were deemed to focus on children’s homes and 123 to focus on other topics (“irrelevant theses”). The titles of the 73 included theses constituted the development set. The development set was analyzed using the Systematic Review Accelerator word frequency analyzer tool and the most commonly found 1 or 2 words keywords were extracted to an Excel document. Each keyword’s ability to correctly identify relevant theses (sensitivity) and correctly exclude irrelevant theses (specificity) was then calculated by emulating Swissbib’s exact keyword search and wildcard searches functions with imbricated COUNTIF().Two search filters were iteratively developed by subjectively selecting and combining keywords with the highest specificity and/or the highest sensitivity. The best “OR” keyword combinations were then sought through trial and error using the dynamic Excel search emulator, trying as best as possible to select keywords leading to inclusion of relevant records only. For all relevant theses titles which could not be found I tried to identify which missing keyword(s) combination(s) could have been used to include them without also including too many irrelevant titles too.
Results:
The highly sensitive search filter achieved 79.45% sensitivity and 95.12% specificity. This search filter found 58 out of 73 (79.45%) relevant theses and adequately excluded 117 out of 123 (95.12%) irrelevant records. The most effective highly specific search filter achieved 69.86% sensitivity and 98.37% specificity. This search filter found 51 out of 73 (69.86%) relevant theses and adequately excluded 121 out of 123 (98.37%) irrelevant records. It is meant to adequately exclude as many non-children’s homes theses as possible. Although a few additional relevant theses with uninformative titles could have been found with children’s homes non-specific keywords this was deemed to be inadequate for this would likely negatively affect the filter performances when/if used in a different dataset or database.
Limitations:
Search filter performances could therefore be slightly different in Swissbib. These search filter performances in other databases including French literature is currently unknown. The performance of a search filter is bounded by the limitations of the data (titles and abstracts) on which it is based; in the current context it is difficult to achieve higher sensitivities when a substantial portion of titles provide little information on the study focus and no abstracts are available. These search filter performances may vary over time if a) keywords in use change or b) graduate theses titles become more or less informative. These search filters are meant to identify children’s homes theses published from 1960 to 2015.A number of French keywords specific to children’s homes such as “foyer de jeunesse” (Canada), “home d’enfants”, “établissement dépositaire”, “Serix” and “maison d’éducation à caractère social (MECS)” (France) were not identified within children’s home theses, which suggests relevant titles can still be missed by these search filters and performances will vary if they are used to search non-Swiss theses. A sample of n=73 children’s homes theses was not enough to identify the full breadth of children’s homes keywords in use in Switzerland from 1960 to 2015. Identifying theses whose focus were children’s homes involved a level of subjectivity, particularly for institutions with mixed populations (children and adults) and other authors may differ with some of the judgements made.
Discussion:
The performances of the two search filters developed in this study should be tested (external validation) in other Swiss databases such as RERO Explore or Renouvaud prior to a more widespread use. HETS Lausanne’s librarians may encourage social work students to use these search filters to identify Swiss children’s homes theses and the Excel search simulator could also be used (and improved) to teach about developing effective search strategies.
HETS students and higher education students could be given more or better guidance on how to make their theses titles more informative to future potential readers if they wish for others to benefits from insights emerging from their work. Swiss social work higher education schools should consider also including theses abstracts in electronic databases to help users identify works they may be interested in. PDF versions of graduate theses would also massively increase their accessibility and both national and international visibility.

No funding was received for this work.

Data and materials: See https://osf.io/dc6xy/files. All other data is otherwise included within this manuscript.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Neurological and Psychiatric Comorbidities Through Orofacial Biomarkers: A Rapid Systematic Review
description:
Background and Rationale
The orofacial region provides a direct, accessible window into central nervous system function. Measurable biological outputs—specifically jaw muscle activation (electromyography), salivary biomarkers, and microscopic facial kinematics—frequently alter in the early stages of major neurological and psychiatric disorders. Conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety, and schizophrenia present distinct orofacial signatures.

While dental clinicians interact with these exact biological signals during routine appointments, they currently play no role in frontline neurological screening. Machine learning architectures have recently demonstrated the capacity to map these complex, non-linear orofacial patterns with high diagnostic accuracy (historically ranging from 72% to 99% in isolated datasets). However, the literature remains fragmented. No comprehensive review has yet synthesized the diagnostic accuracy of these varied AI frameworks specifically for neuro-psychiatric screening, leaving a critical gap between advanced computational models and practical dental clinical applications.

Objectives
This rapid systematic review aims to systematically map and critically evaluate the current state of AI applications using orofacial data for neuro-psychiatric detection. The primary objectives are to:
 • Evaluate the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of existing AI models across distinct orofacial modalities.
 • Determine whether multimodal AI integrations (e.g., combining salivary chemistry with dynamic kinematics) yield superior predictive power compared to standalone single-biomarker models.
 • Identify the methodological barriers preventing the translation of these diagnostic tools from engineering laboratories into physical dental operatories.

Methodology
This study will follow a streamlined rapid review framework adapted from the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines to ensure structural transparency:
 
Search Architecture:
We will execute a systematic search strategy across PubMed, Google Scholar, and Semantic Scholar targeting peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2026.

Eligibility Criteria:
Included studies must utilize machine learning or deep learning algorithms to evaluate human orofacial data (saliva, facial video, or jaw muscle mechanics) for the primary purpose of identifying or tracking a neurological or psychiatric condition. Studies focusing solely on local dental pathologies (e.g., localized temporomandibular joint disorders) or relying purely on standard neuroimaging protocols (such as fMRI) will be excluded.

Data Extraction & Quality Assessment: 
Data regarding model architecture, sample sizing, biomarker categories, and accuracy metrics will be rigorously extracted into a centralized matrix. Risk of bias will be evaluated by assessing study design limitations, sample sizes, and validation methods to contextualize the strength of the current data.

Clinical Significance:
By establishing a clear, evidence-based assessment of AI capabilities in this domain, this review aims to challenge the traditional boundary between dental medicine and neurology. Proving the viability of AI-driven orofacial screening could ultimately allow the routine dental chair to serve as an opportunistic, non-invasive frontline for early neurodiagnostic intervention—a pivot that could fundamentally improve long-term patient prognoses.

title: The Relational Calculus for Green AI
description:
This project is the public home of Relational Calculus, a meta‑mathematical framework that replaces the brute‑force logic of absolute‑scale computation with dimension‑less, capacity‑anchored blueprints. At its heart lies a simple but radical axiom: every system possesses an intrinsic maximum—a “North Star”—and by expressing all observations as fractions of that limit, complexity collapses, efficiency soars, and transfer across domains becomes automatic.

The collection gathers the complete stack: the foundational theoretical paper, a ready‑to‑run Relational Decoder (an open‑source algorithm that probes any black‑box function and extracts its dimensionless template), and five applied case studies that prove the principle in wildly different arenas—number theory (deterministic prime pair lattices), symbolic artificial intelligence (a geometric chess engine that exhibits emergent strategy with zero domain knowledge, gaining 90%+ efficiency), high‑energy physics (scale‑invariant jet tagging that transfers zero‑shot across collision energies with +14.5% AUC), quantum chemistry (80% error reduction in cross‑molecule transfer), and precision oncology (a lightweight XGBoost that achieves 98.4% cross‑species diagnostic accuracy under a 70% hardware‑signal collapse, completely erasing batch effects). A companion paper extends the logic to large language models, proposing Relational‑CoT as a drop‑in replacement for resource‑intensive chain‑of‑thought reasoning.

Every work converges on the same empirical signature: >90% reduction in computational cost, genuine zero‑shot generalization across scales and species, and the proof that Green AI is not an aspiration but an engineering reality. An integrated STEM curriculum for ages 10–14 ensures that the relational lens is taught before the continuous one, inoculating the next generation against the wasteful “math of deviation.”

All code, data, and executable papers are open‑source. The project is intended not as a scholarly gesture but as an enablement instrument for the industrial shift from the Age of Fire—where more compute meant more extraction—to the Era of Relation, where measuring how full a system is replaces the endless pursuit of how much.

title: The Digital Twin Landscape in Medical Diagnosis: A Scoping Review and Bibliometric Analysis of Emerging Applications, Translational Challenges, and Future Theranostic Potential
description:
Amid the growing global demand for precision medicine and personalized healthcare, traditional medical diagnostic models face significant challenges [1, 2]. Current diagnostic methods often rely on empirical judgment and population-based reference data, struggling to capture the dynamic changes and heterogeneous characteristics of individual physiological systems. This leads to frequent issues such as delayed early disease warnings, limited diagnostic accuracy for complex conditions, and suboptimal treatment plan adaptability, which collectively represent critical bottlenecks in improving healthcare quality and efficacy [3-5]. To address these challenges, academia and industry are actively exploring the deep integration of cutting-edge engineering technologies with clinical medicine. Among these, digital twin technology, a hallmark of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, is driving profound transformations in medical diagnostics due to its unique value [6, 7].

Originating from industrial manufacturing, digital twin technology creates digital replicas of physical entities to enable dynamic mapping and optimized control throughout their lifecycle [8, 9]. In recent years, advancements in the Internet of Medical Things, high-precision medical imaging, biosensing technologies, and artificial intelligence algorithms have facilitated the penetration of digital twins into the medical field [10]. The core of this approach lies in integrating multidimensional data—such as genomics, proteomics, imaging, and physiological signals—to construct highly accurate digital twin models of the human body or specific organs. These models enable real-time monitoring, simulation, and precise prediction of physiological states and pathological changes [11]. Compared to industrial applications, medical digital twins must address the complexity and dynamism of biological data, ensuring real-time performance and high fidelity to support precise diagnostics [12].

The primary advantage of digital twins in medical diagnostics lies in their ability to shift from passive diagnosis to proactive prediction and from population-based generalizations to individualized precision [6, 13]. By constructing digital twin models synchronized with patients in real time, clinicians can simulate pathophysiological processes in a virtual environment, avoiding the risks and invasiveness of traditional diagnostic procedures (e.g., biopsies or contrast imaging) [14]. For instance, cardiovascular digital twin models have demonstrated their ability to monitor myocardial electrophysiological activity in real time, not only pinpointing myocardial infarction lesions with precision but also detecting subtle conduction abnormalities early, providing diagnostic evidence for occult pathologies [15]. Moreover, digital twin technology significantly enhances diagnostic workflows and decision-making efficiency. Through virtual simulations, clinicians can pre-optimize diagnostic pathways and parameters before complex procedures or identify early-stage lesions imperceptible to the naked eye by deeply analyzing imaging data [16, 17]. In oncology, digital twins can dynamically track the microscopic evolution and biological behavior of tumors, accurately determining their malignancy, invasion scope, and subtype [12, 18, 19]. Figure 1 illustrates a feedback control system centered on a patient’s digital twin, demonstrating how it achieves precise diagnostics through multisource data integration, with detailed mechanisms discussed further in the main text.

In recent years, medical digital twin technology has shown immense potential in clinical areas such as cardiovascular diseases [17, 20-23], oncology [16, 18, 24, 25], and neurological disorders [26-29]. However, as an emerging interdisciplinary technology, its application in medical diagnostics remains in the early stages of rapid development, facing multiple challenges. For example, the lack of data standardization and sharing hinders the integration of heterogeneous multisource data, limiting model generalizability [30-32]. Incomplete ethical and regulatory frameworks may impede the widespread adoption of digital twins in clinical trials [5, 33]. Additionally, issues such as model accuracy and interpretability, high computational demands, and substantial maintenance costs represent critical barriers to technology translation [34, 35]. Currently, there is a lack of systematic reviews in academia that comprehensively outline the application status, core technologies, research hotspots, and future directions of this field.

Therefore, this study employs a combination of scoping review and bibliometric analysis to systematically examine the global literature on digital twins in medical diagnostics, aiming to address the following core questions:

From the perspectives of global research distribution, international collaboration, core funding, and interdisciplinary integration, what are the macroscopic characteristics of the research landscape in this field?

What are the key data sources, core modeling techniques, and algorithms used to construct digital twin models for diagnostics?

In which disease contexts are digital twins currently applied in medical diagnostics, and at what stage of technological maturity are these applications?

What are the systemic bottlenecks in data, modeling algorithms, and clinical translation that hinder the transition from theory to application, and what are the key future research directions?

Through systematic analysis of these questions, this paper aims to map the global landscape of digital twin applications in medical diagnostics and outline its future development directions. This work seeks to inspire innovative thinking and foster interdisciplinary collaboration to advance this transformative technology toward maturity.

title: How Are AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews Evaluated in Evidence-Based Healthcare? A Scoping Review
description:
This scoping review aims to map and characterize the indicators used to evaluate the performance, reliability, efficiency, validity, or impact of artificial intelligence–assisted systematic review processes in health research. Artificial intelligence technologies, including machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models, are increasingly being applied to different stages of the systematic review process, such as literature searching, deduplication, screening, data extraction, risk of bias and meta-analysis. However, the methods and indicators used to evaluate these applications remain heterogeneous.
The review will include empirical studies that assess the use of artificial intelligence in one or more stages of a systematic review conducted in a health-related field. The included studies shall compare AI-assisted methods with previously published systematic reviews. Data will be charted on the type of AI technology, stage of the review process, comparator or reference standard, and reported performance and quality indicators.
The review will identify commonly used measures, such as sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, accuracy, F1 score, agreement statistics, workload reduction, time savings, reproducibility, reliability, usability, and transparency. It will also examine gaps in current evaluation practices and areas in which standardized indicators may be needed. The findings are expected to support the development of more consistent and transparent approaches for evaluating AI-assisted systematic reviews in health research.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Reporting Quality: Validation of an LLM-Based Tool to Assess STARD 2015 Compliance in Imaging Research
description:
Background: Incomplete reporting in diagnostic accuracy research limits the ability to assess risk of bias, judge clinical applicability, and integrate findings into evidence syntheses. Although the Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) 2015 guideline provides a 30-item checklist to guide transparent reporting, adherence remains suboptimal in imaging research despite widespread endorsement, publication of explanatory materials, and dissemination of author checklists. Existing approaches to improving compliance have yielded only limited and inconsistent improvements, and the editorial infrastructure required to verify adherence at scale is often lacking. Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise for automated reporting guideline assessment, achieving approximately 90% accuracy against human ratings for CONSORT and other guidelines. However, no studies have evaluated whether LLMs can reliably assess adherence to STARD 2015.

Purpose: To evaluate whether AutoReporter, an LLM-based reporting guideline assessment tool, can reliably assess adherence to the STARD 2015 checklist in diagnostic accuracy studies, using previously published human reference ratings as the reference standard.

Methods: This validation study will apply AutoReporter, using the reasoning model o3-mini in a zero-shot, non-retrieval configuration, to two previously published cohorts of imaging-focused diagnostic accuracy studies with available item-level human STARD adherence ratings: Hong et al. (n=41) and Al-Ghita et al. (n=126), yielding a combined dataset of 167 studies. Full-text articles will be acquired from PubMed Central or institutional repositories and preprocessed using XML parsing or PDF-to-text conversion. AutoReporter outputs will be compared against human reference labels, which were assigned in duplicate and resolved by consensus. Binary classification metrics, including accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and Cohen's kappa, will be calculated per checklist item and at the article level, with 95% confidence intervals. Systematic disagreements between AutoReporter and human ratings will be reviewed by the research team to characterize the nature and sources of discordance.

title: Information Sources, Search Strategy, Study Selection and Data Extraction
description:
Information sources and search strategy
The following databases will be searched:
• PubMed/MEDLINE
• Embase
• CINAHL
The search strategy will combine terms for inflammatory bowel disease, malnutrition or nutritional risk, nutritional screening tools, and the selected reference standards. The PubMed strategy will be adapted for Embase and CINAHL using database-specific subject headings and syntax.
Search filters will include humans, publication date from 1 January 2020 to July 2026, and English language or English translation available.
The PubMed search strategy is provided in Appendix 1.
Study selection
Search results from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and CINAHL will be imported into Zotero, where duplicates will be removed. The deduplicated records will then be imported into Rayyan for screening.
Titles and abstracts will be screened by one reviewer against the predefined PICO criteria. Records will be classified as include, exclude or maybe. All records marked include or maybe will proceed to full-text review. A second reviewer will check all records marked include or maybe and a sample of excluded records, using every tenth excluded record.
Full-text screening will be performed against the same eligibility criteria, and each study will be classified as included or excluded. Reasons for exclusion at full-text stage will be recorded. Any disagreements or uncertainties will be resolved by discussion.
The study selection process will be reported using a PRISMA flow diagram.
Data extraction
Data will be extracted into a standardised Excel workbook after full-text review. Each included study will be assigned a study ID using the first author, publication year and a key word from the title.
Study-level data will include basic study details, population demographics, IBD type, clinical setting, nutritional screening tools assessed, comparator used, comparator definition, screening tool cut-off, and whether complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data are available.
Diagnostic accuracy data will be extracted at the study-screening tool-comparator level. Extracted data will include number analysed, reported sensitivity and specificity, TP, FP, FN and TN where available or derivable, and calculated PPV, NPV, accuracy and kappa.
For each study-screening tool-comparator row, it will be recorded whether a complete 2 x 2 table is reported or can be reconstructed. Rows with complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data will be included in the structured diagnostic accuracy synthesis. PICO-eligible studies without sufficient 2 x 2 data will be summarised narratively as supportive evidence.
Extracted rows will be organised by comparator first and then by nutritional screening tool, for example MUST versus GLIM, SaskIBD-NR versus GLIM, and equivalent groups for ESPEN criteria and SGA where available.

title: Benefits and Drawbacks of Modern Educational Approaches Compared with Traditional Teaching Methods for Electrocardiogram Education Among Anesthesia Learners: A Systematic Review
description:
Electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is a core skill for anesthesia trainees and plays an important role in intraoperative patient assessment, detection of cardiac arrhythmias, hemodynamic monitoring, and clinical decision-making during anesthesia. Inadequate ECG interpretation skills may lead to delayed diagnosis and inappropriate management and potentially life-threatening complications for patients.
Traditionally, traditional ECG education has historically relied on passive hub-based instruction such as lecture-based, face-to-face classroom instruction, and printed instructional materials that have only been able to transmit information from the instructor to the learner. However, advances in educational technologies have led to the emergence of innovative instructional approaches, including simulation-based learning, e-learning, web-based learning, mobile applications, gamification, flipped classrooms, case-based learning, problem-based learning, virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and artificial intelligence (AI)-based instructional systems.
Although these educational approaches are increasingly implemented in the education of healthcare professionals and contribute to better education of learners by creating an active and engaged learning environment, a comprehensive review of these methods and their advantages and disadvantages in creating an overall perception has been less discussed and concluded. Modern educational methods may improve knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, overall engagement, confidence, and long-term retention, but they may also increase educational costs, implementation complexity, technological requirements, and cognitive workload.
Therefore, we as a research team concluded that a comprehensive synthesis of available evidence is needed to determine the advantages and disadvantages of modern educational approaches compared to traditional educational methods for ECG training among anesthesia trainees.

title: AI-Enabled EEG for Epilepsy Diagnosis Compared With Clinical Experts: Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis
description:
Background: Electroencephalography (EEG) interpretation for epilepsy diagnosis faces persistent challenges including specialist shortages, variable interpretation accuracy, and limited accessibility. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated interpretation systems promise to address these limitations, yet their diagnostic performance compared to clinical experts remains incompletely characterized.
Objective: To systematically evaluate and meta-analyze the diagnostic accuracy of AI-enabled EEG interpretation compared with human clinical experts for epilepsy detection.
Methods: We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA-DTA and Cochrane MECIR standards, searching PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar through June 2025. Studies directly comparing AI algorithms with human expert interpretation using identical EEG datasets were included. Quality assessment employed QUADAS-AI criteria. Bivariate meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratios, and likelihood ratios.
Results: Three studies encompassing 9,775 EEG examinations met inclusion criteria. AI demonstrated superior pooled sensitivity (0.83–0.85 vs. 0.77–0.80) and specificity (0.83–0.85 vs. 0.72–0.75) compared to human experts. The diagnostic odds ratio for AI was approximately double that of humans (12–13 vs. 6–7). AI exhibited consistently narrower confidence intervals, indicating greater interpretive reliability. For normal versus abnormal EEG classification, AI achieved 86–90% sensitivity with enhanced consistency compared to human evaluators. However, substantial heterogeneity (I²>75%) and methodological limitations were identified across studies.
Conclusions: AI-based EEG interpretation demonstrates diagnostic performance equal or superior to human experts with enhanced consistency, supporting potential implementation as clinical triage tools. However, limited transparency, patient selection bias, and deployment feasibility constraints warrant further investigation before widespread clinical adoption.

title: A collaborative rat functional MRI multi-center study.
description:
In this international collaborative project, we seek to gather the rodent imaging community toward performing a rat fMRI multi-center comparison, within the same template as Grandjean et al. NIMG 2020. We want to examine functional connectivity (FC) parameter distribution at the population level within key networks (somatosensory and default-mode network) of the rat brain, as well as establish connectivity sensitivity and specificity in the collected datasets. To do so, we will gather rat BOLD fMRI datasets from individual labs (n=10, any protocol).
In a desire to push further, we seek to obtain additional datasets pertaining to within-laboratory test-retest (i.e. scans that were collected in the same control animals within a period of 6 months or less), as well as datasets in sensory-stimulation fMRI (limb or whisker stimulation). Finally, we would like to organize a standardized data collection arm of this study for laboratories interested. This would include the de-novo acquisition of a dataset (n=10) using predefined, mutually-agreed, and standardized parameters consistent across all participating laboratories.
The end-goal is to make this as an available resource to researchers and to publish an extensive description of the collective dataset in a peer-reviewed journal.

title: Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory
description:
In the trajectory of human civilization, the relationship between humans and technology has continuously evolved from simple tools that extended physical capabilities to complex systems that augment cognitive processes and decision-making. In the contemporary digital era, this relationship has reached a critical turning point, where the boundaries between human agency and machine intelligence are increasingly intertwined. It is within this transformative context that Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory, originally conceptualized by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) in 2016, emerges as a conceptual framework to understand, interpret, and navigate the deepening integration between human beings and intelligent systems.
The year 2016 represents a pivotal moment in technological development, marked by the acceleration of artificial intelligence, the proliferation of data-driven platforms, and the increasing reliance on algorithmic systems across diverse domains of life. During this period, machines were no longer confined to executing predefined instructions; they began to learn, adapt, and interact in ways that closely resemble human cognitive functions. This shift raised fundamental questions about the nature of human–machine interaction: Are machines merely tools, or are they becoming collaborative agents? How does human identity, autonomy, and decision-making evolve in the presence of increasingly intelligent systems? And most importantly, how can a balanced and mutually beneficial relationship between humans and machines be conceptualized?
Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory was developed as a response to these questions. Rather than framing the relationship between humans and machines as one of competition or replacement, this theory proposes a model of symbiosis an interdependent relationship in which both entities contribute to and benefit from each other’s capabilities. In this framework, humans and machines are not opposing forces but complementary systems, each enhancing the strengths and compensating for the limitations of the other.
At the core of this theory lies the concept of co-evolution. Human capabilities and machine intelligence do not develop independently; they evolve together through continuous interaction. As humans design and interact with machines, they influence the development of technological systems. At the same time, these systems reshape human behavior, cognition, and social structures. This reciprocal relationship creates a dynamic cycle of adaptation and transformation, in which both humans and machines are continuously redefined.
Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), through his 2016 conceptual foundation, identifies three primary dimensions that characterize human–machine symbiosis: cognitive augmentation, adaptive interaction, and systemic integration. These dimensions provide a structured framework for understanding how symbiotic relationships are formed and sustained.
Cognitive augmentation refers to the enhancement of human intellectual capabilities through machine assistance. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, data analytics, and decision-support systems enable individuals to process information more efficiently, make more informed decisions, and extend their cognitive reach beyond natural limitations. In this sense, machines act as amplifiers of human intelligence, enabling new forms of creativity, problem-solving, and innovation.
Adaptive interaction highlights the evolving nature of communication between humans and machines. Unlike traditional tools, which require users to adapt to predefined interfaces, modern intelligent systems are designed to learn from user behavior and adapt accordingly. This creates a more intuitive and personalized interaction, where machines respond to human needs in real time. The adaptive nature of this interaction fosters a sense of collaboration, blurring the distinction between user and system.
Systemic integration, the third dimension, emphasizes the embedding of human–machine relationships within broader socio-technical systems. Symbiosis does not occur in isolation; it is part of a larger ecosystem that includes organizational structures, cultural norms, and technological infrastructures. This dimension highlights the interconnectedness of human and machine activities, demonstrating how symbiotic relationships influence and are influenced by the systems in which they operate.
Together, these dimensions illustrate that human–machine symbiosis is not a static condition but a dynamic and evolving process. It is characterized by continuous feedback loops, where human input shapes machine behavior, and machine output influences human decision-making. This process creates a hybrid form of intelligence one that combines human intuition, creativity, and ethical judgment with machine precision, speed, and analytical capability.
One of the most significant contributions of Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory lies in its humanized perspective. While much of the discourse surrounding artificial intelligence focuses on technological advancement, this theory emphasizes the importance of maintaining a human-centered approach. It recognizes that technology should not only enhance efficiency but also support human values, well-being, and autonomy.
From this perspective, symbiosis is not merely about integration but about alignment. The effectiveness of human–machine relationships depends on the extent to which technological systems are designed to complement human needs and aspirations. This requires a deep understanding of human behavior, cognition, and emotion, as well as a commitment to ethical principles such as transparency, accountability, and inclusivity.
The theory also addresses common concerns about the potential displacement of human roles by machines. Rather than viewing automation as a threat, Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory reframes it as an opportunity for transformation. As machines take over routine and repetitive tasks, humans can focus on activities that require creativity, empathy, and critical thinking. This shift has the potential to redefine the nature of work, education, and social interaction, creating new possibilities for human development.
However, the realization of this potential is not automatic. It requires careful design, governance, and continuous evaluation of human–machine systems. Without these considerations, the integration of technology may lead to unintended consequences, such as loss of autonomy, increased dependency, or reinforcement of existing inequalities. The theory therefore emphasizes the importance of proactive and responsible approaches to technological development.
In addition to its theoretical contributions, Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory has significant practical implications across various domains. In healthcare, for example, symbiotic systems can enhance diagnostic accuracy and patient care by combining human expertise with machine analysis. In education, adaptive learning systems can personalize instruction and support diverse learning needs. In business and marketing, data-driven insights can inform strategy while maintaining a human-centered approach to customer engagement.
These applications illustrate the versatility of the theory and its relevance to contemporary challenges. They also highlight the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration, as the successful implementation of symbiotic systems requires expertise from multiple fields, including technology, social science, and ethics.
Reflecting on the conceptual foundation established in 2016, it is evident that the principles of Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory have become increasingly relevant in the years that followed. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, the emergence of intelligent assistants, and the integration of technology into everyday life have all reinforced the need for a comprehensive framework to understand human–machine relationships.
This opening remark serves as an invitation to explore this framework in depth. It encourages readers to move beyond simplistic narratives of technological determinism or human resistance and to embrace a more nuanced understanding of symbiosis. It challenges us to consider not only how machines can enhance human capabilities but also how humans can shape the development of technology in ways that reflect their values and aspirations.
Ultimately, Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory is about partnership. It is about recognizing that the future of civilization will be shaped not by humans or machines alone, but by the interactions between them. It is about creating systems that are not only intelligent but also meaningful, not only efficient but also humane.
Through the pioneering work of Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), this theory provides a foundation for reimagining the relationship between humans and machines one that is grounded in collaboration, guided by ethical principles, and oriented toward the enhancement of human potential. As we move further into an era defined by technological complexity and rapid change, such a perspective is not only valuable but essential.
