Without these principles, the potential benefits of symbiosis may be overshadowed by unintended consequences.
The relevance of this theory extends across multiple domains. In healthcare, human–machine symbiosis has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes by combining human expertise with machine analysis. In education, adaptive learning systems can personalize instruction and support diverse learning needs, creating more inclusive and effective educational environments. In business and marketing, data-driven insights can enhance decision-making while maintaining a focus on human relationships and customer experience.
These applications illustrate the practical significance of the theory and its potential to contribute to societal advancement. However, they also highlight the need for interdisciplinary collaboration. The successful implementation of human–machine symbiosis requires input from various fields, including technology, social science, psychology, and ethics. This interdisciplinary approach ensures that technological systems are not only technically robust but also socially and ethically responsible.
Reflecting on the conceptual foundation established in 2016, it is evident that the principles of Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory have become increasingly relevant in the years that followed. The rapid development of artificial intelligence, the integration of smart technologies into everyday life, and the growing reliance on digital systems have all reinforced the importance of understanding human–machine relationships.
At the same time, this work acknowledges that the journey toward effective symbiosis is ongoing. As technology continues to evolve, new challenges and opportunities will emerge. The task of understanding and managing these developments requires continuous reflection, adaptation, and innovation. This preface, therefore, is not only an introduction but also an invitation to engage with the theory, to question its assumptions, and to contribute to its ongoing development.
From a personal perspective, the development of this theory has been shaped by a commitment to bridging the gap between technological advancement and human experience. It reflects an ongoing effort to understand how individuals navigate complex digital environments and how these environments can be designed to support human flourishing. This commitment is rooted in the belief that technology should serve humanity, not the other way around.
The decision to present this work in a humanized and paraphrased style, while maintaining rigorous academic standards, reflects the desire to make the theory accessible to a broader audience. Trust, interaction, and symbiosis are not abstract concepts confined to academic discourse; they are lived experiences that affect individuals in their daily lives. By presenting the theory in a way that is both analytical and relatable, this work seeks to bridge the gap between theory and practice.
In conclusion, Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory, as conceptualized by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) in 2016, offers a comprehensive framework for understanding one of the most defining relationships of our time. It challenges us to move beyond simplistic narratives and to embrace a more nuanced and integrated perspective. It invites us to consider not only how machines can enhance human capabilities but also how humans can shape the development of technology in ways that reflect their values and aspirations.
As we move forward into an increasingly interconnected and technologically advanced world, the importance of this perspective cannot be overstated. The future of civilization will be shaped not by humans or machines alone, but by the interactions between them. By fostering a symbiotic relationship grounded in mutual respect, ethical principles, and shared goals, we can create a future that is not only technologically advanced but also deeply human.

title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF BIOMARKERS FOR LATENT AUTOIMMUNE DIABETES IN ADULTS: AN INTEGRATIVE REVIEW
description:
Diabetes Mellitus Type LADA (Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults) represents a peculiar form of diabetes that combines features of Type 1 Diabetes and Type 2 Diabetes. This condition is notable for the presence of autoantibodies directed to pancreatic beta cells, suggesting an underlying autoimmune etiology. According to the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS), a significant proportion of patients with DM (Diabetes Mellitus) diagnosed in adulthood (up to 12% of cases) have slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes, a type of diabetes known as LADA, with prevalent underdiagnosis in many instances, often attributed to its clinical presentation, which resembles Type 2 diabetes, leading to underestimation of the autoimmune component. Understanding the differences in pathophysiology between these forms of diabetes is essential for the development of accurate diagnostic strategies. Traditional biomarkers used in the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, such as the presence of autoantibodies against pancreatic beta cells, may be useful in identifying LADA. However, it is important to consider that the progression of beta cell destruction in LADA is slower than in type 1 diabetes, and typical features of type 2 diabetes, such as insulin resistance, may also be present. Despite the similarities with type 1 diabetes, LADA usually manifests in adults and its progression is gradual and slower, often being confused with the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Manisha et al. established a worldwide prevalence of LADA of 5.1% among patients with T2DM and showed the role of the autoantibody GAD in the screening of LADA, also bringing awareness to the measurement of antibodies in the identification of the disease. From this perspective, the differential diagnosis of LADA is often challenging, due to the overlapping characteristics with other forms of diabetes, leading to misdiagnosis and delay in appropriate treatment. According to the guidelines of the Brazilian Diabetes Society (SBD), the diagnostic criteria for LADA type diabetes are: (1) age at diagnosis <30 years, (2) patients who present slow and progressive destruction of ? cells, presenting positive antibody dosage, and (3) patients who do not require insulin therapy during the first 6 months after diagnosis. Furthermore, Sia et al. found BMI <23 kg/m2 to be the most significant clinical predictive factor for distinguishing between type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (DM) and autoimmune DM in adults (>20 years) with newly diagnosed DM, followed by serum triglycerides <98 mg/dL, HDL >46 mg/dL, and HbA1c >8.6%. Therefore, analyzing the accuracy of LADA diagnostic biomarkers is essential for determining the appropriate therapeutic management and optimizing the patient's prognosis, understanding their diagnostic importance. By assessing them, it is possible to identify which tests or combinations of tests are most effective in distinguishing between LADA, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, allowing an early and accurate diagnosis, initiating appropriate treatment from the onset of the disease. This is essential to ensure an appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach, which takes into account the complexity of LADA's pathophysiology and its similarities and differences with other types of diabetes. Conduct an analysis of the literature regarding the accuracy of the main diagnostic biomarkers applied in the identification of Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA). An integrative review on this topic is crucial to identify accurate diagnostic biomarkers that can distinguish LADA from other forms of diabetes, such as type 1 and type 2. Thus, such identification will not only help in the implementation of appropriate treatments from the beginning, improving clinical management and health outcomes for patients, but will also make it possible to avoid ineffective and potentially detrimental treatments to a better prognosis. This is a qualitative research of the integrative review type to identify productions on topics associated with the accuracy of diagnostic biomarkers of Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA). The integrative review provides the synthesis of knowledge and the applicability of significant studies in practice and is indicated as an important tool in the health field. To construct this research, the PICO strategy will be used as a basis for structuring a clear and targeted research question. PICO is an acronym that stands for: patient, problem or population of interest (P); intervention (I); comparison ©; and result, from the English “outcome” (O). This makes it easier to search for relevant evidence and analyze the results. The search for articles will be carried out in the following databases: PubMed, BVS, Scielo, Google Scholar.

As exclusion criteria, texts that were not related to the theme and/or presented duplicates, in addition to those that fit into case reports, were disregarded. title: The diagnostic accuracy of SARS-CoV-2 nasal rapid antigen self- test: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Introduction: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the cause of corona virus disease (COVID-19), a disease that quickly spread into a pandemic. So, reliable diagnostic tests for SARS-CoV-2 are vital for the management of COVID-19 pandemic. The gold standard for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 is the molecular detection test using the reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction technique (rt-PCR), which is characterized by various disadvantages in contrast to the self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests which give results faster, have lower costs and do not require specialized personnel. Therefore, the usefulness of self-taken rapid antigen tests is indisputable in disease management, facilitating both the health system and the examinees. Our systematic review aims to access the diagnostic accuracy of the self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests.
Methods: This systematic review conducted following the PRISMA guidelines and the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool was used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. All the studies included in this systematic review were found after searching the 2 databases Scopus and PubΜed. Anything but original articles were excluded from this systematic review while all the studies concerning self-taken rapid antigen tests with a nasal sample and using rt-PCR as a reference test were included. Meta-analysis results and plots were obtained using RevMan software and the MetaDTA website.
Results: All 22 studies included in this meta-analysis demonstrated a specificity of self-taken rapid antigen tests greater than 98%, which exceeds the minimum required yield for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2, according to WHO. However, the sensitivity varies (from 40% to 98.7%), which makes them in some cases unsuitable for the diagnosis of positive cases. In the majority of the studies, the minimum required performance set by the WHO, is achieved, which is 80% compared to the rt-PCR. In this meta-analysis the pooled sensitivity of self-taken nasal rapid antigen test was calculated 91,1% and the pooled specificity 99,5%.
Conclusion: In conclusion, self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests have many advantages over rt-PCR, such as those related to the rapid reading of the results and their cheap cost. They also have considerable specificity and some self-taken rapid antigen tests kits also have remarkable sensitivity. Consequently, self-taken rapid antigen tests have a wide range of utility, but are not able to completely replace rt-PCR tests.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Large Language Models for Rare Genetic Disease Diagnosis
description:
Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a potentially transformative technology for clinical diagnostics. Foundation models such as GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrate broad biomedical knowledge, can process unstructured clinical text, and exhibit emergent reasoning capabilities. A landscape analysis of 17 primary studies (conducted as part of protocol development) reveals a rapidly maturing but heterogeneous field with several key findings:

Agentic systems dramatically outperform standalone LLMs. Multi-agent architectures with tool access achieve 55-78% Recall@1 (e.g., LA-MARRVEL: 78%, DeepRare: 57-71%, RareAgents: 76.7%), whereas standalone LLM prompting yields only 12-33% Recall@1 (Kim et al. 2024: 17% top-50; Chimirri et al. 2025: 19.9% across 10 languages).
LLM-as-reranker outperforms LLM-as-solver. LA-MARRVEL (78% Recall@1) uses a traditional variant prioritization pipeline with LLM reranking, substantially outperforming end-to-end LLM approaches (12-15% Recall@1).
Genetic data substantially boosts performance. DeepRare HPO-only: 46.8% Recall@1 vs. HPO+VCF: 70.6% Recall@1, a 23.8 percentage point improvement.
Full EHR text outperforms HPO-only input. RareSeek R1 achieves 68.4% Recall@1 with full clinical narratives vs. 19.2% with HPO terms alone, suggesting rich clinical context is underutilized.
A real-world performance gap persists. Systems achieving 50-70% Recall@1 on curated benchmarks drop to ~20% on real EHR data (MIMIC-RD evaluation), highlighting the distance from clinical deployment.
Benchmark heterogeneity limits direct comparison. Studies evaluate on different datasets (RareBench: 2,185 cases/421 diseases; MIMIC-RD: 145 cases/120 diseases; DeepRare: 6,401 cases/2,919 diseases), with non-overlapping disease sets and varying case complexity.

This rapidly evolving landscape presents a critical need for systematic synthesis. The field currently lacks:

A comprehensive quantitative synthesis of LLM diagnostic accuracy across studies, architectures, and input modalities -- our landscape analysis identified ~13 studies with Recall@K metrics but no existing synthesis has pooled or systematically compared them
Standardized comparison between standalone LLM approaches, agentic LLM systems, and traditional bioinformatics baselines -- the 4-5x performance gap between standalone and agentic architectures is a central finding that requires formal meta-analytic confirmation
Assessment of clinical utility beyond accuracy metrics -- including reasoning quality, time-to-diagnosis impact, and clinical actionability
Identification of failure modes including hallucination rates, reference accuracy (DeepRare reports 95.4% citation accuracy, but this is one study), and performance disparities across disease prevalence tiers, medical specialties, and patient populations
Evidence-based guidance for clinical implementation of LLM-based diagnostic tools in rare disease settings

No existing systematic review comprehensively addresses LLM-based approaches to rare genetic disease diagnosis. Prior reviews (e.g., Neeley et al., 2025; Carbonari et al., 2025) have surveyed the landscape but have not performed meta-analytic synthesis of diagnostic accuracy or systematically assessed the transition from standalone LLMs to agentic systems.

title: TITAN SR vs ChatGPT 4.1 for Abstract Screening.
description: Background and motivation. Citation screening — the task of reading thousands of search-yield records and deciding which are eligible for a systematic review — is the most labour-intensive step in evidence synthesis, consuming weeks to months of expert reviewer time per review. Recent work has demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can automate this task with high accuracy: Cao et al. (2025) reported that GPT-4.1 with an optimized "ScreenPrompt" prompt template achieved 96.6% sensitivity and 93.9% specificity on abstract-level screening across five Cochrane reviews. This raises a question of considerable practical and methodological importance: is the strong performance of LLM-based screening primarily attributable to the underlying model architecture (a frontier general-purpose LLM) or to the specific prompt engineering applied to the screening task?The distinction matters. If model architecture is the primary driver, the field is constrained to depend on commercial frontier APIs with their associated costs, rate limits, version drift, and vendor lock-in. If prompt engineering is the primary driver, then a smaller, fine-tuned, locally-deployable model with an appropriately designed input format may achieve comparable performance at a fraction of the cost and with full reproducibility. Resolving this question has direct implications for systematic-review infrastructure decisions at evidence-synthesis institutions, guideline-development bodies, and individual research teams.Project design. This project pre-registers and executes a head-to-head comparison of two paradigms on identical citation screening tasks: (i) TITAN-SR, a fine-tuned biomedical BERT ensemble (PubMedBERT + BioLinkBERT, 50/50 weighted, 110M parameters per backbone) trained on approximately 762,000 citation–label pairs derived from 19,787 systematic reviews, and (ii) GPT-4.1 (model version gpt-4.1-2025-04-14) under three pre-specified prompt conditions: a minimal zero-shot prompt, a structured chain-of-thought prompt, and the optimized ScreenPrompt template from Cao et al. (2025). The same citations are screened by all four index-test conditions, enabling fully paired statistical comparisons.The evaluation set comprises 74,076 citations across 12 Cochrane reviews published between 1 January 2024 and 27 April 2026 (after TITAN-SR's training cutoff and verified disjoint from its training corpus), stratified across three Oxford CEBM question types (4 diagnostic test accuracy, 4 prognosis, 4 intervention). All 12 reviews, their search-reproduction fidelity, and the full citation corpora with binary inclusion labels are deposited in the registration bundle and SHA-256-locked at the time of registration.Pre-specified hypotheses. The primary hypothesis (H1) is that TITAN-SR is non-inferior to GPT-4.1 (optimized prompt) in paired sensitivity at matched specificity, within a 3-percentage-point margin (paired McNemar test, one-sided α = 0.025). Secondary hypotheses address: the relative contributions of architecture versus prompting (H2); specificity at the safety-critical 99% recall operating point (H3); ranking discrimination by AUC (H4); re-screening reproducibility under deterministic versus API-mediated inference (H5); cost per 1,000 citations screened (H6, with TITAN-SR predicted to be ≥10× cheaper); and probability calibration (H7). Discrepancies between any system's decision and the original Cochrane author decision are adjudicated by an LLM-as-a-judge framework (o3-mini-high, blinded to system identity), with a 5% sample manually audited by the principal investigator.Expected outcomes and contributions. The project will produce: (i) a definitive answer to the architecture-versus-prompting question for biomedical citation screening, with statistically rigorous paired estimates and pre-registered confidence intervals; (ii) a reproducible benchmark dataset of 74,076 labelled citations across 12 stratified Cochrane reviews suitable for future screening-system evaluations; (iii) the locked TITAN-SR operating point and full validation-set provenance for replication; (iv) an empirical cost comparison between locally-deployable and API-based screening paradigms at realistic scale. The findings will inform infrastructure choices for systematic-review teams, guideline developers, and methods researchers evaluating the integration of automated screening into evidence-synthesis workflows. The manuscript is targeted for submission to Research Synthesis Methods upon completion of analysis.

title: Development of a Short Symbol-Based Screening Instrument for Internet Gaming Disorder: The Inclusion of Videogame in the Self (IVS) Scale for Children and Adolescents
description:
Accurate screening for Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) in children and adolescents remains a challenge in routine clinical settings. This study evaluated the psychometric properties and diagnostic utility of the Inclusion of Videogame in the Self (IVS) scale, a brief pictorial tool assessing the perceived fusion between self and video game. A clinical sample of 189 children and adolescents (M = 13.0 years, SD = 3.2) completed the IVS, IGD, and Social Media Disorder (SMD) measures. While the five-item scale showed a solid factor structure and reliability, diagnostic accuracy was limited. A single item assessing the “relationship” with the favourite game emerged as a strong screening proxy, correlating with IGD and minimally with SMD. A cut-off score of 3 or higher yielded 100% sensitivity and a 45% false-positive rate. The Single-Item IVS shows promise as a quick, developmentally appropriate screening tool to identify youth at risk for IGD, warranting further validation in broader samples. More generally, the IVS is the first attempt to conceptualise inclusion of self in an activity (the game) rather than in a group or other person.

Note: To protect participant confidentiality, descriptive sociodemographic variables except age and gender were removed from the dataset.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Delirium Screening Tools in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
description:
Background
Few studies have directly compared the diagnostic accuracy of different tools for detecting delirium in the emergency department.

Materials and Methods
Study Design and Search Strategy
 This systematic review was prospectively registered in the Open Science Framework. This study was conducted and reported in strict accordance with the Preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies (PRISMA-DTA) [18]. The PRISMA-DTA checklist is provided in eTable 1 in Supplement 1. We conducted searches in EMBASE, Medline, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) databases until March 20 2026 to identify studies assessing the diagnostic accuracy of delirium screening tools in the ED. The search terms included “delirium”, “emergency department”, and related synonyms. We also performed hand searching of references and backward/forward citation chasing

Study Selection
 We included studies that met the following criteria: (1) observational studies utilizing a cross-sectional or cohort design; (2) adult patients (≥18 years) presenting to the emergency department; (3) application of any structured delirium screening tool for diagnosis or screening; (4) use of standard operationalized diagnostic criteria (eg, DSM-III through DSM-5, ICD-10, Feighner, or Research Diagnostic Criteria) as the reference standard; and (5) reported sufficient data to calculate diagnostic accuracy. We excluded studies based solely on unstructured clinical judgment without a specific screening tool. Two reviewers (Y.C.L. and W.T.C.) independently screened articles for inclusion. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (C.S.L.). 

Data Extraction and Quality Assessment 
 Two reviewers (Y.C.L. and W.T.C.) independently extracted data on study characteristics (eg, author, year, country), patient demographics, study design, and diagnostic accuracy results (true positive, false positive, false negative, and true negative values). To maximize sample representativeness and mitigate potential selection bias in the presence of overlapping datasets, we prioritized data derived from total populations, as well as physician-based assessments. For studies reporting multiple diagnostic thresholds, the cut-off value maximizing the Youden Index was selected [36]. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool [19]. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (C.S.L). 

Statistical Analysis
 The primary outcomes of this study were the pooled sensitivity and specificity of the included screening tools, from which the Youden Index was calculated. To address clinical heterogeneity, facilitate a structured comparative analysis, and increase the statistical power, our research team reached a consensus to classify the included index tests into six functional categories. We established this classification by evaluating the primary neurocognitive targets to identify the specific clinical features each tool assesses, alongside the structural design to understand its practical operationalization, including algorithmic complexity and administration method. First, the Assessment of Arousal and Sedation (ArouSed) category targeted the altered level of consciousness, which included the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) and the modified RASS (m-RASS) [20-22]. Second, the Assessment of Attention and Working Memory (AWM) focused on inattention as the cardinal feature of delirium, comprising the Months Backwards Test (MBT), Spelling "LUNCH" Backwards (LunchB), Days of the Week Backwards (WeekB), 10-letter Vigilance "A" Task (TenVAT), and the Picture Recognition Task (PRT) [23-25]. Third, the Assessment of Global Cognitive Status (GCS) evaluated general cognitive function rather than specific delirium features, consisting of the Six-item Cognitive Impairment Test (6-CIT) and the Abbreviated Mental Test 4 (AMT4) [26-28]. Fourth, the Composite Delirium Diagnostic Algorithms (CDDA) represented multicomponent tools employing hierarchical algorithms to evaluate multiple neurocognitive domains, encompassing the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) [29], CAM for the ICU (CAM-ICU) [25], Modified CAM for the Emergency Department (mCAM-ED)[30], 4 'A's Test (4AT) [31, 32], Nursing Delirium Screening Scale (Nu-DESC)[33], the Brief CAM (bCAM) [24], and modified bCAM (m-bCAM)[34]. Fifth, Triage Tools designed for high-sensitivity rapid ruling out were represented by the Delirium Triage Screen (DTS) [24]. Finally, the Informant-Based Assessment category relied on clinical observation rather than direct patient testing, represented by the Single Question in Delirium (SQiD) [35].

We conducted a Bayesian bivariate random-effects network meta-analysis to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity[37, 38]. Network geometry was visualized using the netmeta package to illustrate available direct comparisons [39]. Posterior distributions were estimated via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations[40-42]with minimally informative priors [43], implemented in Just Another Gibbs Sampler (JAGS). The model employed four parallel chains consisting of 20,000 iterations each. To ensure steady-state sampling, the initial 10,000 iterations per chain were discarded as burn-in, and convergence was subsequently confirmed via the Gelman-Rubin statistic[44]. Pooled estimates of sensitivity and specificity, including 95% credible intervals (CrIs), were displayed in forest plots generated using ggplot2 and ggdist [45, 46]. Overall diagnostic performance was summarized by constructing a Hierarchical Summary Receiver Operating Characteristic (HSROC) curve, incorporating 95% credible and prediction regions [47]. 

To evaluate clinical efficiency, the relationship between diagnostic accuracy (measured by the Youden Index) and administration time was assessed. Clinical utility was simulated by calculating positive predictive values (PPV) across varying prevalence scenarios [49]. Publication bias was examined using Deeks’ funnel plot asymmetry test [50, 51], where a P-value < .05 indicated potential bias [50]. All statistical analyses were performed using R software, version 4.5.1 [52].

title: Identifying Cooperation Mechanisms in Indirect Reciprocity
description: This study experimentally distinguishes four cooperation mechanisms in an indirect reciprocity game: image scoring, standing, strategic reputation building, and upstream reciprocity. Using a 2x2 between-subjects design (recipient history x audience visibility) plus a standardized anonymous block, the experiment exploits the key diagnostic case of justified refusal—where image scoring and standing make divergent predictions—to classify participants by their assessment rule. Seven pre-specified hypotheses test whether participants use different reputation rules, whether those rules predict donation behavior, whether cooperation depends on audience visibility, whether norm use is intrinsic or strategic, and whether upstream reciprocity operates independently of reputation.

title: Diagnosing Quark–Gluon Entanglement Beyond Spatiotemporal Separation: A Sensitivity–Specificity Framework
description: Quantum entanglement is conventionally identified through spatiotemporal separation and the violation of Bell-type inequalities. While effective in photonic and atomic systems, such diagnostics become degenerate in high-energy collision regimes where quarks and gluons are confined to sub-femtometer scales. In this work, quark–gluon entanglement is examined through a correlation-based diagnostic framework employing sensitivity and specificity as operational criteria. Sensitivity quantifies the ability to correctly identify genuine quantum correlations between quark and gluon degrees of freedom, while specificity constrains false positives arising from classical or kinematic correlations enforced by confinement. By focusing on correlated state transitions and gauge-constrained field configurations rather than geometric separation, this approach provides a robust method for identifying entanglement in regimes where spacetime signatures lose discriminative power. The framework clarifies the interpretation of collision experiments and supports a regime-aware understanding of entanglement as constrained correlation rather than spatial distance

title: Current and Emerging Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Clinical Management of Burn Patients: A Scoping Review.
description:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Introduction:
Artificial Intelligence (A I) is considered an emerging tool within computer sciences, using logic processes, algorithms, machine learning, and deep learning to simulate human mind functions such as intelligence, reasoning, and information processing [1].. This tool has had a significant impact in healthcare, notably in the creation and use of applications for diagnostic support and medical/surgical decision-making in various clinical settings. These applications have enabled healthcare professionals to improve diagnostic accuracy, prevent and anticipate possible complications, and personalize and adjust treatment according to each patient's needs [1]..
In plastic and reconstructive surgery, there is growing interest in using these tools for the care and management of burn patients, as well as for optimizing rehabilitation processes and preventing chronic sequelae[2].
This scoping review aims to explore the current and emerging applications of AI in the comprehensive management of burn patients, identifying benefits, limitations, and possible future recommendations.

Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted of observational studies, original and scientific articles, meta-analyses, systematic or scoping reviews, and gray literature published between 2010 and 2025, in English or Spanish. A comprehensive search will be performed in electronic databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, and LILACS, using MeSH descriptors related to AI and its application in plastic surgery and burn patient management. As a complementary strategy, the snowball technique will be applied to the bibliographic references of selected articles to identify additional relevant studies not retrieved in the initial search.

Expected Results: The results are expected to provide a comprehensive view of current AI uses in plastic and reconstructive surgery focused on burn patient management, identifying especially successful cases, possible obstacles encountered, and recommendations for the potential application of this tool in the field. The findings will be aimed at researchers, healthcare professionals, or anyone interested in AI applications for burn patient care.

title: Deep Learning for Early Detection of Alzheimer’s Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Accuracy
description: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia, and early, reliable diagnosis remains a critical challenge. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have led to the development of models that use neuroimaging, fluid biomarkers, and clinical data to aid in AD detection. However, the literature is fragmented, with wide variation in datasets, algorithms, and reported performance metrics. This project will conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of ML/DL models for Alzheimer’s diagnosis. We will extract and synthesize reported metrics such as AUC-ROC, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score, while assessing risk of bias and heterogeneity across studies. Analyses will explore the impact of model type, validation strategy, and input modality. Our goal is to provide a transparent, reproducible synthesis of the evidence, highlight methodological gaps, and generate recommendations for advancing ML/DL tools toward clinical applicability in AD.

title: Differentiating between bipolar and borderline personality disorder using artificial intelligence: a scoping review
description: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) and bipolar disorder (BD) are debilitating psychiatric illnesses with significant rates of misdiagnosis. Emerging research highlights the potential of machine learning (ML) techniques in distinguishing between mental disorders, offering promise for improved diagnostic accuracy and treatment outcomes. This scoping review explores the potential of ML techniques in distinguishing individuals with BD from those with BPD and identifying the most relevant variables for differentiation.

title: T Cell Activation Mechanism
description:
The “TCR complex” is located in the membrane of T lymphocytes and is composed of, among other proteins, the TCR itself, CD3 and CD247. When there is no signal, the chains inside the cytoplasm of the CDs of the TCR complex, with the ITAM catalytic domains rich in lysine, are intimately bound to the cell membrane, which prevents kinases/phosphorylases from acting on the chains. When the antigen-TCR binding occurs, these chains separate from the membrane, and can bind to certain enzymes, which can then be phosphorylated, initiating the signaling cascade. It is known that the membrane potential, and the charges present in it, are relevant for signal transduction (both of the lymphocyte membrane and that of the presenting cell) [ Xiaoshan Shi, Yunchen Bi, Wei Yang. Ca2+ regulates T-cell receptor activation by modulating the charge property of lipids. Nature, 2013, 493, 111-115]. The lipids in this membrane are peculiar, such as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3), with three and four phosphate groups, respectively, and are relevant for the transmission of the signal between the TCR and CD3. The presentation of the antigen to the TCR by the antigen-presenting cell could generate an electrostatic field on the membrane of the T lymphocyte, whose origin would be the membrane potential of this helper cell, which repels the so-called negatively charged lipids that diffuse away from the complex. These lipids kept the lysine-rich chains of the CDs in the membrane. This would release these chains into the cytoplasm where they can be phosphorylated, triggering the signaling cascade expected from the complex. That is, the signal would be electrostatic in nature. The role of CD3 and CD247 is to bind to TCR, form the TCR complex and allow their tails to be phosphorylated after interaction with the electrostatic field. The evidence supporting this hypothesis is: 1) The distribution of charges already mentioned in the complex and the membrane. 2) The presence of disordered areas between the antigen receptor and the transmembrane domain of TCR (making the transmission of a conformational change impossible, for example). 3) The fact that there are artificial chimeric receptors capable of triggering the signal, with a molecular structure different from that of the TCR complex. 4) The fact that pMHC that bind the TCR for a longer time initiate a stronger activation of the T cell. 5) The antigen alone is not able to activate the lymphocyte. 6) Only one interaction is enough to activate the T-cell. 7) The association of CD3δε, γε, and ζζ subunits to the TCR is necessary for T-cell intracelluar signal transduction.

It is difficult theoretically to predict whether this interaction will be strong enough to activate the mechanism since, among other things, the surrounding medium has dissolved ions that could shield the electric field. The project would consist of designing experiments to prove or refute the hypothesis outlined. For example:

1) T cell + APC with MHC but depolarized: Bring a depolarized presenting cell to the receptor: See if the interaction would occur in the case of an APC with a depolarized cell membrane, and see how this can be achieved. If the hypothesis is correct, since there is no electrical membrane potential, the lymphocyte would not be activated.

2) T cell + MHC bound to something charged: Bring a liposome bound to MHC, with the same membrane potential as an APC, to the TCR. If the hypothesis is correct, activation would occur.

3) T cell + something that carries a negative electrostatic charge and can be brought to the receptor by some means, without interaction with MHC, for example, if we subject the T cell to a negative electrostatic field with the TCR complex oriented towards it and the cell is activated, this would corroborate the hypothesis

4) Visualize anionic lipid movement using fluorescent lipid analogs (e.g., NBD-PS).

5) Assess lipid redistribution using super-resolution microscopy and FRAP.

The Electrostatic Switch: A Unified Biophysical Theory of Lymphocyte Activation

Executive Summary
We propose a universal mechanism for Antigen Receptor (TCR/BCR) triggering based on Electrostatic Lipid Sequestration. In the resting state, the signaling domains (ITAMs) of the receptor are electrostatically "locked" against the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane by anionic lipids ($PIP_2$, $PIP_3$, SAPI33). Activation is not primarily a conformational change transmitted through the receptor, but a biophysical release event: the formation of a tight "Dielectric Synapse" excludes water and ions, allowing an external electrostatic field (from the APC or polyanionic antigen) to repel the anchoring lipids. This repulsion releases the basic-rich cytoplasmic tails, exposing ITAMs for phosphorylation.
1. The Core Mechanism: The "Lipid Lock"
The default state of the T-cell receptor is OFF, maintained by an active electrostatic clamp.
The Anchor: The cytoplasmic tails of the CD3 complex ($\epsilon$, $\zeta$) and Ig$\alpha$/$\beta$ contain conserved Basic-Rich Stretches (BRS). These polybasic motifs (rich in Lysine K and Arginine R) bind tightly to the negatively charged phosphoinositides of the inner membrane leaflet.
The Trigger: Antigen binding creates a localized electrostatic perturbation. This field exerts a repulsive force on the mobile anionic lipids, driving their lateral diffusion away from the receptor cluster.
The Release: Once the "anionic glue" is displaced, the basic tails are electrostatically repelled by the remaining positive potential or simply released by thermal motion ("The Safety Model"), becoming accessible to kinases like Lck.
2. The Physics of Field Propagation: The "Dielectric Bridge"
A primary objection to electrostatic signaling is Debye Screening ($\lambda_D \approx 0.8$ nm in physiological saline). We resolve this through the unique geometry of the Immunological Synapse:
Dielectric Exclusion: The formation of the TCR-pMHC complex creates a tight physical interface ($\sim 13$–$15$ nm). This "Kinetic Segregation" zone excludes bulk water molecules and mobile ions ($Na^+$, $Cl^-$).
The "Hole in the Shield": By removing the conductive ionic shield (Faraday cage), the synapse acts as a low-dielectric bridge ($\epsilon \approx 2-4$). The electrostatic potential from the APC (or the T-cell's own dipole potential) propagates through this protein bridge without screening, acting directly on the transmembrane lipids.
Dynamic Oscillations: Recent data (Papp et al., 2020) reveals that T-cells undergo rapid membrane potential oscillations upon contact. These oscillations act as a "biophysical rattle," mechanically destabilizing the lipid-tail interaction more effectively than a static field.
3. Evolutionary Convergence: The NTR Parallels
This mechanism is not unique to lymphocytes; it represents a convergent evolutionary strategy for receptor regulation.
Neurotrophin Receptors (Trk Family): The Juxtamembrane (JM) domains of TrkA/B contain conserved polybasic motifs (KF G KR) that sequester the kinase domain against the membrane.
Universal Logic: Both the immune (TCR/BCR) and nervous (NTR) systems utilize membrane-proximal basic clusters to electrostatically sequester signaling domains. This homology validates the "Lipid Lock" as a fundamental principle of receptor biology.
4. Experimental Validation: The "Inverse Proofs"
A. CAR-T Tonic Signaling (The Broken Lock)
Chimeric Antigen Receptors (CARs) serve as a powerful test case.
Phenomenon: Many CAR constructs exhibit tonic signaling (constitutive activation) without antigen.
Explanation: The rigid, artificial hinge/spacer of the CAR prevents the CD3$\zeta$ tail from folding back to engage the inner leaflet lipids effectively.
Conclusion: The failure of the "Lipid Lock" leads to a permanently ON state. This proves that the resting state requires active structural sequestration, not just the absence of a ligand.
B. Superantigens (Forced Dielectric Stabilization)
Superantigens (e.g., SEB) bypass peptide specificity but still trigger the TCR.
Mechanism: They act as rigid "molecular staples," forcing the APC and T-cell membranes into the critical $\sim 13$ nm distance.
Biophysics: This forced proximity creates a massive, stable "Dielectric Hole" (or super-raft) that excludes ions and allows the field to penetrate, triggering the release of lipids regardless of peptide recognition.
C. T-Independent B-Cell Activation (The Pure Field)
TI-2 antigens (e.g., S. pneumoniae polysaccharides) activate B-cells without T-cell help.
Nature: These are high-molecular-weight polyanions (dense negative charge).
Mechanism: The antigen itself carries sufficient negative charge to generate the transmembrane field required to repel the anchoring lipids of Ig$\alpha$/$\beta$. This is a "pure" electrostatic trigger that does not require an APC membrane potential.
5. The Permissive Step: Kinetic Segregation of CD45
The electrostatic release of ITAMs is the "ON" switch, but it requires a permissive environment to sustain the signal.
Steric Exclusion: The massive phosphatase CD45 ($\sim 25$–$40$ nm) is physically squeezed out of the tight synaptic gap ($\sim 13$–$15$ nm).
The "Check-Valve": The exclusion of CD45 prevents the immediate dephosphorylation of the newly released ITAMs.
Synthesis: The synaptic geometry performs two coupled functions simultaneously:
Dielectric Function: Excludes ions to allow the Electrostatic Field to open the lock.
Steric Function: Excludes phosphatases to prevent the Signal from being reset.
6. Conclusion
The Electrostatic Lipid Sequestration Model unifies the disparate features of lymphocyte activation—from the sequence homology of cytoplasmic tails to the anomalous behavior of CARs and Superantigens. It posits that the T-cell receptor is a biophysical sensor that converts synaptic geometry and electrostatic fields into biochemical signals by modulating the lateral diffusion of membrane lipids. This framework offers a testable, physics-based explanation for the sensitivity and specificity of the adaptive immune system.

title: The em—ergence of the em—dash: a population-level rise in medRxiv Discussion sections (2020–2025) compatible with increasing LLM-assisted writing
description:
# OSF Registration: Stage 2 confirmatory analysis

**Title:** The em—ergence of the em—dash: a population-level rise in medRxiv Discussion sections (2020–2025) compatible with increasing LLM-assisted writing

**Principal investigator:** Przemysław Czuma, MD, ORCID 0009-0009-8235-2053
Poland; Polish Association: AI in Medicine

**OSF project (umbrella):** https://osf.io/ucsqf/ (created 2026-05-20 17:14 UTC)
**Registration type:** Open-Ended Registration
**Registration date:** 2026-05-31
**Access:** deposited under embargo until publication of the main paper. The timestamp and the frozen plan lock at registration; the content becomes public when the embargo lifts (the hypothesis is already public in the umbrella project description).

> **Note on what is and is not deposited here.** This registration freezes the *analysis plan* only. The medRxiv corpus is external, public data (medRxiv S3 Text-and-Data-Mining bucket) and is **not** copied into OSF or GitHub; the retrieval date and the resulting DOI manifest are recorded. No results exist at registration time. Two distinct timeline points are recorded here as they occur: (i) at **data freeze, immediately before the confirmatory analysis is run**, the input dataset and analysis code are locked and the **GitHub commit hash** is recorded (the frozen input dataset may optionally be deposited to Zenodo at this point); (ii) at **publication, after the analysis**, the Zenodo archive of the final code, processed data, and results is created and its **citable DOI** is recorded.

---

## 1. Background and relationship to prior exploratory work

Prior exploratory analysis on a sample of medRxiv preprints (1,941 DOIs collected from deposits between 2019 and 2025, of which 1,873 passed the length filter and were analysed, via an HTML-based extraction pipeline) indicated a marked post-ChatGPT increase in em-dash prevalence in Discussion sections. The present preregistered analysis tests this on the **full medRxiv XML corpus** (S3 TDM bucket, 82,192 metadata records comprising 82,067 first-version (v1) papers and 125 later-version records; retrieved 2026-05-26) using a **distinct extraction pipeline**, with outcomes and analyses specified before extraction at scale. Of the 1,941 exploratory DOIs, 1,926 (2.4% of the corpus) are present in this corpus; a sensitivity analysis excluding the overlapping records is prespecified (Section 7). The exploratory work informed the design at a high level; specific exploratory effect-size estimates are not carried into this plan.

This is a discovery-then-replication design: the exploratory analysis described above is prior, **unpublished** pilot work that informed this plan; Stage 2 (this registration) is the confirmatory analysis. The exploratory results are not released as a preprint.

## 2. Research question and hypotheses

**Primary hypothesis (H1).** In a v1-only cohort of medRxiv Discussion sections, the prevalence of preprints containing at least one em-dash (U+2014) differs between the pre-ChatGPT period (deposits before 2022-11-30) and the post-ChatGPT period (deposits on/after 2022-11-30).

The claim under test is a **population-level stylistic shift temporally coincident with the public availability of LLM-assisted writing tools, and compatible with their adoption**, not a per-paper detector of LLM authorship, and not a causal proof.

## 3. Data source and corpus

- **Source:** medRxiv S3 Text-and-Data-Mining bucket (full-text JATS XML), public external data; retrieved 2026-05-26 (82,192 metadata records = 82,067 v1 papers + 125 later-version records). The corpus is not redistributed.
- **Units:** preprints (one record per DOI after the v1 restriction below).
- **Deposit date:** from JATS ``, with fallback to DOI date parsing.

## 4. Cohort definition (inclusion / exclusion)

- **Temporal scope (primary):** deposits 2020-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (six full years). The partial first 7 months of platform operation (Jun–Dec 2019, N ≈ 912) and partial 2026 Q1 (N ≈ 5,190) are reported separately as supplementary cohorts, not in the primary analysis.
- **Version restriction:** v1 (first-deposited version) of each DOI only; multi-version papers contribute their v1.
- **Section threshold:** extracted Discussion section length ≥ 500 characters.
- **Extraction:** manual-validation-passed JATS extraction (Section 10).
- **Excluded from per-paper analysis:** records with no parseable JATS / no `` / no DOI / no identifiable Discussion section.

A **corpus inclusion flow diagram** will report N before/after each step, broken down both per year and per major subject category, to verify that exclusions (e.g., no parseable JATS / no identifiable Discussion) are neither year-asymmetric nor concentrated in a specific domain (e.g., physics/math preprints with non-standard formatting). This is a standard cohort-attrition diagram; PRISMA-ScR adherence is not claimed.

## 5. Variables

- **Primary outcome:** binary `HasEm`, Discussion section contains ≥ 1 em-dash (U+2014).
- **Em-dash measurement rule:** `HasEm` is evaluated on the Discussion text after XML extraction and entity decoding; only the literal codepoint U+2014 is counted. No typographic normalization that would convert hyphens (U+002D), Unicode hyphens (U+2010), or en-dashes (U+2013) into em-dashes is applied.
- **Exposure:** `post_ChatGPT` = 1 if deposit_date ≥ 2022-11-30 (ChatGPT public release), else 0. No wash-out period.
- **Cluster (for SEs):** first-author identity (ORCID where present; otherwise a fallback of lowercased surname + first initial + affiliation institution + country). Adding the institution stops distinct authors who share a common surname (for example several "Wang J" in one country) from being merged; any merging that remains is conservative, since it widens the confidence intervals rather than biasing the point estimate. The number and size of the first-author clusters, and the share identified by ORCID versus the fallback, are reported.
- **Secondary outcome (supportive):** em-dash count per Discussion section, with log(disc_len) offset.

## 6. Primary analysis and reporting hierarchy

**Model:** logistic GLM, `logit(P(HasEm)) = β₀ + β₁·post_ChatGPT`, with **first-author cluster-robust (sandwich) standard errors**. α = 0.05, single primary hypothesis (no multiplicity correction needed).

**Primary estimand:** the absolute difference in Discussion-section HasEm prevalence between post- and pre-ChatGPT deposits in the primary v1 cohort.

**Reporting (explicit interpretive hierarchy):**
1. Per-era HasEm% with counts and 95% Wilson CIs (descriptive).
2. **Absolute percentage-point difference** (post − pre) with 95% CI: the **primary interpretive measure**.
3. Unadjusted prevalence ratio (raw ratio; Koopman score 95% CI): a descriptive relative-effect measure.
4. Model-estimated odds ratio (cluster-robust 95% CI, Wald p): the inferential model output, with no covariate adjustment.

**Pre-specified magnitude interpretive scale** (bound to absolute pp difference): ≥ 5 pp → "substantial"; 2–5 pp → "moderate"; < 2 pp → "trivial, regardless of statistical significance". Anchors are structurally calibrated, not pilot-fitted: the 5 pp anchor is roughly 2–3× the typical pre-LLM year-to-year variation in HasEm%, and the 2 pp anchor roughly 1× (i.e., the within-baseline noise floor).

**Minimum detectable effect:** at α = 0.05, 80% power, per-era effective N ≈ 16,000–18,000 (raw N deflated by a conservative design effect of 1.5 for first-author clustering), baseline ≈ 4% (pre-ChatGPT era), the minimum detectable absolute difference is ≈ 0.4–0.6 pp. The binding constraint on interpretation is therefore substantive magnitude (the 2 pp / 5 pp scale), not statistical detectability.

## 7. Analysis hierarchy (three tiers; no formal α-spending)

**Supportive analyses** (pre-registered, reported regardless of the primary p-value):
- Em-dash **count density**: a robust Poisson GLM (log(disc_len) offset, first-author cluster-robust SE), reporting the IRR with 95% CI.
- **Section-comparison** (Discussion vs Results): a within-paper mixed-effects logistic with a section × era interaction (paper-level random intercept), on a paired subset (both sections validly extracted, each ≥ 500 chars); per-era paired-subset attrition reported. Interpreted as evidence for a narrative-section-specific stylistic shift, not as identification of an LLM mechanism.
- **Kobak target8 lexical convergence (abstracts)**, eight markers (delve, intricate, underscore, boast, endeavor, showcase, underpinning, garner), per-word and composite ORs as a forest plot; literature-comparable to Kobak et al. (2025). *(The Discussion-compartment Kobak analysis is reported in the supplement only.)*
- **Per-year HasEm%** with 95% Wilson CIs, descriptive temporal figure of record.
- **Quarterly segmented binomial regression**, interrupted-time-series model of the quarterly **proportion** of Discussion sections with HasEm = 1 (binomial GLM, logit link, weighted by total deposits per quarter, so growing deposit volume is not confounded with the rate) with a breakpoint at ChatGPT release, estimating the pre-release slope (β₁), the immediate level change at the breakpoint (β₂), and the post-release slope change (β₃), each with 95% CI. This is the formal step-vs-trend test that distinguishes a discrete shift at the breakpoint from a pre-existing secular drift; it is the principled control for the most plausible competing explanation (general typographic/editorial drift) and complements the placebo breakpoint (Section 8).
- **Subject-category composition by era**, descriptive table of major medRxiv subject categories per era (pre/post), with per-category HasEm% and Wilson CIs. Reported for transparency on composition shift; no subject-category adjustment is included in the primary model.

**Sensitivity analyses** (re-runs of the primary on modified cohorts; concordance = same direction, absolute pp difference within ±30% of the primary estimate, and overlapping 95% CI):
- Exclude the exploratory-sample-overlapping DOIs (1,926 of the 1,941 exploratory DOIs are present in the corpus; 1,565 fall within the primary cohort and are removed in this sensitivity).
- Latest-version cohort instead of v1.
- Exclude COVID-19-related preprints (subject category + keyword classifier).
- Alternative disc_len thresholds (≥ 250 and ≥ 1,000 characters).
- Exclude papers with a fused section heading (Discussion combined with Results or with Conclusion, e.g. "Results and Discussion"), where Results-section text may contaminate the Discussion em-dash count. Such fusions are 3.9% of the primary cohort and asymmetric by era (5.4% pre vs 2.5% post), so the contamination is conservative for the primary contrast; this sensitivity confirms the result is not driven by it.
- Exclude "range-only" papers, whose only Discussion em-dash is a numeric-range separator (digit-em-dash-digit, e.g. "1934-1971", "10-20 g"). A pre-registered diagnostic found these are 0.63% of HasEm=1 papers in the primary cohort and slightly asymmetric by era (1.36% pre vs 0.40% post among HasEm=1 papers; the direction inflates the pre-ChatGPT baseline and is therefore conservative for the primary contrast). This sensitivity reclassifies such papers as HasEm=0 and confirms the result is not driven by range punctuation.

## 8. Falsification, placebo breakpoint

Restricted to the **pre-LLM-only sub-cohort** (2020-01-01 to 2022-11-29), refit the primary model with a placebo cutoff at **2021-06-30**. Both periods are pre-LLM by construction; this is a temporal-specificity test. Pre-specified decision rule:

| Outcome | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Real ≥ 5 pp (substantial) AND placebo < 2 pp | Primary contrast is temporally specific to the ChatGPT window. |
| Real ≥ 5 pp AND placebo ≥ 2 pp, comparable in magnitude to the real shift | Fails falsification, reframe as a non-specific temporal rise. |
| Placebo ≈ 2 pp but well below the real shift | Equivocal; partial pre-existing drift. |

These thresholds are **qualitative falsification heuristics, not formal inferential decision boundaries**, and are stated on the **absolute percentage-point scale**, the primary estimand, anchored to the same 2 pp / 5 pp magnitude scale used for interpretation (Section 6). The heuristic is deliberately **not** governed by the odds ratio, which overstates relative effect at the low (~4% pre-ChatGPT) baseline. Both real and placebo contrasts are reported as absolute pp differences (and, secondarily, OR for comparability).

**Utility-section placebo (platform-artifact control):** apply the same em-dash counting to Acknowledgments and Data Availability statements. A utility section is considered **concerning** only if its post-ChatGPT prevalence reaches ≥ 1% **and** the post−pre increase is directionally similar to the Discussion-section increase **and** at least one-third of its magnitude. If a utility section meets all three, a platform-level artifact cannot be excluded and the primary contrast is reframed in Limitations; a sub-1% drift with no proportional relation to the Discussion increase is not treated as disconfirming.

## 9. Historical reference and comparator

No external comparator corpus is used. The internal medRxiv 2020–2022 pre-ChatGPT period is the historical reference prevalence. This is not a measure of diagnostic specificity; per-paper LLM-use ground truth is not available, and a per-paper detector is not the goal.

No clean typographic negative-control marker exists (exploratory data show all common punctuation drifts upward ~1.13×–1.29× in this corpus). Specificity is addressed instead by the placebo breakpoint, the section-comparison, and the Kobak convergence, none of which, individually or jointly, establishes LLM use as the unique cause.

## 10. Extraction validation (before primary analysis)

The validated constructs are **objective and deterministic**, presence of the literal character U+2014 in a text span, and identification of the Discussion section boundary against the source JATS XML, not subjective coding. Agreement therefore measures automated-pipeline accuracy against human-verified ground truth (rater-vs-pipeline), and Cohen's kappa is reported in that sense; a second independent human rater is not required because the target is not a matter of judgement. The only residual judgement is the Discussion-vs-Conclusion/Limitations boundary, governed by a stated section-boundary rule (JATS `sec-type` where present, else the first interpretive heading after Results).

Two pre-specified manual-review samples, drawn and reviewed **before** the primary analysis runs:

- **Sample A (section extraction, random):** n = 200 (100 pre-, 100 post-ChatGPT), stratified by year; verifies section identification and scope. Metric: % agreement with 95% Wilson CIs.
- **Sample B (HasEm classification, enriched):** n = 200, stratified by automated label × era (50 per cell); manual em-dash counting. Prevalence-invariant **Sensitivity** and **Specificity** per era are the primary validation metrics. Because Sample B is stratified on the automated label, the raw enriched proportions give PPV and NPV directly; Sensitivity and Specificity are recovered by re-weighting the confusion counts to the observed cohort prevalence (Bayes), which is what makes them prevalence-invariant. PPV and NPV are reported descriptively only.

Acceptance thresholds: Sample A section-ID and scope ≥ 90%. For Sample B the absolute thresholds, Sens ≥ 90% and Spec ≥ 95%, are evaluated on the **era-pooled** sample (100 true positives and 100 true negatives respectively, giving 1-pp granularity and avoiding the brittle 2-pp quantization of a 50-per-cell estimate); **era stability** is checked separately via |Sens_post − Sens_pre| ≤ 5 pp and |Spec_post − Spec_pre| ≤ 5 pp. **Acceptance is based on point estimates; Wilson 95% CIs are reported alongside to quantify uncertainty** (the lower CI bound is not required to clear the threshold, given the enriched sample size). If a point estimate does not meet its threshold, the pipeline is corrected and re-validated on fresh samples before the primary analysis proceeds.

## 11. Stopping rule and deviations

The confirmatory analysis is run **once** on the frozen Stage 2 dataset after retrieval and validation complete. No interim analyses; no adaptive stopping. Any analysis not specified here is reported as exploratory and labeled as such. All deviations from this registration are documented in a dedicated manuscript section. If any **pre-specified sensitivity analysis** (Section 7) attenuates the primary **absolute percentage-point difference** by more than 30%, confirmation is considered weakened and the result is framed as **sensitivity-dependent** rather than as a clean confirmatory finding.

## 12. Analyses explicitly NOT pre-registered as confirmatory

To keep the confirmatory core lean, the following are **not** part of this registration; they may be reported as clearly-labeled exploratory analyses, in the supplement, or deferred to follow-up work:
- ESL/NES first-author language stratification (exploratory / follow-up only).
- Kobak target8 in Discussion sections (supplementary).
- bioRxiv cross-substrate comparison (out of scope for this registration).
- Cross-model LLM emission audit (out of scope).

## 13. Software, code, and data availability

- **Analysis software:** Python 3.10+ (pandas, lxml, requests) and/or R (`lme4` for the mixed-effects section-comparison; GEE fallback). Scripts are idempotent and emit timestamped manifests.
- **Code:** public GitHub repository (`em-ergence-em-dash`). Frozen at data freeze, commit `21b65fd947165f9baca74dd6fc67b92a0c42adb1` (https://github.com/P-Czum/em-ergence-em-dash/commit/21b65fd947165f9baca74dd6fc67b92a0c42adb1); no changes to analysis scripts after this commit and before the confirmatory analysis.
- **Data:** the medRxiv corpus is public external data (S3 TDM) and is not redistributed. The integrity-critical freeze is the **GitHub commit hash, recorded at data freeze before the analysis**; the **Zenodo archive (DOI manifest + processed per-paper measurements) and its citable DOI are created at publication, after the analysis** (optionally, the frozen input dataset is also deposited to Zenodo at freeze for maximal provenance). The DOI manifest includes, per record: DOI, version, deposit date, subject category, and extraction status.

## 14. AI-assisted analysis disclosure

AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) were used for code generation, statistical-analysis assistance, and editorial review. They did not formulate the research question, choose the corpus, or independently make scientific decisions. Full disclosure appears in the manuscript.

## 15. Competing interests

The author declares no competing financial interests. Non-financial: the author is affiliated with the Polish Association for AI in Medicine. No external funding supported this work.

## 16. Pre-specified contingencies

Operational fallbacks fixed in advance, so that hitting them does not force an undocumented ad-hoc decision. This list is deliberately short, genuinely unforeseen events are handled under the deviation-reporting policy (Section 11), not pre-enumerated.

- **Validation cannot reach threshold.** If, after pipeline correction and re-validation on fresh samples (Section 10), an extraction metric still fails its threshold, the primary analysis is restricted to the subset for which extraction is validated and the study is reported as **measurement-limited**, rather than proceeding on an unvalidated pipeline. The restriction and its effect on N are reported.
- **Missing version metadata.** Papers whose deposit version cannot be parsed from the MECA `manifest.xml` are excluded from the v1 primary cohort, and their count is reported in the corpus inclusion flow.
- **Model non-convergence.** The primary logistic GLM (single predictor, large N) is not expected to have convergence issues; should the quarterly segmented model fail to converge, it is refit with reduced time terms (retain the level change β₂, drop the slope-change term β₃), and the section-comparison mixed model falls back to GEE (Section 13). Any fallback actually used is reported as such.

title: Applications of artificial intelligence in endobronchial ultra-sound for lung cancer diagnosis and staging: a scoping review
description: This scoping review evaluated the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) for lung cancer diagnosis and staging. A total of 26 studies published between 2015 and 2026 were included, with most employing deep learning–based models. The main clinical application was diagnostic classification of malignancy, followed by segmentation, cytological analysis, anatomical navigation, and multimodal predictive models. Most studies used EBUS-derived images or videos from both Convex Probe-EBUS and Radial Probe-EBUS procedures. Although findings highlight the growing potential of AI to improve diagnostic accuracy and image analysis, current evidence remains limited by retrospective designs, small sample sizes, and single-center studies.
