title: Strategies for Assessing Post-Hospitalization Outcomes in Trauma Survivors and their Feasibility of Implementation: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
ABSTRACT

Background: Each year, physical trauma affects over one billion people worldwide, generating a substantial burden in terms of mortality, disability, and productivity loss. The period following hospital discharge, encompassing the transition to home as well as outpatient and community-based follow-up care, represents a critical phase in the recovery process for individuals who have experienced traumatic injuries. Yet, this phase remains poorly documented. 

Objective: We aim to 1) map data on assessment strategies for various outcomes among trauma survivors after hospital discharge, including the tools and administration methods used, as well as the resources required, the perceived relevance of these strategies, and the barriers and facilitators to their implementation, and 2) compare the assessment strategies and the feasibility of their implementation in terms of response rates, resource use, costs, and sustainability or continuation beyond the study period.

Methods: We will conduct a scoping review using Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. We will search MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and PsycINFO for studies published since 1990 to reflect the evolution of contemporary follow-up practices, including the emergence of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) and digital tools. There will be no language restrictions. We will consider studies involving any trauma survivors, focusing on the evaluation of post-discharge health indicators. The period following hospital discharge, including the transition to short-term stays in rehabilitation facilities, the return home, and long-term outpatient or community-based follow-up care. Two independent reviewers will screen studies and extract data on population characteristics, assessment strategies, and feasibility dimensions. Results will be analyzed thematically and presented narratively. Counts and proportions of assessment strategies, their characteristics and associated barriers and facilitators will be presented. We also plan to conduct subgroup analyses according to clinical and social determinants and contextual factors. This protocol has been registered on the Open Science Framework.

Expected Results: This review will provide an overview of current practices regarding outcome assessment strategies for trauma patients after hospital discharge. It will provide data on the resources needed and contextual factors influencing the implementation of each assessment strategy. Findings will inform the design of sustainable strategies for monitoring long-term outcomes in trauma populations.

Keywords: (trauma survivors, post-discharge care, health indicators, patient-reported outcomes, feasibility.)

CONTEXTE
Each year, more than one billion people experience traumatic injuries worldwide [1]. Although recent advances in trauma care have significantly reduced post-trauma mortality, survivors still face a substantial ongoing burden [2]. Traumatic injuries are among the leading causes of disability [1, 3, 4], and account for the highest number of productive years of life lost [4].

The period following hospital discharge, including the transition to short-term stays in rehabilitation facilities, the return home, and long-term outpatient or community-based follow-up care, represents a critical phase in the recovery process for individuals who have experienced traumatic injuries. Yet, this continuum of care remains poorly documented.[5-8]. Trauma patients are at risk of developing long-term complications such as a decline in function, persistent pain, and reduced quality of life [9]. These risks may be exacerbated in the absence of appropriate, coordinated post-discharge support, increasing the strain on health systems and society [10]. In this context, the development of integrated, patient-centered models for follow-up outcome assessment, which are distinct from the provision of long-term-care is essential to better capture the functional, psychological, and social recovery of survivors [1, 4, 11].

Current quality of care assessment methods, such as trauma registries, typically focus on health outcomes during hospitalization or in the short term, thus neglecting patients’ long-term continuum of care [12, 13]. Furthermore, follow-up assessments rely primarily on objective health outcomes (e.g. mortality rate, readmissions) or administrative outcomes (service use, costs) [14, 15]. While these dimensions are important, they capture only a limited part of the patient’s long-term lived experience [13, 16]. In this regard, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) can serve as valuable complementary tools, enabling patients to assess their own health status at specific timepoints [17]. When combined with objective health outcomes, they offer a more comprehensive and nuanced view of recovery trajectories [18].

Despite their recognized value, the use of PROMs following trauma care remains inconsistent across jurisdictions. Some trauma systems, such as those in Australia [19] and the Netherlands [13] have successfully integrated longitudinal PROMs collection into routine practice. However, many other regions continue to face significant challenges that lead them to focus on isolated outcome assessment strategies rather than a comprehensive or integrated approach. [18]. Likewise, variability in administration methods (e.g., self-administration vs. professional-led, timing of assessments, type of personnel involved), heterogeneity in the tools used, and multiple barriers associated with data collection processes (e.g., required human and material resources, low patient response rates) have been described [20, 21]. Nonetheless, several facilitating factors have been identified, including the integration of outcome assessment strategies into routine care, the engagement of patients and their families, and the use of new technologies such as digital tools like mobile health applications, web-based monitoring platforms and electronic symptom trackers [7, 17, 19, 22-25]. 

To develop more coherent, accessible, and sustainable long-term outcome assessment strategies in trauma survivors, it is crucial to map existing health outcome measurement tools. Furthermore, describing the resources mobilized for their implementation after discharge, along with barriers and facilitators to their feasibility, will inform future models for follow-up outcome assessment [7, 26, 27]. Ultimately, effective implementation of such models can enhance continuity of care and support long-term recovery for trauma survivors.

METHODOLOGY
We will conduct a scoping review based on the methodological framework developed by Arksey and O’Malley (2005), structured into six stages: (1) identifying the research question, (2) identifying relevant studies, (3) study selection, (4) data extraction and analysis, (5) collating, summarizing, and reporting the results, and (6) stakeholder consultation to enrich or validate the findings [28, 29].

This protocol was developed in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidelines for scoping reviews (JBI Scoping Review Methodology) [30, 31], and the results will be reported following the PRISMA-ScR checklist [30, 32]. This protocol has been pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF).

STEP 1: Identifying the Research Question
This scoping review aims to map the nature and extent of available data on strategies used to measure outcomes in survivors of traumatic injuries following hospital discharge. It will focus specifically on outcome measurement, such as PROMs and other types of clinical, functional, psychological, social, or administrative indicators, obtained from routinely collected data or obtained directly from patients. This review will not address follow-up care delivery, but rather how outcomes are captured and assessed post-discharge.

More specifically, this review seeks to identify:
1) The outcome assessment strategies used to evaluate the long-term outcomes of trauma survivors, including the tools and instruments employed (including, but not limited to, PROMs);
2) The characteristics of these assessment strategies (e.g., type of outcome measured, mode of administration, timing within the care trajectory, frequency and duration of follow-up, individuals responsible for data collection);
3) The human resources involved (e.g., clinical staff, researchers and data analysts, administrative personnel, healthcare professionals or information systems technicians) and material resources required (e.g., standardized measurement tools, data collection software, administrative or clinical databases, computer equipment, remote communication tools) required to implement these strategies;
4) The barriers and facilitators to the implementation of the outcome assessment strategies, including their perceived relevance and the extent to which these strategies are adapted to patients’ needs;
5) The costs associated with their implementation.
6) The sustainability or continuation of the assessment strategies beyond the study period.

Eligibility Criteria
The inclusion and exclusion criteria are based on the population/concept/context framework for scoping reviews, as recommended in the methodological guidelines of the JBI [33]. 

Population: We will include all studies reporting outcome assessment strategies for adult or pediatric patients who have sustained traumatic injuries (i.e., traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, visceral organ injuries, orthopaedic injuries) requiring hospitalization, regardless of injury mechanism. Studies must clearly specify that participants were hospitalized due to physical traumatic injuries. Studies focusing exclusively on patients with burns will be excluded because these patients are often managed by specialized teams distinct from general trauma care. 

Concept: We will focus on structured strategies to assess in the post-discharge period following hospitalization for trauma. Studies must address concrete modalities of health data collection after hospital discharge, whether administered in person, by telephone, electronically, or through alternative patient-centered approaches (e.g., mailed surveys, proxy interviews, community-based assessments). We will include studies that report proxy PROMs (e.g., completed by caregivers or family members) when patients are children or adults physically or cognitively unable to complete them themselves, whether due to injury-related impairment (e.g., severe TBI) or pre-existing conditions (e.g., dementia, intellectual disability) [34-37] 

The types of outcomes/tools considered include (but are not limited to):
• Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs);
• Health indicators (e.g., pain, medical complications);
• Functional indicators (e.g., mobility, autonomy, performance-based measures);
• Psychological indicators (e.g., anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress);
• Social indicators (e.g., social reintegration, return to work/school);
• Administrative indicators (e.g., use of healthcare services, hospital readmissions).

This classification draws on trauma research and health services evaluations, which highlight the need to consider both clinical outcomes and the broader psychosocial and functional dimensions of recovery [15, 18, 38, 39].

To be eligible, studies must document at least one of the following elements:
• Health follow-up outcomes or PROMs assessed post-hospital discharge;
• Detailed information on the outcome assessment strategies used to evaluate the long-term outcomes of trauma survivors (e.g., biological or functional measures, medical examinations, structured interviews, validated or non-validated questionnaires);
• Documentation of data collection modalities (e.g., timing within the care trajectory, frequency, duration, mode of administration [online, paper-based, phone], location);
• Description of the individuals involved in data collection (e.g., healthcare professionals, researchers, clinicians, administrative staff);
• Presentation, where applicable, of the material and human resources mobilized to collect the data;
• Reporting, when available, of:
o The feasibility and perceived relevance of the outcome assessment strategy;
o Response or participation rates;
o Barriers and facilitators;
o Sustainability or continuation of the strategy beyond the study period;
o Adaptation or adjustment strategies based on patients’ needs;
o Costs associated with the implementation of the assessment strategy.

Context: We will include all studies conducted after hospital discharge, across various post-discharge follow-up settings, whether clinical (e.g., outpatient visits, specialized trauma clinics, rehabilitation centers), community-based (e.g., community support services, home care organizations, trauma survivor support groups), or home-based (e.g., home visits by healthcare professionals, telephone follow-up, telemedicine, or digital self-assessment platforms). All geographic locations and models of care will be considered, as long as post-hospital outcomes are documented.

We will exclude studies without a follow-up period after hospital discharge, conducted exclusively in military settings with no intent for generalization, and reporting follow-up conducted solely as part of a research project, without any aim of organizational or systemic integration into a trauma care program. 

We will include publications from 1990 onward to reflect the evolution of contemporary follow-up practices, including the emergence of PROMs and digital tools, such as mobile health applications, web-based monitoring platforms and electronic symptom trackers [40]. There will be no language restrictions. Articles published in languages, other than that of the research team members, i.e. English, Arabic, Dutch, French, Italian, Portuguese, will be translated using the DeepL Translator tool. [41].

Source of evidence selection: All study designs will be considered, including quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies, provided they explicitly document the assessment of outcomes from a perspective applicable to a healthcare system. We will exclude single case studies and conference abstracts (i.e., abstracts without a full article available) and research protocols.

STEP 2: Identifying Relevant Studies

Databases
We will search for relevant studies in the following databases: MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and PsycINFO. Additionally, we will explore dissertations, theses, and academic reports via ProQuest. To ensure comprehensive coverage, we will also screen the reference lists of all included articles, dissertations, and theses to identify any additional eligible studies.

Search Strategy
In accordance with the Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies (PRESS) guidelines [42], a rigorous systematic search strategy will first be developed in collaboration with an information specialist. The strategy will then undergo an independent peer review by a librarian. Our search strategy will be based on a combination of free-text terms and controlled vocabulary, including terms such as: trauma, injury, follow-up, PROMs, feasibility, barriers, and facilitators.
We will begin with a pilot search in MEDLINE (via PubMed) and Embase (via Ovid) to identify additional relevant keywords. Key terms extracted from the titles, abstracts, and full texts of selected studies will be collected and integrated into the final strategy. This enriched strategy will then be applied across all selected databases to ensure comprehensive coverage.

To ensure the sensitivity, specificity, and overall effectiveness of the search strategy, we will use a predefined set of eligibility criteria to select a group of sentinel studies (see Appendix 1). These studies represent a benchmark to evaluate the performance of the strategy. Sensitivity will be assessed by confirming that all sentinel studies meeting the criteria were successfully retrieved. Specificity will be considered by examining whether the strategy avoids retrieving an unmanageable volume of irrelevant citations, which could compromise the feasibility of the screening process. A preliminary version of the search strategy is available in Table 1.

STEP 3: Study Selection
We will use EndNote (version X9.3.3, New York City: Thomson Reuters, 2018) for citation management. Duplicate records will be identified and removed using both automated and manual methods.

Two reviewers (MLS, MAG) will independently screen the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the studies. To ensure the reliability and reproducibility of the selection process, they will follow a systematic and iterative approach, testing the screening process on random samples of 250 citations. This process will be refined until an acceptable level of inter-rater agreement is achieved, based on methodological standards (kappa > 0.8) [43].

In case of disagreements, a senior member of the research team (MB) will be consulted to resolve conflicts. Finally, we will document the search strategy, selection process, and reasons for exclusion in detail using a PRISMA flow diagram [44] to ensure transparency and traceability throughout the study selection process.

STEP 4: Data Extraction
We have developed a standardized data extraction form using the JBI template with Microsoft Excel (version 16.0, Redmond, WA: Microsoft Corporation, 2018), available in Appendix (X). This form will be iteratively tested by two reviewers (MLS, MAG) with both methodological and subject-matter expertise. The test will be conducted on a random sample of five studies representing the diversity of included studies, and the form will be refined until an acceptable level of inter-rater agreement is reached, in line with methodological standards (kappa > 0.8) [43]. Data will be extracted from the original publications along several key dimensions by two reviewers (MLS, MAG). Any discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third team member (MB or LM), if needed.

Regarding the study context, the following information will be collected: country, year of publication, funding source, research design, and the level of implementation (e.g., trauma system, provincial or national health authority, hospital-based, community-based). As for the study population, reviewers will extract the total number of participants and their distribution across various variables: sex, gender, age group, type and severity of trauma, place of residence (urban or rural), ethnocultural background, and socioeconomic status. We will also document the characteristics of the outcome/tool used after hospital discharge. This will include the nature of the indicators assessed, the PROMs used, the timing and frequency of assessments, the mode of administration (in-person, virtual, hybrid), the location where questionnaires were administered (e.g., home, outpatient clinic), as well as any specific adaptations made to meet patients’ particular needs.

In addition, the interventions’ feasibility analysis will be guided by Proctor’s Implementation Outcomes (PIO) framework. Accordingly, the following elements will be extracted: required infrastructure and resources (both human and material), response rate (the proportion of eligible patients who completed the questionnaires), institutional adoption rate, identified barriers and facilitators, as well as associated direct costs (e.g., staff salaries, equipment purchases, software licenses, training expenses) and indirect costs (e.g., time required from clinical personnel, workflow disruptions, or productivity losses related to implementation). The sustainability of the implemented assessment strategies will also be examined [45]. We will extract data aligned with the conceptual domains identified in recent sustainability models, including organizational capacity, ongoing learning, monitoring and feedback, alignment with broader systems, staff engagement, and community involvement. [46] Finally, we will collect information on patient engagement strategies and any equity-related considerations regarding the implementation of the assessment strategies, as well as social determinants that may affect response rates (e.g., sex, age, ethnocultural background, and socioeconomic status)[47]. Where available, we will examine stratified response rates to identify differential participation across subgroups. Particular attention will be given to populations at increased risk of being excluded from follow-up care, such as individuals with no fixed address or those living with mental health or substance use disorders. This will help highlight the barriers faced by these groups and how intersecting determinants influence their experience within the healthcare system.

Any disagreements between reviewers will be resolved through consensus-based discussion. In the event of persistent disagreement, a senior member of the research team (MB or LM) will be consulted to arbitrate the decision. If essential information is missing or unclear, we will contact the first, second, and last authors of the corresponding study, sending up to three emails to request clarification.

STEP 5: Collating, Summarizing, and Reporting the Results
The findings of this scoping review will be compiled, synthesized, and presented using both descriptive and analytical methods, in accordance with the guidelines of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA-ScR reporting framework. As previously mentioned, once study selection is complete, data will be extracted and organized into a summary table structured according to the type of health indicator/tool (e.g., clinical indicators, PROMs, functional, psychological, social, and administrative measures), follow-up modalities, implementation strategies, feasibility factors, and reported outcomes.

The results will be synthesized using a descriptive and thematic approach, highlighting overall trends, variations observed across the included studies and research gaps. To improve the interpretability of the findings, we will construct a mapping table that links the types of outcome assessed (e.g., PROMs, clinical, functional, psychological, social, administrative) and the other modalities involved (e.g., the mode of administration, frequency of assessments) with key feasibility elements such as response rates, timing of follow-up, resources mobilized, and reported costs. This cross-classification will support the identification of patterns between various follow-up indicators and tools, and help compare the feasibility of their implementation.

In addition to this mapping and thematic analysis (qualitative analysis), we will record the frequency of specific characteristics related to the outcomes/tools and the barriers and facilitators associated with their implementation using counts and proportions. This will support a more precise understanding of the key issues to consider in their implementation.

Subgroup analyses will be conducted, data permitting, to explore variations in follow-up strategies and feasibility dimensions across different participant-related and contextual factors. These factors will include the type of trauma, participant age group, mode of administration of the assessment tools (e.g., in-person, online, hybrid), and healthcare system context (e.g., low, middle, and high-income countries). This stratified synthesis will help identify whether certain strategies are more feasible, acceptable, or sustainable depending on the setting and population characteristics, thereby enhancing the contextual relevance and transferability of the findings.

The results will be presented in various formats to support interpretation and dissemination. Descriptive tables will summarize the characteristics of the studies and strategies, their feasibility, and key findings, while figures and graphs will provide a clear illustration of trends and comparisons across strategies.

STEP 6: Stakeholder Consultation
An advisory committee was consulted for the development of this protocol, to ensure the relevance and applicability of the findings. This committee include experts from high-, middle-, and low-income countries representing various disciplines involved in trauma care and post-discharge follow-up, including epidemiology, health data protection and enhancement, trauma surgery, nursing, rehabilitation, psychology, social work and primary care. We have also involved individuals with lived experience as well as healthcare decision-makers and administrators. 

The consultation process aimed to: 1) identify any additional references that could enrich the analysis; 2) gather feedback on elements to include, as well as on the presentation and interpretation of the findings; 3) explore opportunities for knowledge mobilization and practical application of the results in clinical practice and health policy.
To optimize collaboration, we will schedule periodic meetings (in person or virtual) with the members of the advisory committee at key milestones of the review process. These meetings will include structured group discussions and facilitated feedback sessions. In addition, we will use online tools such as questionnaires, shared documents and electronic surveys to systematically collect comments, suggestions, and evaluations. This mixed-methods approach will help capture both individual and collective perspectives and ensure their integration at different stages of the scoping review. This approach is aligned with best practices in stakeholder engagement during knowledge synthesis, which recommend combining synchronous and asynchronous data collection methods to ensure broad participation and integration of diverse perspectives [31, 48, 49].

LIMITATIONS AND MITIGATION STRATEGIES
This scoping review presents certain methodological limitations inherent to its design and the range of studies targeted. In accordance with the methodological recommendations for scoping reviews [28, 30, 33, 44] and due to the wide variety of study designs, we will not conduct a critical appraisal of the methodological quality of included studies. This will limit our ability to assess the strength of individual findings. However, this is in line with recommendations, and we will apply a rigorous selection and evaluation process, including independent dual screening and calculation of inter-rater agreement, ensuring consistency in the application of inclusion and exclusion criteria and maximizing the reliability of the review process.

Secondly, unlike systematic reviews, scoping reviews do not aim to estimate the effectiveness of an intervention, therefore, there will be no meta-analysis. As a result, we will not be able to determine the overall strength of the evidence. While this limits our ability to draw conclusions about the long-term impact of the health indicators/tools assessed, the clear structure of the review, according to the JBI and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, will ensure that findings are presented in a transparent and rigorous manner, thereby maximizing their usefulness for future research and decision-making, including future phases aimed at evaluating the effectiveness of long-term outcome assessment strategies in improving patient outcomes.

Third, the anticipated variability in the health assessment strategies and the methods used may limit comparability across studies. To address this, a standardized data extraction form will be developed based on predefined variables and analytical categories and refined through expert consultation. This process will help identify the key elements to be extracted and validate the analytical framework, thereby strengthening the rigor of the synthesis.

Fourth, the lack of standardization in health indicators and PROMs used across studies may complicate the assessment of post-discharge follow-up feasibility and limit the conclusions that can be drawn. To mitigate this issue, we will develop a mapping table linking the types of indicators assessed with feasibility elements (e.g., response rate, timing of evaluation, resources mobilized), which will contribute to a more structured and effective interpretation of the findings.

Finally, considering the inconsistencies in health assessment follow-up methods across healthcare contexts and systems, some results may not be generalizable to all clinical settings or to less-developed countries. To put this limitation into perspective, we plan to conduct subgroup analyses, when data is available, based on variables such as World Bank country income categories. This will help contextualize the findings according to specific settings.
In addition, an advisory committee composed of healthcare professionals, policymakers, and individuals with lived experience will be involved throughout the process to ensure the relevance and applicability of the findings, thereby enhancing the transferability of knowledge to clinical practice and health policy.

DISCUSSION
The results of this scoping review will provide an up-to-date and structured overview of strategies to assess outcomes in trauma survivors after hospital discharge. By identifying the strategies employed, their characteristics, the resources mobilized, as well as the barriers and facilitators to their implementation, this synthesis will offer an essential knowledge base to support the development of more integrated, accessible, and sustainable long-term assessment tools within trauma care systems.

The expected impacts extend to both research and clinical practice. This review will help inform methodological choices for future evaluation and interventional studies, while also guiding clinicians and decision-makers on favorable conditions for the integration of outcomes and assessment tools into post-trauma care pathways. The findings will also highlight current gaps in the literature, helping to prioritize areas that require further research efforts.

title: Leveraging AI-Driven Neuroimaging Biomarkers for Early Detection and Social Function Prediction in Autism Spectrum Disorders. A Systematic Review
description: This systematic review examines artificial intelligence (AI) applications in neuroimaging for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), addressing the critical need for objective biomarkers that could enable earlier detection and more accurate prediction of developmental outcomes. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive literature search across eight databases, yielding 146 studies from an initial 1,872 records. These studies were systematically analyzed to address key questions regarding AI-neuroimaging approaches in ASD detection and prognosis. Results: Neuroimaging combined with AI algorithms demonstrated significant potential for early ASD detection, with electroencephalography (EEG) showing promise. Machine learning classifiers achieved high diagnostic accuracy (85-99%) using features derived from neural oscillatory patterns, connectivity measures, and signal complexity metrics. Studies of infant populations identified the 9–12-month developmental window as critical for biomarker detection and preceding behavioral symptoms. Multimodal approaches integrating various imaging techniques substantially enhanced predictive capabilities, while longitudinal analyses showed potential for tracking developmental trajectories and treatment response. Conclusions: AI-driven neuroimaging biomarkers represent a promising frontier in ASD research, potentially enabling detection before behavioral symptoms manifest and providing objective measures of intervention efficacy. While technical and methodological challenges remain, advancements in standardization, diverse sampling, and clinical validation could facilitate translation into practice, ultimately supporting earlier intervention during critical developmental periods and improving outcomes for individuals with ASD.

title: Data Analysis and Outcome reporting
description:
Primary outcome
The primary outcome will be the diagnostic performance of predefined nutritional screening tools for identifying GLIM-defined malnutrition in adults with IBD.
Performance will be assessed using study-level sensitivity, specificity and diagnostic odds ratio where complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data are available.
Secondary outcomes
1. Diagnostic performance of the predefined nutritional screening tools against ESPEN criteria and SGA, analysed separately from GLIM-based evidence.
2. The proportion of study-screening tool-comparator rows meeting the predefined screening benchmark of sensitivity >=80%.
3. Supportive diagnostic measures, including PPV and NPV, where available or calculable.
4. Narrative summary of PICO-eligible studies that report relevant performance, agreement or association data but do not provide sufficient data to reconstruct a 2 x 2 table.
Kappa and accuracy may be reported descriptively as supplementary measures but will not be used as primary measures of screening performance.
Data synthesis and analysis
The main synthesis will focus on predefined nutritional screening tools assessed against GLIM-defined malnutrition. Studies using ESPEN criteria or SGA as comparators will be analysed separately and will not be combined with GLIM-based evidence.
Studies with complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data will be included in the structured diagnostic accuracy synthesis. Each row will represent one nutritional screening tool assessed against one comparator within one study.
For each study-screening tool-comparator row, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and diagnostic odds ratio will be calculated where sufficient data are available. Wilson 95% confidence intervals will be calculated for sensitivity and specificity. Diagnostic odds ratios will be presented with 95% confidence intervals. Where zero cells are present, a 0.5 continuity correction will be applied. A diagnostic odds ratio confidence interval excluding 1 will be interpreted as evidence that the screening tool shows discriminatory ability in that cohort.
Results will be presented in structured tables. The primary table will show study-level performance of each nutritional screening tool against GLIM. A secondary table will show performance against ESPEN criteria and SGA.
For each nutritional screening tool against GLIM, results will be summarised descriptively using the median and range of sensitivity and specificity, PPV and NPV ranges, kappa range, the number of studies in which the diagnostic odds ratio confidence interval excludes 1, and the number of rows meeting the predefined sensitivity benchmark of >=80%.
Kappa and accuracy may be reported descriptively as supplementary measures but will not be used as primary measures of screening performance.
Forest plots will be used to display study-level sensitivity and specificity estimates with 95% confidence intervals. No pooled estimate will be calculated.
Formal meta-analysis is not planned. PICO-eligible studies without complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data will be summarised narratively as supportive evidence only.
Exploration of variation
Where necessary, variation in diagnostic performance will be explored descriptively in relation to population demographics, disease activity and clinical setting.
Because the number of studies per nutritional screening tool is expected to be small, formal subgroup analysis, meta-regression and pooled sensitivity analysis are not planned.

title: Scoping Review of Risk Prediction Models for Acute Kidney Injury Following Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation
description:
This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing evidence on risk prediction models for acute kidney injury (AKI) in adult patients following successful resuscitation from cardiac arrest (including both out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [OHCA] and in-hospital cardiac arrest [IHCA]).
Cardiac arrest survivors are at high risk of developing AKI, which is strongly associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stay, and poor neurological outcomes. In recent years, several risk prediction models (such as nomograms, logistic regression-based scores, and machine learning models) have been developed to predict AKI occurrence, progression, or severity in this population. However, the evidence remains sparse, fragmented, and has not yet been systematically synthesized or critically appraised.
The objectives of this scoping review are:
(1) to identify all published and unpublished studies that have developed, validated, or updated risk prediction models for AKI after successful cardiac arrest resuscitation;
(2) to summarize the key characteristics of these models, including study design, sample size, predictors, performance metrics (e.g., AUC/C-index, calibration, sensitivity, specificity, decision curve analysis), and validation approaches (internal/external);
(3) to assess the methodological quality of the included models using the PROBAST tool; and
(4) to highlight current evidence gaps and provide clear directions for future research and clinical application.
This scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Comprehensive searches will be performed in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and other relevant databases, with no language or publication date restrictions.
The findings of this review will provide clinicians, researchers, and guideline developers with a clear overview of the current state of AKI risk prediction modeling in post-cardiac arrest patients and serve as a foundation for the development of more robust, externally validated, and clinically implementable prediction tools.

title: Processo de validação de instrumentos de autoavaliação da voz: Uma revisão de Escopo
description:
Informações sobre a avaliação da validade, confiabilidade e responsividade nos instrumentos de autoavaliação de pacientes com disfonia são importantíssimos, visto que os principais objetivos do tratamento são melhorar a função vocal dos pacientes e seu bem-estar. Este tipo de estudo permite a otimização e o direcionamento das avaliações na prática clínica, diminuindo a sobrecarga ao paciente e ao terapeuta. A responsividade dos testes tem sido realizada nos últimos dez anos, apontando um interesse maior das pesquisas na criação de instrumentos mais sensíveis, para utilização na prática clínica e nos ensaios clínicos.
Portanto, para uma melhor utilização dos protocolos de autoavaliação vocal no diagnóstico ou acompanhamento terapêutico, faz-se necessário compreender as evidências científicas que respaldam a sua utilização, bem como todo o processo de validação que esse instrumento obedeceu. Desta forma, essa pesquisa propõe mapear o processo de validação de instrumentos de autoavaliação vocal, utilizados em pacientes disfônicos adultos, bem como fornecer a pesquisadores e clínicos evidências sobre a qualidade e utilidade clínica dos instrumentos de avaliação da voz utilizados na prática clínica no Brasil.

Diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for CDKN2A homozygous deletion and for distinguishing mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations: a systematic review and bivariate meta-analysis
description:
This OSF project (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/M9PTK) hosts the supplementary materials for a systematic review and bivariate / HSROC meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry (a) as a surrogate for CDKN2A homozygous deletion and (b) for distinguishing mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations. The review is reported to PRISMA-DTA 2020 standards, with risk of bias assessed by QUADAS-2.

The frozen pre-registration is held separately at OSF Registries, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/S7YW4, and is preserved exactly as registered. The controlling methods-of-record for the completed review is protocol amendment v5 (19 June 2026), as amended by protocol amendment v6 (6 August 2026) for changes made in response to peer review; both are deposited here. Between them they document every deviation from, and correction to, the registered plan with its rationale and impact. The primary review questions and the reference standards are unchanged from registration.

REVIEW QUESTIONS

(a) Primary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry, used alone, for detecting CDKN2A homozygous deletion in pleural mesothelioma, taking dual-colour CDKN2A FISH (or an equivalent CNV / NGS reference) as the gold standard? Peritoneal mesothelioma is addressed separately, as a pre-specified and independently reported stratum, and is not pooled with the pleural primary analysis.

(b) Secondary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for distinguishing histologically or cytologically confirmed mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations, taking the integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis as the reference? Peritoneal cohorts are likewise reported separately from the pleural-main secondary pool.

POPULATION AND SPECIMENS

Adult patients with suspected mesothelioma (pleural as the primary target; peritoneal as a pre-specified, separately reported subgroup) undergoing diagnostic biopsy or pleural / peritoneal effusion cytology, in whom MTAP IHC has been applied as part of the ancillary diagnostic workup.

INDEX TEST

MTAP immunohistochemistry on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue or cell block. Pre-specified primary loss definition: complete cytoplasmic loss with positive internal control. Pre-specified sensitivity-analysis convention: each study's own threshold including broader patterns (nuclear loss, focal loss, >=30% cells lost). Antibody clone recorded as a pre-specified subgroup variable (2G4 reference clone; mAb1813; EPR6893; 2B1G6; polyclonal / unspecified).

REFERENCE STANDARD

Primary: CDKN2A homozygous deletion by dual-colour FISH (>=10% nuclei threshold standard). CNV array and targeted NGS panels with explicit CDKN2A copy-number calls are accepted equivalents.

Secondary: integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis per IMIG 2017 / WHO 2021 with at least 12 months follow-up for benign controls. Incorporation bias is acknowledged and addressed in QUADAS-2 domain 3.

OUTCOMES

Primary: pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio (all with 95% CI); summary HSROC curve with 95% confidence and prediction regions.

Secondary: between-study heterogeneity (tau^2, I^2); pre-specified subgroup pooled estimates by antibody clone and specimen format; pooled proportion of uninterpretable MTAP IHC results.

SEARCH (as executed)

PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and a Google Scholar top-up, from inception to 18 June 2026. A single index-test-agnostic concept pair was applied at the database stage — (MTAP OR methylthioadenosine phosphorylase) AND (mesothelioma OR mesothelial); restriction to the MTAP-IHC index test and to an admissible reference standard was performed by manual screening. Per-source yields: PubMed 153, Web of Science 217, Scopus 194, Google Scholar 1, citation tracking 0 — 565 records identified, 20 studies included. The registered protocol named PubMed and Embase to 2 June 2026; Embase access lapsed at the re-run and was replaced by Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar, with the cut-off extended to 18 June 2026. This deviation, and the correction of the earlier two-strand / IHC-term search description to the single executed concept pair, are documented in amendment v5 and in the deposited search log (MTAP_search_strategy_log.md).

DATA EXTRACTION AND VERIFICATION

Two reviewers — V. Tayade (Grant Government Medical College & Sir J.J. Group of Hospitals, Mumbai) and G. Singh (AIIMS Rajkot) — extracted each included study independently from the source articles, and discrepancies between the two independent extractions were resolved by consensus to form the locked dataset. Every 2x2 cell (TP, FP, FN, TN) is transcribed verbatim from the source; no value is fabricated, approximated, inferred, or back-calculated, and manuscript point estimates are drawn only from the locked analysis output (mtap_dta_analysis_FINAL.R -> MTAP_R_output.txt). The locked extraction is deposited as MTAP_2x2_dataset_locked.csv and, in formatted form, as MTAP_Supplementary_Table_S1_2x2.xlsx; MTAP_2x2_dataset_v6.csv supersedes it, carrying the same counts with columns marking which arms contribute to a pooled stratum. (The registered record's description of the second-reviewer step is corrected in amendment v5; see that document.)

RISK OF BIAS

QUADAS-2 (Whiting 2011): four risk-of-bias domains (patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing) and three applicability domains, scored per study. Tally across the 20 included studies: Low 85, High 24, Unclear 31. Workbook deposited as MTAP_QUADAS2_workbook.xlsx.

DATA SYNTHESIS

Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis (Reitsma 2005 / Rutter-Gatsonis HSROC) using the mada package in R, with logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity jointly modelled. Where a pool's specificity is at or near 100% (most or all false positives = 0), the pre-specified summary is the univariate random-effects pooled sensitivity (logit, DerSimonian-Laird), with specificity described as at/near 100%. Peritoneal cohorts are reported separately from the pleural pools, and the Fukuoka University representatives are entered sensitivity-only. Reproducible analysis code is deposited as mtap_dta_analysis_FINAL.R with its output log MTAP_R_output.txt; the SROC plots and the PRISMA-DTA study-flow diagram are deposited as PDF and PNG. The computational environment, and a cross-version check confirming the estimates reproduce under mada 0.5.12 and meta 8.5-0, are recorded in MTAP_sessionInfo.txt.

Pool composition as registered (20 studies / 22 two-by-two tables / five strata):
- Primary, pleural-main (k = 7): Chapel 2020, Chapel 2021, Vrugt 2023, Febres-Aldana 2024, Seker 2026, Broggi 2024, Brcic 2023.
- Primary, peritoneal, reported separately (k = 1): Quaranta 2025 (1% cutoff).
- Secondary, MTAP-alone, pleural-main (k = 9): Berg 2018 (tissue), Berg 2020, Chapel 2022, Lynggard (histology), Lynggard (cytology), Seker 2024, Hiroshima 2021, Amacher 2023, Aoe 2026.
- Secondary, peritoneal, reported separately (k = 2): Alsugair 2022 (biopsy), Quaranta 2025 (secondary).
- Fukuoka University series, sensitivity-only (k = 3): Kinoshita 2020 (tissue), Kinoshita 2021 (cytology), Sa-ngiamwibool 2022.

Pool composition after peer review (19 studies / 21 two-by-two tables; amendment v6): Alsugair 2022 was withdrawn from quantitative synthesis, both arms, because it scored MTAP loss by absent nuclear staining rather than the complete-cytoplasmic-loss convention applied throughout, and therefore does not read the same index test. Peritoneal data are no longer pooled: the k = 2 secondary peritoneal estimate is withdrawn and Quaranta 2025 is reported descriptively, as is the primary peritoneal arm. Three strata are pooled (primary pleural k = 7, secondary pleural-main k = 9, Fukuoka sensitivity-only k = 3) and two peritoneal strata (k = 1 each) are descriptive. Twenty reports remain in the flow diagram and in the study-characteristics table as identified and eligible. No 2x2 cell value changed, and no pooled pleural estimate changed.

PRE-SPECIFIED SENSITIVITY ANALYSES

(i) Exclude Seker 2024 from the secondary main pool. (ii) Stratify by specimen (tissue versus cytology) — performed; see SUBGROUP ANALYSES below. (iii) Stratify by clone (2G4 versus other) — performed; see below. (iv) Primary-pool sensitivity with each study's own threshold; the substituted counts are recorded in amendment v5 §8 and in the deposited dataset, and threshold-substituted re-fits were not performed. (v) Sa-ngiamwibool ID-handling variant. (vi) Lynggard cytology-only sensitivity to bound the effect of the shared TN = 20 reactive mesothelial controls used in both Lynggard arms; the drop-one-arm analyses are deposited as SROC_SECONDARY_drop_Lynggard_cyto.pdf and SROC_SECONDARY_drop_Lynggard_histo.pdf.

SUBGROUP ANALYSES

Performed and reported: specimen format (tissue k = 4 versus effusion cytology k = 5) and antibody clone (2G4 k = 3 versus other k = 6), both within the secondary pleural-main pool. Neither showed a difference in sensitivity. Outputs are deposited as SROC_SECONDARY_specimen_cytology.pdf and SROC_SECONDARY_clone_other.pdf; no SROC is produced for the tissue or 2G4 subgroups, in which every contributor returned zero false positives, so a bivariate model is not applicable and the pre-specified univariate summary applies. Because the single false-positive contributor in the whole pool is simultaneously the cytology arm, a non-2G4 clone and the broader loss threshold, specimen format, clone and threshold are mutually confounded at this number of contributors; both comparisons are therefore descriptive and neither is a test of difference.

Planned but not performed, the number of contributing studies being insufficient to support them: histologic subtype (epithelioid versus sarcomatoid including desmoplastic versus biphasic versus mixed); anatomic site (pleural versus peritoneal) as a pooled comparison; reference-standard modality; and time period (pre-2020 versus 2020 onward).

STATUS

The search, data extraction, QUADAS-2 assessment, and synthesis are complete. The manuscript was submitted to Cancer Cytopathology in June 2026, received a major revision decision in August 2026, and the revision was submitted on 14 August 2026. The registered protocol's status note originally read "synthesis completed; deviations nil"; amendment v5 corrects this to record that deviations and corrections were identified and are documented in full — that is, not nil — superseding the earlier "nil deviations" declaration. Amendment v6 records the further changes made in response to peer review.

FUNDING AND CONFLICTS

No external project funding. The reviewers declare no conflicts of interest, and no relationship with the manufacturer of any antibody clone or FISH-probe vendor.

title: Machine learning models for predicting contraceptive discontinuation among reproductive-age women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
This research project is a systematic review and meta-analysis that aims to evaluate the predictive performance of machine learning (ML) models for identifying contraceptive discontinuation among reproductive-age women. Contraceptive discontinuation remains a major public health challenge because it contributes to unintended pregnancies, unmet family planning needs, and adverse maternal and reproductive health outcomes. Early identification of women at high risk of discontinuation may support targeted counseling and personalized reproductive health interventions. In recent years, ML approaches have increasingly been applied to predict contraceptive discontinuation using large demographic and health datasets; however, evidence regarding their overall predictive accuracy and reliability has not been comprehensively synthesized.

The primary purpose of this study is to systematically identify, critically appraise, and quantitatively synthesize published studies that developed and/or validated ML-based prediction models for contraceptive discontinuation. The review will assess pooled predictive performance measures, including sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), and area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (SROC-AUC). The study will also evaluate heterogeneity across studies and explore differences in predictive performance according to ML algorithms, study settings, predictor variables, and validation methods.

A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Wiley Online Library, and ProQuest for studies published up to August 31, 2025. Eligible studies will include original research involving reproductive-age women and reporting sufficient data on ML model performance. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment using the PROBAST tool.

The expected outcomes of this research include a pooled estimate of the predictive accuracy of ML models for contraceptive discontinuation and identification of factors contributing to variability in model performance. The findings are expected to provide evidence regarding the clinical and public health utility of ML-based prediction tools in family planning services. Additionally, the study may inform future research on predictive modeling and support the development of more robust and generalizable ML approaches for reproductive health applications.

title: Evidence on the utility of artificial intelligence in the interpretation of diagnostic radiological images in low and middle-income countries: a scoping review
description:
Background: In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), access to diagnostic imaging remains limited due to scarce equipment, geographic barriers, inadequate digital infrastructure, and a shortage of trained personnel. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to address these gaps by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, supporting non-specialist health workers, and optimizing workflows. However, the evidence remains fragmented.
Objective: This scoping review aimed to identify and synthesize available evidence on the utility of AI in the interpretation of radiological diagnostic images in LMICs.
Methods: A scoping review was conducted in July 2025 following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Clinical Key for studies published between 2000 and July 2025 in English and Spanish. Eligible studies included clinical applications of AI in radiological imaging within LMICs, reporting diagnostic accuracy, workflow impact, user perception, or implementation factors.
Results: From 620 records, 51 studies met the inclusion criteria, representing 33 LMICs. The majority were published between 2022 and 2025 and focused on ultrasound, X-ray, and computed tomography. Across these modalities, AI consistently improved diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and clinical applicability, particularly for tuberculosis, pneumonia, obstetric care, and oncological screening. Evidence on magnetic resonance imaging was promising but mainly experimental, while mammography research remained scarce. Common limitations included small sample sizes, single-center designs, reliance on public datasets, and limited multicentric validation.
Conclusions: AI demonstrates significant potential to enhance radiological diagnostics in LMICs, particularly in ultrasound, X-ray, and computed tomography. Nevertheless, methodological heterogeneity, infrastructural challenges, and regulatory gaps underscore the need for larger multicenter studies, international collaboration, and context-adapted implementation strategies to ensure sustainable integration.

title: Extracellular Vesicles as Biomarkers for the Diagnosis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune inflammatory disease with a multifactorial etiology, primarily affecting women of childbearing age. It presents as a multisystemic condition, potentially involving the skin, kidneys, and heart. Diagnosis is based on clinical and immunological criteria, such as those established by SLICC and ACR/EULAR; however, it is often delayed due to the complexity of symptoms. A particular group of vesicles, known as extracellular vesicles (EVs), has shown relevance in the diagnosis and treatment of autoimmune diseases, representing a potential diagnostic method that is faster and more accurate for SLE. In this context, this study aims to analyze, through a systematic review, the use of EVs in the diagnosis of SLE, compared to currently available testing methods. The study will be conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The electronic literature search will be conducted until June 2025 using the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Cochrane Library databases to answer the PICO question: “Are extracellular vesicles effective as biomarkers for the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus?” Diagnostic accuracy will be considered the primary outcome. The ideal biological material for EV collection and the biomarker detection method will be included as secondary outcomes. After article selection and data extraction, the data will undergo bias assessment and meta-analysis. It is expected that this study will determine the biomarker potential of EVs for the diagnosis of SLE.

title: Use of Salivary ATR-FTIR Spectroscopy in the Screening and Diagnosis of Systemic Diseases: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Abstract
Objective: This scoping review aims to map and synthesize the existing evidence on the use of salivary ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, alone or in combination with other analytical techniques, for the screening or diagnosis of systemic diseases in human studies.
Methods: The data sources included several databases, such as MEDLINE (PubMed), Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE), The Cochrane Library, Livivo, LILACS, Web of Science, Scopus, Epistemonikos, and Google Scholar (gray literature), to identify articles on the topic. The electronic search was conducted on November 24, 2025, with an update performed on December 24, 2025. No language or publication period restrictions. Two independent researchers will apply eligibility criteria and select studies for inclusion in the scoping review, with a third specialist resolving discrepancies. Data extraction and review will also be conducted by two independent researchers, which will then be analyzed by the third expert researcher in scoping reviews to resolve any potential divergences. Data will be tabulated in an Excel spreadsheet; no specific software will be used for data extraction and management.
Inclusion criteria: Studies involving human participants, conducted in clinical, hospital, laboratory, or outpatient settings, that use salivary samples analyzed by ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, either alone or in combination with other analytical techniques, for the purposes of screening or diagnosis of systemic diseases. Original studies such as clinical trials, observational studies (cross-sectional, cohort, or case-control), pilot studies, diagnostic accuracy research, or methodological validation studies will be considered, with no restriction on language or publication period.
Exclusion criteria: Studies will be excluded if they do not use human saliva as the biological matrix, if they employ spectroscopic methods other than ATR-FTIR, or if they are conducted exclusively in animal models, cell cultures, or other experimental settings without direct clinical applicability. Studies addressing conditions restricted to the oral cavity, such as oral cancer, burning mouth syndrome, oral lichen planus, periodontal disease, gingivitis, dental caries, and other purely local oral disorders, will also be excluded, as these conditions do not reflect systemic diseases. Editorials, letters, protocols without data, guidelines, case reports, case series, reviews, book chapters, theses or dissertations, and full conference abstracts will likewise be excluded.

Methodological quality will be assessed using QUADAS-2 and the PROBAST+AI tool to evaluate risk of bias and data leakage. The findings aim to establish clinical benchmarks for the integration of AI in precision gynecology, aligning with the "Office of the Future" framework for the SOGESP 2026 congress.

title: A mobile-health smartphone application shows high diagnostic accuracy for malignant skin lesions in a Latin American population: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study
description:
This research project is a diagnostic accuracy study designed to evaluate the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based smartphone application for the detection and triage of malignant skin lesions in a Colombian population with broad ethnic diversity and a predominance of Fitzpatrick skin phototypes III–VI. The project was developed in response to the increasing global burden of skin cancer and the growing need for accessible, scalable strategies that facilitate early detection and timely referral to dermatologic care, particularly in regions with limited specialist access.

Globally, skin cancer represents one of the most common malignancies and continues to rise in incidence. Although melanoma accounts for most skin cancer-related deaths, non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), including basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, contributes substantially to morbidity and overall mortality due to its very high incidence. In Colombia, melanoma exhibits distinct epidemiologic characteristics compared to high-incidence countries, including a predominance of acral lentiginous melanoma and a high proportion of advanced-stage diagnoses. Mortality-to-incidence ratios are nearly twice those observed in many high-income countries, reflecting delays in diagnosis and barriers to specialized care. At the same time, artificial intelligence tools for skin lesion classification are rapidly expanding, yet most available algorithms have been trained and validated using datasets derived predominantly from European, North American, and Oceanian populations, with minimal representation of darker skin phototypes or Latin American populations. This lack of demographic diversity raises concerns regarding the generalizability and equity of AI-assisted dermatologic tools.

The primary purpose of this project is therefore to determine the sensitivity and specificity of a mobile-health application that integrates a convolutional neural network with optional dermatologist review for identifying malignant skin lesions in real-world clinical settings involving ethnically diverse populations. The study also aims to evaluate the application’s performance in detecting premalignant lesions and specific skin cancer subtypes, including basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma. In addition, subgroup analyses according to Fitzpatrick phototype were conducted to explore whether diagnostic performance varies across different skin types.

The study was conducted at the Dermatology Unit of San Ignacio University Hospital (HUSI) in Bogotá, Colombia, and complemented by three rural and underserved community health brigades in Mahates (Bolívar), Buenaventura (Valle del Cauca), and Leticia (Amazonas). These regions were intentionally selected because they include Afro-descendant, Indigenous, and mixed Hispanic populations with higher frequencies of darker skin phototypes and historically limited access to dermatologic services. By incorporating participants from both tertiary urban care centers and remote underserved regions, the project seeks to improve representation of populations traditionally excluded from AI validation studies in dermatology.

Eligible participants included adults attending dermatologic consultation who presented with at least one cutaneous lesion suitable for photographic assessment. After informed consent, lesions underwent standardized evaluation including sociodemographic characterization, Fitzpatrick skin phototype classification, dermatologist clinical assessment, and image capture using the smartphone application. The application generated an AI-based risk classification and, when necessary, incorporated remote review by a dermatologist panel. Dermatologists performing the clinical evaluations were blinded to the application results. Lesions suspicious for malignancy underwent biopsy for histopathological confirmation, while benign and premalignant lesions were classified using predefined clinical and histopathologic criteria. Data were collected and managed using REDCap, ensuring secure storage and standardized data acquisition across both urban and remote settings.

The primary expected outcome of this project is to provide robust evidence regarding the diagnostic performance of AI-assisted mobile applications in populations that have been historically underrepresented in dermatologic AI research. Specifically, the study seeks to determine whether this technology maintains acceptable sensitivity and specificity in individuals with darker skin phototypes and diverse ethnic backgrounds. Secondary expected outcomes include generating data on the performance of the application across different lesion categories and cancer subtypes, as well as identifying potential disparities in algorithmic accuracy between phototype groups.

More broadly, this project aims to contribute to the development of more equitable and generalizable AI systems in dermatology. The findings may help inform future validation studies, support safer integration of AI-assisted triage tools into clinical practice, and encourage the inclusion of ethnically and phenotypically diverse populations in dermatologic machine learning datasets. The project also seeks to explore the potential role of smartphone-based AI technologies as accessible screening and referral-support tools in low-resource settings where access to dermatologists is limited.

title: Human learning from predictive AI
description: We examined the effects of predictive AI deployment on the immediate performance and learning of medical novices. In two pre-registered field experiments, we varied whether AI input was provided during the training or practice of lung cancer diagnoses, or both. Our results show that different AI deployments have distinct implications for learning: AI input during training or practice independently improves individuals’ diagnostic accuracy, whereas deployment across both phases yields gains that exceed either approach alone. Furthermore, AI input in both training and earlier practice can improve the accuracy of individuals’ subsequent independent diagnoses. Beyond individual accuracy, AI deployment affects the diversity of errors across individuals, with consequences for the accuracy of group decisions (e.g. when getting a second or third opinion on a diagnosis).

title: Diagnostic Performance of AI-assisted Digital Chest Radiography Interpretation for Pulmonary Nodule Detection in Adults: A Scoping Review
description:
Background: Lung cancer requires early nodule detection to improve patient prognosis. Although chest radiography (CXR) is the primary imaging modality used in primary healthcare, its sensitivity is limited by the superimposition of anatomical structures and inter-reader variability in radiographic interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a diagnostic support tool capable of reducing errors and optimizing diagnostic accuracy. The objective of this study is to map the available evidence on the diagnostic performance of AI applied to the interpretation of digital CXR for pulmonary nodule detection in adults.

For the systematic search, full-text primary studies published between 2016 and 2026 were identified in PubMed, LILACS, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Embase, ProQuest and Google Scholar.

title: Diagnostic performance and feasibility of bowel elastography in the pediatric population: a systematic review
description:
This systematic review evaluates the diagnostic performance and feasibility of bowel elastography in the pediatric population (≤18 years). Ultrasound elastography (strain and shear wave) and MR elastography quantify bowel-wall stiffness and may non-invasively characterize inflammatory versus fibrotic change, but existing syntheses are limited to adults or to Crohn disease. We will systematically review elastography of the bowel wall and appendix across pediatric pathologies — inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, acute appendicitis and intussusception — and in healthy children (normative/feasibility studies).

PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane CENTRAL will be searched from inception, supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists. Two reviewers will independently screen, extract data, and assess risk of bias (QUADAS-2; JBI for case series). Primary outcomes are diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC, correlation with reference standards) and normative values with feasibility/reproducibility. Evidence will be synthesized narratively (SWiM), with quantitative meta-analysis attempted only where studies are sufficiently homogeneous in modality, unit and outcome. Certainty will be graded with GRADE.

Reporting follows PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-DTA.

title: SCOPING REVIEW OF THE EVOLUTION OF DELIRIUM DETECTION, DIAGNOSTIC, AND SEVERITY ASSESSMENT SCALES
description:
The morbidity and mortality associated with delirium, or acute confusional syndrome, and the significant burden it represents at clinical, administrative, and family levels, have been well-documented. Early detection of delirium is critical to enabling timely intervention in its underlying causes and establishing appropriate treatment, which has driven numerous researchers over the past 70 years to develop and refine specific diagnostic tools. This work has resulted in a wide array of assessment methods that have evolved significantly over time in response to the inherent complexities of this syndrome.
In its early stages, diagnostic evaluations involved complex and lengthy batteries, whose application was limited to psychiatry specialists, who could establish a diagnosis through prolonged processes. However, these methodologies proved insufficient to address the growing population affected by delirium. Two main factors underlie this insufficiency: the high incidence of the syndrome, as highlighted by recent studies showing its presence across hospital settings, nursing homes, and home care, and the fluctuating nature of delirium, which complicates the continuous identification of symptoms without constant monitoring by psychiatrists.
The combination of these factors has driven the creation of various diagnostic tools that allow delirium identification by other healthcare professionals and even caregivers and family members. Additionally, the variability of clinical settings in which these patients present has led to the adaptation of these tools for specific populations, such as pediatric patients, patients in critical care units (including those intubated or on mechanical ventilation), and in emergency services, thereby optimizing the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic methods within these contexts. The high workload faced by healthcare professionals has necessitated the simplification of these tools, promoting the development of faster and shorter screening scales.
The considerable number and diversity of diagnostic instruments developed underscore the need for an in-depth analysis to identify and contextualize the primary studies, gathering the original psychometric data of each tool and establishing a timeline that clarifies the evolution of delirium diagnosis. This analysis will provide a solid foundation for comparing and validating new detection instruments, offering a reference framework to evaluate their accuracy and clinical relevance in diagnosing delirium.

Performance of Federated Learning in Health Services Research: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
Protocol for Rapid Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
1. Title and Registration Title: Performance of Federated Learning in Health Services Research: A Rapid Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
Registration: This protocol will be registered with the Open Science Framework (OSF).
2. Background
Federated learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning (ML) approach that enables multi-institutional model development without sharing patient-level data. It has emerged as a promising strategy for clinical modeling in health services research (HSR), particularly under data governance constraints. However, the comparative performance of FL models relative to local and centralized models and the consistency of reporting and implementation practices in HSR remain incompletely summarized.
3. Objectives
To evaluate the performance of FL models in HSR relative to local and centralized models and to assess the transparency of reporting, model sharing practices, and methodological consistency.
4. Methods
4.1 Eligibility Criteria
We will include original peer-reviewed studies applying FL to clinical prediction tasks in HSR, including diagnosis, prognosis, segmentation, and resource allocation. Studies must compare FL models to local and/or centralized models and report at least one model performance metric (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC, F1 score). We will exclude reviews, editorials, commentaries, protocols, and studies not involving human clinical data.
4.2 Information Sources and Search Strategy
We will systematically search Ovid MEDLINE and PubMed from inception to June 10, 2025. Search terms will include: “federated learning,” “machine learning,” “health services research,” “clinical prediction,” and related synonyms. No language restrictions will be applied.
4.3 Study Selection
Two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts. Disagreements will be resolved by consensus.
4.4 Data Extraction and Risk of Bias Assessment
Two reviewers will extract data on study design, country, care setting, FL architecture (e.g., FedAvg, FedSGD), number of participating sites, sample size, type of clinical task, and model performance metrics (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC, F1). Due to the rapid review nature, interrater reliability (e.g., kappa) and formal risk of bias assessment will not be conducted.
4.5 Data Synthesis
We will conduct a narrative synthesis and, where feasible, perform random-effects meta-analyses on pooled performance metrics. Results will be stratified by comparator model type (local vs centralized) and clinical use case (diagnosis, prognosis, segmentation).
5. Limitations
This review will follow rapid review methodology. Limitations include absence of interrater agreement measures, no formal risk of bias or publication bias assessments, and single-reviewer screening confirmation.
6. Dissemination Plans
The findings will be submitted for peer-reviewed publication and shared at relevant academic conferences and via professional networks. The full dataset and extraction code will be made publicly available to promote reproducibility.
7. Funding and Conflicts of Interest
This review is unfunded. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
8. Ethics Approval
Not applicable; this review does not involve primary data collection.

title: Large Language Models in Cardiology Education, Training, and Assessment: Protocol and Supplementary Materials
description:
This project is a scoping review and evidence map of large language models (LLMs) in cardiology-related education, training, and assessment. The review aims to map how LLMs and generative artificial intelligence systems have been studied in learner-centered cardiovascular education, including knowledge assessment, board or certification examinations, case-based learning, feedback, simulation, multimodal interpretation, and other training or assessment applications. 

The review focuses on health professions learners, clinicians, educators, and assessment settings related to cardiovascular medicine. Eligible contexts include general cardiology and relevant subspecialty or training areas. Studies focused solely on patient education, patient-facing communication, clinical decision support, diagnostic accuracy, or general cardiovascular clinical applications without an explicit education, training, or assessment purpose are outside the scope of this review. 

The review was designed in accordance with JBI guidance for scoping reviews and is reported using PRISMA-ScR. The planned information sources include PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science, with English-language records since January 1, 2022. Study selection, data charting, and synthesis focus on the characteristics of included studies, cardiology domains, learner groups, LLM systems, model versions, task formats, comparators, outcomes, reporting transparency, methodological limitations, and evidence gaps. Because the included studies are expected to be heterogeneous in models, tasks, educational settings, and outcomes, results are synthesized descriptively rather than by meta-analysis. 

The expected outcomes of this project are to clarify the current evidence base for LLMs in cardiology education, training, and assessment; identify areas where evidence is concentrated, such as examination or question-bank performance; and highlight gaps related to learner-centered outcomes, assessment validity, multimodal and simulation-based tasks, reproducibility, and responsible implementation. The findings are intended to inform future research design, transparent reporting, and cautious educational use of LLMs in cardiovascular training contexts.
