Diagnostic Variability in Symptoms and Risk Factors of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD): A Scoping Review
description:
Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a severe, cyclical mood disorder characterized by affective, behavioral and somatic symptoms occurring during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle (O'Brien et al., 2011). It is formally recognized in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5), with diagnostic criteria requiring the presence of at least five symptoms, including one core mood symptom and confirmation through prospective daily symptom ratings across at least two menstrual cycles (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

Despite its formal classification, PMDD remains underdiagnosed and inconsistently identified in both clinical and research contexts (Islas-Preciado et al., 2024). One major challenge lies in the variability of diagnostic approaches. While prospective tools such as the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP) are considered the gold standard, many studies and clinical settings rely on retrospective self-report measures, which are associated with recall bias and reduced diagnostic accuracy (Reilly et al., 2024).

Furthermore, symptom presentation in PMDD is heterogeneous, with considerable variation in how symptoms are defined, measured and interpreted across studies (Reilly et al., 2024). Similarly, a range of biological, psychological and social risk factors have been proposed, including hormonal sensitivity, stress exposure and psychiatric comorbidities, yet there is no harmony on how these factors are assessed or their relative contribution to diagnosis (Jadhav et al., 2022; Reilly et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2025).

This inconsistency limits comparability across studies, contributes to variability in prevalence estimates and may hinder effective clinical recognition and management (Reilly et al., 2024). Additionally, there is evidence suggesting that healthcare professionals may lack adequate training and awareness regarding PMDD diagnostic criteria and tools (Islas-Preciado et al., 2024).

To date, no comprehensive synthesis has systematically mapped the diagnostic tools, symptom definitions and risk factor assessments used in PMDD research and practice. Given the methodological diversity and lack of standardisation, a scoping review is warranted to explore the breadth of existing evidence, identify patterns in diagnostic approaches and highlight gaps in the literature.

Understanding diagnostic variability is essential for improving clinical practice, informing guideline development and addressing educational needs among healthcare professionals.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Radiographic Detection of Impacted Maxillary Canines: A Systematic Review of Human Studies
description:
Purpose of the Study:
This systematic review aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms in detecting impacted maxillary canines using dental radiographic imaging. Impacted canines are among the most common dental anomalies, with early and accurate detection being critical for preventing complications such as malocclusion, root resorption, and aesthetic issues. Traditional imaging interpretation is often time-consuming and prone to variability among practitioners. AI-driven tools, especially those utilizing deep learning (e.g., convolutional neural networks or CNNs), have shown potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, the performance and reliability of these systems vary across studies.

Objectives:

To assess the diagnostic accuracy (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC) of AI algorithms in detecting impacted maxillary canines on dental radiographic images.

To compare the performance of different AI architectures and imaging modalities (e.g., CBCT vs. panoramic radiographs).

To evaluate the strengths, limitations, and methodological quality of existing studies applying AI to this diagnostic task.

To identify current research gaps and propose recommendations for future development and clinical integration of AI systems in dental diagnostics.

Methods Overview:
A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, and Google Scholar. Eligible studies include original research involving human subjects, applying AI models for the diagnosis of impacted maxillary canines through radiographic imaging, and reporting quantitative performance outcomes. Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment will be conducted by two independent reviewers. Quality will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool (for diagnostic accuracy) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (for observational studies).

Where appropriate, a meta-analysis using a bivariate random-effects model will be performed to generate pooled estimates of diagnostic accuracy. Narrative synthesis will supplement the quantitative analysis, especially where heterogeneity is high or meta-analysis is not feasible.

Expected Outcomes:

Comprehensive synthesis of current evidence on the diagnostic performance of AI for detecting impacted maxillary canines

Identification of high-performing AI models and preferred imaging modalities

Evaluation of methodological strengths and weaknesses in the literature

Recommendations for future studies including the need for standardized datasets, model validation, and integration strategies for clinical practice

The findings will guide dental researchers, clinicians, and technology developers in improving and implementing AI-based diagnostic tools in clinical settings.

title: The Limits of AI in Medical Imaging: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Bias, and the Irreplaceable Role of the Radiologist
description:
This study examines the reliability and equity of artificial intelligence in medical imaging by testing the hypothesis that AI diagnostic performance is less consistent in real-world and diverse patient populations than in controlled benchmark settings. A structured review and meta-analysis of 30 peer-reviewed studies (2018–2024) was conducted, with quantitative synthesis of sensitivity and specificity in diabetic retinopathy screening and pneumonia detection.

The results show that while AI systems achieve high diagnostic accuracy overall, performance varies significantly across clinical settings, with substantial heterogeneity between studies. Evidence across the literature also reveals consistent patterns of demographic bias, with higher error rates in underserved populations. These findings suggest that current AI systems are better suited to support rather than replace radiologists. This study highlights the importance of evaluating AI not only by accuracy, but by reliability and fairness in real-world healthcare environments.

title: Thoracoscopy versus closed pleural biopsy with Cope needle in undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions: systematic review
description: This systematic review aims to compare thoracoscopy with closed pleural biopsy using a Cope needle in adults with undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions following thoracentesis and initial pleural fluid analysis. Pleural effusion is a common clinical condition associated with diverse pulmonary and systemic diseases, and accurate etiological diagnosis is essential for appropriate management and prognosis. When initial investigations are inconclusive, pleural biopsy becomes a critical diagnostic step. Closed pleural biopsy with a Cope needle remains widely used, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to its low cost and accessibility, although its diagnostic yield is variable. In contrast, medical thoracoscopy (pleuroscopy) enables direct visualization and targeted biopsies, offering higher diagnostic accuracy, especially for malignant pleural disease, albeit with greater infrastructure requirements. This review will systematically evaluate and synthesize available evidence on the overall diagnostic yield and safety profile of these procedures. Secondary outcomes will include diagnostic yield by etiology (malignancy and tuberculosis), complication rates, need for additional diagnostic procedures, and length of hospital stay. The study will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines, assess methodological quality using validated tools, and evaluate the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. By providing a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous comparison, this review aims to inform clinical decision-making and optimize diagnostic strategies, particularly in diverse healthcare settings, including low- and middle-income countries.

title: Establishment of Hematological and Coagulation Reference Intervals in Healthy Yemeni Adults
description:
Project Description

This project aims to establish comprehensive hematological and coagulation reference intervals for healthy Yemeni adults living in Al-Dhale’ Governorate, Yemen. Accurate reference intervals are essential for clinical decision-making, disease diagnosis, and laboratory quality assurance. However, most currently used intervals in Yemen are extrapolated from Western or other regional populations, which may not reflect local genetic, nutritional, and environmental factors.

Objectives

1. To generate population-specific reference intervals for complete blood count (CBC) parameters in healthy Yemeni adults.


2. To determine reference ranges for key coagulation tests (PT, aPTT, INR, fibrinogen).


3. To assess sex- and age-related differences in hematological and coagulation markers.


4. To provide open-access supplementary datasets and R scripts for reproducibility and secondary analyses.



Methodology

Design: Cross-sectional study.

Participants: 258 apparently healthy Yemeni adults (174 males, 84 females), aged 18–50 years.

Exclusion Criteria: History of chronic illness, acute infection, medication affecting blood parameters.

Data Collection: Sociodemographic data, venous blood samples, standardized laboratory procedures.

Laboratory Analysis: CBC performed using automated hematology analyzers; coagulation tests performed manually with inter-operator reliability analysis.

Statistical Analysis: Outlier detection (Tukey/Boxplot), calculation of 2.5th–97.5th percentiles, bootstrapped confidence intervals, and sensitivity analyses excluding endemic-infection regions.


Outputs on OSF

Main dataset (CSV, de-identified).

R scripts for statistical analysis and figure generation.

Supplementary tables (Word/PDF) covering demographic data, QC metrics, and inter-operator reliability.

Figures (TIFF/PNG) illustrating distributions, reference limits, and sex/age differences.


Significance

This study provides the first locally-derived hematological and coagulation reference intervals for Yemeni adults. The open-access dataset and analysis scripts will support:

Improved diagnostic accuracy in Yemeni hospitals and laboratories.

Regional and global comparative hematology research.

Transparency, reproducibility, and secondary analyses by other researchers.

title: Artificial Intelligence's Role in Healthcare Information Systems
description:
Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2021. Artificial Intelligence's Role in Healthcare Information Systems. Telehealth and Medicine Today Publishing, Evanston Book Special Issue, 2021. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/pwyug



"Intelligent Networks: AI's Role in Healthcare Information Systems" by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, published in 2021 by Telehealth and Medicine Today Publishing in Evanston, explores the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on healthcare information systems. The book addresses the increasing integration of AI into health data management, diagnostics, and personalized care, providing insights into how AI enhances efficiency and effectiveness in medical institutions.
Definition and Basic Concepts
The book begins by introducing health information systems and the integration of AI, outlining key concepts and definitions. AI in healthcare refers to the use of advanced algorithms and machine learning models to process health data, support clinical decisions, and improve patient outcomes. The chapter provides an overview of the evolution and development of AI in the healthcare sector.
Underlying Phenomena
The motivation behind this book is the rapid advancement of AI technologies and their growing application in healthcare information systems. The author emphasizes the increasing volume of healthcare data, the need for accurate and timely decision-making, and the demand for personalized patient care as driving forces behind AI integration. The book explores how these technologies can address contemporary healthcare challenges and improve patient outcomes.
Problem Statement
The central problem addressed by the book is the effective integration of AI into healthcare information systems to enhance data management, diagnostics, and personalized care. It examines the challenges and opportunities associated with leveraging AI in healthcare settings, aiming to understand how these technologies can be implemented to improve healthcare delivery while ensuring data security and privacy.
Research Objectives
The book aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the role of AI in healthcare information systems. It explores the applications, benefits, and challenges of integrating AI into health data management, diagnostics, and personalized care. The book seeks to offer practical recommendations for healthcare providers and policymakers on leveraging AI to enhance patient care and operational efficiency.
Indicators
Key indicators of successful AI integration in healthcare, as identified in the book, include improved data management, enhanced diagnostic accuracy, personalized treatment plans, and increased patient satisfaction. The book also highlights the importance of robust data security and privacy measures as critical indicators.
Operational Variables
Operational variables discussed in the book include AI algorithms, data management practices, diagnostic tools, and personalized care protocols. The book also considers variables related to patient outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and the usability of AI technologies in clinical settings.
Determining Factors
Several factors are crucial for the successful implementation of AI in healthcare information systems, including technological advancements, healthcare professionals' readiness to adopt new tools, regulatory support, and patient acceptance. The author emphasizes the importance of continuous innovation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and effective training programs to overcome technical and ethical challenges.
Implementation and Strategy
The book outlines various strategies for integrating AI into healthcare information systems, such as investing in AI research and development, fostering collaboration between technology developers and healthcare providers, and establishing comprehensive training programs for healthcare workers. It also highlights the need for continuous monitoring and evaluation to adapt to evolving technologies and healthcare needs.
Challenges and Supportive Factors
The book identifies several challenges, including data privacy concerns, cybersecurity threats, and the complexity of integrating AI into existing healthcare systems. Supportive factors include ongoing technological innovations, supportive regulatory policies, and positive patient outcomes. The author calls for a balanced approach to address these challenges while leveraging supportive factors to maximize the benefits of AI in healthcare.
Determining Factors of the Book
The relevance and impact of the book are determined by its timely exploration of emerging AI technologies, its comprehensive analysis, and its practical recommendations for healthcare professionals and policymakers. The book’s ability to address ethical considerations and propose actionable strategies also contributes significantly to its importance.
Research Findings
The book presents several case studies demonstrating successful applications of AI in various healthcare settings. These include improved data management through AI-powered systems, enhanced diagnostic accuracy using machine learning models, and effective personalized care through predictive analytics. These findings illustrate the tangible benefits of integrating AI in healthcare, providing evidence of its potential to transform medical practice.
Conclusion and Recommendations
In conclusion, the book emphasizes the vital role of AI in modernizing healthcare information systems. It advocates for the ethical and responsible adoption of AI technologies, emphasizing the need for robust data security measures and regulatory frameworks. The author recommends fostering interdisciplinary collaborations, investing in technological innovations, and developing comprehensive training programs to ensure the successful integration of AI in healthcare.
"Intelligent Networks: AI's Role in Healthcare Information Systems" offers a detailed exploration of how AI can enhance traditional healthcare practices and pave the way for new approaches in patient care. It underscores the importance of innovation, ethical responsibility, and strategic implementation to harness the full potential of these transformative technologies.

title: Machine learning based detection of EGFR mutation and HER2 over expression in metastatic brain adenocarcimoma:a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis explores the innovative application of machine learning techniques in the detection of Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) mutations and Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) overexpression in metastatic brain adenocarcinoma. As these biomarkers play a crucial role in the prognosis and targeted therapy of brain tumors, the study aims to evaluate the efficacy and accuracy of machine learning algorithms in identifying these genetic alterations compared to traditional diagnostic methods. Key metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy are analyzed to provide insights into the potential of these technologies in clinical settings. Additionally, the meta-analysis aims to highlight trends, challenges, and future directions for integrating machine learning into routine diagnostics for brain adenocarcinoma. title: The Comparison of Accuracy and Practicability between Ultrasound and Spiral CT in the Diagnosis of Intestinal Obstruction：A protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
description:

background: Acute abdominal pain is often caused by intestinal obstruction, with high morbidity and mortality, so that the early diagnosis is particularly important. title: Concurrent validity of the directionnal preference phenomenon compared to lumbar discography A Supplementary Analysis of a Diagnostic Accuracy Study
Assessment of Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for ROTEM
description:
This retrospective observational validation study aims to evaluate the accuracy and clinical decision-making performance of artificial intelligence (AI)-based language models in interpreting rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) findings. ROTEM is a point-of-care viscoelastic testing modality widely used in high-risk surgical settings, including cardiac surgery and liver transplantation, to assess hemostatic function and guide transfusion decisions. Although ROTEM-guided algorithms such as Görlinger’s protocol have contributed to improved clinical outcomes, the interpretation of ROTEM results remains complex and highly dependent on clinical expertise.

In this study, de-identified ROTEM datasets previously obtained from adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent elective cardiac surgery or liver transplantation will be retrospectively collected and converted into structured clinical vignettes. Only cases with complete, technically valid ROTEM results will be included. Each case vignette will be assessed by at least three experienced clinicians, forming an expert consensus that serves as the reference standard. Parallelly, the same ROTEM cases will be interpreted by one or more large language models (LLMs) developed for clinical reasoning tasks.

Each AI model will be presented with standardized prompts containing ROTEM parameters and relevant clinical context, including Görlinger’s ROTEM interpretation algorithm, and asked to answer a set of 14 structured clinical questions. These questions aim to identify the presence and type of coagulopathy and to recommend appropriate treatments, such as antifibrinolytics, protamine, fibrinogen, platelets, or coagulation factor replacement. Responses will be limited to binary (“Yes” or “No”) format for consistency across evaluators.

The primary outcome is the agreement between the AI models and the expert panel regarding the decision to initiate treatment. Secondary outcomes include the diagnostic classification of coagulopathies, concordance in specific treatment recommendations, and standard diagnostic accuracy metrics (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, overall accuracy, and Cohen’s Kappa).

As this study involves secondary use of previously collected clinical data, no direct patient interaction or modification of clinical care is involved. All data will be anonymized prior to analysis, and appropriate ethical approvals and waivers will be obtained for retrospective chart review.

The expected outcome of this study is to determine whether large language models can accurately interpret ROTEM findings and make clinically sound transfusion recommendations. These findings may support future integration of AI-assisted decision support tools in perioperative bleeding management.

title: The Visual Revolution in Anal Fistula Management: Mapping the Evolving Role of MRI and Ultrasound in Diagnosis and Prognosis – A Scoping Review
description:
Anal fistula is a chronic, debilitating inflammatory condition characterized by an anomalous tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin, or occasionally other pelvic structures. Its prevalence is significant, negatively impacting patients' quality of life with symptoms like persistent pain, purulent discharge, pruritus, and recurrent infections. While predominantly cryptoglandular, a challenging subgroup manifests in patients with fistulizing perianal Crohn's disease (FPC), where underlying intestinal inflammation exacerbates the complexity and recalcitrance of the fistulous disease.

Accurate diagnosis and precise characterization of anal fistulas are intrinsically linked to successful treatment. However, evaluation is notoriously difficult due to the complex three-dimensional anatomy of the anorectal region, involving the delicate sphincter system and the potential for multiple fistulous tracts, secondary ramifications, and occult abscess collections. Physical examination, though fundamental, often underestimates the true extent of the disease, leading to incomplete surgical interventions and high recurrence rates. Thus, an accurate understanding of the main tract, its extensions, the location of internal openings, and its relationship with the sphincters is indispensable for guiding therapeutic decisions and monitoring treatment response.

In recent years, diagnostic imaging has witnessed remarkable advancements, with new techniques and optimization of existing modalities, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and various ultrasound (US) technologies, including 3D and contrast-enhanced approaches. Given the rapid evolution and diversity of these tools, and the need to understand their comparative performance and ideal applications, this scoping review is justified.


This scoping review aims to:

Map and correlate the most recent findings (published between 2020-2026) from studies evaluating imaging modalities for anal fistula and FPC.
Analyze the diagnostic accuracy, prognostic value, and clinical impact of MRI and various US modalities in this context.
Provide an updated synthesis of evidence to support evidence-based clinical practice and identify current research trends and gaps.


A scoping review methodology will be employed, following the guidelines of the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR).

Search Strategy: A systematic search will be conducted in three main electronic databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus. The search strategy will be developed with the assistance of a specialized librarian and adapted for each database. The last search will be conducted in [Preencher com a data da sua última busca].
Eligibility Criteria: Studies published from January 2020 to December 2024 focusing on emerging imaging methods for anal fistula diagnosis and characterization will be included. Exclusion criteria will comprise animal/in vitro studies, conventional methods in isolation, case reports/series with <10 patients, editorials, letters, and non-peer-reviewed literature.
Study Selection: A two-stage selection process will be carried out by two independent reviewers (title/abstract screening followed by full-text evaluation), with discrepancies resolved by consensus or a third reviewer. Rayyan software will be used for selection and blinding.
Data Extraction: Data will be extracted by two independent reviewers using a standardized form developed a priori. Categories for extraction include study identification, characteristics, population, diagnostic method details, reference standard, primary/secondary outcomes, statistical analysis, risk of bias, certainty of evidence (where applicable), clinical applicability, and conflicts of interest.
Quality Assessment: Methodological quality and risk of bias of included studies will be assessed independently by two reviewers. QUADAS-2 will be used for diagnostic accuracy studies, ROBINS-I for observational studies, and ROB 2 for randomized clinical trials. For consensus studies, narrative evaluation of methodology will be performed.
Data Synthesis: Data will be synthesized narratively due to expected heterogeneity across studies. Results will be organized by imaging modality, presenting study characteristics, diagnostic accuracy measures, and identified limitations. Evidence tables will be constructed where appropriate.


This project expects to:

Identify dominant imaging modalities (MRI, US) and their specific strengths in anal fistula and FPC diagnosis.
Highlight the high diagnostic accuracy of MRI for complex anatomical characterization and its prognostic value.
Demonstrate the competitive accuracy and cost-effectiveness of advanced US techniques, particularly for superficial lesions and initial assessments.
Map the current landscape of research, including geographical distribution, study designs, and the predominant use of surgical findings as a gold standard.
Conclude that while significant advancements have been made, the overall certainty of evidence remains predominantly low to moderate, urging for more prospective, multicenter studies.
Ultimately, the findings will provide a current synthesis to guide clinical decision-making, optimize therapeutic planning, and improve patient outcomes by informing the selection of appropriate imaging strategies.
Keywords: anal fistula, perianal Crohn's disease, MRI, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound, US, diagnostic imaging, scoping review, diagnostic accuracy, prognosis, PRISMA-ScR.

title: Self-sampling for HPV detection in cervical screening in women aged 25 to 65 years – Scoping Review
description:
Introduction: 
Cervical cancer is one of the leading causes of morbimortality in women worldwide, with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection as its main etiological factor. Although traditional screening tests are essential for early diagnosis, their use has been affected by accessibility barriers and sociocultural factors. In response to this, self-sampling for HPV detection has emerged as an alternative, with a primary care approach to address equity and social determinants, strengthening individual capacities and facilitating access to screening. Therefore, a scoping review is needed to synthesize the evidence and guide the strengthening of cervical screening programs by integrating this self-sampling tool with high potential for impact on public health. 

Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the methodology of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed studies, reviews, and gray literature with empirical evidence published between 2015 and 2025 in Spanish or English will be included. Searches will be conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and BIREME, using MeSH/DeCs descriptors and Boolean operators. The selection will be carried out in three phases: elimination of duplicates, review of titles/abstracts, and reading of full texts, documenting said results using the PRISMA-ScR diagram. The data will be extracted into a standardized template and synthesized using narrative analysis and thematic categorization.

Expected results: This review is expected to gather and synthesize the most recent evidence on self-sampling for HPV detection as a cervical screening strategy, identifying the different methods and devices available, describing their diagnostic accuracy compared to sampling performed by healthcare personnel, and analyzing parameters such as sensitivity, specificity, and coherence. It will also evaluate women's acceptability, perception, and adherence, as well as the barriers and facilitators associated with the use of self-sampling, especially in populations with low access to traditional screening.

title: Validation of a deliberative multi-LLM Delphi panel for safe automated title/abstract screening in systematic reviews: a study protocol
description: This pre-registration introduces Delph-AI — a deliberative multi-LLM Delphi panel — and pre-registers a retrospective, multi-dataset diagnostic accuracy study evaluating its capacity for autonomous, safe exclusion of records during title and abstract screening in systematic reviews. Performance is assessed against published human screening decisions from completed systematic reviews used as the reference standard. Unlike active-learning tools that prioritize records for human inspection, Delph-AI is evaluated for autonomous classification against pre-specified safety thresholds, with mandatory human review restricted to irrecoverable technical failures. The pipeline operates on atomized eligibility criteria across a panel of three large language models from distinct architectural families. Primary validation requires the simultaneous satisfaction of three pre-specified thresholds, evaluated as the median across confirmatory systematic reviews: a safe auto-exclusion rate of ≥40% of records, a sensitivity of ≥95.0%, and a negative predictive value lower bound of ≥99.0%. Pre-specified component ablations isolate the contributions of multi-round deliberation (versus single-round majority voting) and criterion atomization (versus monolithic record-level evaluation). The protocol follows PRISMA-P 2015, STARD-AI 2025, and TRIPOD+AI 2024 reporting guidance, and proposes the Delphi-LLM Validation Extension (Appendix A; DL-1 to DL-20) as a complementary reporting checklist for deliberative multi-LLM screening systems. Pre-registered via OSF Open-Ended Registration. Protocol v1.0, April 2026. A Freeze Date amendment will be filed upon dataset, model, and prompt finalization.

title: Bridging the Pediatric Neurology Gap: Teleneurology for Screening, Referral, and Diagnostic Workup of Global Developmental Delay and Epilepsy in Children in LMICs — A Scoping Review
description:
Study Type: Scoping Review (PRISMA-ScR / JBI Methodology)
Target Journal: Frontiers in Pediatrics, Special Issue: Global Child Health: Innovations Within Our Reach (Topic ID: 80206)
Search Window: 2016– 2026
Language: English only
Reporting Standard: PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al., 2018); JBI Scoping Review Methodology (Peters et al., 2020)

Background
In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), a significant proportion of children with global developmental delay (GDD) and epilepsy go undiagnosed or receive delayed diagnoses due to a scarcity of pediatric neurologists and severely restricted access to specialist neurological services. Globally, 8.4% (95% UI 7.7–9.1) of children under five years have developmental disabilities — a category encompassing epilepsy, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, and hearing and vision loss — with approximately 95% of affected children residing in LMICs.[1] GDD specifically, defined as significant delay in two or more developmental domains in children under five years, affects 1–3% of children globally.[1] The period from ages 2–5 represents a critical but frequently missed window for neurodevelopmental detection and intervention — yet only 25.4% of children in LMICs receive adequate nurturing care during this period, and fewer than one in three attend early childhood care and education programmes.[2]
Childhood epilepsy incidence in LMICs is approximately threefold higher than in high-income countries, driven by birth asphyxia, CNS infections, neonatal encephalopathy, and malaria.[3] Both conditions share a common structural barrier: in Africa, there are only 0.007 child neurologists per 100,000 population in the lowest-resourced settings — with a continental median of 0.01 per 100,000 and 73% of low-income countries having no access to child neurologists whatsoever — compared to a median of 0.59 per 100,000 across high-income countries.[4] Both conditions are time-sensitive — early detection and intervention during the neuroplastic window of the first five years of life directly alters long-term neurological outcomes.
Telemedicine, portable diagnostic tools, and task-shifting to non-specialist providers offer a pathway to extend specialist neurological reach. However, three relevant bodies of evidence — tele-neurology for pediatric conditions, task-shifting for neurodevelopmental screening, and digital tools for GDD and epilepsy detection — exist in isolation from each other and have not been synthesised. No review has mapped the critical transition from community-level clinical suspicion to neurologist-confirmed diagnosis and structured workup via telemedicine in LMIC settings.

Objectives
This scoping review aims to:
 1. Map existing evidence on the use of telemedicine and tele-neurology for the identification, referral, and diagnostic workup of GDD and epilepsy in children aged 0–18 years in LMICs and analogous low-resource settings from 2015–2025.
 2. Characterise provider roles and task-shifting models within telemedicine-supported pediatric neurology pathways.
 3. Identify the specific evidence gap at the transition from community detection to specialist neurological diagnosis and workup, and to propose a structured research agenda and a conceptual implementation framework for pediatric tele-neurology referral pathways in LMICs.

Methods
This scoping review follows JBI scoping review methodology (Peters et al., 2020) and will be reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist (Tricco et al., 2018).
Search Strategy
JBI recommends a three-step search strategy. Step 1 involves a limited preliminary search of PubMed and Embase to identify relevant keywords and index terms from the titles and abstracts of retrieved articles, which will then inform the full search string. Step 2 consists of a full systematic search across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Global Health (CAB Abstracts), using all identified keywords and index terms. Step 3 involves reference list scanning of all included studies to identify additional relevant sources. Grey literature will be searched through WHO IRIS, UNICEF publications, World Bank reports, and ILAE resources. The search period covers January 2015 to May 2025.
Eligibility Criteria — PCC Framework
Population: Children aged 0–18 years with confirmed or suspected GDD or epilepsy.
Concept: Any telemedicine, tele-neurology, or digital health intervention used for screening, referral, diagnosis, workup, or follow-up of GDD or epilepsy.
Context: LMIC settings as defined by the World Bank income classification at the time of publication. Studies from rural or remote low-resource settings in high-income countries will be considered where the telemedicine model is explicitly designed for specialist-scarce, low-connectivity environments analogous to LMIC peripheral health systems. Studies conducted in well-resourced high-income settings without relevance to resource-constrained environments will be excluded.

Exclusion Criteria
Studies exclusively in adults without pediatric subgroup data will be excluded. Studies set exclusively in well-resourced high-income settings without relevance to access gaps will be excluded. Studies without a telemedicine or digital health component will be excluded. Single case reports (n < 5) will be excluded. Conference abstracts without extractable data will be excluded. Studies published before January 2015 will be excluded. Studies not published in English will be excluded. This language restriction is acknowledged as a potential source of selection bias, particularly given the volume of relevant research published in Portuguese, French, and Spanish from LMIC settings in Latin America, West Africa, and Southeast Asia.
Evidence Domains
Three domains will be mapped simultaneously. Domain 1 covers tele-neurology delivery models for pediatric epilepsy and GDD in low-resource settings, including delivery model type, outcomes, equity data, and scalability. Domain 2 covers task-shifting and community health worker roles in neurodevelopmental screening and epilepsy detection, including competencies, training models, and supervision structures. Domain 3 covers digital and portable tools for GDD and epilepsy detection and diagnostic workup in low-resource settings, including tele-EEG, AI-assisted diagnosis, and neurodevelopmental assessment platforms.
Study Selection
Screening of titles/abstracts and full texts will be performed by the principal investigator using Rayyan systematic review software. A random subset of 20% of records will be independently screened by a second reviewer to assess reliability, with inter-rater agreement reported as percent agreement or Cohen’s kappa statistic. A PRISMA-ScR flow diagram will document all records identified, screened, assessed for eligibility, and included at each stage, with reasons for exclusion recorded at the full-text review stage.
Data Charting and Synthesis
A standardised data charting form will capture study characteristics including author, year, country, World Bank income group at time of publication, study design, and sample size. It will also capture setting (urban, rural, or mixed), telemedicine model type (synchronous, asynchronous, mHealth, AI-assisted, or hybrid), provider roles (community health worker, nurse, clinical officer, primary care physician, or pediatric neurologist), diagnostic workup access (EEG modality, neuroimaging, metabolic and genetic testing — whether accessible via telemedicine or requiring in-person attendance), outcomes reported (diagnostic accuracy, feasibility, acceptability, cost, time to diagnosis, equity indicators), and equity data where reported.
Narrative synthesis will be organised thematically across five implementation domains: burden and unmet need; telemedicine delivery model; provider roles and task-shifting; diagnostic workup access; and equity and scalability.
No meta-analysis is planned. Consistent with JBI scoping review methodology, formal critical appraisal of included sources will not be performed; however, study designs and methodological characteristics will be charted to contextualise findings. Results will be presented using tables, figures, and a conceptual evidence map aligned with the three evidence domains.
Expected Outcomes
Based on preliminary searches, a substantive evidence base is anticipated for tele-epilepsy follow-up predominantly from high-income settings, emerging evidence on portable EEG and AI-assisted epilepsy diagnosis in LMICs, sparse evidence on tele-neurodevelopmental assessment for GDD in low-resource settings, and a critical absence of integrated models linking community screening to pediatric neurologist-guided diagnostic workup.
The review will produce a synthesised evidence map across the three domains and identify priorities for a research agenda and conceptual implementation framework for tele-neurology referral pathways targeting children with GDD and epilepsy in LMICs. The framework will be developed inductively from synthesised evidence, structured around five implementation pillars: burden and unmet need, telemedicine delivery model, provider roles and task-shifting, diagnostic workup access, and equity and scalability.

Language Restriction
Only studies published in English will be included due to resource constraints on translation. This constitutes a potential source of selection bias and will be explicitly acknowledged as a limitation of this review, particularly given the volume of relevant research published in Portuguese, French, and Spanish from LMIC settings.

AI Use Disclosure
Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2025), and OpenEvidence were used for ideation, literature finding and structural drafting during protocol development. All content has been independently verified, critically evaluated, and rewritten by the author. All cited statistics have been confirmed against primary peer-reviewed sources. Disclosed per Frontiers in Pediatrics author guidelines, to be stated in both the Acknowledgements and Methods sections of the final manuscript according to the Publisher rules.

title: Content-routed hybrid extraction from free-text pathology reports in Brazilian Portuguese: a human-anchored internal and external validation study
description:
STUDY DESIGN:
Diagnostic accuracy study (STARD-AI compliant). Retrospective analysis of free-text pathology reports in Brazilian Portuguese.

SOURCE COHORT:
848,987 pathology reports (2015-2025) from a private pathology laboratory (Lâmina Lab) in Brasília, Brazil. Reports include anatomopathological (AP), immunohistochemistry (IHC), cytology, and molecular biology exams across breast, gastric, thyroid, cervical, and other domains.

SYSTEM UNDER VALIDATION:
Hybrid AI extraction system with 4 components:
1. Content-based routing (validates IHC reports by conclusion content, not specimen metadata — addressing 27% misrouting rate found in development)
2. Domain-selective extraction: regex + LLM for breast AP/IHC; regex-only for gastric; regex + LLM-subtypes for thyroid; regex-first for cervical
3. Ontological canonicalization (behavior_class replacing benign/malignant; dual HER2/Ki-67 representation)
4. Reconciliation with discordance flagging

Models: Claude Sonnet 4 (primary extractor), Claude Opus 4 (secondary dual reader — does not correct primary output).

DATASETS:
- Development set: 145 reports (used for prompt iteration)
- Internal benchmark: 656 reports (used for pipeline decisions — NOT test data)
- Frozen holdout: 980 reports (seed=51, zero overlap with above) — PRIMARY EVALUATION
- Challenge set: 100 reports (separate stress test, not included in success thresholds)
- External validation: ~400 reports from independent laboratory (Diagnose)

HOLDOUT COMPOSITION:
- Breast AP: 200 (80 biopsy carcinoma, 60 surgical, 60 benign)
- Breast IHC: 200 (20 HER2 3+, 30 HER2 2+, 30 triple-negative, 80 luminal, 40 non-breast IHC)
- Gastric: 180 (60 OLGA 0, 50 OLGA I, 40 OLGA II, 15 H.pylori+, 15 dysplasia)
- Thyroid Bethesda: 200 (25 Cat I, 25 Cat II, 40 Cat III, 40 Cat IV, 35 Cat V, 35 Cat VI)
- Cervical: 200 (80 NILM, 40 ASC-US, 20 ASC-H, 25 LSIL, 25 HSIL, 10 AGC)

REFERENCE STANDARD:
- Primary: Pathologist 1 (P1) — blinded annotation of ALL 980 holdout reports
- Reliability: Pathologist 2 (P2) — blinded annotation of 150 reports (30 per domain, stratified)
- Adjudication: Pathologist 3 (P3) — resolves P1↔P2 discordances in the 150 subsample
- External: P1 reviews 100% of ~400 Diagnose reports

PRIMARY ENDPOINTS (per domain):
- Breast AP: behavior_class, tipo_hist_canonical, margem_status, invasive_malignancy
- Breast IHC: re_status, rp_status, her2_status
- Gastric: h_pylori, olga, displasia
- Thyroid: bethesda_category
- Cervical: resultado_bethesda, adequabilidade

SUCCESS THRESHOLDS:
- F1/macro-F1 ≥ 0.90 for primary categorical/binary variables per domain
- Weighted kappa ≥ 0.85 for ordinal variables
- ICC ≥ 0.85 for numeric variables
- Inter-rater reliability (P1↔P2) kappa ≥ 0.80
- Study passes if ≥ 4 of 5 domains meet all primary thresholds

ANALYSIS PLAN:
- Metrics computed after ontological canonicalization; raw agreement reported in supplement
- CIs via stratified bootstrap (2,000 iterations)
- Secondary analyses: inter-AI agreement (Sonnet↔Opus), performance by pathologist/period, challenge set

FROZEN PIPELINE:
Version v5.2.1 — No further tuning of prompts, regex, routing, ontology, or canonicalization rules after this registration. Any post-hoc deviations will be documented and reported.

ETHICS:
Protocol submitted to CEP/FEPECS (12/02/2026). Broad scope. Waiver of informed consent.

DATA AVAILABILITY:
Raw reports contain PHI and cannot be shared. Will provide: prompts, regex code, canonicalization rules, anonymized outputs, analysis code.

title: From “hands up” to “pencils down”: An investigation of student academic performance in the wake of a fatal police shooting
description:
This project examines associations between a nearby fatal police shooting and the academic performance of public-school students in the district in which the shooting occurred. We draw on a rich dataset from an education technology provider that includes information about daily lessons students complete (including lesson duration and pass rate) as well as their performance on thrice-yearly standardized (“diagnostic”) assessments. Temporal and geographic distance from the shooting are examined as moderators, as are student age and ethnoracial group and school subject (math or reading).

Assessing impacts within one academic year and one school district, this study examines the acute effects of nearby police violence. We identify students as treated or exposed to this violence if their schools are proximate to the shooting (as described below) and ask whether their academic performance suffers in the immediate aftermath (days to weeks) of the incident. We note that this acute focus differs somewhat from existing work that has examined impacts in the academic year that followed a high-profile killing (Gershenson & Hayes, 2018) and from studies that have identified impacts on adult mental health among Black adults living in the same state in which an unarmed Black individual was killed by police (Bor, Venkataramani, Williams, & Tsai, 2018).

School distance from shooting events will be an important measure for determining which schools were “treated.” We anticipate that residing or going to school in the same neighborhood as a fatal police shooting would be even more disruptive to a child than residing in the same city as the incident or hearing about it on the news. However, the definitions of proximity included in some prior work on exposure to neighborhood violence (i.e., distance from a child’s home) suggest that neighborhood may be quite small: within 1,000 feet (Sharkey, Tirado-Strayer, Papachristos, & Raver, 2012) or less than half of a mile (2,640 ft) (Heissel, Sharkey, Torrats-Espinosa, Grant, & Adam, 2017). According to the US Department of Transportation, the majority of children living in urban areas travel one mile or more to school (2008). This statistic has at least two implications for our study design: First, there may be few, if any, schools within half a mile of a fatal police shooting. Additionally, the students who live closest to the shooting may go to school several miles from their home. In other words, a child's home and school may, or may not, share the same immediate neighborhood context. This phenomenon brings us to a classic situation of balancing between sensitivity and specificity: we want to draw neighborhood boundaries large enough that they contain the students whose home or school environments were most directly impacted by a fatal police shooting, but not so large that it dilutes the true effect of this exposure.

Importantly, Black Americans are at disproportionate risk of experiencing violence during police encounters (by some estimates over three times more likely to be killed than whites; Schwartz & Jahn, 2020). Among the fatal police shootings we examine, all victims were Black. For this reason, while we imagine proximity to such an event could be distressing for any young person, we anticipate these incidents would be particularly upsetting for Black students.

title: “Non-Infectious Causes of Rash Mimicking Infectious Diseases: A Clinical Review for Undergraduate Medical Training “
description:
Background: Rashes are a frequent clinical presentation in both ambulatory and hospital settings. While infectious diseases are often presumed to be the primary cause, numerous non-infectious conditions mimic infectious exanthems, leading to diagnostic errors, unnecessary antibiotic use, and delayed management of the true underlying disorder.
Objective: To provide an evidence-based, undergraduate-level clinical review of the major non-infectious causes of rash that resemble infectious diseases, and highlight key differentiating features that aid accurate diagnosis.
Methods: A comprehensive review of established dermatology and internal medicine literature was conducted, focusing on conditions commonly presenting with exanthematous or infection-like rashes. Key data from standard textbooks, clinical guidelines, and peer-reviewed sources were synthesized. Conditions were categorized into drug reactions, autoimmune diseases, allergic disorders, systemic diseases, dermatologic disorders, environmental causes, and nutritional deficiencies. Diagnostic clues distinguishing non-infectious rashes from infectious counterparts were summarized.
Results: The analysis identified several high-yield non-infectious mimickers—including drug eruptions, autoimmune vasculitides, Kawasaki disease, contact dermatitis, erythema multiforme, psoriasis variants, photodermatitis, and nutritional deficiencies. Distinguishing clinical clues include onset relative to drug exposure, distribution patterns, pruritus, mucosal involvement, presence or absence of fever, systemic symptoms, and exposure history. A consolidated comparison table between infectious and non-infectious rashes enhances diagnostic clarity.
Conclusion: Non-infectious rashes frequently resemble infectious exanthems, posing a diagnostic challenge for clinicians and trainees. Understanding their characteristic patterns and key differentiating features can significantly reduce misdiagnosis, prevent unwarranted antimicrobial therapy, and improve patient outcomes. This review provides a concise, structured framework to support undergraduate medical students in developing diagnostic accuracy in dermatologic presentations.

title: Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine
description:
Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2021. Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine. Perspectives in Health Information Management Publishing, Chicago Book Special Issue, 2021. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/ryz6q
"Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine" by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, published in 2021 by Perspectives in Health Information Management Publishing in Chicago, examines the transformative impact of Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) technologies on modern medicine. This book was written in response to the growing interest and significant advancements in VR and AR technologies, emphasizing their potential to revolutionize healthcare practices and patient outcomes.
Definition and Basic Concepts
The book provides a foundational understanding of VR and AR technologies, tracing their historical development and technological evolution. VR is defined as a simulated experience that can mimic or differ from the real world, while AR overlays digital information onto the real world. Both technologies are explored within the medical context, highlighting their capabilities to enhance healthcare delivery.
Underlying Phenomena
The driving force behind this book is the rapid development and adoption of VR and AR technologies in healthcare. The increasing need for advanced training tools, accurate diagnostic methods, and innovative therapeutic solutions are key phenomena that underscore the significance of VR and AR in modern medicine. The author highlights the potential of these technologies to address critical healthcare challenges and improve patient care.
Problem Statement
The primary issue addressed by the book is the integration of VR and AR into healthcare practices. It seeks to understand how these technologies can be effectively utilized to enhance medical training, diagnostics, surgical procedures, rehabilitation, and patient care, while also considering the potential social and psychological impacts.
Research Objectives
The book aims to explore the various applications of VR and AR in healthcare, providing a comprehensive analysis of their benefits, challenges, and future potential. It seeks to offer insights into how these technologies can be implemented to improve healthcare outcomes and to provide recommendations for their ethical and effective use.
Indicators
Key indicators of successful VR and AR integration in healthcare, as identified in the book, include enhanced medical training outcomes, improved diagnostic accuracy, safer and more efficient surgical procedures, and more effective rehabilitation therapies. The book also emphasizes the importance of understanding the social and psychological impacts of these technologies on patients.
Operational Variables
Operational variables discussed in the book include VR and AR hardware and software, medical training programs, diagnostic tools, surgical aids, and rehabilitation protocols. The book also considers variables related to patient outcomes, such as recovery rates, psychological well-being, and overall treatment efficacy.
Determining Factors
Several factors are crucial for the successful implementation of VR and AR in healthcare, including technological advancements, healthcare professionals' willingness to adopt new tools, regulatory support, and patient acceptance. The book highlights the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and continuous innovation to overcome challenges and maximize the benefits of these technologies.
Implementation and Strategy
The book outlines strategies for integrating VR and AR into healthcare, such as developing robust training programs for healthcare professionals, investing in cutting-edge VR and AR technologies, and fostering collaborations between technology developers and medical practitioners. It also emphasizes the need for regulatory frameworks and ethical guidelines to ensure responsible use.
Challenges and Supportive Factors
The book identifies several challenges, including the high cost of VR and AR technologies, potential technical issues, and the need for comprehensive training for healthcare professionals. Supportive factors include ongoing technological innovations, supportive policies and regulations, and positive patient outcomes. The author calls for a balanced approach to leverage supportive factors while addressing challenges effectively.
Determining Factors of the Book
The relevance and impact of the book are determined by its timely exploration of emerging technologies, its comprehensive analysis, and its practical recommendations for healthcare professionals and policymakers. The book’s ability to address ethical considerations and propose actionable strategies contributes significantly to its importance.
Research Findings
The book presents numerous case studies demonstrating successful applications of VR and AR in healthcare. These include enhanced surgical training through virtual simulations, improved diagnostic accuracy using 3D visualizations, and effective rehabilitation therapies in controlled virtual environments. These findings highlight the tangible benefits of VR and AR in transforming healthcare delivery.
Conclusion and Recommendations
In conclusion, the book emphasizes the vital role of VR and AR in modernizing healthcare. It advocates for their ethical and responsible adoption, emphasizing the need for continuous education and adaptation among healthcare professionals. The author recommends fostering interdisciplinary collaborations, investing in technological innovations, and developing comprehensive regulatory frameworks to ensure the successful integration of VR and AR in healthcare.
"Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine" offers a detailed exploration of how VR and AR can enhance traditional medical practices and pave the way for new approaches in healthcare. It underscores the importance of innovation, ethical responsibility, and strategic implementation to harness the full potential of these transformative technologies.

In Scopus, the search was conducted in the title, abstract, and keyword fields, using the following expression: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score")) AND NOT TITLE-ABS-KEY(review OR survey OR "systematic review" OR "meta-analysis" OR conceptual OR theoretical). This formulation prioritizes thematic specificity by restricting the search to the most informative metadata and by excluding, even in the initial retrieval, secondary studies and works of a non-empirical nature.

In IEEE Xplore, the strategy maintained the conceptual core, since the database shows strong adherence to the domain of networks, security, and applied computing. The expression used was: ("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score") NOT (review OR survey OR "systematic review" OR "meta-analysis"). In this database, subsequent refinement by year, language, and publication type contributes to reducing the presence of ineligible materials without compromising sensitivity.

In the ACM Digital Library, an equivalent formulation was adopted, adjusted to the platform's text search logic: ("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score") NOT (review OR survey). This adaptation sought to balance comprehensiveness and precision, preserving the essential concepts of the review without excessively expanding the retrieval of tangential studies.
In SpringerLink, the strategy was more controlled, due to the greater tendency of this database to retrieve occurrences distributed throughout the full text. The expression used was: ("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score") NOT (review OR survey OR "systematic review" OR "meta-analysis"). This version maintains conceptual consistency with the other databases, but sought to contain the noise resulting from the broader indexing characteristic of SpringerLink.
In ScienceDirect, the search expression was simplified due to the platform's limitation to a maximum of eight Boolean operators and the lack of support for wildcard characters. For this reason, a condensed version was used: ("cross-dataset" OR "multi-dataset") AND (hybrid OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic") AND evaluation. Based on this, the other eligibility criteria, such as exclusion of revisions, time limits, language, and document type, were handled by native filters and manual screening of the retrieved records.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for CDKN2A homozygous deletion and for distinguishing mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations: a systematic review and bivariate meta-analysis
description:
This registration documents a systematic review and bivariate / HSROC meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry in mesothelioma pathology. The review was conducted to PRISMA-DTA 2018 standards. The synthesis was executed against a locked v12 dataset between 3 and 4 June 2026, and the present OSF registration follows completion of the synthesis prior to journal submission, in the absence of an active PROSPERO Diagnostic Test Accuracy template at the time of synthesis completion. The full locked protocol, search strategy, locked dataset, analysis code, and analysis-output files are deposited as project files.

REVIEW QUESTIONS

(a) Primary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry, used alone, for detecting CDKN2A homozygous deletion in pleural and peritoneal mesothelioma, taking dual-colour CDKN2A FISH (or equivalent CNV / NGS reference) as the gold standard?

(b) Secondary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for distinguishing histologically or cytologically confirmed mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations, taking the integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis as the reference?

POPULATION AND SPECIMENS

Adult patients with suspected mesothelioma (pleural primary; peritoneal as a pre-specified subgroup) undergoing diagnostic biopsy or pleural / peritoneal effusion cytology, in whom MTAP IHC has been applied as part of the ancillary diagnostic workup.

INDEX TEST

MTAP immunohistochemistry on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue or cell block. Pre-specified primary loss definition: complete cytoplasmic loss with positive internal control. Pre-specified sensitivity-analysis convention: each study's own threshold including broader patterns (nuclear loss, focal loss, ≥30% cells lost). Antibody clone recorded as a pre-specified subgroup variable (2G4 reference clone; mAb1813; EPR6893; 2B1G6; polyclonal / unspecified).

REFERENCE STANDARD

Primary: CDKN2A homozygous deletion by dual-colour FISH (Vysis LSI CDKN2A/CEP9 most common; ≥10% nuclei threshold standard). CNV array and targeted NGS panels with explicit CDKN2A copy-number calls are accepted equivalents.

Secondary: integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis per IMIG 2017 / WHO 2021 with at least 12 months follow-up for benign controls. Incorporation bias acknowledged and addressed in QUADAS-2 D3.

OUTCOMES

Primary: pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio (all with 95% CI); summary HSROC curve with 95% confidence + prediction regions.

Secondary: between-study heterogeneity (τ², I²); pre-specified subgroup pooled estimates by antibody clone, specimen format, MTAP loss threshold, anatomic site, time period; pooled proportion of uninterpretable MTAP IHC results.

SEARCH

PubMed and Embase from inception to 2 June 2026. Two-strand strategy: (1) core ("MTAP" OR "methylthioadenosine phosphorylase") AND ("mesothelioma" OR "mesothelial") AND (immunohistoch* OR IHC), 149 records; (2) sensitivity expansion same intersection without IHC term, 104 records. Full strategy with date stamps deposited in MTAP_search_strategy.md.

DATA EXTRACTION AND DUAL-REVIEWER VERIFICATION

Two independent reviewers (V. Tayade, Grant Government Medical College, Mumbai; G. Singh, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Rajkot). First-reviewer extraction across twelve audit iterations (v1 to v12) into the structured workbook MTAP_locked_dataset_v12.xlsx. Second-reviewer independent re-extraction returned 100% cell-level agreement across all four data sheets (948 of 948 cells). Agreement pathway: text confirmation between the two reviewers followed by mechanical mirroring of the locked first-reviewer dataset into the second-reviewer workbook artefact, in lieu of independent direct population of a blanked template. This procedural deviation from the standard direct-population workflow is disclosed in full in agreement_provenance.md and is acknowledged in the manuscript Limitations section.

RISK OF BIAS

QUADAS-2 (Whiting 2011), four domains (patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing), each scored for risk of bias and applicability.

DATA SYNTHESIS

Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis (Reitsma 2005 / Rutter-Gatsonis HSROC) using the mada package in R. Logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity jointly modelled. Step-6 uninterpretable-proportion synthesis via metaprop (meta package), logit transformation, continuity correction. Reproducible analysis code deposited as MTAP_analysis_code.R; analysis-output files deposited as MTAP_pooled_estimates.csv and the six forest / SROC PDFs.

Primary pool composition (pleural HD, MTAP-alone, k=6): Chapel 2020, Chapel 2021, Vrugt 2023, Febres-Aldana 2024 (mAb1813 arm), Şeker 2024 (broad threshold), Broggi 2024. Aoe 2025 primary subset in pre-specified sensitivity-only pool.

Secondary pool composition (MM vs RMP, MTAP-alone, k=6): Lynggård 2022 (histology + cytology arms), Berg 2020, Quaranta 2025 peritoneal cyst cohort, Aoe 2025, Şeker 2024. Fukuoka cluster in sensitivity-only pools.

PRE-SPECIFIED SENSITIVITY ANALYSES

(i) Exclude Şeker 2024 from secondary main pool. (ii) Stratify by specimen (tissue versus cytology). (iii) Stratify by clone (2G4 versus other). (iv) Primary-pool sensitivity with each study's own threshold. (v) Sa-Ngiamwibool ID-handling variant. (vi) Lynggård 2022 cytology-only sensitivity to bound the effect of the shared TN=20 reactive mesothelial controls used in both Lynggård arms.

SUBGROUP ANALYSES

Specimen (tissue versus cell block versus effusion); histologic subtype (epithelioid versus sarcomatoid including desmoplastic versus biphasic versus mixed); anatomic site (pleural versus peritoneal); MTAP clone; MTAP loss threshold (strict cytoplasmic versus broader); reference standard modality; time period (pre-2020 versus 2020 onward).

STAGE AT REGISTRATION

Data acquisition complete; second-reviewer dual extraction complete with 100% cell-level agreement; risk-of-bias assessment complete; LOCK declaration effective 4 June 2026 on joint reviewer ratification (G. Singh WhatsApp confirmation on briefing v3); synthesis complete; manuscript v1 drafted. Journal submission pending OSF registration.

FUNDING AND CONFLICTS

No external project funding. The reviewers declare no conflicts of interest. No relationship with manufacturers of any antibody clone or FISH probe vendor.

DEPOSITED FILES

MTAP_protocol_v3.md (locked protocol); MTAP_search_strategy.md; MTAP_PRISMA_flow.svg; MTAP_locked_dataset_v12.xlsx; MTAP_LOCK_audit.md; agreement_provenance.md; MTAP_analysis_code.R; MTAP_pooled_estimates.csv; MTAP_uninterpretable.csv; six forest / SROC PDFs.

title: DEEP LEARNING MODELS FOR THE DETECTION OF CLEFT PALATE ON PANORAMIC RADIOGRAPHS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
Background: Cleft lip and palate (CLP) is a congenital craniofacial anomaly that requires continuous dental follow-up from birth. Panoramic radiography (PR) is widely used in the monitoring of these patients due to its accessibility, low cost, and reduced radiation exposure, allowing the identification of alterations such as alveolar clefts (AC). However, image interpretation may be impaired by the superimposition of anatomical structures and by radiologists’ workload, which may lead to visual fatigue and potential diagnostic errors. In this context, deep learning (DL) models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have emerged as promising tools to support diagnostic decision-making.
Objective: This scoping review aims To evaluate the effectiveness of deep learning models applied to panoramic radiography for the detection of cleft palate.
Methods: The protocol will be registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). The search strategy will include the descriptors “cleft palate,” “panoramic radiography,” and “deep learning,” combined using Boolean operators in the PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, EMBASE, and Google Scholar databases. Observational studies that applied supervised DL models to detect CLP on PRs and directly compared their performance with human professionals will be included. Two calibrated reviewers will independently perform study selection and data extraction, including methodological characteristics, cleft type, model architecture, image acquisition parameters, and diagnostic accuracy metrics.
Conclusion: The results are expected to support the clinical use of artificial intelligence, contributing to more accurate diagnoses and a reduction in errors related to human limitations.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of cone-beam computed tomography in detecting root perforations: a systematic review
description:
Background and Rationale
Endodontic root perforations represent a severe iatrogenic or pathological complication characterized by an unnatural communication between the aseptic root canal system and the highly vascularized periodontal apparatus. If not immediately diagnosed and repaired, these defects rapidly precipitate microbial colonization, localized inflammatory responses, and crestal bone loss, ultimately jeopardizing the survival of the tooth. While conventional two-dimensional (2D) periapical radiography is the standard frontline diagnostic tool, it is intrinsically constrained by anatomical superimposition, often rendering perforations on the buccal or lingual root surfaces imperceptible. Although Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) has revolutionized three-dimensional maxillofacial imaging, its specific diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) for detecting root perforations remains inconsistently reported in the literature, particularly regarding the profound confounding variables of spatial resolution and beam-hardening artifacts caused by intracanal radiopacities.

Purpose and Objectives
The primary objective of this systematic review is to comprehensively aggregate, synthesize, and critically evaluate the diagnostic test accuracy (Sensitivity and Specificity) of CBCT specifically for the detection of endodontic root perforations.

The secondary objectives are to determine how diagnostic accuracy is modulated by specific technical and clinical parameters, namely:

The obturation status of the root canal system (evaluating the detrimental impact of photon starvation and beam-hardening artifacts caused by gutta-percha, heavy-metal sealers, and metallic posts).

The spatial resolution of the CBCT scan (comparing high-resolution versus low-resolution voxel sizes).

The anatomical localization of the defect (e.g., furcal, lateral, strip, or apical perforations).

The comparative accuracy of CBCT against alternative diagnostic modalities, specifically Electronic Apex Locators (EALs) and digital periapical radiography.

Methodological Scope
To ensure strict statistical homogeneity, this review utilizes a specialized PIRD (Population, Index test, Reference standard, Diagnosis of interest) framework. The analysis will be strictly limited to primary diagnostic accuracy studies utilizing extracted permanent human teeth (in vitro and ex vivo laboratory models) validated by an absolute, independent physical reference standard (e.g., digital calipers or stereomicroscopy). Continuous linear measurement studies and animal models are explicitly excluded. The methodological quality and external applicability of the included literature will be independently appraised utilizing the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) framework.

Expected Outcomes and Clinical Significance
The anticipated outcome of this systematic review is the establishment of the first definitive, evidence-based clinical imaging guidelines for the detection of root perforations.

This project is expected to demonstrate that while CBCT significantly outperforms 2D radiography in anatomical "blind spots," its application must be highly strategic. We anticipate the data will formulate the following clinical directives:

For non-obturated teeth: Low-resolution CBCT is highly efficacious and should be utilized to strictly adhere to the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation dosimetry principle.

For obturated teeth: The expected data will likely prove that CBCT accuracy is severely compromised by artifact scatter, necessitating either high-resolution scanning protocols to mitigate partial volume averaging, or a multimodal diagnostic approach prioritizing radiation-free Electronic Apex Locators (EALs) and eccentric multi-angle periapical radiography during active retreatment procedures.

title: Role of AI in the Detection of Dental caries in Pediatric Dentistry
description:
Early identification of dental caries in children is essential for preventive care and minimally invasive treatment. Detecting carious lesions at an early stage allows clinicians to intervene before extensive damage occurs. Conventional diagnostic methods, including visual-tactile examination and radiographs, are reliable but often require clinical expertise, specialized equipment, and in-person visits. These limitations may delay timely diagnosis, especially in rural or underserved communities where access to pediatric dental care is restricted.
Recent progress in artificial intelligence and mobile health technologies offers innovative alternatives for screening and early detection. AI-enabled mobile applications use smartphone cameras to capture intraoral photographs, which are then analysed with trained algorithms to identify early carious changes. These tools can support parents, caregivers, and community health workers in recognizing suspicious lesions outside the dental clinic, ensuring prompt referral to pediatric dentists. Beyond detection, such applications can provide preventive advice, caries risk assessment, and follow-up reminders, promoting better oral health practices and patient engagement.
However, challenges remain before clinical adaptation. Variability in image quality, lighting conditions, and differences in children’s oral anatomy can affect diagnostic accuracy. Concerns about data privacy, ethical use of AI, and the need for regulatory approval also present barriers. Integration into healthcare systems will require user compliance and interdisciplinary collaboration.
AI-powered mobile applications have strong potential to complement conventional diagnostic methods. With further research, validation, and policy support, these tools could significantly enhance access to early caries detection in pediatric dentistry.
