title: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models and Human Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Specialists Using Balanced Clinical Vignettes
description:
Title:
Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models and Human Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Specialists Using Balanced Clinical Vignettes
1. Overview
This preregistration describes a two-part study designed to evaluate diagnostic performance in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery (OMFS) using standardized, expert-validated clinical vignettes.
Both parts will use the same vignette dataset, gold standard criteria, and scoring methodology to ensure comparability.
Part 1 – Model-to-Model Evaluation: Head-to-head comparison of multiple large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-3.5, and Google Gemini, for diagnostic accuracy.
Part 2 – Human-to-AI Evaluation: Comparative diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-4 versus independent OMFS specialists (≥5 years post-qualification) under blinded conditions.
2. Background and Rationale
Accurate diagnosis of OMFS lesions is critical for effective patient management. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in various medical domains, systematic benchmarking against both competing AI models and human experts in OMFS is limited.
A balanced vignette design minimizes selection bias and allows robust cross-category comparison.
The two complementary parts of this study will together provide a comprehensive performance benchmark for AI in OMFS diagnostics.
3. Objectives
Part 1: Compare the diagnostic accuracy and reasoning clarity of multiple LLMs on a standardized OMFS vignette dataset.
Part 2: Compare the diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-4 with that of independent OMFS specialists.
Identify recurring diagnostic error patterns across both AI and human participants.
Explore differences in performance across lesion categories.
4. Methods
4.1 Study Design
Cross-sectional diagnostic performance study using balanced, expert-validated clinical vignettes.
Each vignette represents one OMFS lesion and is text-based, containing essential clinical information but no images.
Equal number of vignettes per diagnostic category to reduce selection bias.
4.2 Vignette Development
Six diagnostic categories:
Odontogenic infections
Inflammatory bone lesions
Odontogenic cysts/tumors
Salivary gland disorders
Oral mucosal lesions
Malignant neoplasms
10 vignettes per category (total = 60 vignettes).
Developed and validated by 3 OMFS specialists (not participating in Part 2 comparisons).
Gold standard diagnosis established by consensus.
4.3 Participants and Comparators
Part 1:
ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI), ChatGPT-3.5 (OpenAI), Google Gemini (Google).
All models accessed in the same month to minimize version drift.
Part 2:
Three independent OMFS specialists (≥5 years post-qualification), blinded to gold standards, not involved in vignette development.
4.4 Prompting and Response Capture
Standardized zero-shot prompt: “Based on the following clinical information, provide the most likely diagnosis.”
AI outputs recorded verbatim; human responses collected via structured Google Form.
4.5 Outcome Measures
Primary Outcome: Diagnostic accuracy (% correct vs. gold standard).
Secondary Outcomes:
Cohen’s κ for inter-rater agreement (humans) and AI–human agreement.
Qualitative analysis of reasoning clarity in AI outputs.
Error pattern classification (overgeneralization, underspecificity, underestimation of malignancy, etc.).
4.6 Statistical Analysis
Accuracy comparisons: McNemar’s test for paired comparisons.
Agreement: Cohen’s κ with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
Between-model/human differences: Chi-square or Fisher’s exact as appropriate.
Error pattern frequencies summarized descriptively.
5. Ethics
The study protocol was reviewed by the Institutional Ethics Committee, Dr. Hedgewar Smruti Rugna Sewa Mandal's Dental College and Hospital, Hingoli, Maharashtra, which granted exemption on 15 March 2025.
No identifiable patient information is used.
6. Sample Size Justification
For a 95% confidence level, ±10% margin of error, and expected accuracy of 70%, the minimum sample size is 81 vignettes.
We will use 60 vignettes (10 per category) for feasibility in this phase, with future expansion planned.
7. Data Management and Availability
All vignette text and gold standard diagnoses will be uploaded as supplementary material upon study acceptance.
Raw anonymized outputs from AI models and human raters will be made publicly available on OSF post-publication.
8. Timeline
March–April 2025: Vignette development and validation.
May 2025: AI and human evaluation.
June 2025: Data analysis.
July–August 2025: Manuscript drafting (Part 1).
August–September 2025: Manuscript drafting (Part 2).
9. Planned Publications
Part 1 – Model-to-Model Evaluation: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models in Oral and Maxillofacial Lesions: Balanced Vignette Study (Part 1 – Model-to-Model Evaluation)
Part 2 – Human-to-AI Evaluation: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of ChatGPT-4 and Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Specialists: Balanced Vignette Study (Part 2 – Human-to-AI Evaluation)
Both will reference this OSF registration.

title: Validation of the UK English Oxford Cognitive Screen-Plus in Sub-Acute and Chronic Stroke Survivors.
description:
Stroke survivors are routinely screened for cognitive impairment with tools that often fail to detect subtle impairments. The Oxford Cognitive Screen-Plus (OCS-Plus) is a brief tablet-based screen designed to detect subtle post-stroke cognitive impairments. We examined its psychometric properties in two stroke cohorts (subacute: <3 months post-stroke, chronic: >6 months post-stroke).
Patients and Methods
This study included 347 stroke survivors (mean age = 73 years; mean education = 13 years; 43.06% female presenting; 74.42% ischaemic stroke). The OCS-Plus was completed by 181 sub-acute stroke survivors and 166 chronic stroke survivors. All participants also completed the Oxford Cognitive Screen (OCS) and a subset completed the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and further neuropsychological tests. 
Results
First, convergent construct validity of all OCS-Plus tasks against task-matched standardized neuropsychological tests was confirmed. Second, we evaluated divergent construct validity of all OCS-Plus subtasks. Third, we report the sensitivity and specificity of each OCS-Plus subtask compared to neuropsychological test performance. Fourth, we found that OCS-Plus detected cognitive impairments in a large proportion of those classed as unimpaired on MoCA and OCS.
Discussion and Conclusion
The OCS-Plus provides a valid screening tool for sensitive detection of subtle cognitive impairment in stroke patients. Indeed, the OCS-Plus detected subtle cognitive impairment at a similar level to validated neuropsychological assessments and exceeded detection of cognitive impairment compared to standard clinical screening tools.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of metagenomic next-generation sequencing for osteomyelitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Osteomyelitis is a common and severe infectious disease in orthopedics. Traditional diagnostic methods primarily rely on microbial culture; however, these methods exhibit low positive rates (approximately 30–50%) and prolonged turnaround times (7–14 days), leading to diagnostic challenges and delayed clinical treatment. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), as an unbiased pathogen detection technology, has demonstrated significant potential in the diagnosis of infectious diseases in recent years. Previous studies have indicated that mNGS exhibits high detection rates in bone and joint infections, yet a systematic evaluation specifically focusing on the diagnostic accuracy of mNGS for osteomyelitis remains lacking.

title: The Use of AI-Assisted Digital Otoscopes for Evaluating Pediatric Patients in Rural Settings: A Scoping Review
description:
Introduction: Otitis media (OM) is one of the most prevalent infectious diseases in childhood and represents a significant public health problem due to its association with hearing loss, developmental complications, and frequent antibiotic use. In this context, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology for evaluating the tympanic membrane using digital otoscopes, showing great potential for improving diagnostic accuracy and expanding access to specialized care in rural settings. However, the implications of these technologies extend beyond their diagnostic performance and include aspects related to their implementation, feasibility, acceptance, and applicability in resource-limited settings. Therefore, the objective of this project is to map the available evidence on the use of AI-assisted digital otoscopes for the evaluation of the tympanic membrane in pediatric patients, identifying their applications, benefits, limitations, challenges, and future opportunities.
Objective: To map and synthesize the available evidence on the use of AI-assisted digital otoscopes for evaluating the tympanic membrane in pediatric patients in rural settings
Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the methodology of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Databases such as PubMed, 


Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, and BIREME will be searched using MeSH and DeCS terms related to AI, digital otoscopy, and middle ear pathology in pediatrics. Scientific articles, reviews, and technical and institutional reports published between 2015 and 2025 will be included.
Expected results: The study aims to generate a comprehensive mapping of the available evidence on the characteristics and diagnostic performance of AI-assisted digital otoscopes in the pediatric population; the types of devices and AI systems used; the reported diagnostic performance indicators; the contexts of use and the feasibility of implementation in rural settings; as well as the advantages, barriers, and challenges to their adoption. The results will provide relevant evidence for educators, clinicians, health policy makers, and researchers interested in the digital transformation of pediatric care in rural areas.

title: Biomarkers in Pediatric Neuropsychiatric Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Systematic Review
description:
This is the protocol for a systematic review aiming To evaluate and synthesize current evidence on the diagnostic, predictive, or disease-monitoring value of biomarkers in pediatric patients with neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (pNPSLE).
Inclusion criteria

Population: Children and adolescents (≤18 years old) diagnosed with SLE and presenting neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Study Types: Original peer-reviewed studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional).
Intervention/Exposure: Measurement of biomarkers related to neuropsychiatric involvement in SLE.
Outcomes: Diagnostic accuracy, association with NP symptoms, or prognostic relevance of biomarkers.
Exclusion criteria

Case reports, case series, review articles.
Studies without separate pediatric data.
Animal studies or non-human participants.
Studies without data on relevant biomarkers.
Databases and Search Strategy

Databases searched: We followed the PRISMA guidelines to perform a systematic literature search of articles relevant to pediatric NPSLE and biomarkers in four databases

PubMed (n=24)
EMBASE (n=24)
Scopus (n=7)
Google Scholar (n=48)
A total of 29 studies were selected for data extraction and narrative synthesis.Data were extracted manually from full texts and supplementary materials. Extracted information included: author, year, country, study design, population size, NP symptomatology, biomarker type and measurement method, sensitivity/specificity, and association with NP outcomes.The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) adapted for cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies was used. Quality grading followed the AHRQ thresholds. Most studies were of poor quality due to small samples and lack of control for confounding.A qualitative synthesis was performed. No meta-analysis was conducted due to high heterogeneity in study designs, biomarkers, and outcome measures.

title: Current overview of the use of AI-assisted digital stethoscopes for early cardiovascular assessment in primary care: a scoping review
description:
Introduction: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Cardiac auscultation in primary care settings serves as the first line of screening for valvular heart disease and structural abnormalities; however, its accuracy is highly dependent on the experience and training of the examining clinician. Consequently, the development of digital stethoscopes integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms has emerged as a promising tool for objectifying acoustic analysis, enabling early detection and timely referral from primary care.
Objective: To map and summarise the available scientific evidence on the use, diagnostic accuracy and barriers to implementation of AI-assisted digital stethoscopes for cardiovascular assessment in adult patients within the primary care setting.
Methodology: A scoping review of original articles, diagnostic validation studies and observational studies published in databases such as PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science. The search strategy will utilise MeSH/DeCS terms and keywords associated with artificial intelligence, cardiac auscultation, digital stethoscopes and primary care.
Expected outcomes: The aim is to produce a comprehensive overview describing how these technologies are being implemented in primary care, to identify the most frequently detected conditions, and to analyse the technological barriers and barriers to adoption by medical staff.

title: Diagnostic performance of urinary biomarkers in reducing unnecessary prostate biopsies in men with suspected prostate cancer: a scoping review
description:
: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common malignancy in men worldwide and one of the leading causes of male cancer-related morbidity and mortality. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) remains the principal initial screening tool, but its low specificity leads to a high number of prostate biopsies in men without clinically significant disease, with the consequent risk of procedure-related complications (infection, sepsis, bleeding). Given this scenario, various complementary risk-stratification strategies have emerged, including multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging and, more accessibly, non-invasive urinary biomarkers such as prostate cancer antigen 3 (PCA3), the ExoDx Prostate IntelliScore (EPI), and SelectMDx, aimed at reducing unnecessary biopsies without compromising the detection of clinically relevant disease.
Objective: To map and synthesise the available scientific evidence on the diagnostic performance, clinical utility and limitations of urinary biomarkers (PCA3, ExoDx/IntelliScore, SelectMDx and the Michigan Prostate Score (MiPS)) in reducing unnecessary prostate biopsies in adult men with suspected prostate cancer.
Methodology: A scoping review of original articles, diagnostic accuracy studies, clinical utility studies and systematic reviews published in databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Bireme. The search strategy will use MeSH/DeCS terms and keywords associated with urinary biomarkers, prostate cancer and prostate biopsy.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Generative and Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Models in Chest Radiograph Interpretation: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Bivariate Hierarchical Meta-analysis
description:
This registration covers the systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic performance of Generative AI (Large Language Models) and Multimodal AI (Vision-Language Models) in interpreting chest radiographs.

Purpose:
The primary goal is to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of these models compared to human radiologists or clinical reference standards. We focus on common thoracic pathologies, including pneumonia, pneumothorax, and tuberculosis, providing an evidence-based synthesis of current GenAI capabilities in medical imaging.

Methodology:
Following PRISMA-DTA guidelines, we searched major medical databases (PubMed, SciELO, BVS) to identify relevant diagnostic studies. Data extraction focused on raw 2x2 contingency tables. We employed a bivariate hierarchical random-effects model (Reitsma et al.) estimated by Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) to calculate summary estimates and generate SROC curves, accounting for the correlation between sensitivity and specificity.

Expected Outcomes:
The study provides a comprehensive overview of the current diagnostic accuracy of LLMs and VLMs in radiology, identifying strengths in specific diagnostic tasks and highlighting methodological gaps for future research. All source code, raw data, and analytical pipelines used for these findings are hosted in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Borghi2000/metaanalysis) to ensure full transparency and scientific reproducibility.

title: Evaluating the Diagnostic Accuracy and Integration Potential of Multiple Artificial Intelligence Models in Medicine Ward Patients: A Multi-Hospital Pilot Study in Pakistan
description: This pilot study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of multiple artificial intelligence (AI) models—ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini—in independently diagnosing inpatient medicine ward cases across six teaching hospitals in Pakistan. By comparing AI-generated diagnoses to physician-confirmed diagnoses, the study will assess both accuracy and efficiency, including steps, time taken, and additional tests requested. The study also explores the feasibility of integrating AI models into real-time hospital workflows, identifying potential operational barriers and informing methodology for future large-scale trials. This project addresses the lack of evidence on AI performance in real-world inpatient settings in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Neuropsychologycal Assessment Through Videoconferencing
description: With the emergence of COVID-19, significant changes have occurred in the day-to-day functioning of society around the world. Psychologists had to adapt their interventions to a new format, using web-based videoconferencing to assess and intervene with their patients. Although this procedure may provide a convenient solution, it has not been standardized or validated for remote use. While there is preliminary evidence to suggest that the scores obtained from digital administrations of the instrument are equivalent to traditional paper and pencil versions, emerging research suggests that this may not be the case. Thus, this project aims to validate remote cognitive assessment through a videoconference procedure, create standards for the European Portuguese population, study the reliability and the sensitivity and specificity of this procedure for the diagnosis of clinical impairment.

title: Clinical Resources for Cantonese Morphology

title: Diagnostic accuracy of D-dimer testing for splanchnic vein thrombosis: a systematic review
description: D-dimer testing is integral to the diagnostic algorithm for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. However, its utility for splanchnic vein thrombosis (SVT) remains controversial due to confounding factors including hepatic dysfunction and local inflammation. This study’s objective was to systematically evaluate D-dimer diagnostic accuracy across different SVT locations, clinical contexts, assay methods, and in combination with other biomarkers.

title: The EVIDENCE Framework: A Pre‑registered Protocol for Detecting and Preventing Evidence Recycling in AI‑Assisted Systematic Reviews and Meta‑Analyses
description:
Purpose: The EVIDENCE Framework is an eight domain editorial checklist (Evaluation of originality, Verification of sources, Integrity in synthesis, Diversity of data, Ethical AI use, Novel contribution, Contextual relevance, Editorial responsibility) designed to detect evidence recycling – the AI driven paraphrasing of existing research findings that creates an illusion of novel evidence without new data. This pre registered protocol outlines the prospective validation of the framework.
Methods: We will conduct a diagnostic accuracy study using 100 systematic reviews or meta analyses that declared use of generative AI. Two independent reviewers will apply the EVIDENCE Framework (index test) blinded to a reference standard. The reference standard consists of a three expert panel manually auditing all sources for evidence recycling using semantic similarity tools. Primary outcomes are sensitivity, specificity and inter rater reliability (Cohen’s κ). Secondary outcomes include feasibility (median completion time) and positive/negative predictive values.
Expected outcomes: We anticipate that the EVIDENCE Framework will demonstrate high sensitivity (>80%) and substantial inter rater reliability (κ > 0.7) for detecting evidence recycling. The protocol includes pre specified editorial action thresholds (e.g., any “Not met” on Verification of sources triggers mandatory dependency matrix submission). Results will inform journal policies on AI assisted evidence synthesis.
Data sharing: De identified dependency matrices, EVIDENCE scores and reference standard judgments will be deposited on OSF with a CC BY license upon publication.

title: The role of artificial intelligence in neurodegenerative disorders detection and diagnosis: a systematic review
description:
Dementia represents a healthcare challenge, as pathological changes often emerge years before overt symptoms. Early manifestations such as Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and Subjective Cognitive Decline (SCD) are critical transitional stages between normal aging and dementia. 
Thus, distinguishing these conditions (i.e. MCI, SCD) and whether they could evolve to dementia remains crucial. However, to date, the clinical tools available, chiefly among them neuroimaging and the neuropsychological assessment remain not always clearly interpretable and resource intensive as well. 
In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has shown promising capabilities in enhancing early detection, predicting progression, and supporting differential diagnosis across neurodegenerative disorders.
This systematic review aims at synthesizing the current evidence on the extent to which AI-based approaches are being applied to improve diagnostic accuracy and prognostic assessment in dementia. A comprehensive literature search of studies published between 2015 and 2025 was carried out across major scientific databases following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and studies were evaluated with respect to data modality, methodological rigor, performance metrics, and clinical applicability. 
The results highlight that AI models, particularly DL architectures applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiological signals, speech and language features, biomarker profiles, and digital behavioral data, consistently achieve high diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing MCI, Alzheimer’s disease, and healthy aging. Moreover, predictive models demonstrate potential in predicting conversion from MCI to dementia and in monitoring real-world cognitive and functional trajectories using wearable or smart-home technologies. However, the evidence also reveals substantial heterogeneity, limited external validation, and methodological inconsistencies that constrain clinical translation. 
In conclusion, this review highlights that AI is a rapidly evolving and promising tool for the early detection and monitoring of neurodegenerative disorders. Binding together the studies reported in this review, underscore the need for standardized pipelines, larger multicenter datasets, and explainable AI frameworks to support a real clinical implementation of this technology.

title: Tuberculosis (TB) Research Signals from the Union Conference 2025: A Map Toward End TB 2035 Using Transparent Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Synthesis
description:
Project overview

This project aims to develop and evaluate a structured, transparent and human-supervised artificial intelligence framework for synthesising scientific evidence presented at the Union World Conference on Lung Health 2025. The conference contains a large and diverse body of emerging tuberculosis research, including clinical trials, diagnostic studies, implementation research, epidemiology, mathematical modelling, health-systems research, community and lived-experience evidence, policy discussions, and early-stage scientific innovations.

Conference evidence is highly valuable because it often includes new findings before they are fully published. However, the volume and heterogeneity of conference presentations make it difficult for researchers, clinicians, policymakers, funders and affected communities to identify the most reliable findings, distinguish mature evidence from preliminary claims, and understand which developments could realistically contribute to ending tuberculosis.

The project therefore uses a multi-stage, AI-assisted evidence-synthesis workflow to convert conference presentations and transcripts into a structured and auditable evidence map. The objective is not to replace scientific reviewers or conduct a conventional systematic review of published literature. Rather, the project will assess whether artificial intelligence can support a rapid, reproducible and evidence-weighted synthesis of an entire major scientific conference while maintaining explicit human oversight.

Purpose and research objectives

The primary purpose is to identify the most credible, decision-relevant and potentially scalable tuberculosis evidence signals presented at the conference and assess their relevance to global End TB priorities.

The specific objectives are to:

Create a structured dataset of individual conference presentations and their principal scientific claims.
Classify each presentation by study design, intervention, population, setting, evidence maturity and thematic area.
Assess each presentation using a predefined six-domain evidence-scoring framework.
Distinguish reliable evidence from promising but immature findings, contextual information and claims requiring human adjudication.
Map conference findings to the WHO End TB Strategy, the 2023 United Nations High-Level Meeting commitments and the current global tuberculosis progress gaps described by WHO.
Identify areas in which scientific innovation is advancing faster than implementation, policy adoption or equitable access.
Identify populations and research questions that remain underrepresented, including children, pregnant and lactating women, people with HIV, people with drug-resistant or extrapulmonary TB, migrants, refugees, incarcerated populations and other underserved groups.
Produce a transparent conference-to-evidence synthesis framework that could be adapted for future tuberculosis conferences and other global health fields.
Evidence sources

The primary evidence source is the scientific content presented at the Union World Conference on Lung Health 2025. The source corpus includes cleaned conference transcripts, session information and structured extraction tables covering symposia, plenaries, TBScience sessions, late-breaker presentations and spotlight sessions.

The current combined dataset contains approximately 247 individual presentations. Each row represents a presentation or evidence unit and may contain:

session and talk identifiers;
presentation title;
speaker and institutional affiliation;
collaborating organisations or research networks;
country or geographical setting;
study design and research question;
intervention or exposure;
study phase or evidence maturity;
population and sample size;
main findings;
statistical results;
limitations and uncertainties;
relevance to End TB goals; and
AI-generated and human-reviewed evidence scores.

The conference evidence will be interpreted against three principal normative sources:

the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025;
the 2023 Political Declaration of the United Nations High-Level Meeting on the Fight Against Tuberculosis; and
WHO documentation summarising the commitments and targets arising from the 2023 High-Level Meeting.

These documents provide the reference framework for assessing whether conference findings address major gaps in tuberculosis prevention, diagnosis, treatment, research, financing, equity, social protection and implementation.

AI-assisted evidence-synthesis workflow

The project uses generative artificial intelligence as a structured research-assistance tool rather than as an autonomous decision-maker.

Stage 1: Transcript preparation and evidence extraction

Conference transcripts are cleaned and organised by session and presentation. A large language model is used to extract structured information from each presentation, including the research question, study design, population, intervention, outcomes, numerical findings, statistical methods, limitations and End TB relevance.

The extraction prompt requires the model to preserve uncertainty, identify unclear terminology, flag speaker or study-name ambiguities and avoid inventing information not present in the source material.

Stage 2: Presentation-level evidence scoring

Each presentation is scored independently across six domains from 1 to 5:

A. Leadership and institutional credibility

Assesses whether the accountable institutions have relevant tuberculosis expertise, research infrastructure, operational capability and an established record of delivering research, policy or implementation work.

B. Collaboration breadth and implementation reach

Assesses the geographical and institutional breadth of the collaboration, including involvement of high-burden settings, national programmes, community organisations, implementation partners and multicentre networks.

C. Potential near-term impact and decision relevance

Assesses the likelihood that the finding could influence policy, clinical practice, product development, programme delivery or research decisions within approximately five years.

D. Methodological robustness

Assesses alignment between the research question and design, appropriateness of comparators, sampling, outcome definitions, bias control, confounding adjustment and transparency of limitations.

E. Data and statistical adequacy

Assesses sample size, denominators, uncertainty estimates, analytical methods, prespecification, handling of missing data and whether the reported effect is clinically or programmatically interpretable.

F. External validation, generalisability and reproducibility

Assesses replication across datasets or settings, external validation, transferability, consistency with prior evidence and whether the methods could be reproduced.

Institutional prominence and collaboration breadth are treated as contextual confidence modifiers. They are not permitted to compensate for weak methodology, inadequate statistical support or lack of validation.

Stage 3: Evidence-quality guardrails and tier classification

The following quantities are calculated:

context and reach subtotal: A + B;
decision-impact score: C;
evidence-quality subtotal: D + E + F; and
total score: A + B + C + D + E + F.

Presentations are classified as:

Tier 1 — Must capture

Total score of at least 24, with C, D and E each at least 4, F at least 3, and an evidence-quality subtotal of at least 12.

Tier 2 — Capture and verify carefully

Total score of 18–23, or a higher total that fails one of the evidence-quality guardrails. This category can include high-impact early-stage work with strong methodology but insufficient external validation.

Tier 3 — Usually exclude from principal claims

Total score of 17 or below, or C, D or E of 2 or below.

Within each tier, evidence is ranked first by the evidence-quality subtotal, followed by near-term impact, collaboration breadth and institutional credibility. This prevents institutional prestige from outranking stronger empirical evidence.

Stage 4: Independent audit and conservative rescoring

The initial AI-generated evidence table is independently reviewed using a second analytical stage. The audit checks:

row matching and duplicated presentations;
missing or inconsistent fields;
scoring and spreadsheet formula accuracy;
study-design classification;
whether the main claim exceeds the available data;
whether observational associations are incorrectly expressed as causal effects;
whether exploratory, interim or post-hoc analyses are overstated;
whether preclinical findings are framed as clinically actionable;
whether modelled impact is confused with observed impact;
whether diagnostic accuracy is incorrectly equated with improved patient outcomes; and
whether weak or absent external validation is sufficiently acknowledged.

Conservative score caps are applied where the source material consists of expert commentary, advocacy, protocols without results, incomplete transcripts, preclinical evidence, interim analyses or claims without adequate numerical support.

Stage 5: Claim-level signal classification

The presentations are converted into claim-level evidence signals and classified as:

Core evidence signal: mature, methodologically robust and quantitatively supported evidence;
Probable evidence signal: credible and decision-relevant evidence requiring limited verification;
Promising but immature signal: potentially important early-phase, preclinical, exploratory or modelled evidence;
Controversial or human-adjudication signal: an important claim with unresolved methodological, statistical, safety, generalisability or interpretive concerns; or
Low-confidence or contextual finding: information insufficient to support a principal scientific or policy claim.

Presentations arising from the same trial, dataset or research programme are consolidated to avoid double counting.

Thematic framework

Evidence is organised into six major End TB themes:

Diagnostics and screening
Treatment and regimen optimisation
Prevention, tuberculosis preventive treatment and infection control
Vaccines and immunology
Implementation, community engagement, equity and health systems
Surveillance, modelling, epidemiology and financing

Each signal is mapped to one primary theme and, where necessary, one secondary theme.

Mapping to End TB goals

Each evidence signal is mapped to the End TB Strategy pillars and to specific WHO and UN commitments, including:

reductions in tuberculosis incidence and mortality;
at least 90% treatment coverage;
at least 90% tuberculosis preventive treatment coverage among eligible populations;
universal initial testing with WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostics;
improved diagnosis and treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis;
development and equitable access to a new tuberculosis vaccine;
universal health and social-benefit coverage;
elimination of catastrophic costs;
meaningful engagement of affected communities;
increased annual financing for tuberculosis services;
increased annual investment in tuberculosis research; and
stronger surveillance, accountability and multisectoral action.

Signals are additionally classified according to their likely contribution:

direct acceleration of an End TB target;
enabling health-system or policy change;
contribution to the research and product-development pipeline; or
contextual or descriptive contribution.

Implementation readiness is categorised as immediate, medium term, long term or uncertain.

Human oversight and adjudication

Human review is retained as an essential component of the project.

High-priority human adjudication is required for:

all Tier 1 evidence;
all signals proposed for the final Top 10;
safety or non-inferiority findings;
incomplete or technically compromised transcripts;
influential mathematical or economic models;
claims that could materially affect clinical or programme decisions;
evidence with conflicting denominators or statistical interpretations;
exploratory subgroup analyses; and
claims that appear inconsistent with current WHO recommendations.

For each flagged signal, the framework generates a specific adjudication question identifying what must be checked in the original abstract, presentation slides, trial registration, publication or dataset before inclusion in the manuscript.

Expected outputs

The planned outputs are:

A complete scoring and audit dataset

A structured table containing all included conference presentations, extracted evidence, original and audited scores, evidence tiers, maturity classifications, cautions and human-review priorities.

A theme-level evidence map

A claim-level synthesis of the strongest evidence across the six End TB themes, including evidence type, quantitative findings, evidence strength, limitations, implementation readiness and End TB relevance.

A consolidated Top 10 evidence-signal list

A ranked set of the most reliable and strategically important findings, with overlapping presentations consolidated by trial or research programme.

A human-adjudication queue

A prioritised list of claims requiring expert review before manuscript inclusion, together with explicit verification questions and the potential consequences of overstatement.

An End TB target-gap matrix

A comparison between official global commitments, current progress, conference evidence, remaining evidence gaps and recommended actions for 2026–2027, 2028–2030 and 2031–2035.

A manuscript-ready scientific synthesis

A structured Results and Discussion synthesis describing the strongest areas of convergence, the most important unresolved gaps, the balance between innovation and implementation, underrepresented populations and a strategic roadmap towards 2035.

A methodological framework

A reusable and adaptable framework for AI-assisted conference evidence synthesis, including prompts, extraction fields, scoring rules, audit procedures and human-review safeguards.

Open-science materials

Where conference permissions and intellectual-property restrictions allow, the project will share the protocol, scoring rubric, analysis prompts, data dictionary, decision rules, audit templates and de-identified derived evidence tables. Full transcripts or copyrighted conference materials will not be publicly redistributed without permission.

Expected contribution and significance

The project addresses a gap between conventional conference reporting and formal evidence synthesis. Conference summaries commonly describe selected highlights but rarely assess all presentations using explicit methodological and statistical criteria. Conventional systematic reviews, in contrast, generally rely on published studies and may not capture emerging conference evidence for months or years.

This project tests a middle approach: a rapid but conservative conference-scale evidence synthesis that identifies emerging signals without treating unpublished conference findings as definitive evidence.

The project is expected to contribute in three areas.

First, it will provide a broad picture of the direction of global tuberculosis research and implementation at a major international conference.

Second, it will identify which findings are sufficiently mature to inform near-term decisions and which require further validation, replication or implementation research.

Third, it will evaluate a reproducible model for responsible use of generative AI in scientific synthesis, with explicit attention to transparency, auditability, uncertainty and human accountability.

The project may represent one of the first tuberculosis-specific attempts to combine conference-wide transcript analysis, claim-level evidence grading, multi-stage AI review, policy-target mapping and structured human adjudication in a single workflow.

Limitations

The project has several anticipated limitations.

Conference presentations are not equivalent to peer-reviewed full publications. Important information on study design, denominators, statistical uncertainty, missing data, adverse events and subgroup definitions may be absent from transcripts or slides.

Transcript quality may vary, and automated transcription can introduce errors in speaker names, terminology, study names and numerical values.

The scoring framework is designed for evidence triage and prioritisation. It is not a validated replacement for formal risk-of-bias tools.

The corpus contains heterogeneous evidence types. Clinical trials, diagnostic studies, modelling, qualitative research, community evidence and policy discussions cannot be evaluated identically. Scores will therefore be interpreted according to the type and purpose of the evidence.

Large language models may produce extraction errors, inconsistent scores or unsupported interpretations. For this reason, AI outputs will be retained as auditable intermediate products rather than accepted as final judgements.

Evidence presented at the conference may later change following peer review, final data analysis, regulatory review or publication.

Implementation readiness estimates are judgement-based and depend on factors not always captured in scientific presentations, including manufacturing, affordability, regulatory approval, health-system capacity, financing, political commitment and community acceptability.

Overall anticipated outcome

The anticipated final outcome is an evidence-weighted roadmap showing what the Union 2025 conference indicates about progress towards ending tuberculosis, which innovations could realistically influence practice before 2030, which developments may contribute closer to 2035, and where major scientific, implementation, equity and financing gaps remain.

The project will not present artificial intelligence as a replacement for tuberculosis expertise. Its intended contribution is a scalable and transparent first-pass synthesis system that helps experts focus their limited time on the findings with the greatest potential impact and the greatest risk of misinterpretation.

title: Implementation of AI-Powered Computer-Aided Detection for Tuberculosis Chest X-ray Screening in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Scoping Review Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR 2.0)
description:
This project contains the protocol, data, and materials for a scoping review examining the implementation of AI-powered computer-aided detection (CAD) for tuberculosis chest X-ray screening in low- and middle-income countries.

While existing reviews have evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of CAD tools for TB, none has applied an implementation science framework to systematically map the real-world deployment evidence. This review uses the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR 2.0) to structure the extraction and analysis of evidence on barriers, facilitators, workflow integration, cost, health worker and patient perceptions, policy environments, and sustainability of CAD deployment across LMICs.

The review follows JBI scoping review methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Five electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Global Index Medicus, CINAHL) are searched alongside systematic grey literature searches of WHO, FIND, Global Fund, Stop TB Partnership, and national TB programme reports. Implementation outcomes are classified using the Proctor et al. (2011) taxonomy.

Project contents:
- Scoping review protocol (registered)
- Search strategies for all databases
- CFIR 2.0 coding guide and data charting form
- Screening decisions and PRISMA-ScR flow diagram
- Extracted data and analysis outputs
- Manuscript drafts and supplementary materials

title: Artificial intelligence for detecting periapical lesions in dental imaging: a scoping review protocol (PRISMA-ScR, JBI) — Retrospective OSF registration
description:
Project overview

Title: Artificial intelligence for detecting periapical lesions in dental imaging: a scoping review (PRISMA-ScR, JBI)
Modalities: intra-oral periapical radiographs (IOPA), panoramic radiographs (OPG), cone-beam CT (CBCT).
Purpose: Map and synthesize the evidence on AI methods for detecting periapical lesions across dental imaging modalities; summarize performance and evaluation practices; assess reporting transparency; and identify gaps that affect clinical translation.

Rationale

Research on AI for periapical pathology is growing but highly heterogeneous in tasks, datasets, reference standards, units of analysis, and metrics. This variability hinders comparison and practical adoption. A structured scoping review will organize the field and provide actionable guidance for future studies and clinical pathways.

Methods (summary)

Scoping review per PRISMA-ScR and JBI (PCC); PRISMA-S for search reporting.
Inclusion: English-language, human, primary AI studies (2010–present) that develop, fine-tune, or evaluate AI for periapical lesion tasks (classification/detection/segmentation) on IOPA/OPG/CBCT.
Process: Dual independent screening and data charting (e.g., Rayyan) with consensus/third reviewer.
Data items: modality; task; dataset/source; unit of analysis (tooth/region/patient); reference standard (e.g., expert consensus, histology, CBCT confirmation); sample sizes/splits (patient-level where applicable); external validation/multicenter; augmentation; model family; transparency (code/data).
Synthesis: Descriptive (no meta-analysis). We will report sensitivity/specificity, AUC, accuracy, F1 (and Dice/IoU for segmentation), and map reporting completeness against key CLAIM/MI-CLAIM concepts.

Timeframe & six-week plan (actual timeline)

Coverage: 2010 → present.

Week 1 — 1–7 Aug 2025: Preparation (define PCC, eligibility, draft protocol outline; select databases).

Week 2 — 8–14 Aug 2025: Protocol drafting; PRISMA-S strategy drafting (v0.9); small sanity-check queries.

Week 3 — 15–21 Aug 2025: Pilot search (~100 records) + pilot screening; refine eligibility; finalize strategies (v1.0).

Week 4 — 22–28 Aug 2025: Full multi-database search and cross-database deduplication; create Rayyan project.

Week 5 — 29 Aug–4 Sep 2025: Title/abstract screening; full-text retrieval; pilot extraction (10 sources); lock data-charting template (4 Sep).

Week 6 — 5–11 Sep 2025: Full extraction (data charting) and initial descriptive synthesis; draft PRISMA-ScR flow.
Finalization & registration: 12–15 Sep 2025 — verify counts; re-run update search (15 Sep 2025) for currency; register on OSF.

Expected outcomes

Narrative synthesis with evidence tables/figures by modality and task.

PRISMA-ScR flow diagram.

Comparative view of performance metrics and evaluation rigor (patient-level splits, external validation, multicenter use).

Gap analysis + a minimum-practice checklist to improve reproducibility and clinical relevance.

Practical recommendations for dataset reporting and reference standards in dental imaging AI.

Registration & timeline

Retrospectively registered on OSF. Initiation: 1 Aug 2025 (protocol drafting and early preparation). OSF registration: 15 Sep 2025. Planned manuscript submission: 18 Sep 2025.

Data/materials availability

Search strategies (with exact run dates), anonymized screening logs, the data-charting template, and the PRISMA-ScR flow will be deposited on OSF; the charted dataset will be shared subject to publisher policy.

Ethics, funding, conflicts

No human/animal intervention; ethics approval not required. No specific funding; authors declare no conflicts of interest.

title: What are the most frequently reported clinical signs and symptoms in individuals diagnosed with motor neurone disease? A scoping review
description:
Overview
Motor Neurone Disease (MND) is a progressive and incurable neurodegenerative disorder that results in the degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, leading to debilitating loss of muscle function, mobility, speech, and ultimately prematurely ending life. Although MND encompasses a spectrum of subtypes including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), progressive muscular atrophy (PMA), primary lateral sclerosis (PLS), progressive bulbar palsy (PBP), and flail limb variants each presents with variable clinical signs and symptoms, leading to significant delays in diagnosis and overall condition management.
Despite existing guidelines from NICE (2016) highlighting the importance of early recognition and referral, diagnostic delays persist, averaging 12 months from initial symptom onset. Misdiagnosis is common due to the overlap of MND symptoms with those of other neuromuscular and neurological disorders. Recognising the full range of signs and symptoms associated with MND is essential to improving diagnostic accuracy, enhancing care pathways, and potentially providing earlier access to supportive treatments and clinical trials.
Purpose
The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, describe, and map the range of clinical signs and symptoms reported in individuals diagnosed with MND. This includes an exploration of motor, bulbar, respiratory, cognitive, and any atypical or under-recognized symptoms documented across MND subtypes. The review aims to clarify these symptoms and consolidate the evidence with the aim of informing future clinical guidelines.
Research Objectives
1. To explore how the current literature describes the clinical signs and symptoms of MND.
2. To map which specific signs and symptoms aid healthcare professionals in recognising patients with MND.
Methodology

This review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and adhere to the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The five-stage framework by Arksey & O’Malley (2005) will be employed, including identifying the research question, searching and selecting studies, charting the data, and summarising the results.
A comprehensive search using MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo, CINAHL Ultimate, Academic Search Ultimate, and SPORTDiscus, followed by hand-searching reference lists and Google Scholar will be carried out. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed literature that reported numerical data on clinical signs and symptoms in individuals with a confirmed MND diagnosis, using clinical-epidemiological or descriptive study designs.
Expected Outcomes
• A comprehensive map of signs and symptoms across MND subtypes.
• A clearer understanding of symptom prevalence.
• Identification of knowledge gaps to guide future research and inform clinical training materials.
Significance
This scoping review will support earlier and more accurate recognition of MND by consolidating evidence on its signs and symptoms. It will also contribute to refining diagnostic criteria, educating clinicians, and ensuring timely access to multidisciplinary care, supportive services, and clinical trials for people living with MND.

title: Under-diagnosis of Dementia in Nursing Home Residents: A scoping Review
description:
As per the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-5 (DSM-5), dementia is diagnosed when there is evidence of decline in activities of daily living (ADL) as well as decline in cognitive ability in one or more of the following domains: complex attention, executive ability, learning and memory, language, perceptual - motor - visual perception, praxis and social cognition (1). Progression of these deficits to the extent one’s ability to conduct activities of daily living is impaired is one of the major reasons for older individuals transition to residential aged care facilities (RACF) or nursing homes (2,3,4,5). 
Dementia is a significant public health issue in Australia and a health condition that is highly prevalent amongst residents of RACF (6,7). Under-diagnosis of dementia may affect the quality of care provided to the RACF residents, eventually impacting their health-related outcomes (8). Overarching this issue is the fact that funding allocation to RACF for the care of residents is dependent on whether the diagnosis of dementia is present or not (9). 
 It is estimated that three quarters of people living with dementia globally are living without the diagnosis made (7,8). More than 50% of residents living with dementia in RACF are said to have not been diagnosed as living with dementia (8,9,10,11). The issue of under-diagnosis likely begins before entry into the RACF given that a 2017 meta-analysis of 23 studies found that more than 63% of people living with dementia in the community had not been diagnosed with dementia (12). The same study also revealed that the true prevalence of dementia in RACF was double that reported, meaning that half of the residents were not diagnosed (12). Similar results were also reported by another study focusing on diagnosis of dementia in RACF residents (13). 
Findings from Australian studies have identified similar gaps in the diagnosis of dementia. The South Australian Longitudinal Frailty In Residential Sector over Time [FIRST] Study of RACF residents speculated that dementia might not have been diagnosed in almost half of the residents given that 75.6% of residents were identified as possibly living with dementia when using the Dementia Severity Rating Scale (DSRS), whilst a diagnosis of dementia was recorded in the medical records for only 37.1% residents (14). In another Australian study, 83% of residents scored 4 or more on the Psychogeriatric Assessment Scale (PAS-cog) suggesting the presence of dementia but only 65% had a recorded diagnosis of dementia (15). Clearly, the degree of under-diagnosis reported varies according to the method used to identify dementia (16). Methods that are used to make the diagnosis of dementia in RACF can range from a diagnosis recorded in medical records, to scales used to screen for dementia risk and all the way up to a more definitive diagnosis by clinical experts (e.g., geriatricians, neurologists or expert panels). 
It is important to be cognizant of the fact that screening tools such as the DSRS and PAS-cog only identify the risk of dementia and that too with varying performance. The DSRS for example, was able to differentiate between mild cognitive impairment and dementia with a sensitivity of 41% and specificity of 79% or a post-test probability of 74% (16). Additionally, the study design can also influence the reported prevalence for dementia with prevalence varying depending on if the prevalence was estimated at the time of admission to RACF or cross-sectionally, where the prevalence of dementia was determined for all residents at the time the study was conducted (16).
Ensuring that those living with dementia are diagnosed in a timely manner is important (15,16) as a missed diagnosis could result in the resident missing out on funding allocations (e.g., dementia supplement) that would enable the resident to receive increased care hours (17,18,19,20). A timely diagnosis also facilitates conversations regarding the medical management of residents including future care planning (21). It is no surprise therefore that timely diagnosis has been identified as an essential care requirement as per the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) guidelines (21). Timely dementia diagnosis has also been highlighted as a priority area for action in the National Framework for Action on Dementia (22).

description:
Introduction: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most prevalent complications of diabetes mellitus (DM) and one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide. Its high epidemiological burden emphasizes the need to improve early detection and diagnosis strategies to mitigate the onset of irreversible changes. The limitations of the current approach to DM in identifying complications such as DR in a timely manner reinforce the importance of incorporating innovative detection strategies. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool, demonstrating high levels of early diagnostic accuracy to optimize the quality of health services, mainly in developing countries. 

Methodology: Through a scoping review, scientific articles, reviews, technical literature, and gray literature published between 2019 and 2025 will be analyzed, covering the available evidence on artificial intelligence modalities in the automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy in adults worldwide. The PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and BIREME databases will be included, using MeSH and DeCS descriptors. 

Expected results: We expect to provide a comprehensive overview of the main types of artificial intelligence used for the automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy in adults worldwide, identifying benefits, limitations, and future opportunities. The findings will generate useful evidence for healthcare professionals and service planners, facilitating the design of strategies and interventions aimed at contributing scientific knowledge in this area, opening up horizons for improvement in healthcare.

title: ENSURE-AI: Independent Evaluation of AI tools for Prostate Cancer in Pathology
description:
Background
Increasing uptake of digital pathology has opened the door for the introduction of novel AI-based tools to support the diagnostic workflow.(1,2) These technologies have the potential to streamline workflow efficiency, alleviate workload pressures, reduce costs, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and improve patient outcomes.(3-5) One necessary step in proving clinical benefit is to demonstrate high levels of accuracy and generalisability for each tool. 
 
At present, there are at least 26 AI-based tools for analysing Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) digital pathology images that have received regulatory approval as medical devices to be placed on the UK market.(6) However, there is limited information available on the performance of devices approved for clinical use, and the quality of evaluation studies used to test their performance is variable.(6) Additionally, whilst a product may perform well on some data sources, this may change when utilised on different data in a different setting.(7) Evaluation on UK NHS data is important prior to widespread deployment of such tools. 
 
One of the most mature areas of the commercial market for AI-based products in digital pathology is in the prostate cancer field. There are currently multiple products with regulatory approval for placement on the EEA/GB market that interpret H&E images of prostate core needle biopsies and predict cancer location and Gleason grade. 

Study aims
1. To develop a framework and recommendations for performing retrospective evaluations using hidden datasets for AI products for diagnostic tasks in digital pathology 
2. To develop the technical infrastructure and processes for performing evaluations of multiple AI products within NPIC 
3. To engage with industry to perform balanced assessments of AI products and ensure their participation, whilst maintaining independence in the evaluations. 
4. To design an output report to describe evaluations and results for individual products 

Study summary
Obtaining the full benefit of AI for patients, whilst ensuring safe adoption into busy clinical laboratories is of great importance in pathology. There are many challenges to be faced by healthcare providers when deciding whether to purchase products with existing regulatory approvals and to introduce these to the clinical workflow. 
 
At the time of writing, the authors are not aware of a standardised accepted framework for the evaluation of AI for adoption into a clinical pathology laboratory. External validation studies of such AI products so far are variable in terms of their approach, whether they include UK NHS data and are often not conducted in a way that is independent from the vendor.(6) 
 
This is an evaluation study of prostate cancer AI products on a multicentre retrospective dataset of prostate biopsies. This project aims to evaluate the performance of multiple AI products with existing regulatory approval for prostate cancer diagnosis in pathology. A further aim is to develop an evaluation framework that could be replicable in other disease areas and within different laboratories. 
 
This work is broken down into six workpackages to perform the project set up, data curation, evaluation across multiple centres and a usability assessment. The final assessment will be summarised and made publicly available, along with details of the evaluation framework that is developed.

Lay summary
To diagnose cancer, samples of tissue are often taken from patients. This tissue is processed in a laboratory to fit on a glass slide. New digital scanning technology means that glass slides can now be "digitised" to become an electronic image. A pathologist can then view the tissue as a detailed image on a computer screen, instead of using a microscope. Increasing availability of these digital images of tissue has created more opportunities to develop and use artificial intelligence (AI) to help with a diagnosis, because AI tools can analyse these images automatically. 
 
In the UK, 97% of pathology laboratories do not have enough staff to meet the demand for quick and accurate diagnoses.(8) AI could help by providing key information in a diagnosis. It could also automate tasks to assist a pathologist when examining a case. The potential of AI to improve cancer diagnosis is very exciting. However, before use in routine patient care, this technology must be tested and evaluated to ensure it is safe, accurate and useful. 
 
This project aims to evaluate the performance and usefulness of existing prostate cancer AI products with regulatory approval and to develop a framework for evaluating AI products in pathology in general. 

Study location
This is a hospital-based study coordinated by the National Pathology Imaging Co-operative (NPIC) at Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, in collaboration with other hospitals within the NPIC network. www.npic.ac.uk

title: Thoracoscopy versus closed pleural biopsy with Cope needle in undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions: systematic review
description: This systematic review aims to compare thoracoscopy with closed pleural biopsy using a Cope needle in adults with undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions following thoracentesis and initial pleural fluid analysis. Pleural effusion is a common clinical condition associated with diverse pulmonary and systemic diseases, and accurate etiological diagnosis is essential for appropriate management and prognosis. When initial investigations are inconclusive, pleural biopsy becomes a critical diagnostic step. Closed pleural biopsy with a Cope needle remains widely used, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to its low cost and accessibility, although its diagnostic yield is variable. In contrast, medical thoracoscopy (pleuroscopy) enables direct visualization and targeted biopsies, offering higher diagnostic accuracy, especially for malignant pleural disease, albeit with greater infrastructure requirements. This review will systematically evaluate and synthesize available evidence on the overall diagnostic yield and safety profile of these procedures. Secondary outcomes will include diagnostic yield by etiology (malignancy and tuberculosis), complication rates, need for additional diagnostic procedures, and length of hospital stay. The study will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines, assess methodological quality using validated tools, and evaluate the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. By providing a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous comparison, this review aims to inform clinical decision-making and optimize diagnostic strategies, particularly in diverse healthcare settings, including low- and middle-income countries.

title: A Scoping Review of Applications of Machine Learning for the Diagnosis and Classification of Multiple Myeloma
description:
This review systematically maps how machine learning (ML) has been applied to improve the diagnosis of multiple myeloma through serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) and immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE), two tests that remain central but heavily dependent on expert interpretation. By reviewing ML applications ranging from early neural-network models to modern deep learning systems, the study captures the full landscape of automated M-protein detection, band classification, and electrophoretic pattern recognition. Through rigorous scoping review methodology, it synthesizes evidence from diverse datasets, model architectures, diagnostic objectives, and performance outcomes, offering the first comprehensive overview of this rapidly evolving field.

Early and accurate detection of multiple myeloma is often limited by human interpretation, variable expertise, and resource constraints, particularly in settings with uneven access to trained laboratory personnel. ML models consistently demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy—sometimes surpassing expert readers—yet their clinical readiness, generalizability, and integration remain unclear without a consolidated evidence base. Understanding where these models excel, where they fail, and what methodological gaps persist is essential for guiding responsible adoption of AI in diagnostic laboratories. This review is therefore crucial for identifying strengths, limitations, and unrealized opportunities such as explainable AI, multi-centre validation, workflow integration, and multimodal diagnostic approaches.

The review establishes that ML has strong potential to enhance or even automate components of electrophoresis-based myeloma diagnostics, but real-world impact depends on addressing key gaps in generalizability, transparency, and clinical deployment. It delivers an evidence map, highlights methodological weaknesses, and outlines a clear research roadmap to support future development of trustworthy, scalable AI tools. Ultimately, this project provides essential groundwork for improving diagnostic equity and accelerating early detection of multiple myeloma, especially in resource-limited healthcare systems, while informing laboratories, clinicians, and policymakers considering AI adoption

Background: Colon cancer is a common malignant tumor of the gastrointestinal tract. Therefore, a clear diagnosis is particularly important for the treatment of colon cancer. title: On the Equivalency of Factor and Network Loadings
description: Recent research has demonstrated that the network measure node strength or sum of a node’s connections is roughly equivalent to confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) loadings. A key finding of this research is that node strength represents a combination of different latent causes. In the present study, we sought to circumvent this issue by formulating a network equivalent called network loadings. In two simulations, we evaluated the extent to which network loadings could effectively (1) separate the effects of multiple latent causes and (2) estimate the population or true factor loading matrix of factor models. We demonstrate that the network loadings could effectively separate multiple latent causes and estimate the population factor loadings. We also leveraged the second simulation to derive effect size guidelines for network loadings. In a third simulation, we evaluated the similarities and differences between factor and network loadings when the data generating model was a random or network model. We found sufficient differences between the loadings, which allowed us to develop an algorithm called Loadings Comparison Test (LCT). The LCT had high sensitivity and specificity when predicting the true data generating model. In sum, our results suggest that network loadings can provide similar information to factor loadings when the data are generated from a factor model and therefore can be used in a similar way (e.g., item selection, measurement invariance, factor scores). Moreover, we found that network loadings may be a general case that can be effectively applied to any data generating model.

title: Hemodynamic Significance of Carotid Artery Ultrasound Predictors in Assessing Volume Status in Critically Ill Patients: A Scoping Review
description:
Abstract

Background: Accurate, timely, and non-invasive assessment of volume status in critically ill patients, including those on mechanical ventilation (MV) or in shock, is crucial for effective hemodynamic management and the prevention of multiorgan failure. Traditional static markers of preload, such as central venous pressure (CVP), have definitively demonstrated their pathophysiological and clinical inadequacy in predicting fluid responsiveness. Meanwhile, classic dynamic parameters based on heart-lung interaction, such as pulse pressure variability (PPV) and stroke volume variability (SVV), require invasive arterial monitoring and are subject to strict physiological limitations. In recent years, point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the carotid artery (CA) has gained significant popularity as an innovative, accessible, and non-invasive method for predicting fluid responsiveness.

Objectives: To conduct a comprehensive scoping review to map existing evidence regarding the diagnostic accuracy, physiological limitations, "grey zone" sizes, and reproducibility (both intra- and inter-operator) of various carotid artery ultrasound parameters in patients within the intensive care unit (ICU).

Methods: In accordance with the PRISMA-ScR methodology, a systematic search will be conducted across the MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases. The analysis will include studies evaluating corrected flow time (FTc), respiratory variability of peak systolic velocity, carotid blood flow (CBF), velocity-time integral (VTI), and carotid artery diameter variability in combination with dynamic tests, such as the passive leg raise (PLR) test, end-expiratory occlusion test (EEOt), and fluid bolus.Expected Results: The review is expected to synthesize data demonstrating that carotid artery Doppler indices possess moderate to high predictive value. It is anticipated that parameters based on flow time (FTc) and relative peak velocity variation ($\Delta$Vpeak) will outperform absolute carotid blood flow (CBF) calculations due to their lower dependence on the insonation angle and reduced mathematical errors associated with vessel diameter measurement. The issue of "grey zones," which can reach 61% for certain parameters, will be described in detail, as this critically limits their isolated use at the bedside.

Conclusions: Ultrasound assessment of the carotid artery is a promising tool in the intensive care armamentarium. Nevertheless, high inter-operator variability among novice specialists, the impact of vascular compliance in geriatric patients, and the presence of broad zones of diagnostic uncertainty necessitate the standardization of scanning protocols and cautious interpretation of data within the context of comprehensive multimodal hemodynamic monitoring.

title: Use of extracellular vesicles as biomarkers for the diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a multifactorial autoimmune inflammatory disease with a polyarticular pattern, characterized by joint stiffness, chronic pain, and synovitis mainly affecting the small proximal synovial joints. The repercussions of this disease are systemic, and there may be extra-articular and constitutional manifestations. Regarding the diagnosis of RA, clinical biomarkers are currently used which have limitations, mainly regarding sensitivity and specificity. Therefore, exosomes are being studied as promising biomarkers for more efficient diagnosis and monitoring of RA. Exosomes are extracellular vesicles (EVs) secreted by almost all cell types physiologically and pathologically, playing a major role in RA. Therefore, this research aims to evaluate, by a systematic review, the effectiveness of EVs as a biomarker for the diagnosis of RA. To this end, the study will be conducted based on the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). The electronic literature search will be carried out using the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Cochrane Library databases, which will be carried out until March 2025 to answer the PICO question: “Would the use of extracellular vesicles as a biomarker be more efficient than the markers used currently used for the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis?” Efficacy in diagnosis will be considered the primary outcome. The biological material used as the source of EVs and the method for biomarkers will be included in the secondary outcomes. After selecting the articles and extracting the data, they will be subjected to bias analysis and meta-analysis. It is expected to determine the effectiveness of EVs as a biomarker for the diagnosis of RA.
